  • August 6, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

What is the arithmetic intensity of \([B, D] \times [B, D, F] \to [B, F]\) — a separate weight matrix per batch element — and what is the lesson?

Answer In int8, the work is the same \(2BDF\) — these are \(B\) independent \([D] \times [D, F]\) products — but the traffic is \(BD + BDF + BF\), dominated by the \(BDF\) weight term. So \[\mathrm {Intensity} = \frac {2BDF}{BD + BDF + BF} \approx 2\] constant. Batching bought nothing: \(B\) appears in numerator and denominator and cancels, leaving you comms-bound at every batch size. The lesson is that a matmul's intensity comes entirely from amortizing one weight load across many tokens. Give every token its own weights and the amortization disappears — which is why per-example weights, and anything shaped like them, never reach the flat roof.

Card. The sharded-matmul threshold falls on D, not B [EIZJ]

  • August 6, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

Two chips split \(X[B, D]\) and \(Y[D, F]\) along \(D\), each computing a partial sum and exchanging it. When is this compute-bound, and why is the threshold surprising?

Answer Each chip does half the contraction, \(T_{\mathrm {math}} = BDF / 1.97 \times 10^{14}\), then ships its \([B, F]\) partial sum across the interconnect, \(T_{\mathrm {comms}} = 2BF / 4.5 \times 10^{10}\). Compute-bound means \[\frac {BDF}{2BF} = \frac {D}{2} > \frac {1.97 \times 10^{14}}{4.5 \times 10^{10}} = 4377 \implies D > 8755\] The surprise is that the threshold depends on \(D\), not \(B\): the batch scales FLOPs and bytes-sent identically and cancels out. Same roofline machinery as a single-chip matmul, but because the relevant bandwidth is now the network, a different dimension decides whether Tensor Parallelism pays for itself — the contracted dimension has to be large enough to hide the exchange.

Card. VMEM moves the ridge point [D1X1]

  • August 10, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

VMEM vs HBM bandwidth: what is the ratio, and what does it do to the roofline?

Answer VMEM\(\to \)MXU bandwidth is roughly \(22\times \) HBM bandwidth, so the critical arithmetic intensity for peak FLOPs drops from ~240 to ~10–20. Worked, with int8[16384,4096] weights on v5e: FLOPs-bound at \(B > 267\) out of HBM, but only \(B > 11\) out of VMEM — call it 20 in practice, since you cannot spend all of VMEM's bandwidth on weights. The consequence is VMEM prefetch: load the FFW weights during attention and the load disappears behind compute. The limit is capacity — VMEM is tiny, so a layer's weights have to be small or sharded enough to fit with room to spare.

Card. Decode is bounded by the weight read [YK3Y]

  • August 10, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

200B parameters in bf16 across 32 TPU v4p. What is the lower bound on per-step sampling latency?

Answer \[2\ \text {bytes} \times 200\mathrm {e}9 = 400\mathrm {e}9 \text { bytes} \;\longrightarrow \; \frac {12.5\mathrm {e}9 \text { bytes/chip}}{1.23\mathrm {e}12 \text { B/s}} \approx 10\ \mathrm {ms}\] It is a bound because every decode step has to re-read all the parameters from HBM into the MXU, so no step can beat the weight-load time. At small batch it is close to achievable, too: decode is HBM-bandwidth-bound, not FLOPs-bound, which is the whole reason batching pays.

What is a TPU?

  • August 6, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

Definition. TPU memory hierarchy [IO2I]

  • August 11, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

The TPU memory hierarchy is entirely software managed with no cache. Memory movement is controlled by the compiler and Operator fusion is like ASIC caching.

Notably, in Pallas, you tile the memory transfer and define the pipeline from HBM to VMEM.

Definition. TensorCore (TPU) [OGCRQ]

  • May 22, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios
  • Vector register file each register is 8x128 vector registers with 8 horizontal lanes and 128 vertical lanes. There are typically 64 of these registers.

Definition. Systolic array [SXP6]

  • August 11, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

A grid of processing elements in which every operand moves by one hop per cycle to a fixed neighbour, and nothing is addressed. A PE multiplies what arrives at it, adds what arrived from above, and passes the result on. There is no register file to name, no arbitration, and no scheduler: the dataflow is the wiring, and the only freedom in the design is which of the three operands you decide to hold still.

Hold the output still and each PE owns one entry of the result, accumulating in place while both inputs stream past. Hold the weights still — the choice the Matrix Multiply Unit (MXU) makes — and each PE pins one \(w_{ij}\) for the whole tile while activations stream in from the left and partial sums fall downward. The second is the one worth being able to draw from memory, because the staggering it requires is where every systolic-array bubble comes from:

The stagger is the whole trick. Row \(i\) of the activation tape is held back \(i\) cycles, so that \(x_k\) arrives at PE(\(k\), \(j\)) on precisely the cycle the running sum for column \(j\) reaches that row. The set of PEs firing on cycle \(t\) is therefore the anti-diagonal \(i + j = t\), and a finished dot product falls out of the bottom of column \(j\) having been accumulated on the way down — never written to memory, never read back.

What you pay for that is the fill and the drain. An \(N \times N\) array streaming \(M\) samples is busy for \(M + 2N - 2\) cycles but does only \(M N^2\) useful multiply-accumulates, so utilisation is

\[\frac {MN^2}{(M + 2N - 2)N^2} = \frac {M}{M + 2N - 2}.\]

For the four-by-four array above, four samples give 40%. On a real \(128 \times 128\) MXU the fill is \(2N - 2 = 254\) cycles, so one isolated \(8 \times 128\) tile — the shape of the native op — would run at \(8/262\), near three per cent. That number is not what the hardware achieves, and the gap is the point: consecutive tiles stream in back-to-back with no bubble between them, so the fill is paid once per run of matmuls rather than once per tile. This is the fill bubble, and it is why the cost of a small matmul is dominated by a fixed charge that a large one amortises away.

Definition. Matrix Multiply Unit (MXU) [OGCRP]

  • May 22, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

A core component of the TPU architecture responsible for performing matrix multiplication via a weight stationary Systolic array.

  • \(128 \times 128\) — 16,384 multiply accumulate units, each multiplying and adding in one cycle. v6e/Trillium widens the array to \(256 \times 256\), i.e. 65,536.
  • The native op is one bf16[8,128] @ bf16[128,128] -> f32[8,128] every 8 cycles, or about \(5e13\) bf16 FLOPs/s per MXU at 1.5 GHz. A v5e chip has enough MXUs to reach ~\(2e14\).
Remark. The side length is fixed in hardware, so every dimension has to be tiled down to it and any axis shorter than it is padded up to it, wasting the FLOPs spent on the padding. The order is
  1. Tiling the matrix to load from HBM to VMEM.
  2. Compiler tiles from VMEM to \(128 \times 128\) tiles to load into the MXU.

Card. Why the MXU pads everything to 128 [HPSO]

  • August 10, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

What is the native op of one Matrix Multiply Unit (MXU), and why does that force padding to 128?

Answer One bf16[8,128] @ bf16[128,128] -> f32[8,128] every 8 cycles, on a \(128 \times 128\) systolic array — \(256 \times 256\) on v6e/Trillium. The array's side length is fixed in hardware, so any matrix axis shorter than 128 (256 on v6e) is padded up to it, and the FLOPs spent on the padding are simply wasted. With 2–4 MXUs per core, tiling dimensions want to exceed \(128 \times \) the MXU count. Scale: roughly \(5e13\) bf16 FLOPs/s per MXU at 1.5 GHz, so about \(2e14\) per v5e chip. int8 runs ~\(2\times \) faster, int4 ~\(4\times \).

Card. The systolic array fill bubble [R3DP]

  • August 10, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

Sketch the dataflow through a \(128 \times 128\) systolic array (Matrix Multiply Unit (MXU)). Where does the pipeline bubble come from?

Answer A 2D grid of 16,384 ALUs, each doing one multiply-add per cycle.
  • Weights (RHS, \(128 \times 128\)) are pushed down from the top.
  • Activations (LHS, \(8 \times 128\)) stream in from the left.
  • Each cell multiplies its overlapped pair, adds the partial sum arriving from above, and passes the result down.
The bubble: both operands are loaded diagonally, so the array needs a fill period before every cell is busy. Once filled, new LHS/RHS stream in back-to-back with no further bubble — which is why large matrices amortize the fill and small ones do not.

Definition. Vector Processing Unit [OGCRN]

  • May 22, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

A core component of the TPU architecture responsible for elementwise operations.

  • 2D SIMD execution, where each of 1024 sites execute same program in lockstep.
  • Each site contains 4 ALUs, enabling 4096 FLOPs.
  • Fed a 8x128 Vector Register in one cycle.

Card. The VPU is thirty times smaller than the MXU [JFWY]

  • August 10, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

Vector Processing Unit: what is its shape and throughput relative to the Matrix Multiply Unit (MXU), and which reductions are cheap?

Answer Shape \((8\ \text {sublanes}, 128\ \text {lanes})\), with 4 independent ALUs per position and most ops at 1/cycle: \[8 \times 128 \times 4 \times 1.75\mathrm {e}9 \approx 7\mathrm {e}12 \text { FLOPs/s}\] on v5p — about \(30\times \) less than the ~\(2e14\) MXU FLOPs/s per core. VPU work is fp32. Reductions along the sublane axis (the 8) are cheap: an intra-lane shuffle by 4/2/1 plus three pairwise adds. Cross-lane reductions need the separate XLU, which is slow and expensive. Control is skewed the other way: a single scalar core fetches and dispatches everything and can issue only one DMA request per cycle. Efficient, but it blocks data-dependent vectorization.

Card. The three units and the one data path [MZIY]

  • August 10, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

What are the three units inside a TPU TensorCore (TPU), and what is the data path from HBM to compute?

Answer
  • MXU — matrix multiply on a systolic array. Nearly all of the FLOPs.
  • VPU — elementwise ops (ReLU, add, mul) and reductions.
  • VMEM — an on-chip scratchpad in the TensorCore, like L1/L2 but far larger (~128 MiB on v5e) and programmer-controlled rather than a cache.
The path is HBM \(\to \) VMEM \(\to \) VREGs \(\to \) MXU/VPU \(\to \) VMEM \(\to \) HBM. Nothing computes directly out of HBM. All of it is pipelined — the copies overlap with MXU work, so the array never stalls waiting on memory.

Card. Four communication tiers, four budgets [026G]

  • August 10, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

Name the four communication tiers on a TPU, fastest to slowest, with per-chip v5p numbers.

Answer
  1. HBM \(\leftrightarrow \) TensorCore — \(2.8e12\) B/s.
  2. ICI (Inter-chip interconnect, chip to nearest neighbors) — \(9e10\) B/s per axis one-way, across 3 axes on v5p.
  3. PCIe (host to its tray of chips) — \(1.6e10\) B/s, about \(100\times \) slower than HBM.
  4. DCN (host to host) — \(6.25e9\) B/s.
The design rule that falls out: keep the bytes crossing each channel proportional to that channel's speed. Note also that a TPU\(\to \)TPU transfer over DCN pays the whole chain — PCIe, NIC egress, NIC ingress, PCIe again.

Card. Which TPU axes actually wrap around [590O]

  • August 10, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

Inter-chip interconnect topology: which generations get which torus, and when do you actually get wraparound links?

Answer
  • 2D torus, 4 neighbors — v2, v3, v5e, v6e. A pod caps at \(16 \times 16\); past that, pods talk over DCN.
  • 3D torus, 6 neighbors — v4, v5p. Superpods are \(16 \times 16 \times 16\) (v4) and \(16 \times 20 \times 28\) (v5p), built from reconfigurable \(4 \times 4 \times 4\) cubes joined by optical links.
Wraparounds exist only on full-cube multiples (\(4 \times 4 \times 4\), \(4 \times 4 \times 8\) — not \(2 \times 2 \times 4\), since the optical switches only exist on a full cube), or on a v5e/v6e axis of exactly 16, so an \(8 \times 16\) slice wraps the long axis only. Losing the wraparound roughly doubles comms time. Links are nearest-neighbor only and bypass the hosts entirely, so distant chips hop through the chips between them — unlike a GPU's switch hierarchy.

Sharded Matrices and How to Multiply Them

  • August 6, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

Card. An unsharded contracting axis needs no comms [QJX1]

  • August 12, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

Sharded matmul, case 1: neither multiplicand has a sharded contracting dimension. What communication is required, and what is the output sharding?

Answer None at all. Each device does a local block matmul and the result is already sharded correctly: \[A[I_X, J] \cdot B[J, K_Y] \to C[I_X, K_Y]\] The contracting axis \(J\) is unsharded, so every device holds complete contracting slices and the computation does not depend on the sharding. The output simply inherits the input shardings. The one caveat: this holds only if the two inputs' non-contracting dimensions are not sharded over the same mesh axis — that case is invalid.

Definition. AllGather [VSDZ]

  • August 12, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

An AllGather gets resources from all devices onto one device. In TPU's Ring topology, this is done in \(\frac {N}{2}\) hops via each TPU sending its shard to the neighboring chip.

Assuming we have \(X\) shards and the total bytes is \(N\), then each chip must send \(\frac {N}{X}\) bytes. If we have an ICI bandwidth of \(W_{\text {ICI}}\), then for each chip to send to its neighbor will be \[T_{1\text { hop}} = \frac {N}{X\cdot W_{\text {ICI}}}\] Now each chip must send across \(X\) hops, which gives \(T = X\cdot T_{1\text { hop}} = \frac {N}{W_{\text {ICI}}}\).This does not change if we use the bi-directional bandwidth because then we have \(2N\) bytes but only need to send at most \(\frac {X}{2}\) hops!

Remark. A super fun trick from [scaling-book, Ex 3.2]: If you have an unused replicated dimension, then you can shard the replicated axis and perform an AllGather over both dimensions to double your bandwidth!

Card. AllGather costs the same at any device count [RBEJ]

  • August 12, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

AllGather: signature, mechanism, and cost?

Answer

Signature \([A_X, B] \to [A, B]\) — it removes a subscript, reassembling shards so every device on that axis holds a full copy. It can drop just one of several axes: \(A[I_{XY}, J] \to A[I_Y, J]\).

Mechanism: pass each shard around the ring, \(N-1\) hops in one direction or about \(N/2\) bidirectionally.

Cost, when bandwidth-bound: \(T = V / W_{\mathrm {ici}}\) on bidirectional bandwidth, or \(V / (W_{\mathrm {ici}} \cdot N_{\mathrm {axes}})\) across several mesh axes. The takeaway is that this is independent of the device count \(X\) — each hop sends \(V/X\) bytes but you make \(X/2\) hops. Only array size and link bandwidth matter.

Latency-bound regime: about \(1\mu \mathrm {s}\) intrinsic cost per hop, so \(T = \max (T_{\min } \cdot \sum _i |X_i| / 2,\; V / (W \cdot N_{\mathrm {axes}}))\). On v5e (\(4.5e10\) unidirectional) anything under ~45 kB is latency-bound.

Card. Gather before, or reduce after [JO4V]

  • August 12, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

Sharded matmul, case 2: one multiplicand has a sharded contracting dimension, \(A[I, J_X] \cdot B[J, K] \to C[I, K]\). Which primitive, and what is the alternative?

Answer AllGather the sharded input first, then matmul locally: \(\mathrm {AllGather}_X(A[I, J_X]) \to A[I, J]\), then \(A[I, J] \cdot B[J, K] \to C[I, K]\). You cannot just multiply the local shards, because the sum over \(J\) is split across \(X\) and each device holds only a partial sum. The alternative is to treat it like case 3: do the local partial matmul and AllReduce or ReduceScatter the result. That shards the FLOPs but usually costs more comms. For \(X[B,D] \cdot Y[D_X,F]\), the gather moves \(2DF\) bytes and the reduce moves \(2 \cdot 2BF\), so the reduce path wins roughly when \(D > 2B\). Rare in practice, though — the other input is usually sharded along the same axis anyway, as under FSDP.

Card. A mesh axis may appear only once [QBBA]

  • August 12, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

Sharded matmul, case 4: both multiplicands have a non-contracting dimension sharded along the same mesh axis, \(A[I_X, J] \cdot B[J, K_X]\). Why is this invalid, and how do you resolve it?

Answer A mesh axis may appear at most once in a sharding. Writing \(C[I_X, K_X]\) would give shard \(i\) only the \((i,i)\) block — the block diagonal. The off-diagonal blocks of \(C\) exist nowhere, so the result is unrecoverable. The fix is to AllGather one of the two inputs along \(X\) first, so that \(X\) appears once in the output:
  • \(\mathrm {AllGather}_X(A) \to A[I, J]\), giving \(C[I, K_X]\).
  • \(\mathrm {AllGather}_X(B) \to B[J, K]\), giving \(C[I_X, K]\).
Which one you pick is decided by the sharding the downstream ops want.

Definition. AllReduce [U351]

  • August 12, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

Card. Matching contracting shards give partial sums [KIRV]

  • August 12, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

Sharded matmul, case 3: both multiplicands are sharded along the contracting dimension on the same mesh axis, \(A[I, J_X] \cdot B[J_X, K]\). What happens, and which primitive fixes it?

Answer The local shards can be multiplied — they share contracting indices — but each device ends up with only a partial sum, written \(C[I, K]\{U_X\}\), "unreduced along \(X\)": \[A \cdot B = \sum _i A[:,i] \otimes B[i,:]\] Device \(i\) owns the \(i\)-th column block of \(A\) and the \(i\)-th row block of \(B\), so it computes exactly the \(i\)-th term of that sum. The fix is AllReduce along \(X\) for a replicated \(C[I, K]\) — or the cheaper \(\mathrm {ReduceScatter}_{X,K} \to C[I, K_X]\) if you can leave the output sharded. That is half the cost, and defers the gather, possibly forever.

Definition. ReduceScatter [CAGW]

  • August 12, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

The collective that resolves partial sums along a mesh axis and leaves the result sharded rather than replicated: \([A, B]\{U_X\} \to [A_X, B]\). It is the reduction half of an AllReduce, and the transpose of an AllGather. Same ring pass, same cost \(V / W_{\mathrm {ici}}\), except each device sums the shard arriving from its left neighbour into its own copy instead of merely keeping it.

Notation. Because it introduces a subscript, you have to say where it goes: \(\mathrm {ReduceScatter}_{X,K}\) reduces along mesh axis \(X\) and shards the result along \(K\). That freedom is the whole argument for preferring it. Namely, whenever the consumer can accept a sharded input, stopping at the ReduceScatter costs half what an AllReduce does and defers the gather, possibly forever.

The mechanism is easiest to see as a schedule. Each device starts holding a full-size buffer that is only a partial sum, and on every step forwards one chunk rightward and folds in the chunk arriving from its left. After \(N-1\) steps device \(b\) holds chunk \(b\) summed over all \(N\) partials and has forwarded the rest away, which is also why the resident memory falls by \(N\).

Question. How do we know what chunk to send to who?
Answer.It is actually remarkably easy. If there are \(N\) devices, then you just compute which device is \(N - 1\) hops away from you. You send that chunk to your right neighbor. Each chunk then propagates through the ring and will end up with the completed chunked sum on the correct device

Note that the steps are not \(N-1\) rounds of moving a whole buffer: every link carries one chunk in the same direction at the same time, so the cost is \(N-1\) chunk-times, and the \(N\) in the chunk size cancels the \(N-1\) in the step count. Nothing is ever broadcast, which is the sense in which the ring is optimal and the reason a ReduceScatter is not merely an AllReduce with a slice at the end.

Card. ReduceScatter is AllGather transposed [HIDN]

  • August 12, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

ReduceScatter: signature, relationship to AllGather, and cost?

Answer Signature \([A, B]\{U_X\} \to [A_X, B]\) — it resolves partial sums along \(X\) and leaves the result sharded along a dimension of your choosing. It introduces a subscript, which is why you have to say where: \(\mathrm {ReduceScatter}_{X,K}\). Mechanism: the same ring pass as an AllGather, except you sum the incoming shards instead of keeping them. Cost is therefore identical, \(V / W_{\mathrm {ici}}\). Duality: AllGather and ReduceScatter are transposes of each other, hence each other's derivative — an AllGather in the forward pass means a ReduceScatter on the reverse-mode gradients, and vice versa. (Broadcast is \(u \otimes I\), reduce is \(u^\top \otimes I\).)

Card. AllReduce is two collectives, not one [MJ7A]

  • August 12, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

AllReduce: signature, decomposition, and cost relative to an AllGather?

Answer Signature \([A_X, B]\{U_Y\} \to [A_X, B]\) — it removes the "unreduced" suffix, leaving every device on the axis holding the same fully-summed value, unsharded along \(Y\). It is not really a primitive: an AllReduce is a ReduceScatter followed by an AllGather. \[A[I_X, J]\{U_Y\} \xrightarrow {\ \mathrm {ReduceScatter}_{Y,J}\ } A[I_X, J_Y] \xrightarrow {\ \mathrm {AllGather}_Y\ } A[I_X, J]\] Cost \(2V / W_{\mathrm {ici}}\), exactly \(2\times \) an AllGather — which is the practical argument for stopping at the ReduceScatter whenever the consumer can accept a sharded output. The AllGather can then be deferred, or skipped entirely.

Definition. AllToAll [T470]

  • August 12, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios
🌱 Stub — this concept is referenced but not yet written.

Card. AllToAll is a quarter of an AllGather [IOUR]

  • August 12, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

AllToAll: signature, when it shows up, and why is it cheaper than an AllGather?

Answer Signature \([A, B_X] \to [A_X, B]\) — a sharded transposition, which moves a subscript from one logical axis to another. When: never out of a sharded matmul. It is for resharding between regions of a computation with incompatible layouts — classically MoE routing. Cost \(V \cdot \max (A, B, C, \ldots ) / (4 N W_{\mathrm {ici}})\); on a 1D mesh that is \(V / (4 W_{\mathrm {ici}})\), a quarter of an AllGather, and it scales down further in 2D+ with the shortest axis. Why cheaper, as \(2 \times 2\): each device need not send its whole shard everywhere, so the sum becomes \(D + (D-1) + \cdots + 1\) instead of \(D\) repeated \(D\) times — a factor of 2. And bidirectionality buys \(4\times \) here rather than the \(2\times \) it buys an AllGather, since blocks travel at most \(D/2\) hops in either direction. Equivalently: two random nodes on a ring are about \(N/4\) hops apart.

Collectives summary [41OF]

  • August 14, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

The four collectives that sharded matmuls actually need, in the [scaling-book] notation: a subscript is a mesh axis the array is split along, and \(\{U_X\}\) marks an array that is unreduced along \(X\) — every device holds a full-size partial sum. A collective is then a rewrite of that decoration, and its cost is a function of how many bytes have to cross the ICI to do it.

Operation Description Syntax Runtime
AllGather Gathers all the shards of a sharded array along an axis, removing a subscript. \([A_X, B] \to [A, B]\) \(\text {bytes} / (W_{\mathrm {ici}}^{\text {bidi}} \cdot \text {num\_axes})\)
ReduceScatter Sums a partially summed array along an axis and shards it along another axis, adding a subscript. \([A, B]\{U_X\} \to [A_X, B]\) Same as AllGather
AllReduce Sums a partially summed array along an axis, removing the \(\{U_X\}\). Combines an AllGather and a ReduceScatter. \([A_X, B]\{U_Y\} \to [A_X, B]\) \(2 \times \) AllGather
AllToAll Gathers (replicates) an axis and shards a different dimension along the same axis. \([A, B_X] \to [A_X, B]\) AllGather / 4 for a bidirectional ring

Only two of these are primitives. An AllReduce is a ReduceScatter followed by an AllGather, which is exactly why it costs twice as much, and the practical consequence is that you should stop at the ReduceScatter whenever the consumer can accept a sharded input. AllGather and ReduceScatter are transposes of each other and hence each other's derivative, so a forward-pass AllGather implies a ReduceScatter on the reverse-mode gradients.

Remark. The runtime column is written relative to the AllGather because every entry is the same ring pass over the same \(V\) bytes — the only thing that changes is how far each byte travels. An AllToAll is \(4\times \) cheaper because a shard's destination is on average a quarter of the ring away rather than all the way around, and no byte is broadcast to every device [scaling-book, Ex 3.10]. The \(\text {num\_axes}\) factor in the AllGather row is the trick from [scaling-book, Ex 3.2]: gathering over two mesh axes at once buys you both axes' bandwidth.
Remark. Notice what is absent from the runtime column: the number of devices. A ring collective moves \(V\) bytes off each chip regardless of how big the ring is, so cost depends on the array and the link, not the mesh size, which is what makes these affordable at pod scale and why the roofline question is comms-vs-FLOPs rather than comms-vs-devices.

Transformer Math

  • August 6, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

Card. Every axis label appears once in the FLOP count [LARD]

  • August 18, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

An einsum contracts \(C[GHIJKL]\) with \(D[GHMNKL]\), where \(GH\) are batching axes and \(KL\) are contracting axes. How many FLOPs?

Answer Two times the product of every distinct label, each counted once: \[2 \cdot GH \cdot IJ \cdot MN \cdot KL\] Why. Every output element is a dot product over the contracted axes, and a dot product spends one multiply and one add per term — that is the factor of two. The batch axes index independent subproblems, so they multiply the total work but appear only once in the product, exactly as the contracted axes do. The vocabulary is what makes the rule mechanical. A contracting label appears in both inputs and is absent from the output; a batching label appears in both inputs and the output. Everything else is a free axis of one input. Once the labels are sorted that way, the count is read off the einsum string without thinking about the shape of the loop nest. Caveat. With no contracting axes there is no dot product — the operation is an elementwise product, and the factor of two goes away.

Card. The backward pass is two matmuls, not one [92HA]

  • August 18, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

One matmul \(C = AB\) with \(A[N,P]\), \(B[P,M]\) costs \(2NPM\) FLOPs at inference but \(6NPM\) in training. Where do the other two thirds come from?

Answer The forward pass contracts over \(P\) and costs \(2NPM\). Backpropagation then needs two matmuls of exactly that size, not one:
  • \(\partial L/\partial B = A^{\top }(\partial L/\partial C)\), contracting over \(N\) — the parameter gradient;
  • \(\partial L/\partial A = (\partial L/\partial C)B^{\top }\), contracting over \(M\) — not a parameter gradient at all, but the signal handed to earlier layers.
Each of the three contracts a different axis of the same \(N \times P \times M\) box, so each costs \(2NPM\) and the total is \(6NPM\), three times the forward pass. It is easy to remember only the first backward matmul and land on \(4NPM\); the activation gradient is the one that goes missing. Why the constant is worth memorising. \(PM\) is the parameter count of that matrix and \(N\) is the token count, so \(6NPM\) is precisely the \(6 \cdot \mathrm {params} \cdot \mathrm {tokens}\) rule of thumb — the whole training cost of a Transformer is a sum of such terms.

Card. Gating splits the up-projection in two [Y4Y8]

  • August 18, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

For one Transformer layer with a gated MLP, what are the parameter count and training FLOPs — and why is the coefficient three rather than two?

Answer Parameters: \(3DF\), from \(W_{in1}[D,F]\), \(W_{in2}[D,F]\), \(W_{out}[F,D]\). Training FLOPs: \(18BTDF\) — three matmuls at \(6BTDF\) each, by the \(6NPM\) rule. Where the third matrix comes from. A Gated Linear Unit (GLU) splits the up-projection into two matrices whose outputs are multiplied elementwise, \(\sigma (AW_{in1}) \odot (AW_{in2})\), so one of them acts as a gate on the other. LLaMA, DeepSeek and most current models do this. A non-gated MLP has a single \(W_{in}\) and so \(2DF\) params — and typically scales \(D\) and \(F\) up to compensate, which is why the two families cost about the same at equal quality. The gate itself is \(O(BTF)\) — elementwise, no contraction, and negligible against \(BTDF\).

Card. GQA saves cache, not projection FLOPs [59OV]

  • August 18, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

Per layer, what do the QKVO projections cost in parameters and training FLOPs under Group Query Attention with \(N\) query heads, \(K\) key/value heads, and head dimension \(H\)?

Answer Parameters: \(2D(N+K)H\), from \(W_Q[D,N,H]\) and \(W_O[N,H,D]\) at \(DNH\) each, plus \(W_K, W_V[D,K,H]\) at \(DKH\) each. Training FLOPs: \(12BTD(N+K)H\) — each projection is \(6BTD \cdot (\text {heads}) \cdot H\). The variants are one knob. \(K = N\) is plain multi-head attention; \(K = 1\) is MQA; \(1 < K < N\) with \(K \mid N\) is grouped-query, with group size \(G = N/K\). Read the formula for what shrinking \(K\) actually buys. It touches only the \(K\) term, so the projection cost falls from \(2N\) to \(N + K\) — at most a factor of two, and usually far less. That is not why anyone uses GQA. The payoff is the KV-cache, which scales with \(K\) alone and is the binding constraint at generation time.

Card. Attention dominates only past 8D tokens [CRO4]

  • August 18, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

Dot-product attention costs \(12BT^2NH\) FLOPs in training. At what sequence length does it start to dominate the matmul FLOPs, and why that number?

Answer Past \(T > 8D\). With the usual proportions \(F = 4D\), \(D = NH\), \(N = K\), the ratio of attention to everything else is \[\frac {12BT^2NH}{18BTDF + 24BTDNH} = \frac {12BT^2D}{72BTD^2 + 24BTD^2} = \frac {T}{8D}\] What that means in practice. At \(D \approx 8\mathrm {k}\) attention only takes over past roughly 64k tokens; Gemma-27B, with \(D = 4608\), crosses at about 37k. Larger models push the crossover further out, so the quadratic term is not what stops large models training on long context — the KV-cache at inference is a much earlier wall. The \(12BT^2NH\) is two matmuls, \(QK^{\top }\) and \(SV\), each \(6BTSNH\) and each batched over \(B\) and the head axis.

Card. The KV cache scales with K, and is per-sequence [J65M]

  • August 18, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

How large is a KV-cache, and which dimension actually drives it?

Answer The cache has shape \([2, S, L, K, H]\) per sequence — the leading 2 is keys and values — so in int8 it is \(2SLKH\) bytes. Worked: \(S = 8\mathrm {k}\), \(L = 64\), \(KH = D = 8192\) gives \(2 \cdot 8192 \cdot 64 \cdot 8192 \approx 8\) GiB for a single sequence. Two things in that expression decide inference planning. It scales with \(K\), the number of key/value heads, and not with the \(N\) query heads — which is the whole argument for Group Query Attention and MQA at \(K \ll N\). And it is per sequence, so unlike the weights it cannot be amortised over the batch: it competes with batch size for the same High bandwidth memory budget, and generation is bandwidth-bound on streaming it.

Card. Remat buys memory with a third more FLOPs [WCLV]

  • August 18, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

What does block-level gradient checkpointing cost, and what does it save?

Answer Saves: only the input to each layer is kept — one checkpoint per layer instead of the roughly twenty intermediate nodes a layer produces. In the book's setting (\(BT = 4\)M, \(L = 64\), \(D = 8192\), bf16) that is 84 TB of activations down to 4.2 TB. Costs: the forward pass is run a second time inside the backward pass, so training goes from about \(6 \cdot \mathrm {params} \cdot \mathrm {tokens}\) to about \(8\) — a third more FLOPs for a twentyfold cut in activation memory. Why twenty nodes. Backpropagation needs whatever the derivative mentions. For \(f(x) = \exp (g(x))\) we have \(df/dx = \exp (g(x)) \cdot dg/dx\), so both \(g(x)\) and \(\exp (g(x))\) have to survive to the backward pass. Counting every such intermediate across a layer lands around twenty. The middle setting is usually the right one: save just the outputs of the big matmuls — about seven per layer — and no large matmul is ever recomputed, only the cheap elementwise work between them.

Card. The running max makes the chunk merge exact [6UFW]

  • August 18, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

In flash attention, what running statistics travel between KV chunks, and how are two chunks merged?

Answer Each query block carries three: \(M\), the running maximum of \(q \cdot k\); \(L\), the running softmax denominator; and \(O\), the running output. Merging chunks with local maxima \(M^1, M^2\) and sums \(L^1, L^2\) rescales each to the shared maximum: \[L = e^{M^1 - \max (M^1, M^2)}L^1 + e^{M^2 - \max (M^1, M^2)}L^2\] This is exact, not an approximation. It is only \(\sum _i e^{a_i + b} = e^b \sum _i e^{a_i}\): pulling a constant out of a sum of exponentials. The maximum is subtracted for numerical stability and put back by the same identity — see Online Softmax for the one-pass version of the argument. The payoff is memory, not FLOPs. The \([B,T,S,N]\) attention matrix is never materialised, so memory is \(O(1)\) in the number of chunks while the FLOP count stays quadratic. The query block sits in VMEM and only the KV chunks stream in, which is also what raises the arithmetic intensity.

Card. Sparsity sets the batch an MoE needs [2NWW]

  • August 18, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

A Mixture of Experts (MoE) has \(E\) experts and top-\(k\) routing, int8 weights on a TPU v5e (ridge point around 240 FLOPs/byte). What batch size does it need to be compute-bound, and what is that for DeepSeek v3?

Answer \(B > 120E/k\) tokens. For DeepSeek v3, with \(E = 256\) routed experts and \(k = 8\), that is \(B > 3840\) tokens — a startlingly large batch to require at generation time. Per weight matrix: a full batch touches every expert, so all \(E\) copies get loaded — \(EDF\) bytes — while only \(k\) experts fire per token, so the work is \(2kBDF\) FLOPs. The arithmetic intensity is therefore \[\frac {2kBDF}{EDF} = \frac {2kB}{E}\] and int8 weights against bf16 arithmetic need that above roughly 240, giving \(kB/E > 120\). The framing that makes this obvious: an MoE is a dense model with \(E\) MLP blocks per layer. Total parameters scale with \(E\); parameters activated per token scale with \(k\). The sparsity \(E/k\) — typically 8 to 64, and 32 for DeepSeek v3 — is exactly the factor by which the required batch inflates. The other cost is routing: two AllToAlls per MoE block, out to the experts and back.

Exercise 1.1. int8 matmul

  • August 5, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

Multiplying \(X (B \times D)\) and \(Y (D \times F)\) in int8.

  1. How many bytes loaded from memory?
  2. How many total OPs performed?
  3. What is arithmetic intensity?
  4. What is roofline estimate for \(T_{math}\) and \(T_{comms}\)? What are reasonable upper and lower bounds for runtime of whole operation?
Solution
  1. The only difference here from before is that the loaded / written bytes are divided by \(2\). This means we load \(BD\) bytes for \(X\) and \(DF\) bytes for \(Y\), which is a total of \(BD + DF\) bytes.
  2. The same number of total ops is performed. Namely, for each element in the output matrix (\(BF\) of them) we must perform \(2D\) OPs. This leaves a total of \(2DBF\) OPs.
  3. The arithmetic intensity is now just \(2 \times \) the old arithmetic intensity because we are loading half as many bytes i.e. \(\frac {2DBF}{BD + DF + BF}\).
    4. Remark. After looking at the solution, they also mention that the rule on batch size to saturate arithmetic intensity remains unchanged. Namely, using the heuristic \(B \ll D, F\), we can get that the arithmetic intensity \(\approx \frac {2DBF}{DF} = 2B\). One may think that this means that we can use smaller batch size. However, recall that our in8 peak OPs/s has now doubled to \(3.94e14\). Therefore, the computation is effectively \[2B > \frac {2 \cdot \text {Peak OPs / s}}{\text {HBM Bandwidth}} \iff B > \frac {\text {Peak OPs / s}}{\text {HBM Bandwidth}} = 240\]
    Question. So what is the point of int8?
    Answer.Within each batch, we are actually performing FLOPs \(2 \times \) as fast. Therefore, our computation is actually twice as fast wall clock time!
  4. From above, we know that we are performing \(2DBF\) FLOPs. Assuming our int8 peak OPs/s is \(3.94e14\), this gives \(T_{math} = \frac {2DBF}{3.94e14}\). Similarly, we have that \(T_{comm} = \frac {BD + DF + BF}{8.2e11}\). We know that \(\max \{T_{max}, T_{comm}\} \) is a good lower bound, and that \(T_{max} + T_{comm}\) is a good upper bound.

Exercise 1.2. int8 + bf16 matmul

  • August 5, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

In practice we often do different weight vs. activation quantization, so we might store our weights in very low precision but keep activations (and compute) in a higher precision. Say we want to quantize our weights in int8 but keep activations (and compute) in bfloat16. At what batch size do we become compute bound? Assume \(1.97e14\) bfloat16 FLOPs/s.

Solution

Following the computation in the above remark / from the notes, the only thing that changes is now in the bytes loaded we have \(2BD + DF + 2BF\). Using the approximation, this gives us once again that the computational intensity is \(2B\). However, unlike in the previous question, we now remain doing computation at the speed of bf16 which means the previous cancellation no longer occurs. Thus, we have that

\[2B > \frac {\text {Peak FLOPs / s}}{\text {HBM Bandwidth}} \implies 2B > 240 \implies B > 120.\]

Taking the setup from Question 1.2, make a roofline plot of peak FLOPs/s vs. BB for F=D=4096F=D=4096 and F=D=1024F=D=1024 . Use the exact number of bytes loaded, not an approximation.

Exercise 1.4. Batched matrices

  • August 5, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

What if we wanted to perform int8[B,D] \(\cdot \) int8[B,D,F] \(\to \) int8[B,F] where we imagine having a different matrix for each batch element. What is the arithmetic intensity of this operation?

Solution

This dramatically reduces arithmetic intensity because it requires loading \(B \times \) more bytes from memory. In particular, we now have \(BD + BDF + BF\) total bytes moved. Even making the same approximation as before, this gives \(\frac {2BDF}{BDF} = 2\). Recall to saturate TPU we need this to be greater than \(240\)...

Exercise 1.5. Memory rooflines for GPUs

  • August 5, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

For the H100 SXM, calculate the batch size at which a bfloat16 matrix multiplication will become compute-bound. Note that the Tensor Core FLOPs numbers are twice the true value since they’re only achievable with structured sparsity.

Solution

We only need to find two quantities in the spec sheet 1. the bf16 peak FLOPs/s and 2. the HBM bandwidth. From the spec sheet, a bf16 tensor core on the H100 sxm can achieve \(1.979e15\) FLOPs / s and has a memory bandwidth of \(3.35e12\) bytes / s. Using the approximation from above, we will become compute bound when \(B > \frac {1.979e15}{3.35e12} \approx 591\).

Remark. From the solution, the number we used was with sparsity. It turns out the true number is \(9.89e14\), which gives \(295\) instead of \(590\).

What is a TPU? [scaling-ch2]

  • August 5, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

Exercise 2.1. bounding LLM latency

  • August 5, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios
 Say you want to sample from a 200B parameter model in bf16 that’s split across 32 TPU v4p. How long would it take to load all the parameters from HBM into the systolic array? Hint: use the numbers above.
Solution

I am a bit stumped to start. However, since we only care about loading the parameters, the relevant number is HBM BW (1.2e12). Since there is no communication between chips yet (I think). ICI bandwidth is not yet relevant? Since each chip has its own HBM, the effective bandwidth should be \(32 \cdot 1.2e12 = 3.84e13\). Therefore, we should have

\[(2e11 \cdot 16) / 3.84e13 = 0.0833\text {s}\]
Remark. After looking at solution, this turned out right?

Exercise 2.2. TPU details

  • August 5, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios
 Consider a full TPU v5e pod. How many total CPU hosts are there? How many TPU TensorCores? What is the total FLOPs/s for the whole pod? What is the total HBM? Do the same exercise for TPU v5p pod.
Solution

TPU v5e. From the TPU specs, a TPU v5e has a pod size of \(16\times 16\) and a host size of \(4\times 2\). Therefore, I believe this means that there are \(8\) CPU hosts. The v5e is an inference chip, so it only has one tensor core per chip. Across \(16\times 16\) chips this gives \(256\) tensor cores. Similarly, from the TPU specs I think we can just multiply the FLOPS/s per chip and HBM per chip to get \(256\cdot 1.97e14\) bf16 FLOPs/s and \(256\cdot 8.2e11\) bytes/s.

TPU v5p. The only distinction here besides swapping the numbers is that each chip has two tensor cores. Combining this with the larger pod size, we get \(2\cdot 16\cdot 20\cdot 28\) tensor cores per pod.

Remark. After looking at solution, it seems I misunderstood what host size meant. The host size is the topology of the subunit connected to a single host. So the number of hosts is actually the pod size / host size. This gives \((16\cdot 16) / (4\cdot 2)\) for the v5e and \((16\cdot 20\cdot 28) / (2\cdot 2\cdot 1)\) for the v5p.

Exercise 2.3. PCIe operational intensity

  • August 5, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios
 Imagine we’re forced to store a big weight matrix \(A\) of type bf16[D,F], and a batch of activations \(x\) of type bf16[B,D] in host DRAM and want to do a matrix multiplication on them. This is running on a single host, and we’re using a single TPU v6e chip attached to it. You can assume B≪DB≪D , and F=4DF=4D.
Solution

I assume this is streaming directly from PCIe without any tiling in VMEM / HBM? Relevant number TPU v6e can do \(9.2e14\) FLOPs/s. From previous chapter, we know that for bf16 matmul we need

\[B = \text {intensity}(\text {computation}) \geq \text {intensity}(\text {accelerator}) = (\text {FLOPs/s}) / (\text {bytes/s})\]

Therefore, we need

\[B \geq \frac {9.2e14}{1.6e10}\]

This is a very large batch size compared to HBM we saw in the previous chapter.

Exercise 2.4. General matmul latency

  • August 5, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios
 Let’s say we want to multiply a weight matrix int8[16384, 4096] by an activation matrix of size int8[B, 4096] where B is some unknown batch size. Let’s say we’re on 1 TPU v5e to start.
  1. How long will this multiplication take as a function of B?
  2. What if we wanted to run this operation out of VMEM? How long would it take as a function of B?
Solution

For the first part, we need to load

\[16384 \cdot 4096 + 4096B~\text {bytes}\]

and store \(B \cdot 16384\) bytes. We need to perform

\[2\cdot B\cdot 16384\cdot 4096~\text {FLOPs}\]

Therefore, the communication time is

\[T_{comm} = (16384 \cdot 4096 + 4096\cdot B + 16384\cdot B)/8.2e11\]

and the math time is

\[T_{math} = (2\cdot B\cdot 16384\cdot 4096)/3.94e14\]

The total computation time will then be \(\max \{T_{math}, T_{comm}\}\) and the ridge point is when \(T_{math} = T_{comm}\). This gives us

\[ \begin {align*} \frac {2\cdot B\cdot 16384\cdot 4096}{3.94e14} &= \frac {16384 \cdot 4096 + 4096\cdot B + 16384\cdot B}{8.2e11} \\ &\iff B = 259 \end {align*} \]

For the second part, VMEM is \(10\times \) faster than HBM. Therefore, our batch size can be \(10\times \) smaller.

Remark. The solution says that VMEM is \(22\times \) faster. So the numbers are adjusted accordingly.

Exercise 2.5. ICI Bandwidth

  • August 5, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios
 Let’s say we have a TPU v5e 4x4 slice. Let’s say we want to send an array of type bf16[8, 128, 8192] from TPU{0,0} to TPU{3, 3}. Let’s say the per-hop latency for TPU v5e is 1μs.
  1. How soon will the first byte arrive at its destination?
  2. How long will total transfer take?
Solution

I believe since we have wrap-around links in the Torus topology we can make it from \((0,0) \to (3,3)\) in \(4\) hops. If each hop latency is \(1\mu s\) then it should take \(4 \mu s\).

From TPU specs, the TPU v5e has ICI bandwidth \(4.5e 10\). We need to transfer \(2\cdot 8\cdot 128\cdot 8192\) bytes. Naively, I am going to say that this means it will take

\[\frac {2\cdot 8\cdot 128\cdot 8192}{4.5e 10} s,\] factoring in latency this gives \(372 + 4 \mu s\).
Remark. So the wraparound links are actually only on pods of \(16 \times 16\) or larger. This means it is actually \(6\) hops from \((0,0) \to (3,3)\). Also, we can use the bi-directional capabilities of the network to half the time it will take to send the whole array.

Exercise 2.6. pulling it all together

  • August 5, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios
 Imagine you have a big matrix \(A\): int8[128 * 1024, 128 * 1024] sharded evenly across a TPU v5e 4x4 slice but offloaded to host DRAM on each chip. Let’s say you want to copy the entire array to TPU{0, 0} and multiply it by a vector bf16[8, 128 * 1024]. How long will this take?
Solution

From the question wording, we are assuming the vector is already on TPU{0,0}.

From TPU specs, the host configuration for TPU v5e is \(4 \times 2\). I believe this means in a \(4 \times 4\) pod there will be \(2\) CPUs. If this is the case, then for the half of chips on the other host, we first have to transfer to our host via DCN which has bandwidth \(3.125e 9\) for v5e. Since it is sharded evenly, this would be \((1/2) \cdot 128 \cdot 128 \cdot 1024 \cdot 1024\) bytes we must send over DCN, taking

\[\frac {(1/2) \cdot 128 \cdot 128 \cdot 1024 \cdot 1024}{3.125e 9} = 2.75 s\]

However, now looking at the notes again, we only use DCN for chips not connected via ICI (which makes sense because it clearly slow AF).

Instead, we can first transfer all the bytes to the respective chips over PCIe and then to TPU{0,0} over ICI. To load into HBM, PCIe bandwidth is \(1.6e 10\) bytes/second. Since we can divide across all 16 chips, it will take

\[\frac {128 \cdot 128 \cdot 1024 \cdot 1024}{16\cdot 1.6e 10} = 67.1ms\]

Now to actually get all of the weights onto a single chip, we can follow the previous part. Using bi-directional bandwidth \(9e 10\), we have

\[\frac {128 \cdot 128 \cdot 1024 \cdot 1024}{9e 10} = 190.9ms\]

The remaining time comes from \(\max \{T_{comm}, T_{math}\}\), which are \[T_{math} = \frac {2\cdot 128\cdot 1024\cdot 128 \cdot 1024\cdot 8}{1.97e 14} = 1.39ms\] and \[T_{comm} = \frac {128\cdot 1024\cdot 128\cdot 1024 + 2\cdot 8\cdot 128\cdot 1024 + 2\cdot 128\cdot 1024\cdot 8}{8.2e 11} = 20.9ms \]

Thus, the total is \(67.1 + 190.9 + 20.9 = 278.9ms\).

Remark.

I think I might be so fucking him it is actually unbelievable. My numbers are all off, but the process seems pretty much the same. I also SNIPED the DCN stuff.

However, it seems there is a bit more nuance to the ICI links than I thought. In particular, our number is a lower bound dependent on the amount of utilized inbound links. Since \((0,0)\) is a corner, it only has \(2\) links and that is why the denominator is \(2\cdot 4.5e 10\) and is not because of bi-directional bandwidth. I imagine if there were wraparound links then we could divide the ICI time by \(2\) because there are \(4\) total inbound links.

Exercise Pop Quiz. Calculating VPU throughput

  • August 5, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

Using the above information, calculate how many vector FLOPs/s a TPU v5p can perform. A TPU v5p has a clock speed of about 1.75GHz.

Solution

From our discussion on VPU architecture, each site has 4 ALUs and there are \(8 \times 128\) sites. Therefore, we have

\[4 \cdot 8 \cdot 128 \cdot 1.75e9 = 7.168e12\]

Exercise Pop Quiz. 2D sharding across 1 axis

  • August 5, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios
 Consider an array fp32[1024, 4096] with sharding \(A[I_{XY},J]\) and mesh {'X': 8, 'Y': 2}. How much data is held by each device? How much time would it take to load this array from HBM on H100s (assuming 3.4e12 memory bandwidth per chip)?
Solution

The notation indicates that we are sharding the first axis \((1024)\) across both \(x\) and \(y\)? This means we are dividing into fp32[64, 4096] chunks or \(4\cdot 64\cdot 4096\) bytes per device, which would then take

\[\frac {4\cdot 64\cdot 4096}{3.4e12} = .308 \mu s\]

Exercise Pop Quiz. 2D sharding across 1 axis of 3D mesh

  • August 5, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios
 Let \(A\) be an array with shape int8[128, 2048], sharding \(A[I_{XY},J]\), and mesh Mesh({'X': 2, 'Y': 8, 'Z': 2}) (so 32 devices total). How much memory does \(A\) use per device? How much total memory does \(A\) use across all devices?
Solution

Since there is no sharding across the Z axis. I assume this means it is replicated. This still gives \(8\cdot 2048\) bytes per device but now total memory is still multiplied by \(32\) giving \(32\cdot 8\cdot 2048\) bytes across all devices.

Exercise Pop Quiz. AllGather

  • August 5, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios
 How long does it take to perform the AllGatherY([EY, F]) → [E, F] on a TPU v5e with a 2D mesh {'X': 8, 'Y': 4}, for \(E = 2048\), \(F = 8192\) in bf16? What about for \(E = F = 256\)?
Solution

For the large \(E\) and \(F\), we will clearly not be latency bound, so we can just perform the ICI cost. We will have \(N = 2\cdot 2048\cdot 8192\) bytes and the TPU v5e uni-directional bandwidth is \(4.5e 10\). Since we are only gathering over \(1\) dimension, we do not get any additional bandwidth. Thus, it will take \(\frac {N}{4.5e10} = 3.72\text {ms}\).

For the small \(E\) and \(F\), we now need to consider the latency time given by

\[T_{\text {latency}} = \frac {|Y|\cdot T_{\min }}{2} = 2\mu s.\]

Computing the ICI cost, we have \(N = 2\cdot 256\cdot 256\) bytes and \(T_{\text {ICI}} = \frac {N}{4.5e 10} = 0.73 \mu s\). Thus, the total time is \(T = \max \{T_{\text {latency}}, T_{\text {ICI}} = 2\mu s\).

Remark. I divided the latency time by \(2\), when once again the TPU v5e sub-mesh does not support wrap-around links and therefore the hop count is NOT upperbounded by \(|Y|\). Also the hop count is actually \(|Y| - 1\) not \(|Y|\), so the correct answer was just \(T_{\text {min}}\cdot (|Y| - 1) = 3\mu s\).

Exercise 3.1. replicated sharding

  • August 5, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios
 An array is sharded \(A[I_X,J,K,…]\) (i.e., only sharded across \(X\) ), with a mesh Mesh({'X': 4, 'Y': 8, 'Z': 2}). What is the ratio of the total number of bytes taken up by \(A\) across all chips to the size of one copy of the array?
Solution It is sharded across \(X\), so that on each chip there is only \(1/4\) of \(A\). However, it must be replicated across \(Y\) and \(Z\) which are \(8\cdot 2 = 16\) copies. This leaves us with \(16 \times \) the total number of bytes across all copies.

Exercise 3.2. AllGather latency

  • August 5, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios
 How long should \(\text {AllGather}_{X}([B_X,D_Y])\) take on a TPU v4p 4x4x4 slice with mesh Mesh({'X': 4, 'Y': 4, 'Z': 4}) if \(B=1024\) and \(D=4096\) in bfloat16? How about \(\text {AllGather}_{XY}([B_X,D_Y])\) How about \(\text {AllReduce}_{Z}([B_X,D_Y]\{U_Z\})\)?
Solution

  1. We cannot use bi-directional because we are on a non-16 dim axes on TPU v4p. Therefore, the ICI bandwidth is \(W_{\text {ICI}} = 4.5e10\). From AllGather, we know that the communication time is independent of \(|X|\) and is \(\frac {N}{W_{\text {ICI}}}\). For this problem, we have \(N = 1024\cdot 4096\cdot 2\). Thus, it will take \(.186\text {ms}\).

    Remark. I do not understand wrap-around rules at allor maybe they are just highly unintuitive, but we actually do have bi-directional bandwidth. I also needed to take into consideration that \(|X|\) cancels out but we only have \(N/|Y|\) bytes. Correct answer is \[\frac {1024\cdot 4096\cdot 2}{9e10\cdot |Y|}\]

  2. In this case, we now have double the bandwidth because we are reducing across both dimensions. However, the total number of bytes is now \(4\times \), which means this will be double the previous part.

  3. An AllReduce requires each device to send the full \(A\) across \(Z\). This should be \(\frac {2BD}{W_{\text {ICI}}}\) or \(2 \times \) the previous part.
    Remark. Completely misunderstood this question. For starters, when reducing along the \(Z\) axis, we still stay sharded across \(x\) and \(y\) and therefore do not make hops across those links. Therefore, we must divide by \(|X| \cdot |Y|\). Also, I guess the heuristic that AllReduce is roughly \(2 \times \) AllGather is used in calculations, which gives final answer \[\frac {4BD}{|X|\cdot |Y|\cdot W_{\text {ICI}}}\]

Exercise 3.3. latency-bound AllGather

  • August 5, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios
 Let’s say we’re performing an \(\text {AllGather}_X([B_X])\) but \(B\) is very small (say 128). How long should this take on a TPU v4p 4x4x4 slice with mesh Mesh({'X': 4, 'Y': 4, 'Z': 4}) in bfloat16?
Solution

Since \(|X| = 4\), the hop latency time is \(\approx 4 \mu \)s. We have \(N = 2\cdot 128 = 256\)bytes and \(W_{\text {ICI}} = 9e10\). This gives \(.0028 \mu \)s. So we are severely latency bound.

Remark. Only need to do \(2\) hops in bi-directional case, so true answer is \(\approx 2\mu s\): still latency bound.

Exercise 3.4. matmul strategies

  • August 5, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios
 To perform \(X[B,D]\cdot _D Y[D_X,F] \to Z[B,F]\), in this section we tell you to perform \(\text {AllGather}_X(Y[D_X,F])\) and multiply the fully replicated matrices (Case 2, Strategy 1). Instead, you could multiply the local shards like \(X[B,D_X]\cdot _D Y[D_X,F] \to Z[B,F]\{U_X\}\) (Case 3, Strategy 2), and then \(\text {AllReduce}_X(Z[B,F]\{U_X\})\). How many FLOPs and comms does each of these perform? Which is better and why?
Solution

Case 2, strategy 1. In this case, the AllGather will take \(\frac {DF}{W_{\text {ICI}}}\) for communication over \(ICI\) and \(BD + DF + BF\) over HBM with \(2BDF\) FLOPs.

Case 3, strategy 2. For local shards, each will only need to do \(\frac {2BDF}{X}\) FLOPs and \(BD + D_X F + BF\) HBM cost. However, the ICI cost would then be the whole matrix which is \(X \times \) as much over ICI.

Remark.

I was roughly correct. However, an important distinction (and gap in my understanding I gues) is that we have been ignoring HBM cost when communicating over ICI because these transfers are done concurrently and are therefore bottlenecked by the slower one (ICI).

Exercise 3.5. minimum latency

  • August 5, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios
 Let’s say I want to do a matmul \(A[I,J]\cdot JB[J,K]\to C[I,K]\) on a TPU v4p 4x4x4 with the lowest possible latency. Assume the inputs can be sharded arbitrarily but the result should be fully replicated. How should my inputs be sharded? What is the total FLOPs and comms time?
Solution

My initial intuition is we do not want to shard along the contracting dimension. If we have a large enough matrix, then I think the best sharding strategy would be to shard \(A[I_{XYZ}, J], B[J, K]\). The multiplication then requires no communication, and the only communication is an AllGather across all \(3\) axis, which should triple bandwidth. Since we shard over every axis of our mesh, we do not have any additional replicated bytes. This gives us \(N = 2IK\)bytes in bf16. Since we are on a \(4\times 4\times 4\) cube, we have bi-directional bandwidth availability. Therefore, the communication time on TPU v4p is \(\frac {2IK}{3\cdot 9e10}\). The total flops is still just \(2IJK\).

Exercise 3.6. comparing shardings

  • August 5, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios
 Let’s say we want to perform \(A[I_X,J_Y]\cdot _J B[J_Y,K]\to C[I_X,K]\) on TPU v5e 4x4. What communication do we perform? How much time is spent on communication vs. computation?
  • What about \(A[I_X,J]\cdot _J B[J_X,K_Y]\to C[I_X,K_Y]\)? This is the most standard setting for training where we combine data, tensor, and ZeRO sharding.
  • What about \(A[I_X,J]\cdot _J B[J,K_Y]\to C[I_X,K_Y]\)? This is standard for inference, where we do pure tensor parallelism.
Solution

  1. Since this is a matmul over the sharded axis, we need to perform a reduction at some point. After performing the matmul, we should have \(C[I_X, K]\{U_Y\}\). Therefore, we need to do an AllReduce over \(Y\). This is then a ReduceScatter and an AllGather. For computation, each chip does the partial sum, which takes \(\frac {2IJK}{|X||Y|}\) FLOPs. For communication, the AllReduce is \(2 \times \) an AllGather. We are still sharded over \(X\), so the total bytes is \(N = \frac {2IK}{|X|}\). We do not have bi-directional because the v5e is a 2d topology and \(4 \times 4\) is not full in either axis. Thus, the communication is

    \[\frac {2\cdot N}{W_{\text {ICI}}} = \frac {4IK}{4.5e10\cdot |X|}\]

    To see where we are bound, the v5e can do \(1.97e 14\) bf16 FLOPs/s. Therefore, we are compute bound when

    \[ \begin {align*} \frac {2IJK}{|X|\cdot |Y|\cdot 1.97e 14} > \frac {4IK}{4.5e10\cdot |X|} \iff J > \frac {8 \cdot 1.97e 14}{4.5e10} .\end {align*} \]

    Thus, we are almost surely communication bound because it is determined by the contracting dimension, which is \(d_{\text {model}}\) in practice.

    Remark. No solutions available. Prayers up this right...

  2. This is Case 1 with an additional sharding over the contracting dim in \(B\). I believe this means when we do the matmul, we are gonna end up with scattered partial sums i.e. unlike in the ReduceScatter case, where we have partial sums the same dimension as \(C\), the partial sums will now be \(\frac {I}{|X|} \times \frac {K}{|Y|}\). Another ReduceScatter would cause this smaller matrix to be further divided and scattered, so it is not what we want.

    Instead, we should just perform \(\text {AllGather}_X(B[J_X, K_Y])\). Then, this will directly reduce to Case 1 and we will need no further communication. We only need to send \(N = \frac {2JK}{|Y|}\) bytes. Once again, we do not have bi-directional bandwidth. Thus, the communication is

    \[\frac {N}{W_{\text {ICI}}} = \frac {4JK}{4.5e10\cdot |Y|}\]

    The FLOPs per-device are still \(\frac {2IJK}{|X|\cdot |Y|}\). To see where we are bound, the v5e can do \(1.97e 14\) bf16 FLOPs/s. Therefore, we are compute bound when

    \[ \begin {align*} \frac {2IJK}{|X|\cdot |Y|\cdot 1.97e 14} > \frac {2JK}{4.5e10\cdot |Y|} \iff I > \frac {4 \cdot 1.97e 14}{4.5e10} .\end {align*} \]

    Thus, we have a smaller bound than the previous part but are now dependent on \(I\) instead of \(J\). This is likely in practice because \(I\) corresponds to sequence length, which can get very large.

  3. This is pure case 1 with no communication, so we instead need to worry about memory instead of communication overhead.

Exercise 3.7. transformer block

  • August 5, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios
 A typical Transformer block has two matrices \(W_{in}[D,F]\) and \(W_{out}[F,D]\) where \(F \gg DF \gg D\) . Say we have a batch size B. Then the full block is \(In[B,D]\cdot W_{in}[D,F]\cdot W_{out}[F,D]\). Let’s pick D=8192 , F=32768, and B=128 and assume everything is in bfloat16. Assume we’re running on a TPU v5e 2x2 slice but let’s pretend each TPU only has 300MB of free memory. How should In, \(W_{in}\), \(W_{out}\), and Out be sharded to stay below the memory limit while minimizing overall time? How much time is spent on comms and FLOPs? Hint: the final output doesn’t need to be fully replicated, but it should be sharded the same as the input so the “layer” can be repeated.
Solution

To start, lets compute how big everything is.

\[ \begin {align*} In &= 2\cdot B\cdot D \\ &= 2\cdot 8192\cdot 128 = 2^{21} \\ W_{in} &= 2\cdot D\cdot F \\ &= 2\cdot 8192\cdot 32768 = 2^{29} \\ W_{out} &= 2\cdot D\cdot F \\ &= 2\cdot 8192\cdot 32768 = 2^{29} \end {align*} \]

and each TPU has \(300\)MB \(\approx 300 \cdot 2^{20} \approx 2^{28}\) in this example. Therefore, each TPU can fit just over one half of \(W_{in}\) and \(W_{out}\), which leads us to have to fully shard both across \(X\) and \(Y\). The remaining \(11 \cdot 2^{22}\) can fit \(\text {In}\). However, we need to satisfy the constraint that \(\text {Out}\) is sharded in the same way as \(\text {In}\). We adopt the following strategy:

  1. Shard \(\text {In}[B_{XY}, D]\), \(W_{in}[D,F_{XY}]\)
    • First, we need to AllGather \(\text {In}\) along \(B\).
    • Then, we have \(\text {In}[B, D]\cdot W_{in}[D, F_{XY}]\to \text {Tmp}[B, F_{XY}]\)
  2. Shard \(W_{out}[F_{XY}, D]\)
    • Now we have \(\text {Tmp}[B, F_{XY}]\cdot W_{out}[F_{XY}, D] \to \text {Out}[B, D]\{U_{XY}\} \)
    • Then we need to do a ReduceScatter over \(XY\) in the \(B\) axis to get back to our input shape.

Now lets count up the communication cost.

  1. First, we have an AllGather over \(XY\) of \(\text {In}\). This is \(N = 2\cdot B\cdot D\) bytes. We only have unidirectional bandwidth. However, we are gathering over 2 axes, which doubles our bandwidth. Thus, this will take \[\frac {2\cdot 128\cdot 8192}{2\cdot 4.5e 10} = 23.3\mu s\]
  2. Then we have a ReduceScatter of \(\text {Out}[B, D]\{U_{XY}\}\), which takes the same time as AllGather and is another \(23.3 \mu s\).

Thus, the whole communication cost is only \(46.6 \mu s\).

Remark. In the solution, they instead propose to shard \(\text {In}[B, D_{XY}]\), which is equivalent in communication cost. According to Claude, there is a subtle distinction.
  1. If you are in decoding (i.e. \(B = 1\)), then you cannot even shard along \(B\) but can still shard along \(D\).
  2. However, it seems preferable to shard over \(B\) if you can. This way, for activations / reductions over \(D\) you do not need any communication.

Exercise 3.9. another strategy for sharded matmuls

  • August 5, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios
 Above we claimed that when only one input to a matmul is sharded along its contracting dimension, we should AllGather the sharded matrix and perform the resulting contraction locally. Another strategy you might think of is to perform the sharded matmul and then AllReduce the result (as if both inputs were sharded along the contracting dimension), i.e. \(A[I,J_X]\cdot _J B[J,K]\to C[I,K]\) by way of
  1. \(C[I, K]\{U_{X}\} = A[I, J_{X}]\cdot B[J_{x}, K] \)
  2. \(C[I, K]\{U_{X}\} = \text {AllReduce}(C[I,K]\{U_{X}\})\)
Answer the following
  1. Explicitly write out this algorithm for matrices \(A[N,M]\) and \(B[M,K]\), using indices to show exactly what computation is done on what device. Assume \(A\) is sharded as \(A[I,J_X]\) across ND devices, and you want your output to be replicated across all devices.
  2. Now suppose you are ok with the final result not being replicated on each device, but instead sharded (across either the N or K dimension). How would the algorithm above change?
  3. Looking purely at the communication cost of the strategy above (in part 2, not 1), how does this communication cost compare to the communication cost of the algorithm in which we first AllGather A and then do the matmul?
Solution
  1. On the device, we can only make use of the \(J_{X}\) rows of \(B\) and compute the corresponding partial sums. This corresponds to the outer product \[C'[i] = \sum _{n=i\cdot \frac {J}{ND}}^{i(\frac {J}{ND} + 1)} A_{:,n} \oplus B_{n,:}\]
  2. The above algorithm would change by replacing the AllReduce with a ReduceScatter. This is better communication wise because AllReduce is two collectives, not one.
  3. The communication cost is the same because ReduceScatter has the same communication cost as AllGather, but it is likely preferable if you are compute bound because you can distribute computation across devices.
    Remark. In the solutions, they make the (excellent) point that in the ReduceScatter case we are sending the output \(N\times K\) matrix, whereas in the AllGather case we are sending the \(N\times M\) matrix. Therefore, if we have a large contraction dim, then the second case might also be preferable.

Exercise 3.10. Fun with AllToAll

  • August 5, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios
 In the table above, it was noted that the time to perform an AllToAll is a factor of 4 lower than the time to perform an AllGather or ReduceScatter (in the regime where we are throughput-bound). In this problem we will see where that factor of 4 comes from, and also see how this factor would change if we only had single-direction ICI links, rather than bidirectional ICI links.
  1. Let’s start with the single-direction case first. Imagine we have D devices in a ring topology and want to do either an AllGather or a ReduceScatter on an N x N matrix \(A[I_X,J]\) (say D divides N for simplicity). Describe the comms involved in these two collectives, and calculate the total number of scalars (floats or ints) which are transferred across a single ICI link during the entirety of this algorithm.
  2. Now let’s think about an AllToAll, still in the single-directional ICI case. How is the algorithm different in this case than the all-gather case? Calculate the number of scalars that are transferred across a single ICI link in this algorithm.
  3. You should have found that the ratio between your answers to part (a) and part (b) is a nice number. Explain where this factor comes from in simple terms.
  4. Now let’s add bidirectional communication. How does this affect the total time needed in the all-gather case?
  5. How does adding bidirectional communication affect the total time needed in the AllToAll case?
  6. Now simply explain the ratio between AllGather time and AllToAll time in a bidirectional ring.
Solution
  1. The communication involved in either of these collectives is each chip in the ring sending a chunk of \(A\) of size \(\frac {N^2}{D}\) to the right neighbor. A single ICI link sees every chunk and therefore \(N^2(D-1)\) scalars must cross a single ICI link. The \(D - 1\) comes from the fact that each device already owns one \(\frac {N^2}{D}\) chunk.
  2. AllToAll differs than AllGather because each subsequent forwarding is \(\frac {N^2}{D^2}\) less bytes. Namely, each device has an \(\frac {N^2}{D}\) shard of \(A\). Then in AllToAll, you forward to a neighbor who takes a \(\frac {1}{D}\) of this chunk and forwards the remaining. Therefore, a single ICI link only sees the following bytes of ICI traffic \[\frac {N^2}{D} \sum _{i=1}^{D} (D - i) = \frac {N^2\cdot D(D-1)}{2D} = \frac {N^2(D-1)}{2}\]
  3. From the previous 2 parts, we see that the ratio is exactly \(\frac {1}{2}\). This comes from the fact that, for farther devices, a link needs to transfer a much smaller number of bytes in AllToAll. Whereas, in AllGather, you must see all bytes of a chunk for every device uniformly.
  4. In the AllGather case, bidirectional communication still requires each link to see every byte. Therefore, only the ICI bandiwdth changes and not the total bytes seen per-link.
  5. In the AllToAll case, each chip only needs its sub-chunk of each chunk. Therefore, we can divide the chunk into the front and back half and send in each direction. This halves the total bytes seen per link, reducing to \(\frac {N^2(D-1)}{4}\).
  6. In the bidirectional case, we can effectively reduce our AllToAll to 2 unidirectional AllToAll's of half the size. This then halves the bytes-per-link, which was already half of an AllGather. Since every device needs every byte of each chunk in the AllGather case, it gets no reduction in the bidirectional case.
