Definition. Softcapping [39ZN]

  • July 16, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

Softcapping is a stability trick in the attention mechanism. It is a way to ensure that the softmax does not explode. \[\mathrm {logits} = \mathrm {softcap} \cdot \tanh \left ( \frac {\mathrm {logits}}{\mathrm {softcap}} \right ) \]

Stabilizing Softmax in Attention [7TMH]

  • July 16, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

The softmax is ill-behaved due to the exponentials. In the transformer, we have two softmaxes: one at the end and one in the attention.

  • For the first, note \[\log \sigma (\mathbf {x})_i = \log (x_i) - \log \underbrace {\sum _{j=1}^{d} e^{x_j}}_{D(\mathbf {x})}\] The only problem is the denominator term. The idea is to enforce the \(D(\mathbf {x}) = 1\) by regularizing via a penalty on \(\log D(\mathbf {x})\) ie. \[\mathcal {L}_{\text {aux}} = 10^{-4} \log ^2(D(\mathbf {x}))\] With the \(\nabla D(\mathbf {x})\) should be \(0\) and we are effectively only considering the non-exponential term.
  • For the attention, they primarily operate on the logits prior to the softmax. One way is via layer norm before the softmax. Another is via Softcapping

Question. What is the role of weight decay in training large models? [U52K]

  • July 16, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

Since there is so much data, it is not feasible to train your model for multiple epochs. This is actually nice in the sense that we do not have to worry about overfitting and performing regularization.

However, many of the large models are still trained with weight decay. Tatsu claims that this is not to do with regularization but actually due to some weird interaction with the learning rate schedule. I am not sure I entirely understood this part.

Computing FFN and MHA in parallel is free speedup [ZAR4]

  • July 16, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

Another small trick is to parallelize computation. Traditionally, one computes the \(\mathrm {MHA}\) output and then passes this to the \(\mathrm {FFN}\) i.e. \[\mathbf {y} = \mathbf {x} + \mathrm {FFN}(\mathrm {LN}(\mathbf {x} + \mathrm {MHA}(\mathrm {LN}(\mathbf {x})))).\] However, this requires waiting for the \(\mathrm {MHA}\) to complete before performing the \(\mathrm {FFN}\) computation. It has been found that performing these in parallel does not cause any severe degradation in performance. Explicitly, instead they do \[\mathbf {y} = \mathbf {x} + \mathrm {FFN}(\mathrm {LN}(\mathbf {x})) + \mathrm {MHA}(\mathrm {LN}(\mathbf {x}))\]

Activations [9X1X]

  • July 16, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

Despite a long list of activations, the two focused on are ReLU and GELU.

Definition. Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU) [BEA2]

  • July 14, 2025
  • Kellen Kanarios

The rectified linear unit(ReLU) is defined as \[\mathrm {ReLU} : \mathbb {R}^d \to \mathbb {R}^d, \quad \mathbf {x} \mapsto \max (0, \mathbf {x}),\] where the \(\max \) is done elementwise i.e. \(\mathrm {ReLU}(\mathbf {x})_i = \max (0, x_i)\) This provides "nice" gradients, making it common when training neural networks.

Definition. Gaussian Error Linear Unit (GELU) [5SPM]

  • July 14, 2025
  • Kellen Kanarios

The Gaussian Error Linear Unit (GELU) is a slight modification to the ReLU to account for the non-differentiability at \(0\). Namely, \[\mathrm {GELU}(\mathbf {x}) : \mathbb {R}^d \to \mathbb {R}^d, \quad \mathbf {x} \mapsto \mathbf {x} \cdot \psi (\mathbf {x}),\] where \(\psi (\mathbf {x}) = \mathrm {CDF}(\mathcal {N}(\mathbf {x}, \mathbf {I}))\)

Definition. Swish Activation [OZD8]

  • July 14, 2025
  • Kellen Kanarios

The Swish activation is given by \[\mathrm {Swish}(\mathbf {x}) : \mathbb {R}^d \to \mathbb {R}^d, \quad \mathbf {x} \mapsto \mathbf {x} s(\mathbf {x}),\] where \(s : \mathbb {R}^d \to \mathbb {R}^d\) is the sigmoid function.

Remark. The extra computation required by GELU or Swish is a non-factor because FLOPS are dominated by matrix multiplication and there is no increase in memory pressure.

Definition. Gated Linear Unit (GLU) [K2N7]

  • July 14, 2025
  • Kellen Kanarios

A gated linear unit is an activation function combined with an elementwise multiplication i.e.

  • \(\mathrm {ReGLU} = \mathrm {ReLU}(\mathbf {x}) \otimes \mathbf {V} \mathbf {x},\)
  • \(\mathrm {SwiGLU} = \mathrm {Swish}(\mathbf {x}) \otimes \mathbf {V} \mathbf {x},\)
where \(\mathrm {ReLU}\) is the ReLU activation and \(\mathrm {Swish}\) is the Swish activation respectively.

Remark. The matrix \(\mathbf {V}\) introduces additional learnable parameters. Therefore, an architecture that uses gating typically reduces their other parameters by a factor of \(\frac {2}{3}\).

Card. Gating splits the up-projection in two [Y4Y8]

  • August 18, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

For one Transformer layer with a gated MLP, what are the parameter count and training FLOPs — and why is the coefficient three rather than two?

Answer Parameters: \(3DF\), from \(W_{in1}[D,F]\), \(W_{in2}[D,F]\), \(W_{out}[F,D]\). Training FLOPs: \(18BTDF\) — three matmuls at \(6BTDF\) each, by the \(6NPM\) rule. Where the third matrix comes from. A Gated Linear Unit (GLU) splits the up-projection into two matrices whose outputs are multiplied elementwise, \(\sigma (AW_{in1}) \odot (AW_{in2})\), so one of them acts as a gate on the other. LLaMA, DeepSeek and most current models do this. A non-gated MLP has a single \(W_{in}\) and so \(2DF\) params — and typically scales \(D\) and \(F\) up to compensate, which is why the two families cost about the same at equal quality. The gate itself is \(O(BTF)\) — elementwise, no contraction, and negligible against \(BTDF\).

Norms [7JRP]

  • July 16, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

Pre-norm vs. Post-norm. The first architecture variation discussed is when to apply the layer norm. As can be seen in the figure below, rather than apply the layer norm in the residual stream. They instead place it before the FFN and MHA layers.

They actually found that adding layer normalization before and after the MHA and FFN works the best. This is known as double norm.

RMSNorm vs. LayerNorm. Another useful trick is to use the RMSNorm instead of LayerNorm.

Definition. RMS Norm [1XNO]

  • July 14, 2025
  • Kellen Kanarios

The RMS norm is simply the layer norm without the added bias term and centering i.e. \[\mathrm {RMSNorm}: \mathbb {R}^d \to \mathbb {R}^d, \quad \mathbf {x} \mapsto \frac {\mathbf {x}}{\sqrt {\mathrm {Var}[\mathbf {x}_i] + \epsilon }}*\gamma .\] This is used to spare memory movement of layernorm, where the bias term \(\beta \in \mathbb {R}^d\) and has been found to be empirically almost if not as good.

One might wonder if matrix multiplies are the only thing that matters what can such a small change really accomplish.

  • Due to memory movement, despite being .17% of FLOPS, provided 25% speedup in runtime!!
Remark. Most people apparently just drop the bias term and keep the centering i.e. subtracting the mean. This makes sense because computing the mean does not require loading any additional information back to memory.

Review: The Mezzanine [HGRL]

  • July 15, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

This was a very different read for me. A short book (only 135 pages) that goes into great detail the work day at the Mezzanine. I have some gripes with the description of readable on the cover. I found the incredibly vivid imagery sometimes hard to follow. It seems the intent of the book was to highlight the thoughts of an ordinary working man throughout the day. However, some of these thoughs were so far from ordinary it lost the relatable, funny read it was going for. Some chapters were pure gold (the urinal) but others were a huge miss for me.

Overall, I enjoyed the book and would recommend. 6.5/10.

MLIR [IR7B]

  • July 15, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

An extensible compiler infrastructure: rather than one instruction set, a framework in which each domain defines its own dialect of operations, types, and attributes, all sharing one syntax and one pass infrastructure. That shared syntax is why an unfamiliar dialect is still readable on sight: the op grammar is fixed even when the ops are not, and Five sigils make any dialect readable is most of what reading one takes.

Collection of resources

  • https://llvm.org/devmtg/2020-09/slides/MLIR_Tutorial.pdf
  • https://www.lei.chat/posts/mlir-linalg-dialect-and-patterns/
  • https://www.lei.chat/posts/mlir-vector-dialect-and-patterns/

Dialects. This is effectively a syntax. For your given DSL, you must write each of the operations in this MLIR dialect in order to inherit the benefits of the MLIR ecosystem.

The whole structured CodeGen paradigm in MLIR prefers co-designing op semantics and transformations and let ops structurally encode and guarantee certain properties to simplify analyses and transformations.
— Lei Zhang

The general paradigm. It seems that when you are writing a DSL backed by MLIR that you

  1. Write an MLIR dialect for your DSL
  2. You can write custom compiler passes for your MLIR dialect.
    • This is what is done in Triton.
    • Triton has two custom MLIR dialects: ttir and ttgir.
      • The ttir dialect is the backend agnostic IR.
      • The ttgir dialect is the Triton GPU IR.
  3. Write a lowering pass from your MLIR dialect to the MLIR dialect of an MLIR with codegen backing i.e.
    • MLIR has an LLVM dialect
    • Alternatively, XLA ingests StableHLO, which is an MLIR dialect. In theory, this means that if your DSL is similar to that of a JAX / LinAlg dialect, then you can get a lot of the optimizations Google has come up with for free.
      • However, XLA works by translating StableHLO to HLO (via the internal mhlo dialect, chlo desugars, stablehlo is stable, mhlo is internal), which is then optimized by XLA. HLO is NOT an MLIR dialect and therefore in order to use XLA your backend needs to have an appropriate conversion from HLO to an executable on their backend.
      • This is what is done for trainium. Namely, the neuronx-cc compiler performs the translation from optimized HLO to optimized executable code on their ASIC.
    • Triton and the GPU backend for XLA are the LLVM + NVVM MLIR, which is the MLIR dialect for LLVM with added GPU instructions.

Reading a dump

  • July 15, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

Because the dialect is open-ended, what you can rely on is the structure: one op syntax (One shape for every op), five sigils (Five sigils make any dialect readable), regions for nesting, attributes for compile-time data, and a location on every op. That fixed part is enough to read a dialect whose documentation you have never opened.

Card. One shape for every op [JE7W]

  • August 22, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

In MLIR's generic form, what does each part of %0 = "foo.add"(%a, %b) : (i32, i32) -> i32 mean?

Answer Every op, in every dialect, prints to one shape: 
results = "dialect.opname"(operands) ({regions}) {attributes} : (operand types) -> result types
  • The quoted name is always dialect.op. The prefix is what makes an unfamiliar op findable — it names the dialect whose docs define it.
  • The type after the colon is a function type: operand types before the arrow, result types after. So the signature is always readable off the one line.
  • Only operands sit in the parens. Attributes are the brace dictionary and are compile-time constants, not Static single assignment values — that split is exactly what is known at compile time versus what flows at runtime.
Learn this shape once and any dialect is parseable; the pretty forms are sugar over it (The pretty form is optional, the generic form always works).

Card. The pretty form is optional, the generic form always works [T1YS]

  • August 22, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

Why does the same op print two different ways — arith.addi %a, %b : i32 versus "arith.addi"(%a, %b) : (i32, i32) -> i32?

Answer An op may define a custom pretty printer and parser; the generic form (One shape for every op) is the fallback that always works. Most dialects define one, so most dumps are pretty. The consequence when reading a dump. The type after the colon in pretty form is whatever the op's printer chose to show — usually just the element or result type, not the full signature. Operands, regions, and attributes may all be elided or rearranged. When a pretty form is ambiguous, re-dump with --mlir-print-op-generic (Print generic, print locations, disable threading) and read the unambiguous version.

Card. Five sigils make any dialect readable [KWH2]

  • August 22, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

What do the five MLIR sigils %, ^, @, #, ! mark?

Answer
  • % — an Static single assignment value (SSA names are printing hints).
  • ^ — a block label (Block arguments replace phi nodes).
  • @ — a symbol: function, global (Symbols are looked up, values are defined).
  • # — an attribute or attribute alias: #map0, #stablehlo.dot<...>, #tpu.memory_space<vmem>.
  • ! — a type or type alias: !llvm.ptr, !tt.ptr<f32>.
This is the whole trick to reading an unfamiliar dialect. MLIR is extensible in ops, types, and attributes, so you will constantly meet names you do not know — but the sigil tells you which kind of thing it is, and therefore where it may legally appear. # and ! in particular are the escape hatches every dialect uses for its own metadata (The prefix says which side of layout assignment, Mosaic is explicit memory spaces and explicit copies).

Card. A multi-result op binds one name and indexes into it [OBP3]

  • August 22, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

In an MLIR dump, what is %2#1?

Answer The second result — index 1 — of the op that defined the value group %2. A multi-result op binds one name and you index into it: 
%2:3 = "foo.split"(%x) : (tensor<6xf32>) -> (tensor<2xf32>, tensor<2xf32>, tensor<2xf32>)
then %2#0, %2#1, %2#2. The declaration syntax %2:3 means "three results named %2", not a type annotation. This is MLIR's alternative to HLO's tuple-plus-get-tuple-element idiom (get-tuple-element is free aliasing): multiple results are native, so no packing op is needed.

Card. SSA names are printing hints [MOVC]

  • August 22, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

Are MLIR value names like %arg0, %c0_i32, %lhs semantically meaningful?

Answer No. They are printing hints only. Internally Static single assignment values are positional and unnamed; the asm printer reconstructs a name from a name-hint interface, which is why constants come out as %c0_i32 or %cst and block arguments as %arg0. Two things follow, and both bite when reading dumps:
  • %arg0 in two different functions or regions are unrelated. The name is scoped to its region and carries no identity across one.
  • The numbering is not stable across passes. Diffing two per-pass dumps (Per-pass dumps find the pass that broke it) on value names produces noise; diff on structure instead.
The Locations are the provenance of an op is the stable thing to key on — it survives the passes that renumber values.

Card. Block arguments replace phi nodes [QZFU]

  • August 22, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

Read this line: ^bb1(%arg0: i32, %arg1: f32):

Answer A block label with block arguments. MLIR has no phi nodes — instead each predecessor passes the merged values as branch operands: 
cf.br ^bb1(%x, %y : i32, f32)
Block arguments are the Static single assignment merge mechanism. The trade is that a value's incoming edges are recorded at the branches rather than collected at the merge, which makes CFG edits local: rewriting one predecessor touches one op. The entry block of a function-like op takes the function's parameters this same way, which is why %arg0 is the conventional name for a function argument.

Card. A region is nesting, not a flat CFG [MKYF]

  • August 22, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

What is a region in MLIR, and which ops have them?

Answer A region is an ordered list of blocks nested inside an op, written in braces. It is how MLIR encodes structured control flow and nesting instead of flattening everything into one CFG.
  • func.func — one region, the body.
  • scf.for — one region (iter_args and yield are the mutable accumulator); scf.if — two, then and else (Both scf.if regions must yield the same types).
  • stablehlo.reduce — one region holding the reducer (reduce takes a computation, not an enum).
Every block in a region ends in a terminator: scf.yield, func.return, cf.br. Regions are the structural reason MLIR can host both high-level tensor dialects and low-level CFGs in one module — a pass lowering scf.for to blocks is just replacing a region with a CFG.

Card. Position separates attributes from regions [CZBE]

  • August 22, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

In an MLIR dump, how do you tell an attribute dictionary from a region?

Answer By what is inside, and in generic form by position. Content. An attribute dict is {name = value, name2 = value2} — every entry is key = constant. A region contains operations, and possibly block labels (Block arguments replace phi nodes). Position. In generic form (One shape for every op) the slots are fixed: 
"scf.if"(%cond) ({ ...then... }, { ...else... }) {some_attr = 1} : (i1) -> ()
Regions come in parens straight after the operands; attributes come after the regions, before the colon type. The distinction matters because it is the compile-time / runtime line: an attribute is known to the compiler now, a region is code that runs.

Card. Symbols are looked up, values are defined [45LB]

  • August 22, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

In MLIR, what is @foo versus %foo?

Answer @foo is a symbol reference — a name resolved by lookup in a SymbolTable (a func.func, a global). %foo is an Static single assignment value defined earlier in the same region. Nested symbols use @parent::@child. The distinction shows up in the type list, which is the tell when reading a call: 
func.call @foo(%a) : (i32) -> i32
The callee is a symbol, not an operand, so it does not appear in the operand types — only %a does. A symbol is resolved at compile time; a value flows at runtime.

Card. Every dump is wrapped in a module [R2O9]

  • August 22, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

What wraps every MLIR dump, and what does a named one look like?

Answer A builtin.module. Printed bare as module { ... }, or with a name and attributes: 
module @jit_f attributes {mhlo.num_partitions = 1 : i32} { ... }
The outer braces are a region (A region is nesting, not a flat CFG), so the module is an ordinary op — there is nothing special about the top level. Read the module attributes first. In a JAX or XLA dump they carry the information the body assumes: partition and replica counts, Sharding configuration, target features. A body that looks like it does too little often makes sense once you see num_partitions up here.

Card. Three attribute positions on a function [ZZHW]

  • August 22, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

Decode the three annotation positions in func.func @main(%arg0: tensor<8xf32> {jax.arg_info = "x"}) -> (tensor<8xf32> {jax.result_info = ""}) attributes {llvm.emit_c_interface}

Answer Three different kinds of attribute, distinguished only by where they sit:
  1. Argument attributes — braces after an argument's type. Per-argument metadata.
  2. Result attributes — braces after a result's type, inside the result parens. Per-result metadata.
  3. Op attributes — after the keyword attributes. These belong to the function op itself.
JAX uses the first two to record what tracing threw away: the original Python argument names, donation, and per-argument Sharding. When you need to know which HLO parameter (parameter(i) is positional) was which Python argument, jax.arg_info is the record.

Card. An affine map separates dimensions from symbols [51XY]

  • August 22, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

Read #map = affine_map<(d0, d1)[s0] -> (d0 * s0 + d1)>

Answer An affine map: a multi-dimensional affine function used for indexing and loop bounds.
  • (d0, d1) — dimension operands: loop induction variables, indices. These vary within the iteration space.
  • [s0] — symbol operands: quantities loop-invariant over the map's use, such as sizes and strides.
  • The results are affine expressions over both — addition, subtraction, multiplication by a constant, floordiv, ceildiv, mod.
The dimension/symbol split is the point. Restricting to affine expressions of dims and symbols is what makes dependence analysis decidable, which is what lets the affine dialect tile, fuse, and interchange loops automatically. You will meet these on affine.load, affine.for bounds, and linalg indexing_maps, where the map says how the iteration space lands in memory.

Card. An unrealized cast that survives is a missing pattern [Y070]

  • August 22, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

What does builtin.unrealized_conversion_cast mean when you see it in an MLIR dump?

Answer A placeholder bridging two type systems mid-conversion — tensor to memref (A memref names storage, a tensor is a value), a dialect type to !llvm.ptr. The dialect conversion framework inserts them so that a partial conversion still verifies while some ops are converted and others are not. If one survives to the end of the pipeline, that is the bug. It means no pattern claimed the op on one side of the cast, so the conversion never closed. Chase the missing pattern rather than the cast. Mid-pipeline, in a --mlir-print-ir-after-all dump (Per-pass dumps find the pass that broke it), they are expected noise; at the boundary where the IR is supposed to be one dialect, they are a failure.

Locations

  • July 15, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

Value names are printing hints and instruction order changes every pass, so provenance has to be carried explicitly. The location is the only thing in the IR that survives rewriting well enough to answer "which line of Python produced this op".

Card. Locations are the provenance of an op [NRD2]

  • August 22, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

What does loc("model.py":42:8) on an MLIR op tell you, and how do you get locations printed?

Answer It is the op's Location — the provenance the compiler carries for diagnostics and for mapping generated code back to source. An op that was never given one prints loc(unknown). Print them with --mlir-print-debuginfo, or --mlir-print-debuginfo --mlir-pretty-debuginfo for a compact form (Print generic, print locations, disable threading). Why it is the tool that matters. Value names are unstable (SSA names are printing hints) and op ordering changes every pass, but a location survives rewrites — passes are expected to propagate it, fusing into fused and inlining into callsite (Fused means merged, callsite means inlined). So "which line of Python produced this op" is a location question, and only a location question. It is the MLIR analogue of HLO's metadata field (op_name is the trace path back to Python).

Card. Fused means merged, callsite means inlined [SE0U]

  • August 22, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

What do these two location forms mean? loc(fused["a.py":1:1, "b.py":2:2]) and loc(callsite("inner" at "outer"))

Answer fused — the op came from several source ops that a pass merged: Operator fusion, canonicalization, a rewrite that collapsed a chain. A fused location may carry a tag naming the culprit, loc(fused<"fusion">[...]). callsite — an inlining chain. Read it inner-to-outer: the callee's location first, then the site it was called from. Chains nest one level per inlining. Both are how a Locations are the provenance of an op stays honest under transformation: rather than picking one survivor and losing the rest, the location grows to record what happened. So a long fused location is itself the evidence that this op is several of your source ops.

Card. Aliases are deduplicated printing [7Z9D]

  • August 22, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

What are the #loc3 = loc(...) lines at the bottom of an MLIR dump?

Answer Location aliases. The printer hoists a repeated Locations are the provenance of an op into a named definition, and ops then reference it as ... loc(#loc3). It is the same mechanism as attribute aliases (#map0, An affine map separates dimensions from symbols) and type aliases (!my_type): purely printing deduplication, with no semantic content. Two ops sharing #loc3 have equal locations, nothing more. Practically: when you jump to an op and find loc(#loc3), the answer is at the bottom of the file, not missing.

The type system

  • July 15, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

The type grammar is where a dump's abstraction level is written down. Tensors mean you are above bufferization, memrefs mean storage and therefore aliasing, vectors mean register width and proximity to the hardware.

Card. Question mark is a dynamic dimension, star is unknown rank [L3F6]

  • August 22, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

What do tensor<4x?xf32>, tensor<*xf32>, and tensor<f32> mean?

Answer
  • 4x?xf32 — ranked, with the second dimension dynamic: ? means unknown at compile time.
  • *xf32 — unranked; even the rank is unknown.
  • tensor<f32> — a rank-0 tensor, which is not the same type as a bare f32.
The rank-0 distinction is the one that catches people. A scalar tensor is still a tensor and takes tensor ops; f32 is a scalar and takes arith ops. Conversions between them are explicit. A tensor is a value with no memory location — it cannot alias, so a pass may duplicate or reorder it freely. That freedom is exactly what a memref gives up (A memref names storage, a tensor is a value). By contrast HLO has no dynamic shapes at all: every dimension is known at compile time (An HLO line is self-contained).

Card. A memref names storage, a tensor is a value [B1A1]

  • August 22, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

Read memref<8x128xf32, strided<[128, 1], offset: ?>, #tpu.memory_space<vmem>>

Answer A buffer reference: shape and element type, then two optional slots.
  • strided<[128, 1], offset: ?> — the layout. Strides are in elements, not bytes; the offset is dynamic. Strides of [128, 1] on an 8x128 shape is the contiguous row-major case, the MLIR spelling of HLO's {1,0} (The layout is minor-to-major).
  • #tpu.memory_space<vmem> — which memory this lives in (VMEM / smem / hbm on TPU; 1 and 3 for shared and global on GPU).
The difference from a tensor is aliasing. A memref names storage, so two of them may refer to the same bytes and a pass must prove otherwise before reordering. A tensor is a value and cannot alias (Question mark is a dynamic dimension, star is unknown rank). Bufferization is the pass that trades the second for the first, and it is where most "why did a copy appear" questions live.

Card. Vectors are register-level, tensors are abstract [1XJ4]

  • August 22, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

Distinguish vector<4x8xf32>, vector<[4]xf32>, and tensor<4x8xf32>

Answer A vector is a fixed-size, register-level SIMD value — always ranked, always static. A tensor is an abstract n-dimensional value that still needs bufferization and lowering (Question mark is a dynamic dimension, star is unknown rank). Brackets around a dimension, [4], mark it scalable: the length is 4 * vscale, fixed by the hardware at run time rather than compile time. That is the SVE / RVV style of vector target, where the register width is not known when you compile. What seeing vector types tells you about the dump. You are past the tensor level and close to hardware — the shapes are now register tiles, not logical arrays. On TPU that is the 8x128 native tile you see all through a Mosaic dump (Mosaic is explicit memory spaces and explicit copies).

Card. Signedness lives in the op, not the type [I4UP]

  • August 22, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

Why is it arith.divsi and arith.divui rather than one divide over a signed type?

Answer Because integer types in MLIR are signless: i32 is thirty-two raw bits and nothing more. Signedness lives in the operation, not the type. So the op suffix is the interpretation — si signed, ui unsigned — and it appears exactly on the ops where it changes the answer: divide, remainder, comparison, widening extension, shift right. Addition and multiplication need no suffix, because two's complement makes them agree. Why design it this way. One type means one canonical form, so a pattern that matches i32 matches everything, and frontends with different signedness rules can share the dialect. Some dialects do carry si32 and ui32 for frontend fidelity, but core arith is signless plus typed ops.

Card. index is the type of sizes and offsets [2QC3]

  • August 22, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

What is the index type in MLIR and where does it show up?

Answer A target-dependent-width integer for sizes, offsets, and loop induction variables. It lowers to i32 or i64 depending on the target, so the IR does not have to commit to a pointer width. You will see it constantly in the shape of 
%c0 = arith.constant 0 : index
feeding memref.dim, scf.for bounds (iter_args and yield are the mutable accumulator), tensor.extract indices, and memref.subview offsets. Read it as a type-level statement of intent: this value addresses the iteration space, it is not data. That is why index and i32 do not implicitly convert — arith.index_cast is required, and its appearance in a dump marks the boundary where an index became a number or the reverse.

Card. A scalar inside dense is a splat [5B7I]

  • August 22, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

Read these three MLIR constants: dense<[1, 2, 3, 4]> : tensor<4xi32>, dense<0.000000e+00> : tensor<8x128xf32>, dense_resource<__elided__> : tensor<1024x1024xf32>

Answer
  • Bracketed list — a full elementwise literal, one entry per element, with one level of bracket nesting per dimension: a rank-2 constant is a list of rows.
  • A single scalar inside dense<> — a splat: every element takes that value. This is the common case and is stored as one number, not as the expanded array.
  • dense_resource<__elided__> — the printer dropped the payload because it was large. The data still exists in the real module; only the text you are reading lost it.
Elision is controlled by --mlir-elide-elementsattrs-if-larger=N. Raise it when you actually need to see the weights, and leave it alone otherwise — a dump of a real model is otherwise mostly constants. HLO does the same thing, printing a big constant as {...} (iota builds indices without a constant).

Structured control flow

  • July 15, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

The scf dialect keeps a loop as one op with a region rather than as a CFG, which is what lets a pass reason about it as a loop. The carry is explicit and typed — the same design the jaxpr scan (consts, then carry, then xs) and the HLO while (A while loop's whole state is one tuple) arrive at independently.

Card. iter_args and yield are the mutable accumulator [ON39]

  • August 22, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

Read this loop: %r = scf.for %i = %c0 to %c8 step %c1 iter_args(%acc = %init) -> (f32) { %n = arith.addf %acc, %x : f32; scf.yield %n : f32 }

Answer A structured loop that carries state.
  • %i is a block argument of the loop body (Block arguments replace phi nodes), not a value from the enclosing scope.
  • iter_args(%acc = %init) declares the loop-carried values and initialises them once, before the first iteration.
  • scf.yield supplies the next iteration's iter_args and, on the final iteration, the loop's results %r.
So iter_args plus scf.yield is the functional spelling of a mutable accumulator. Nothing is stored; each iteration produces a new value. That is what keeps the loop in Static single assignment form and lets it be analysed and rewritten as a pure region (A region is nesting, not a flat CFG). Both the jaxpr scan (consts, then carry, then xs) and the HLO while (A while loop's whole state is one tuple) use the same idea — the carry is explicit and typed — differing only in how the carried values are packed.

Card. Both scf.if regions must yield the same types [1U5S]

  • August 22, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

How does an scf.if produce a value?

Answer By declaring result types on the op and having both regions (A region is nesting, not a flat CFG) terminate in scf.yield with matching types: 
%v = scf.if %pred -> (f32) { scf.yield %a : f32 } else { scf.yield %b : f32 }
If the op has no results, the else region may be omitted entirely and the yields are empty. The type match is the invariant worth remembering. It is what makes the construct an expression rather than control flow — the op has one well-defined type regardless of which branch runs, so it composes like any other value-producing op (iter_args and yield are the mutable accumulator). A verifier error on scf.if is almost always the two branches disagreeing.

Debugging a lowering

  • July 15, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

Card. Print generic, print locations, disable threading [7R2Y]

  • August 22, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

Which MLIR debugging flags do you reach for when a lowering looks wrong?

Answer
  • --mlir-print-ir-after-all (or --mlir-print-ir-after-change, or -before=<pass>) — IR snapshots per pass. The MLIR counterpart to --xla_dump_hlo_pass_re (Per-pass dumps find the pass that broke it).
  • --mlir-print-op-generic — removes pretty-printer ambiguity (The pretty form is optional, the generic form always works).
  • --mlir-print-debuginfo — locations, so ops trace back to source (Locations are the provenance of an op).
  • --mlir-disable-threading — serialises the pass manager so per-pass output is ordered and readable.
  • --debug-only=<pass-name> — pattern-level tracing, in a debug build only.
Turn off threading first. Without it, per-pass dumps from parallel op processing interleave, and you spend the session reading a file whose disorder is the tooling's, not the compiler's.

Programmed I/O [9RLX]

  • July 13, 2026

Simplified I/O Device Protocol: requires three "registers". One is the status register that tells the OS whether the device is ready or currently performing an operation. The second is the command register, which tells the device what we want to do. Lastly, is the data register that stores the actual data we want moved. The procedure operates as follows [arpaci2018operating, 36.3]

  1. OS polls status register in while loop until status == READY
  2. OS writes data register with data to be moved
  3. OS writes command register with command to be performed
  4. Device begins command and sets status = BUSY
  5. OS polls status register in while loop until status == READY

The above protocol requires that the CPU polls the device. This is a huge waste if the device is very slow because the CPU is unable to do any work while waiting. One solution is to use interrupts. In particular, the CPU follows the above procedure but after writing the command it resumes doing other work. Upon completion, the device issues an interrupt to the CPU to tell it that it has finished the command and that the CPU can resume working on that line of instructions.

Question. How is copying memory to device actually done in programmed I/O? Is the device address space mapped into the CPU address space and the CPU has 1. load from CPU address space to register, 2. write to device address from register?
Answer.There are two ways. The first is there are special I/O instructions (typically protected) that allow the CPU to directly write to the device. In x86, these are in, out. The second way is through memory-mapped I/O (MMIO). This is where the device is actually allocated a region of virtual address space and writing to / reading this region is routed to the device rather than the on-chip memory hierarchy [arpaci2018operating, 36.6].

Operator fusion is like ASIC caching [PMIC]

  • July 13, 2026

On a traditional CPU, the hardware manages caching to ensure that data that is reused does not roundtrip through DRAM. On an ASIC accelerators, we forego the complexity of caching to allow for more execution units. However, now if we have two operations i.e. elementwise add \(\to \) softmax this would

  1. Load the input tensors from memory (HBM on TPU).
  2. Perform the elementwise add.
  3. Store the output tensor to memory.
  4. Load the input tensors from memory.
  5. Perform the softmax.
  6. Store the output tensor to memory.

On a CPU, the input tensors would remain in the cache. However, this must be done explicitly on ASIC (or by the compiler in the case of Google / XLA).

Card. The false dependencies renaming removes [2RO9]

  • July 11, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

What false dependencies does register renaming eliminate?

AnswerWrite-after-write (\(\mathrm {WAW}\)) and write-after-read (\(\mathrm {WAR}\)) hazards — the false dependencies that arise from reusing an architectural register, not from real data flow. Removing them exposes more Register renaming breaks false dependencies to the scheduler.

Construction of universal fixed rated code [OGCSN]

  • July 11, 2026
  • with contributions from Kellen Kanarios

To construct, a universal fixed rate code, we need a code that satisfies (i) and (ii) from Fixed rate universal code.

  • Let \( |\mathcal {X}|=m \), and for any \( n\geq 1 \) and a given \( R>0 \), define \( R_n=R-m \frac {\log n+1}{n}\)
  • Consider the subset \(A_n \subset \mathcal {X}^n\), defined as \[A_n = \{x^n \in \mathcal {X}^n \mid H(\hat {P}_{x^n} \leq R_n)\} \]
  • Then just define the encoder in the usual way i.e. for encoder \(e_n\) give every \(x^n \in A_n\) a unique code and everything else map to the same code.
  • Then the decoder can easily identify everything in \(A_n\) and it suffices to show that in the limit the probabilities concentrate around \(A_n\).

Theorem. The type-based fixed-rate code is universal [006L]

  • March 30, 2025
  • Kellen Kanarios

The code constructed above is a universal fixed-rate code, such that \( \lim _{n\to \infty }\mathbb {P}_{X^{n}\sim P^{n}}(f_{n}(e_{n}(X^{n}))\neq X^{n})=0 \) for all \( P \) with \( H(P)<R \).

Theorem. Entropy is concave [TVGU]

  • July 11, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

Entropy is a concave functional of the distribution: for \(\lambda \in [0,1]\), \[H(\lambda P_1+(1-\lambda )P_2)\ \geq \ \lambda H(P_1)+(1-\lambda )H(P_2).\] Mixing two distributions never destroys uncertainty — the entropy of a mixture is at least the mixture of entropies.

This is the mirror image of KL divergence is jointly convex. Writing \(H(P)=\log |\mathcal {X}|-D_{\mathrm {KL}}(P\,\|\,U)\) against the uniform law \(U\), concavity of \(H\) is exactly convexity of \(P\mapsto D_{\mathrm {KL}}(P\|U)\). Concavity is what makes the maximum in The uniform distribution maximizes entropy well-behaved — a concave objective on the simplex has a unique maximizer.

Theorem. KL divergence is jointly convex [WV2P]

  • July 11, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

The KL divergence \(D_{\mathrm {KL}}(P\,\|\,Q)\) is convex in the pair \((P,Q)\) jointly: for any two pairs and \(\lambda \in [0,1]\), \[D_{\mathrm {KL}}\left (\lambda P_1+(1-\lambda )P_2\ \|\ \lambda Q_1+(1-\lambda )Q_2\right )\ \leq \ \lambda D_{\mathrm {KL}}(P_1\|Q_1)+(1-\lambda )D_{\mathrm {KL}}(P_2\|Q_2).\]

This drops out of the Log-Sum Inequality applied termwise. Joint convexity is the strong statement: it immediately gives individual convexity in either argument (fix the other and set the two copies equal), and — via \(D_{\mathrm {KL}}(P\|U)=\log |\mathcal {X}|-H(P)\) against the fixed uniform law — it makes Entropy is concave a corollary.

Theorem. The uniform distribution maximizes entropy [6FHG]

  • July 11, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

Over a finite alphabet \(\mathcal {X}\), entropy is bounded by the log of the alphabet size, \[H(X)\ \leq \ \log |\mathcal {X}|,\] with equality iff \(X\) is uniform. No distribution on \(\mathcal {X}\) is more uncertain than the uniform one.

Again a face of Gibb's inequality: measuring \(P\) against the uniform law \(U(x)=1/|\mathcal {X}|\), \[D_{\mathrm {KL}}(P\,\|\,U)\ =\ \log |\mathcal {X}| - H(X)\ \geq \ 0,\] so \(H(X)\leq \log |\mathcal {X}|\), and Gibbs' equality condition \(P=U\) pins down the maximizer. This is the discrete base case of the general maximum-entropy principle: absent constraints, the flattest distribution wins.

Theorem. Entropy is subadditive [C6M8]

  • July 11, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

The joint entropy of a collection never exceeds the sum of the individual entropies: \[H(X_1,\dots ,X_n)\ \leq \ \sum _{i=1}^{n} H(X_i),\] with equality iff the \(X_i\) are mutually independent.

Expand the joint entropy by the chain rule, \(H(X_1,\dots ,X_n)=\sum _i H(X_i\mid X_1,\dots ,X_{i-1})\), and apply Conditioning reduces entropy term by term: each \(H(X_i\mid X_{<i})\leq H(X_i)\). Conditioning on the past can only shrink each term, so dropping the conditioning gives an upper bound.

Theorem. Conditioning reduces entropy [H7J5]

  • July 11, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

Observing another variable can only lower entropy on average: \[H(X\mid Y)\ \leq \ H(X),\] with equality iff \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent.

Immediate from Mutual information is nonnegative and the identity \(I(X;Y)=H(X)-H(X\mid Y)\): since \(I(X;Y)\geq 0\), the conditional entropy cannot exceed the unconditional one. The caveat is that this holds on average over \(Y\) — a particular outcome \(Y=y\) can raise the entropy of \(X\); it is only the expectation \(H(X\mid Y)=\mathbb {E}_Y[H(X\mid Y=y)]\) that is guaranteed to drop.

Theorem. Mutual information is nonnegative [TB4P]

  • July 11, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

For any pair of random variables, \(I(X;Y)\geq 0\), with equality iff \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent.

This is Gibb's inequality in disguise: mutual information is the KL divergence between the joint distribution and the product of marginals, \[I(X;Y)\ =\ D_{\mathrm {KL}}\left (P_{XY}\,\|\,P_X P_Y\right )\ \geq \ 0,\] and Gibbs' inequality forces every KL divergence to be nonnegative, vanishing exactly when the two arguments coincide — i.e. when \(P_{XY}=P_XP_Y\). It is the root fact from which Conditioning reduces entropy follows.

Definition. Markov chain as conditional independence [UWYD]

  • July 11, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

The information-theoretic reading of a Markov chain: three variables form a chain \(U\to V\to W\) when \(W\) depends on \(U\) only through \(V\), \[P(W=w\mid U=u, V=v)\ =\ P(W=w\mid V=v).\] Equivalently, \(U\) and \(W\) are conditionally independent given \(V\), written \((U\perp W)\mid V\): \[P(U=u, W=w\mid V=v)\ =\ P(U=u\mid V=v)\,P(W=w\mid V=v).\]

Two consequences make this the right object for information theory. The relation is reversible — \(U\to V\to W \iff W\to V\to U\) — because conditional independence is symmetric in \(U\) and \(W\). And any estimator forms a chain \(X\to Y\to \hat X\): an estimate \(\hat X\) is computed from the observation \(Y\) alone, never touching \(X\) directly. That structure is exactly what the data processing inequality needs — you cannot manufacture information about \(X\) by processing \(Y\).

Theorem. Second-order optimality conditions [U3L4]

  • July 11, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

Let \(f:\mathbb {R}^n\to \mathbb {R}\) be twice continuously differentiable in an open neighborhood of \(\mathbf {x_\star }\).

Necessary. If \(\mathbf {x_\star }\) is a local minimizer, then \[(i)\ \nabla f(\mathbf {x_\star })=\mathbf {0};\qquad (ii)\ \nabla ^2 f(\mathbf {x_\star })\succeq \mathbf {0}.\] That is, it is a stationary point whose Hessian is positive semidefinite.

Sufficient. If instead \(\nabla f(\mathbf {x_\star })=\mathbf {0}\) and \(\nabla ^2 f(\mathbf {x_\star })\succ \mathbf {0}\) (Hessian strictly positive definite), then \(\mathbf {x_\star }\) is a strict local minimizer. The gap between \(\succeq \) and \(\succ \) is exactly the ambiguity the first-order condition alone cannot resolve.

Theorem. First-order optimality condition [I6DT]

  • July 11, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

If \(\mathbf {x_\star }\) is a local minimizer of \(f:\mathbb {R}^n\to \mathbb {R}\) and \(f\) is continuously differentiable in an open neighborhood of \(\mathbf {x_\star }\), then \(\mathbf {x_\star }\) is a stationary point: \[\nabla f(\mathbf {x_\star })\ =\ \mathbf {0}.\]

This is only necessary: a stationary point may be a maximizer or saddle, which is what the second-order conditions disambiguate. Under convexity it becomes sufficient as well — a stationary point of a convex function is a global minimizer.

Definition. Frobenius norm [4M9J]

  • July 11, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

The entrywise Euclidean norm of a matrix — treat \(\mathbf {A}\) as a long vector and take its 2-norm: \[\|\mathbf {A}\|_F\ =\ \sqrt {\sum _{i,j}A_{ij}^2}\ =\ \sqrt {\langle \mathbf {A},\mathbf {A}\rangle }\ =\ \sqrt {\mathrm {tr}(\mathbf {A}^{\top }\mathbf {A})}.\] It is the norm induced by the matrix inner product, and in terms of singular values it is the \(p=2\) Schatten norm, \(\|\mathbf {A}\|_F=\sqrt {\sum _i\sigma _i^2(\mathbf {A})}\) — the Euclidean length of the singular-value vector, dual in that family to the spectral norm (\(p=\infty \)).

Definition. Spectral norm [3U43]

  • July 11, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

The operator norm of a matrix induced by the Euclidean norm on both sides, \(\|\mathbf {A}\|_{2\to 2}\), usually written just \(\|\mathbf {A}\|\). It equals the largest singular value, \[\|\mathbf {A}\|\ =\ \sup _{\|\mathbf {x}\|_2\leq 1}\|\mathbf {A}\mathbf {x}\|_2\ =\ \sigma _1(\mathbf {A}),\] i.e. the most any unit vector can be stretched by \(\mathbf {A}\). As a Schatten norm it is the \(p=\infty \) case, \(\|\mathbf {A}\|_{\mathrm {S}_\infty }=\|\sigma (\mathbf {A})\|_\infty \), sitting opposite the Frobenius norm (\(p=2\)) in that family.

Definition. Matrix trace [PDX6]

  • July 11, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

For a square matrix \(\mathbf {M}\in \mathbb {R}^{n\times n}\), the trace is the sum of its diagonal entries: \[\mathrm {tr}(\mathbf {M}):=\sum _{i=1}^{n}M_{ii}.\]

Two identities make it the workhorse of matrix calculus. It is invariant under cyclic permutation of a product, \[\mathrm {tr}(\mathbf {A}\mathbf {B})=\mathrm {tr}(\mathbf {B}\mathbf {A}),\qquad \mathrm {tr}(\mathbf {A}_{1}\mathbf {A}_{2}\cdots \mathbf {A}_{n})=\mathrm {tr}(\mathbf {A}_{\pi (1)}\cdots \mathbf {A}_{\pi (n)})\] for any cyclic permutation \(\pi \) of \(\{1,\dots ,n\}\); and it computes the matrix inner product, \[\langle \mathbf {X},\mathbf {Z}\rangle =\mathrm {tr}(\mathbf {X}^{\top }\mathbf {Z})=\mathrm {tr}(\mathbf {X}\mathbf {Z}^{\top }).\]

Definition. Matrix inner product [WWMR]

  • July 11, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

The inner product on \(\mathbb {R}^{m\times n}\), obtained by treating a matrix as a long vector and summing the entrywise products: \[\langle \mathbf {X},\mathbf {Z}\rangle \ :=\ \sum _{i=1}^{m}\sum _{j=1}^{n}X_{ij}Z_{ij},\] the direct generalization of the vector case \(\langle \mathbf {x},\mathbf {z}\rangle =\sum _i x_i z_i\). It is the inner product whose induced norm is the Frobenius norm, \(\|\mathbf {X}\|_F=\sqrt {\langle \mathbf {X},\mathbf {X}\rangle }\).

It has a compact trace form (see Matrix trace): \[\langle \mathbf {X},\mathbf {Z}\rangle \ =\ \mathrm {tr}(\mathbf {X}^{\top }\mathbf {Z})\ =\ \mathrm {tr}(\mathbf {X}\mathbf {Z}^{\top }).\]

Page clustering [YMHF]

  • July 11, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

An amortization trick for the write side of page replacement. Writing one dirty page to swap at a time pays a full disk I/O per eviction, and small random writes are the worst case for a disk. Page clustering batches them: the OS collects a group of dirty pages from the global dirty list and writes them out together in a single larger, more sequential I/O. The per-page cost of paging out falls because the fixed overhead of a disk write is spread across the whole batch.

Segmented FIFO [HF6H]

  • July 11, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

A process-aware refinement of LRU and the clock algorithm. Pure FIFO is a global policy — it does not distinguish memory by owner, so one greedy process can evict everyone else's pages. Segmented FIFO instead maintains a per-process FIFO queue capped at that process's resident set size, bounding how much physical memory any single process can hold.

Evicted pages are not discarded outright; they move to one of two secondary lists:

  1. Clean page free list — evicted pages that were never modified.
  2. Dirty page list — evicted pages that must be written back before reuse.

The secondary lists act as a victim cache: if a process faults on a page still sitting on the dirty list, it can be reclaimed without going to disk. The resident-set cap gives fairness; the secondary lists soften the cost of capping it too aggressively.

Migratory-sharing optimization collapses read-then-write into one coherence transaction [20SW]

  • July 11, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

A common access pattern is migratory: a core reads a line and then writes it — think a lock or a hand-off variable that passes from core to core. Handled naively this costs two cache-coherence transactions: a read miss that fetches the line shared, then a write miss that upgrades it to modified. Upgrade-miss detection spots the pattern and, on the read miss, transitions the line straight to a migratory-exclusive state, so the following write is silent — one transaction instead of two.

Remark. The same optimization hurts producer–consumer sharing, where one core writes and several read. There the right move on a read miss is to downgrade the previous writer rather than invalidate it, so later readers source the line from the last writer instead of racing to own it. The lesson generalizes: coherence optimizations are workload-shaped — a win for one sharing pattern is a loss for another.

Directory protocols expose transient states because transactions span multiple hops [Z32G]

  • July 11, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

Because a directory transaction takes several hops (requestor → home → owner → …), a line spends observable time in transient states between the stable ones — e.g. \(\mathrm {MI}^{A}\) ("modified, going to invalid, waiting on an acknowledgment"). These are not an implementation detail to wave away: concurrent transactions to the same line race, and the protocol must define a correct outcome for every interleaving. That combinatorial state space is what makes directory protocols hard to get right.

Example. L holds a dirty copy and starts a writeback to home H. Concurrently R sends a read to H. R sits in \(\mathrm {S}^{D}\) ("shared, waiting for data") until the race resolves.
Remark. Never resolve these races with NACKs — they cause starvation. The Implementing Directory-based MESI in Murphi Murphi implementation works through the channel-separation arguments that keep the transient-state space deadlock-free.

Sparse directories keep coherence metadata from scaling with memory [QSWW]

  • July 11, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

A directory must remember which caches hold each line, and the naive encoding — a sharer bitmap per cache line — does not scale: at 256 nodes that is 32 bytes of metadata per line, so roughly half of memory goes to coherence bookkeeping. Two ideas bring it back down. Limited-sharer encoding exploits the fact that most lines have ≤4 sharers: track those exactly and fall back to broadcast for the rare widely-shared line. Sparse directories go further and cache the directory entries themselves — an entry missing from the directory cache means nobody holds the line at all, and evicting an entry invalidates the corresponding lines. The directory then scales with the number of actively cached lines rather than with total memory.

A reconvergence stack sequences a warp's divergent paths and can deadlock [KY0M]

  • July 11, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

When a warp diverges, the hardware needs to remember where the split paths rejoin. The classical mechanism is a reconvergence stack: each entry holds a next-PC, a reconvergence PC (the post-conditional join point), and an active mask. On a divergent branch the hardware pushes both sides and executes them one at a time, popping back to the reconvergence point as each side completes; entries are pushed largest-mask-first to bound stack depth.

The stack has a fatal flaw. A thread that exits a loop diverges and is stacked below threads still spinning inside it — so if those spinning threads wait on a lock the exited thread already holds, neither can proceed and the program deadlocks. This is why modern NVIDIA hardware abandons the stack for a barrier-based scheme: each divergence point is tracked by a 32-bit participation mask, letting the scheduler switch between branches arbitrarily and guarantee independent thread progress.

An operand collector serializes register reads to dodge register-file bank conflicts [7QAW]

  • July 11, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

A warp's 32 threads each read 2–4 registers per instruction, but the register file is banked and cannot serve two reads to the same bank in one cycle. An operand collector absorbs this: it gathers a warp's register reads across multiple cycles and routes the collected values to the lanes once all are available, turning what would be a stall into a few cycles of latency the scheduler hides anyway.

These register-file bank conflicts are invisible to the programmer — unlike shared-memory bank conflicts, which the programmer controls directly — but they shrink as register pressure drops. Fewer registers per thread means fewer simultaneous reads competing for banks, one more reason low register pressure raises throughput.

A two-loop scheduler makes warp readiness a constant-time scoreboard check [7SGF]

  • July 11, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

Deciding which warp to issue each cycle by scanning every warp's operands against the scoreboard would be prohibitive — 64 warps against 4 operands each is 256 comparisons. A two-loop scheduler makes the readiness check constant-time instead. The first loop selects a warp with room in its instruction buffer, looks up its PC, and fetches; a small per-warp bit-vector of outstanding register dependencies rides alongside the fetched instruction and clears as writes retire. The second loop issues any buffered instruction whose dependency vector is clean.

Because readiness is a single per-warp bit-vector test rather than a global scan, the scheduler stays cheap even with dozens of resident warps — the design tradeoff that lets a GPU keep far more work in flight than a CPU's CAM-based wakeup-select ever could. It is the scheduling-side counterpart to why the scoreboard replaces a CPU's dependency-tracking hardware.

Occupancy bounds how much latency a GPU can hide [EPUD]

  • July 11, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

Occupancy is the ratio of a GPU SM's active warps to the maximum it can hold. It is the ceiling on latency hiding: every resident warp is a candidate to switch to when another stalls, so higher occupancy gives the scheduler more runnable work, while low occupancy stalls the SM whenever its few resident warps all wait on the same transaction. For latency-bound workloads — most GPU code — raising occupancy is the first-order optimization. What caps it is per-warp resource use: registers and shared memory are finite per SM, so heavier kernels fit fewer warps, which is why cutting register pressure can raise throughput even when it does no less work.

Warp scheduling hides memory latency by switching among resident warps [1PWL]

  • July 11, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

A GPU keeps many warps resident on each Streaming Multiprocessor (SM) and switches between them on every stall. When a warp issues a memory op that misses cache it is dead for hundreds of cycles — but with dozens of resident warps the scheduler always has a runnable one, so aggregate throughput stays high even though single-warp latency is awful. This is the Thread-level parallelism design point cashed out on the GPU: spend silicon on resident warp state rather than on latency-reduction machinery. The switch is free because each SM's register file is large enough to hold every resident warp's registers at once, so a context switch is just changing which warp the scheduler picks — not saving state to memory the way a CPU context switch must.

Two things bound how well this works. Occupancy — how many warps are resident — sets the ceiling on latency hiding: with too few warps the scheduler runs out of runnable candidates. And the scheduler itself must stay cheap enough to choose a warp every cycle, which it does with a two-loop scoreboard check, marshalling each issued instruction's register reads through an operand collector.

Opening a file in UNIX [JQ3C]

  • July 9, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

For more details, see [bartlettProgrammingGround].

Open a file with the open syscall. Must be called with the following:

  • eax contains system call number.
  • ebx contains pointer to string with name of file to open.
  • ecx contains the options for opening the file.
  • edx contains permissions used to open the file.

Pointers to all command line arguments are stored on the stack.

  • Number of arguments is stored at \(8\)(esp),
  • Name of program at \(12\)(esp),
  • Arguments at \(16\)(esp) on.

These are the argv array in C.

fd (int) → fd table → struct file → struct inode
   per-process         "open file        the actual file
                       description"      (one per file)

What happens during a function call [OGBJ]

  • July 8, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

For this note, we will assume we are using the C calling convention. More details in [bartlettProgrammingGround].

The first thing we do is push the arguments onto the stack (in reverse order). Then execute a call instruction. The call instruction does two things:

  1. It pushes the return address onto the stack. This is the address of the next instruction after the function call.
  2. It then modifies eip to point to the function to be called.

Now we have jumped to the function to be called. However, there is still some bookkeeping that must be done within a function. Namely, we must keep track of where the stack started on a function call. To do so, we copy esp (stack pointer) into ebp (base register). This allows us to access each parameter stored to the stack by the caller via \(N*4 + 4\) ebp.

Finally, we simply allocate space on the stack by subtracting the size of the arguments from esp. This is the new stack pointer.

Now we have to return from the function. To do so, we first store the return value in the special register eax. Then, we must return to where we left off prior to calling the function. Recall that we saved the next instruction address at the top of the stack when we first called the function. There are now other local variables, etc. in the stack so we have to unwind it back. We can do this simply by 

movl %ebp, %esp
popl %ebp
ret
Here, the ret instruction just pops whatever is on the top of the stack and sets rip to it.

We are now back in the calling code with the return value stored in eax. However, remember that the caller pushed the function parameters onto the stack. Therefore, we must also pop all of these parameters off before continuing execution.

Components of a function [VSAV]

  • July 8, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

Summarized from [bartlettProgrammingGround].

Local variables. Local variables are data storage that a function uses while processing that is thrown away when it returns. It’s kind of like a scratch pad of paper. Functions get a new piece of paper every time they are activated, and they have to throw it away when they are finished processing. Local variables of a function are not accessible to any other function within a program.

Static variables. Static variables are data storage that a function uses while processing that is not thrown away afterwards, but is reused for every time the function’s code is activated. This data is not accessible to any other part of the program. Static variables are generally not used unless absolutely necessary, as they can cause problems later on.

Global variables. Global variables are data storage that a function uses for processing which are managed outside the function. For example, a simple text editor may put the entire contents of the file it is working on in a global variable so it doesn’t have to be passed to every function that operates on it.2 Configuration values are also often stored in global variables. return address The return address is an "invisible" parameter in that it isn’t directly used during the function. The return address is a parameter which tells the function

Return address. The return address is an "invisible" parameter in that it isn’t directly used during the function. The return address is a parameter which tells the function. where to resume executing after the function is completed. This is needed because functions can be called to do processing from many different parts of your program, and the function needs to be able to get back to wherever it was called from. In most programming languages, this parameter is passed automatically when the function is called. In assembly language, the call instruction handles passing the return address for you, and ret handles using that address to return back to where you called the function from.

Return value. The return value is the main method of transferring data back to the main program. Most programming languages only allow a single return value for a function.

Warp divergence serializes both sides of a branch [OGCSM]

  • July 6, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

When threads in a warp take different branches of a conditional, the warp does not split into smaller warps. Instead, the active mask selects which lanes execute each branch; lanes on the inactive side run dummy instructions until the warp reconverges at the post-conditional join point. The programmer writes ordinary scalar code with if/else, and the hardware silently masks the inactive lanes.

This is the chief ergonomic win over SIMD: the compiler does not have to prove that all lanes will take the same path. The cost is that divergent code pays for both sides — a 32-wide warp where 16 threads take the if-branch and 16 take the else-branch executes both branches sequentially with half the lanes idle each time.

The hardware sequences the two paths with a reconvergence stack — or, on recent GPUs, a barrier-based equivalent that avoids its deadlocks. The standard software mitigation is Warp Specialization: group threads with the same control-flow trajectory into one warp so the branch never diverges in the first place.

My Current Workflow (constantly changing) [OGCSJ]

  • June 25, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

I have been using todoist and habitify. I decided on these tools primarily because of their API availability. I wanted to be able to add / complete / see outstanding tasks or habits for the day without the allure of everything else my browser has to offer. Also visualization for my Weeknotes.

  • I had Claude write a little script to have my next tasks listed when clicked in my status bar, so I do not have to open the browser to check what I need to do today.

It seems how to properly use these (todoist in particular) is the subject of much debate. Here, I will outline what I converged to / works for ME right now. I have broken down my system into a hierarchy:

  1. Higher level: how to actually choose what to do.
  2. Lower level: how to actually do the chosen task.

Figuring out what to do

  • June 25, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

This is effectively a task management system.

Work streams. I took this name from my investment banker friends (sounds cool / important). Basically, these are groupings I have made and allocated time for each day. They roughly consist of the following:

  • Research / work (first thing in the morning):
    • Active work towards new artifact or paper i.e. coding up ideas.
    • In the absence of ideas, studying existing relevant papers.
  • Deliberate practice:
    • Name taken from Cal Newport.
    • Basically, something I need to understand or master for research that is not novel i.e. writing or optimizing a known kernel.
  • Extraneous Study:
    • Things not directly related to research, but I am curious about.
    • I try to maintain study of related computer science fields. Primarily, studying a textbook in something like OS, computer architecture, etc.
  • Habits / daily upkeep:
    • Mainly consists of reviewing Anki cards daily that come from extraneous study / deliberate practice.
    • Necessary to stay on top of, but it normally takes \(< 30\)min if active.

To decide on the next task, I use a priority-based systemThis idea is mainly based on the MLFQ, which has been proven effective for balancing response / turnaround time:

  1. Things I will be working on today / until they are done. At most ONE thing per work stream.
  2. The backlog of things to do next
    • An index to find things to move to priority 1 for the next day
    • Keep relatively small to avoid the crippling nature of choice - roughly on the order of things I want done this week.
  3. A larger backlog of things - should be completed in the next month or so.
  4. Things I am not working on right now, or have any need to be completed any time soon.

To maintain this system, I have reviews each day and week (tracking with habitify) to make sure I stay consistent.

Algorithm. Weekly review.
Algorithm. Daily review.
  • For each work stream,
    • If I finished the allocated task for the day, get new task from priority 2.
    • Else, do nothing and continue with the current task.
  • Review inbox and move new tasks to corresponding work stream for review on Friday.
    • If immediately important, can move directly to priority 1 / 2.
  • Look at calendar for next day and timeblock work streams for the next day.
    • Since PhD work is so hard to predict, I have found timeblocking any further than one day in advance to be a futile effort.
  • Typically done on Fridays, so that I can dynamically allocate time on weekends if needed.
  • For each work stream,
    1. Look in remaining priority 2 and priority 3 tasks.
    2. Define what I think a successful week would look like (e.g. if I get all these things done next week I will be happy).
      • Look at calendar for week to guide this decision.
    3. Get rid of at least two of those tasks (initial plan always too ambitious).
    4. Move / keep remaining tasks in priority 2.
  • Write Weeknotes for the week.

What to do when actually working on a task

  • June 25, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

This is the harder part (and requires the most discipline). When working on a task, especially a more open-ended one like research, it is very common that a million other things come up that seem immediately important. All of the sudden, you have a great idea for the research project you haven't worked on in months.

It is crucial to collect and forget about these things until they are scheduled. This is the one thing I did take from Getting Things Done. The system should flow like water. Making this achievable is where the todoist API becomes crucial.

  • I have a script bound by dwm that pops up vim for me to write down the task and, on save, it sends it to my inbox in todoist.
  • I have more involved ones that allow me to actually allocate it to the specific work stream / priority if it is immediately obvious.

Another thing that I have found useful to actually achieving this watery flow is the pomodoro technique. This basically lets me gaslight myself into thinking I can go to the other things as soon as the timer ends (which is intentionally always just close enough). By the end, I often no longer have this urge and can continue on the scheduled tasks.

My Notes on Productivity [7BUX]

  • June 24, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios
  • 6 min read

Due to the unstructured nature of PhD life / knowledge work in general, I have been trying to come up with the most effective system to ensure I am Getting Things Doneironically I found this system actually not that helpful.

git bisect [T1JM]

  • June 17, 2026

Useful tool for finding a breaking commit. Writeup taken from here.

Use two terminals. One is used for the bisection process and the other is used to run the program to tell whether the current commit is good or bad.

  1. Start with git bisect start to initialize the bisection process.
  2. Find a good commit and mark it with git bisect good <commit>.
  3. Run git bisect bad <commit> to mark the bad commit.
  4. Repeat until you find the breaking commit.
  5. Use git bisect reset to restore to the state you started from.
Remark. Can use git bisect skip to skip a specific commit, or git bisect visualize --oneline to see current progress.

Definition. Virtual Function Table (C++) [OGCSH]

  • June 9, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

Each class with a virtual function gets a virtual table: a static, per-class, array of function pointers with one entry per virtual function.

The virtual table is created by the compiler and is stored in the object's memory.

vtable layout:
  [ offset-to-top  ]   // slot -2
  [ type_info*     ]   // slot -1  ← RTTI
  [ &virtual_fn_0  ]   // slot  0
  [ &virtual_fn_1  ]   // slot  1
  ...
Remark. The type_info pointer is needed to support runtime type-checking / dynamic casting .

During construction, the vptr is initialized to point to the base class's vtable. In each classes vtable, there is a thunk (offset-to-top) that tells

Example. 
struct A {
    virtual void f();
    int a;
};

struct B {
    virtual void g();
    int b;
};

struct D : A, B {
    void g() override;   // overrides B::g
    int d;
};
offset 0:   [ vptr_A ]   ← D's primary vtable (A subobject)
offset 8:   [ a      ]
offset 16:  [ vptr_B ]   ← D's secondary vtable (B subobject)
offset 24:  [ b      ]
offset 32:  [ d      ]

Remark. The type_info pointer is needed to support runtime type-checking / dynamic casting .

During construction, the vptr is initialized to point to the base class's vtable. In each classes vtable, there is a thunk (offset-to-top) that tells

Example. 
struct A {
    virtual void f();
    int a;
};

struct B {
    virtual void g();

};

struct D : A, B {

offset 0:   [ vptr_A ]   ← D's primary vtable (A subobject)
offset 8:   [ a      ]
offset 16:  [ vptr_B ]   ← D's secondary vtable (B subobject)
offset 24:  [ b      ]
offset 32:  [ d      ]

Every object of a class with a virtual function carries a hidden vptr (virtual pointer) that points to the class's virtual table.

Example. Consider the following class hierarchy: 
struct Base {
    virtual void f();
    virtual void g();
    int x;
};

struct Derived : Base {
    void f() override;   // overrides Base::f
    void h();            // non-virtual, not in vtable
    int y;
};
This yields the following components for each type of object: 
Base object:        Derived object:
[ vptr ]            [ vptr ]      → points to Derived's vtable
[ x    ]            [ x    ]
                    [ y    ]

Definition. Sufficient Statistics [T7T7]

  • June 4, 2026

A statistic \(T(X)\) is sufficient for \(\theta \) if the conditional distribution of the data \(X\) given \(T(X) = t\) does not depend on \(\theta \). Intuitively: if someone hands you \(T(X)\), they could regenerate a fresh dataset with the same distribution without knowing \(\theta \) — so \(T\) lost nothing about \(\theta \).

Example. Bernoulli. \(p(\mathbf {x}; \theta ) = \theta ^{\sum _{i} x_i}(1 - \theta )^{n - \sum _{i} x_i}\). The distribution only depends on \(\mathbf {x}\) through \(\sum _{i} x_i\), so this is a sufficient statistic.

Theorem. Behavior cloning error bound (with distribution shift) [OGCSA]

  • June 3, 2026

If \(\pi (a | s)\) is trained via ERM on \(s \sim d^{\pi _{\beta }}(s)\) and optimal labels \(a^*\), and attains generalizationerror \(\epsilon \) on \(s \sim d^{\pi _{\beta }}(s)\), then \(\ell (\pi ) \leq C + H^2 \epsilon \) is the best possible bound.

Definition. Global History Register [T8B9]

  • June 3, 2026

The global history register (GHR) is a hardware structure in a CPU that records the recent outcomes of conditional branches, typically as a shift register of single bits where 1 means "taken" and 0 means "not taken." Each time a branch resolves, its outcome is shifted into the register, evicting the oldest bit. So if the GHR is 8 bits wide and the last eight branches went taken, not-taken, taken, taken, not-taken, not-taken, taken, taken, the register holds 10110011.

The GHR is then passed as input in Branch prediction. The reason this is useful is that branches in real programs are highly correlated. Whether a given branch is taken often depends on what other branches did just before it.

Example. A classic example: 
if (x < 7)  ...      // branch A
if (x > 9)  ...      // branch B
If A is taken (meaning x < 7 was true), then B is guaranteed not taken. A predictor that only looks at branch B's own past behavior misses this. A predictor that looks at recent global history sees the pattern and learns the correlation.

Exceptions (error handling) [D770]

  • June 3, 2026

In C++, exceptions are thrown via the throw keyword.

The throw keyword transfers control to exception handler. This then proceeds as

  1. Allocate heap memory for the exception object.
  2. Invoke the unwinder.
    1. Walk the stack frame-by-frame to checking to see if any frame has a catch with matching type.
    2. Walks the stack again, restoring registers / SP per frame.
      • Cleaning up all the invalid stack frames between the throw and catch.
    3. Transfers control to the catch block.

If no matching catch block is found, the program calls std::terminate

You can annotate a function with noexcept to indicate that it never throws exceptions. This is mainly used as an annotation to enable better choices by the compiler

Example. The compiler may call copy constructor instead of move constructor if the move constructer is not marked noexcept; If an exception were thrown during moving, then the object would be in a broken state.

Distributed Shared Memory (GPU) [OGCS8]

  • June 1, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

Because the CTAs in a cluster live on neighboring SMs connected by a dedicated SM-to-SM network, the shared memory of all CTAs in the cluster is exposed as a single logical address space. A thread in one CTA can read/write/atomic into another CTA's shared memory directly, without round-tripping through global memory (L2/DRAM).

cooperative_group.cu
#include <cooperative_groups.h>
namespace cg = cooperative_groups;

__global__ void __cluster_dims__(2,1,1) kernel(...) {
    cg::cluster_group cluster = cg::this_cluster();
    extern __shared__ int smem[];

    // Get a pointer to another CTA's shared memory
    unsigned int rank = cluster.block_rank();      // my CTA's id in cluster
    int *remote = cluster.map_shared_rank(smem, /*target rank=*/ rank ^ 1);

    // Now read/write the neighbor's shared memory
    remote[threadIdx.x] = threadIdx.x;

    cluster.sync();   // cluster-wide barrier
}

  • June 1, 2026

A Graphics Processing Cluster (GPC) is a top-level hardware partition inside an NVIDIA GPU. It's one level up from the SM in the chip's hierarchy.

As of Hopper, SMs located in the same GPC are connected via an SM-to-SM network, enabling DSMEM.

CUDA Hierarchy [OGCS4]

  • June 1, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

Grid: Top-level define how many blocks are needed to cover the computation across SMs.

Block: Ensures all warps in a block are resident on the same SM and have the same shared memory.

Warp: A group of 32 threads that execute the same instruction.

Thread: A single thread within a warp.

Definition. Cooperative Thread Array (CTA) [W2D5]

  • June 1, 2026

NVIDIA's hardware-level term for what CUDA programmers call a thread block.

A CTA is a group of threads that execute on the same Streaming Multiprocessor (SM), can synchronize via barriers (__syncthreads()), and share fast on-chip shared memory (Shared memory (GPU)). Threads within a CTA are scheduled and executed in groups of 32 called warps.

Union (C++) [W375]

  • June 1, 2026

A union is a struct in which all members are allocated at the same address. This ensures that the union occupies only as much space as its largest member.

A union can hold a value for only one member at a time.

Problem. You can only read the active member of a union. 
union U { int i; float f; };
U u;
u.i = 42;
float x = u.f;  // UB — reading the inactive member
Problem. No automatic lifetime management for non-trivial types. If a union holds an object with a non-trivial constructor/destructor (like std::string), the compiler won't call them for you. You must manually placement-new and explicitly call the destructor, and getting this wrong causes leaks or corruption. 
union U { std::string s; int i; };  // destructor not called automatically
Remark. Avoid "naked" unions; opt for "tagged" unions. 
struct Value {
    enum class Type { Int, Float, Str } tag;
    union {
        int   i;
        float f;
        char  s[32];
    };
};
This along with lifetime management is the basis of std::variant.

User-defined types

  • June 1, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

C++ gives several ways to bundle data into a named type. A class is the workhorse — it separates interface from implementation through access control, and carries the constructor/destructor machinery that ties resource lifetime to scope. A struct is the same mechanism with public defaults, a union overlays members in shared storage, and an enumeration names a fixed set of values.

Union (C++) [W375]

  • June 1, 2026

A union is a struct in which all members are allocated at the same address. This ensures that the union occupies only as much space as its largest member.

Problem. You can only read the active member of a union. 
union U { int i; float f; };
U u;
u.i = 42;
float x = u.f;  // UB — reading the inactive member

You must manually placement-new and explicitly call the destructor, and getting this wrong causes leaks or corruption.

struct Value {
