Concrete and abstract types

  • June 1, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

The pivotal design axis is whether a type's representation is part of its definition. A concrete class commits to its layout, so it can live on the stack and be copied by value; an abstract type hides representation entirely behind pure virtual functions, which forces heap allocation and pointer-based use. The container is the running example that both build on.

Definition. Concrete Class (C++) [OGCSC]

  • June 5, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

A class that behaves "just like built-in types". The defining characteristic of a concrete type is that its representation is part of its definition.

Because the representation is fixed you can

  1. Allocate objects directly on the stack.
  2. Copy and assign them by value
  3. Have them as direct members of other classes.
Example. complex, vector, and string are concrete classes.

Definition. Container (C++) [OGCSE]

  • June 5, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

A container is a concrete class that exists to hold elements..

Example. We call vector a container.

Initialization

  • June 5, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios
 We can initialize a container via std::initializer_list, where you directly pass the list of elements via {1,2,3,4,...}. Alternatively, containers may support additional methods like push_back().

Definition. Abstract type (C++) [OGCSF]

  • June 5, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

An abstract type is a type that completely insulates a user from implementation details.

Since we do not know anything about the representation (in particular, the size) we must allocate everything on heap.

Example. Below is an abstract implementation of a container class. 
  class Container {
  public:
    virtual double& operator[](int) = 0; // pure virtual function
    virtual int size() const = 0; // const member function
    virtual ˜Container() {} // destructor
  };

Runtime polymorphism

  • June 1, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

Abstract types are only useful because of dynamic dispatch. A virtual function call is resolved through a hidden per-object pointer into a per-class virtual function table, which also carries the type information that makes dynamic casting possible.

Definition. Virtual Function (C++) [OGCSG]

  • June 9, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

Definition. Virtual Function Table (C++) [OGCSH]

  • June 9, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

Each class with a virtual function gets a virtual table: a static, per-class, array of function pointers with one entry per virtual function.

The virtual table is created by the compiler and is stored in the object's memory.

vtable layout:
  [ offset-to-top  ]   // slot -2
  [ type_info*     ]   // slot -1  ← RTTI
  [ &virtual_fn_0  ]   // slot  0
  [ &virtual_fn_1  ]   // slot  1
  ...
Remark. The type_info pointer is needed to support runtime type-checking / dynamic casting .

During construction, the vptr is initialized to point to the base class's vtable. In each classes vtable, there is a thunk (offset-to-top) that tells

Example. 
struct A {
    virtual void f();
    int a;
};

struct B {
    virtual void g();
    int b;
};

struct D : A, B {
    void g() override;   // overrides B::g
    int d;
};
offset 0:   [ vptr_A ]   ← D's primary vtable (A subobject)
offset 8:   [ a      ]
offset 16:  [ vptr_B ]   ← D's secondary vtable (B subobject)
offset 24:  [ b      ]
offset 32:  [ d      ]

Every object of a class with a virtual function carries a hidden vptr (virtual pointer) that points to the class's virtual table.

Example. Consider the following class hierarchy: 
struct Base {
    virtual void f();
    virtual void g();
    int x;
};

struct Derived : Base {
    void f() override;   // overrides Base::f
    void h();            // non-virtual, not in vtable
    int y;
};
This yields the following components for each type of object: 
Base object:        Derived object:
[ vptr ]            [ vptr ]      → points to Derived's vtable
[ x    ]            [ x    ]
                    [ y    ]

Idea. Shift work from every run on every user's machine to once on the build machine.

Remark. A constexpr function is not forced to run at compile time. It is only done only when the arguments are const.

  1. When you want to make the type visible clearly to the readers of your code.
  2. You want to be explicit on the variable range or precision i.e. auto x = 1; will be an int. If you want to enforce a double, then you must specify so explicitly.

Error handling

  • June 1, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

Exceptions (error handling) [D770]

  • June 3, 2026

In C++, exceptions are thrown via the throw keyword.

The throw keyword transfers control to exception handler. This then proceeds as

  1. Allocate heap memory for the exception object.
  2. Invoke the unwinder.
    1. Walk the stack frame-by-frame to checking to see if any frame has a catch with matching type.
    2. Walks the stack again, restoring registers / SP per frame.
      • Cleaning up all the invalid stack frames between the throw and catch.
    3. Transfers control to the catch block.

If no matching catch block is found, the program calls std::terminate

You can annotate a function with noexcept to indicate that it never throws exceptions. This is mainly used as an annotation to enable better choices by the compiler

Example. The compiler may call copy constructor instead of move constructor if the move constructer is not marked noexcept; If an exception were thrown during moving, then the object would be in a broken state.

Flash Attention (Fwd) [OGCS0]

  • May 27, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

Unlike in the online softmax, we are not interested in the outputted probability vector \(\mathbf {p}\). Instead we are interested in the entire output matrix \(O\) given by

\[O = \mathrm {softmax}(QK^T) V\]

For more details see self-attention.

Notation. In correspondence with the notation in the online softmax, we define the following: \[x_{i,j} = \mathbf {q}_i \cdot \mathbf {k}_j,\] where \(\mathbf {q}_i\) is the \(i\)th row of \(Q\) and \(\mathbf {k}_j\) is the \(j\)th row of \(K\). Similarly, \(\mathbf {o}_i\) is the \(i\)th row of the output matrix \(O\) given by \[\mathbf {o}_i = \sum _{j = 1}^{n} \frac {\exp (x_{i,j} - m_n)}{d_n} \cdot \mathbf {v}_j \]

Now following the template provided by the online softmax, we must find a recurrence for \(\mathbf {o}_i\). Namely, we will consider the sequence \(\mathbf {o}_{i,k}'\) given by \[\mathbf {o}_{i,k}' = \sum _{j = 1}^{k} \frac {\exp (x_{i,j} - m_k)}{d_k} \cdot \mathbf {v}_j, \] such that \(\mathbf {o}_{i,n}' = \mathbf {o}_n\)

Claim. We have the following recurrence for \(\mathbf {o}_{i,k}'\): \[ \mathbf {o}_{i,k}' = \mathbf {o}_{i, k-1} \cdot \frac {d_{k - 1} \cdot \exp (m_{k-1} - m_{k})}{d_k} + \frac {\exp (x_{i,j} - m_k)}{d_k} \cdot \mathbf {v}_k \]
Proof. We will proceed by directly rewriting the recurrence for \(\mathbf {o}_{i,k}'\) as \[ \begin {align*} \mathbf {o}_{i,k}' &= \sum _{j = 1}^{k} \frac {\exp (x_{i,j} - m_k)}{d_k} \cdot \mathbf {v}_j \\ &= \left (\sum _{j = 1}^{k - 1} \frac {\exp (x_{i,j} - m_{k-1})}{d_{k-1}} \cdot \mathbf {v}_j\right ) \frac {d_{k - 1} \cdot \exp (m_{k-1} - m_{k})}{d_k} + \frac {\exp (x_{i,k} - m_k)}{d_k} \cdot \mathbf {v}_k \\ &= \mathbf {o}_{i, k-1} \cdot \frac {d_{k - 1} \cdot \exp (m_{k-1} - m_{k})}{d_k} + \frac {\exp (x_{i,k} - m_k)}{d_k} \cdot \mathbf {v}_k .\end {align*} \]

Thus, we are left with the following algorithm

flash_attention.py
for i in range(N):                      # one query row at a time
    m = float("-inf")                    # running max of the logits
    d = 0.0                              # running softmax denominator
    o = zeros(head_dim)                  # running output accumulator
    for j in range(M):                   # stream over keys/values
        x = q[i] @ k[j]                  # logit x_{i,j}
        m_new = max(m, x)
        d_new = d * exp(m - m_new) + exp(x - m_new)
        o = o * (d * exp(m - m_new) / d_new) + (exp(x - m_new) / d_new) * v[j]
        m, d = m_new, d_new
    out[i] = o
Remark. A key benefit of this algorithm is that it is entirely parallelizable across rows. This means that we can loop across entire tiles like in the GEMM case.

Flash Attention (Bwd) [OGCRZ]

  • May 27, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

The forward pass of flash attention avoids materializing the \(N \times N\) attention matrix by streaming an online softmax. The backward pass has to pull the same trick twice over, because the naive gradient computation wants two \(N \times N\) matrices — \(\mathbf {P}\) and \(d\mathbf {P}\). Getting there means first writing down every gradient we need, then finding a way to recompute rather than store each one.

Notation. Following the notation in the original paper, \[\mathbf {S} = \mathbf {Q} \mathbf {K}^T, \quad \mathbf {P} = \mathrm {softmax}(\mathbf {S}), \quad \mathbf {O} = \mathbf {P} \mathbf {V},\] where \(\mathbf {Q}, \mathbf {K}, \mathbf {V}, \mathbf {O}\) are \(N \times d\) and \(\mathbf {S}, \mathbf {P}\) are \(N \times N\). For a scalar loss \(\phi \) we abbreviate the gradient with respect to any matrix \(\mathbf {X}\) as \[d\mathbf {X} = \frac {\partial \phi }{\partial \mathbf {X}},\] and write \(\mathbf {L}_i\) for the softmax denominator of row \(i\) saved by the forward pass, so that \(\mathbf {P}_{ij} = \exp (\mathbf {Q}_i \cdot \mathbf {K}_j) / \mathbf {L}_i\).

The gradients we need for FlashAttention [4QZE]

  • August 3, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

Everything downstream is chain rule; the only step with any content is differentiating through the softmax. We take the gradients in dependency order, starting from \(d\mathbf {O}\) which arrives from the layer above.

\(d\mathbf {P}\) and \(d\mathbf {V}\) from \(\mathbf {O} = \mathbf {P}\mathbf {V}\)

  • August 3, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

Both fall straight out of the product rule for matrices:

\[ d\mathbf {P} = \frac {\partial \phi }{\partial \mathbf {O}} \frac {\partial \mathbf {O}}{\partial \mathbf {P}} = d\mathbf {O} \mathbf {V}^T, \qquad d\mathbf {V} = \frac {\partial \phi }{\partial \mathbf {O}} \frac {\partial \mathbf {O}}{\partial \mathbf {V}} = \mathbf {P}^T d\mathbf {O}. \]

The shapes are a useful sanity check. \(d\mathbf {O}\) has one entry per output, so it is \(N \times d\); \(\mathbf {V}^T\) is \(d \times N\); their product is \(N \times N\), matching \(\mathbf {P}\). Likewise \(\mathbf {P}^T d\mathbf {O}\) is \(N \times d\), matching \(\mathbf {V}\).

Componentwise, from \(\mathbf {O}_{ik} = \sum _j \mathbf {P}_{ij} \mathbf {V}_{jk}\),

\[ \begin {align*} d\mathbf {P}_{ij} &= \sum _{k} \frac {\partial \phi }{\partial \mathbf {O}_{ik}} \cdot \frac {\partial \mathbf {O}_{ik}}{\partial \mathbf {P}_{ij}} = \sum _{k} d\mathbf {O}_{ik} \mathbf {V}_{jk}, \\ d\mathbf {V}_{jk} &= \sum _{i} \frac {\partial \phi }{\partial \mathbf {O}_{ik}} \cdot \frac {\partial \mathbf {O}_{ik}}{\partial \mathbf {V}_{jk}} = \sum _{i} d\mathbf {O}_{ik} \mathbf {P}_{ij} = \sum _{i} \frac {\exp \left (\mathbf {Q}_{i} \cdot \mathbf {K}_{j}\right )}{\mathbf {L}_{i}} d\mathbf {O}_{ik} .\end {align*} \]

That last line is worth noting already: \(d\mathbf {V}\) never needs \(\mathbf {P}\) stored, only the ability to re-evaluate \(\mathbf {P}_{ij}\) from \(\mathbf {Q}\), \(\mathbf {K}\), and \(\mathbf {L}\).

\(d\mathbf {S}\) through the softmax

  • August 3, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

Softmax acts row by row, so drop into the scalar case with \(\mathbf {s}\) and \(\mathbf {p}\) single rows. The softmax Jacobian is \(\partial \mathbf {p}_i / \partial \mathbf {s}_j = \mathbf {p}_i(\delta _{ij} - \mathbf {p}_j)\), giving

\[ \begin {align*} d\mathbf {s}_j &= \sum _{i} d\mathbf {p}_i \cdot \frac {\partial \mathbf {p}_i}{\partial \mathbf {s}_j} \\ &= \sum _{i} d\mathbf {p}_i \cdot \mathbf {p}_i (\delta _{ij} - \mathbf {p}_{j}) \\ &= d\mathbf {p}_{j} \mathbf {p}_{j} - \mathbf {p}_{j}\sum _{i} d\mathbf {p}_{i} \mathbf {p}_{i} .\end {align*} \]

As a row vector this is \(d\mathbf {s} = \mathbf {p} \odot (d\mathbf {p} - \mathbf {p} \cdot d\mathbf {p})\), where the subtracted term is the scalar \(\mathbf {p} \cdot d\mathbf {p}\) broadcast across the row. Collecting those scalars into a column \(\mathbf {D}\) with \(\mathbf {D}_i = \mathbf {P}_i \cdot d\mathbf {P}_i\) recovers the matrix form

\[d\mathbf {S} = \mathbf {P} \odot (d\mathbf {P} - \mathbf {D}).\]

\(\mathbf {D}\) is the piece that will cause trouble later: it is a dot product over an entire row of \(\mathbf {P}\), which is exactly the thing we refuse to materialize.

\(d\mathbf {Q}\) and \(d\mathbf {K}\) from \(\mathbf {S} = \mathbf {Q}\mathbf {K}^T\)

  • August 3, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

One more chain rule, and the sums run over opposite indices:

\[ \begin {align*} d\mathbf {Q}_{i} &= \sum _{j} d\mathbf {S}_{ij} \mathbf {K}_{j} = \sum _{j} \mathbf {P}_{ij} \left (d\mathbf {P}_{ij} - \mathbf {D}_i\right ) \mathbf {K}_{j}, \\ d\mathbf {K}_{j} &= \sum _{i} d\mathbf {S}_{ij} \mathbf {Q}_{i} = \sum _{i} \mathbf {P}_{ij} \left (d\mathbf {P}_{ij} - \mathbf {D}_i\right ) \mathbf {Q}_{i} .\end {align*} \]

Recomputing instead of storing

  • August 3, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

Every gradient above is expressed through \(\mathbf {P}_{ij}\) and \(d\mathbf {P}_{ij}\), both \(N \times N\). Materializing either one is exactly the quadratic memory cost the forward pass went to such lengths to avoid, so the backward pass has to be able to produce those entries on demand.

Insight. Both are recoverable from the \(N \times d\) tensors already resident in memory. The forward pass saved \(\mathbf {L}\), so \[\mathbf {P}_{ij} = \frac {\exp \left (\mathbf {Q}_{i} \cdot \mathbf {K}_{j}\right )}{\mathbf {L}_{i}},\] and \(d\mathbf {P}\) is just an inner product of two rows, \[d\mathbf {P}_{ij} = \sum _{k} d\mathbf {O}_{ik} \mathbf {V}_{jk} = d\mathbf {O}_{i} \cdot \mathbf {V}_j.\] Neither ever requires an \(N \times N\) intermediate.

Substituting both into the previous section leaves \(d\mathbf {Q}\) and \(d\mathbf {K}\) in terms of \(\mathbf {Q}\), \(\mathbf {K}\), \(\mathbf {V}\), \(d\mathbf {O}\), \(\mathbf {L}\), and \(\mathbf {D}\) alone:

\[ \begin {align*} d\mathbf {Q}_{i} &= \sum _{j} \frac {\exp \left (\mathbf {Q}_{i} \cdot \mathbf {K}_{j}\right )}{\mathbf {L}_{i}} \left (d\mathbf {O}_{i} \cdot \mathbf {V}_j - \mathbf {D}_i\right ) \mathbf {K}_{j}, \\ d\mathbf {K}_{j} &= \sum _{i} \frac {\exp \left (\mathbf {Q}_{i} \cdot \mathbf {K}_{j}\right )}{\mathbf {L}_{i}} \left (d\mathbf {O}_{i} \cdot \mathbf {V}_j - \mathbf {D}_i\right ) \mathbf {Q}_{i}. .\end {align*} \]

Getting \(\mathbf {D}\) for free

  • August 3, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

One problem survives. \(\mathbf {D}_i = \mathbf {P}_i \cdot d\mathbf {P}_i\) is a dot product over a full row, so computing it inside the streaming loop would mean a reduction over all \(j\) before any tile of \(d\mathbf {Q}_i\) could be finished. This is the same global dependency the online softmax was designed to break.

The way out is that the row sum has already been computed once, in the forward pass. Expanding and pulling \(d\mathbf {O}_i\) out of the sum:

\[ \begin {align*} \mathbf {D}_i &= \mathbf {P}_{i} \cdot d\mathbf {P}_{i} \\ &= \sum _{j} \frac {\exp \left (\mathbf {Q}_{i} \cdot \mathbf {K}_{j}\right )}{\mathbf {L}_{i}} d\mathbf {P}_{ij} \\ &= \sum _{j} \frac {\exp \left (\mathbf {Q}_{i} \cdot \mathbf {K}_{j}\right )}{\mathbf {L}_{i}} \left (d\mathbf {O}_{i} \cdot \mathbf {V}_{j}\right ) \\ &= d\mathbf {O}_{i} \cdot \sum _{j} \frac {\exp \left (\mathbf {Q}_{i} \cdot \mathbf {K}_{j}\right )}{\mathbf {L}_{i}} \mathbf {V}_{j} \\ &= d\mathbf {O}_{i} \cdot \mathbf {O}_{i} .\end {align*} \]

The inner sum is precisely the definition of \(\mathbf {O}_i\). So \(\mathbf {D}\) is a single elementwise product of \(d\mathbf {O}\) and \(\mathbf {O}\) summed along the head dimension — one \(O(Nd)\) pass over tensors we already have, done once before the backward loop begins.

Summary

  • May 27, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

Forward pass. Store \(\mathbf {O}\) and the softmax denominators \(\mathbf {L}\), both \(O(Nd)\).

Between the passes. Receive \(d\mathbf {O}\) from the layer above (automatic in JAX), then precompute \(\mathbf {D}_i = d\mathbf {O}_i \cdot \mathbf {O}_i\) in \(O(N)\) memory.

Backward pass. Stream over tiles, recomputing \(\mathbf {P}_{ij}\) from \(\mathbf {Q}, \mathbf {K}, \mathbf {L}\) and \(d\mathbf {P}_{ij}\) from \(d\mathbf {O}, \mathbf {V}\) as needed:

  1. \(d\mathbf {V}_j = \sum _i \mathbf {P}_{ij} d\mathbf {O}_i\), accumulated over query tiles.
  2. \(d\mathbf {Q}_i = \sum _j \mathbf {P}_{ij}(d\mathbf {O}_i \cdot \mathbf {V}_j - \mathbf {D}_i)\mathbf {K}_j\), accumulated over key tiles.
  3. \(d\mathbf {K}_j = \sum _i \mathbf {P}_{ij}(d\mathbf {O}_i \cdot \mathbf {V}_j - \mathbf {D}_i)\mathbf {Q}_i\), accumulated over query tiles.

Each accumulator is \(O(d)\) per row or column, so the whole backward pass stays linear in \(N\).

Memory Tiling (GPU) [OGCRV]

  • May 25, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

An example of how to tile a matrix multiplication, our tile partitions the output matrix \(M \times N\) by block sizes BS_N and BS_M as seen in the image below (drawn using excalidraw)

The block size of \(k\) BS_K is then basically the accumulation axis, where we loop over \(k\) if we cannot fit the whole row / column of \(A\) and \(B\) into shared memory.

Bank conflicts serialize shared-memory accesses to the same bank [OGCRU]

  • May 25, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

Shared memory is divided into banks (typically 32). Each bank can service one access per cycle. If two threads in a warp access different addresses in the same bank, the accesses serialize — a bank conflict.

Three behaviors when warp threads access shared memory:

  • Different banks: full parallelism. No conflict.
  • Same bank, same word: hardware broadcasts the word to all threads. No conflict.
  • Same bank, different words: serialize.
Question. How to avoid bank conflicts?
Answer.Change the access pattern so threads hit different banks (often by transposing or by adding padding to break the stride that causes the conflict).

Flash Attention (v1) [R0PM]

  • May 25, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios
  • 17 min read

This will be a brief tour through all the fundamentals needed to understand the first instantiation of FlashAttention as introduced in FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness.

Online Softmax [PI7N]

  • May 20, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

This covers the math behind the online softmax algorithm required by Flash Attention (v1).

Safe softmax

  • May 20, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

The first thing we must consider is numerical precision. Namely, the original softmax operation is given by

\[\mathrm {softmax}(\mathbf {x}) = \frac {\exp (\mathbf {x})}{\sum _{i=1}^n \exp (\mathbf {x}_i)}\]

However, when operating with low precision data types (i.e. float16) the maximum value is \(65536\). Therefore, with \(\exp \) we can easily get numerically overflow.

To get around this, the online softmax algorithm adheres to the safe softmax. For safe softmax, we simply multiply the numerator and denominator by \(\exp (-m)\), where \(m = \max \{x_{1}, \ldots , x_n\}\). This gives

\[\mathrm {softmax}(\mathbf {x}) = \frac {\exp (\mathbf {x} - m)}{\sum _{i=1}^n \exp (\mathbf {x}_i - m)}\]

Since \(x_i - m \leq 0\), this ensures that each \(\exp (x_i - m)\) is bounded in a safe range.

Problem. Note that computing the \(\max \) over \(\mathbf {x}\) means that we must have all of the logits in a row of \(QK^T\) materialized in SMEM, or first loop over all of them to compute the max before computing the normalization constant.

Fusing the max and normalization

  • May 20, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

The online softmax algorithm fuses the max reduction into the normalization pass, so a single sweep over the row suffices to compute the normalization with the max. The key difficulty is that the denominator depends on \(n\) for each \(i\) i.e.

\[d = \sum _{i=1}^{n} \exp (x_i - m_n)\]

Therefore, we must find a recursive relationship such that \(d_{i+1} = f(d_i, m_i, x_{i+1})\) for some function \(f\). This would then allow us to locally compute \(d_{i+1}\) with only the local information of current \(x_{i+1}\) and the two running statistics \(d_i\) and \(m_i\). This is exactly the kind of algorithm that is conducive to memory tiling.

Question. What is \(f(d_i, m_i, x_{i+1})\)?
Answer.Consider \(d_{i+1} = d_i \cdot \exp (m_{i} - m_{i + 1}) + \exp (x_{i + 1} - m_{i + 1})\).
Proof. This can be seen by directly rewriting \(d_{i + 1}\). \[ \begin {align*} d_{i + 1} &= \sum _{j = 1}^{i+1} \exp (x_j - m_{i + 1}) \\ &= \left (\sum _{j = 1}^{i} \exp (x_j - m_{i+1})\right ) + \exp (x_{i+1} - m_{i+1}) \\ &= \left (\sum _{j = 1}^{i} \exp (x_j - m_{i})\right )\exp (m_{i} - m_{i + 1}) + \exp (x_{i+1} - m_{i+1}) \\ &= d_{i} \exp (m_{i} - m_{i + 1}) + \exp (x_{i+1} - m_{i+1}) \end {align*} \]

The running denominator \(d\) is rescaled by \(e^{m - m_{\text {new}}}\) each time a new maximum is found, keeping it consistent with the safe-softmax shift.

online_softmax.py
m = float("-inf")                    # running max of the logits
d = 0.0                              # running softmax denominator
for i in range(n):                   # one fused sweep for the stats
    m_new = max(m, x[i])
    d = d * exp(m - m_new) + exp(x[i] - m_new)
    m = m_new
p = [exp(x[i] - m) / d for i in range(n)]   # second pass: normalized probs
Remark. Unfortunately, we cannot get around the second pass to compute the normalized output for \(\mathbf {p}\). However, this is not the case in Flash Attention (v1).

Flash Attention (Fwd) [OGCS0]

  • May 27, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

Unlike in the online softmax, we are not interested in the outputted probability vector \(\mathbf {p}\). Instead we are interested in the entire output matrix \(O\) given by

\[O = \mathrm {softmax}(QK^T) V\]

For more details see self-attention.

Notation. In correspondence with the notation in the online softmax, we define the following: \[x_{i,j} = \mathbf {q}_i \cdot \mathbf {k}_j,\] where \(\mathbf {q}_i\) is the \(i\)th row of \(Q\) and \(\mathbf {k}_j\) is the \(j\)th row of \(K\). Similarly, \(\mathbf {o}_i\) is the \(i\)th row of the output matrix \(O\) given by \[\mathbf {o}_i = \sum _{j = 1}^{n} \frac {\exp (x_{i,j} - m_n)}{d_n} \cdot \mathbf {v}_j \]

Now following the template provided by the online softmax, we must find a recurrence for \(\mathbf {o}_i\). Namely, we will consider the sequence \(\mathbf {o}_{i,k}'\) given by \[\mathbf {o}_{i,k}' = \sum _{j = 1}^{k} \frac {\exp (x_{i,j} - m_k)}{d_k} \cdot \mathbf {v}_j, \] such that \(\mathbf {o}_{i,n}' = \mathbf {o}_n\)

Claim. We have the following recurrence for \(\mathbf {o}_{i,k}'\): \[ \mathbf {o}_{i,k}' = \mathbf {o}_{i, k-1} \cdot \frac {d_{k - 1} \cdot \exp (m_{k-1} - m_{k})}{d_k} + \frac {\exp (x_{i,j} - m_k)}{d_k} \cdot \mathbf {v}_k \]
Proof. We will proceed by directly rewriting the recurrence for \(\mathbf {o}_{i,k}'\) as \[ \begin {align*} \mathbf {o}_{i,k}' &= \sum _{j = 1}^{k} \frac {\exp (x_{i,j} - m_k)}{d_k} \cdot \mathbf {v}_j \\ &= \left (\sum _{j = 1}^{k - 1} \frac {\exp (x_{i,j} - m_{k-1})}{d_{k-1}} \cdot \mathbf {v}_j\right ) \frac {d_{k - 1} \cdot \exp (m_{k-1} - m_{k})}{d_k} + \frac {\exp (x_{i,k} - m_k)}{d_k} \cdot \mathbf {v}_k \\ &= \mathbf {o}_{i, k-1} \cdot \frac {d_{k - 1} \cdot \exp (m_{k-1} - m_{k})}{d_k} + \frac {\exp (x_{i,k} - m_k)}{d_k} \cdot \mathbf {v}_k .\end {align*} \]

Thus, we are left with the following algorithm

flash_attention.py
for i in range(N):                      # one query row at a time
    m = float("-inf")                    # running max of the logits
    d = 0.0                              # running softmax denominator
    o = zeros(head_dim)                  # running output accumulator
    for j in range(M):                   # stream over keys/values
        x = q[i] @ k[j]                  # logit x_{i,j}
        m_new = max(m, x)
        d_new = d * exp(m - m_new) + exp(x - m_new)
        o = o * (d * exp(m - m_new) / d_new) + (exp(x - m_new) / d_new) * v[j]
        m, d = m_new, d_new
    out[i] = o
Remark. A key benefit of this algorithm is that it is entirely parallelizable across rows. This means that we can loop across entire tiles like in the GEMM case.

Flash Attention (Bwd) [OGCRZ]

  • May 27, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

The forward pass of flash attention avoids materializing the \(N \times N\) attention matrix by streaming an online softmax. The backward pass has to pull the same trick twice over, because the naive gradient computation wants two \(N \times N\) matrices — \(\mathbf {P}\) and \(d\mathbf {P}\). Getting there means first writing down every gradient we need, then finding a way to recompute rather than store each one.

Notation. Following the notation in the original paper, \[\mathbf {S} = \mathbf {Q} \mathbf {K}^T, \quad \mathbf {P} = \mathrm {softmax}(\mathbf {S}), \quad \mathbf {O} = \mathbf {P} \mathbf {V},\] where \(\mathbf {Q}, \mathbf {K}, \mathbf {V}, \mathbf {O}\) are \(N \times d\) and \(\mathbf {S}, \mathbf {P}\) are \(N \times N\). For a scalar loss \(\phi \) we abbreviate the gradient with respect to any matrix \(\mathbf {X}\) as \[d\mathbf {X} = \frac {\partial \phi }{\partial \mathbf {X}},\] and write \(\mathbf {L}_i\) for the softmax denominator of row \(i\) saved by the forward pass, so that \(\mathbf {P}_{ij} = \exp (\mathbf {Q}_i \cdot \mathbf {K}_j) / \mathbf {L}_i\).

The gradients we need for FlashAttention [4QZE]

  • August 3, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

Everything downstream is chain rule; the only step with any content is differentiating through the softmax. We take the gradients in dependency order, starting from \(d\mathbf {O}\) which arrives from the layer above.

\(d\mathbf {P}\) and \(d\mathbf {V}\) from \(\mathbf {O} = \mathbf {P}\mathbf {V}\)

  • August 3, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

Both fall straight out of the product rule for matrices:

\[ d\mathbf {P} = \frac {\partial \phi }{\partial \mathbf {O}} \frac {\partial \mathbf {O}}{\partial \mathbf {P}} = d\mathbf {O} \mathbf {V}^T, \qquad d\mathbf {V} = \frac {\partial \phi }{\partial \mathbf {O}} \frac {\partial \mathbf {O}}{\partial \mathbf {V}} = \mathbf {P}^T d\mathbf {O}. \]

The shapes are a useful sanity check. \(d\mathbf {O}\) has one entry per output, so it is \(N \times d\); \(\mathbf {V}^T\) is \(d \times N\); their product is \(N \times N\), matching \(\mathbf {P}\). Likewise \(\mathbf {P}^T d\mathbf {O}\) is \(N \times d\), matching \(\mathbf {V}\).

Componentwise, from \(\mathbf {O}_{ik} = \sum _j \mathbf {P}_{ij} \mathbf {V}_{jk}\),

\[ \begin {align*} d\mathbf {P}_{ij} &= \sum _{k} \frac {\partial \phi }{\partial \mathbf {O}_{ik}} \cdot \frac {\partial \mathbf {O}_{ik}}{\partial \mathbf {P}_{ij}} = \sum _{k} d\mathbf {O}_{ik} \mathbf {V}_{jk}, \\ d\mathbf {V}_{jk} &= \sum _{i} \frac {\partial \phi }{\partial \mathbf {O}_{ik}} \cdot \frac {\partial \mathbf {O}_{ik}}{\partial \mathbf {V}_{jk}} = \sum _{i} d\mathbf {O}_{ik} \mathbf {P}_{ij} = \sum _{i} \frac {\exp \left (\mathbf {Q}_{i} \cdot \mathbf {K}_{j}\right )}{\mathbf {L}_{i}} d\mathbf {O}_{ik} .\end {align*} \]

That last line is worth noting already: \(d\mathbf {V}\) never needs \(\mathbf {P}\) stored, only the ability to re-evaluate \(\mathbf {P}_{ij}\) from \(\mathbf {Q}\), \(\mathbf {K}\), and \(\mathbf {L}\).

\(d\mathbf {S}\) through the softmax

  • August 3, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

Softmax acts row by row, so drop into the scalar case with \(\mathbf {s}\) and \(\mathbf {p}\) single rows. The softmax Jacobian is \(\partial \mathbf {p}_i / \partial \mathbf {s}_j = \mathbf {p}_i(\delta _{ij} - \mathbf {p}_j)\), giving

\[ \begin {align*} d\mathbf {s}_j &= \sum _{i} d\mathbf {p}_i \cdot \frac {\partial \mathbf {p}_i}{\partial \mathbf {s}_j} \\ &= \sum _{i} d\mathbf {p}_i \cdot \mathbf {p}_i (\delta _{ij} - \mathbf {p}_{j}) \\ &= d\mathbf {p}_{j} \mathbf {p}_{j} - \mathbf {p}_{j}\sum _{i} d\mathbf {p}_{i} \mathbf {p}_{i} .\end {align*} \]

As a row vector this is \(d\mathbf {s} = \mathbf {p} \odot (d\mathbf {p} - \mathbf {p} \cdot d\mathbf {p})\), where the subtracted term is the scalar \(\mathbf {p} \cdot d\mathbf {p}\) broadcast across the row. Collecting those scalars into a column \(\mathbf {D}\) with \(\mathbf {D}_i = \mathbf {P}_i \cdot d\mathbf {P}_i\) recovers the matrix form

\[d\mathbf {S} = \mathbf {P} \odot (d\mathbf {P} - \mathbf {D}).\]

\(\mathbf {D}\) is the piece that will cause trouble later: it is a dot product over an entire row of \(\mathbf {P}\), which is exactly the thing we refuse to materialize.

\(d\mathbf {Q}\) and \(d\mathbf {K}\) from \(\mathbf {S} = \mathbf {Q}\mathbf {K}^T\)

  • August 3, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

One more chain rule, and the sums run over opposite indices:

\[ \begin {align*} d\mathbf {Q}_{i} &= \sum _{j} d\mathbf {S}_{ij} \mathbf {K}_{j} = \sum _{j} \mathbf {P}_{ij} \left (d\mathbf {P}_{ij} - \mathbf {D}_i\right ) \mathbf {K}_{j}, \\ d\mathbf {K}_{j} &= \sum _{i} d\mathbf {S}_{ij} \mathbf {Q}_{i} = \sum _{i} \mathbf {P}_{ij} \left (d\mathbf {P}_{ij} - \mathbf {D}_i\right ) \mathbf {Q}_{i} .\end {align*} \]

Recomputing instead of storing

  • August 3, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

Every gradient above is expressed through \(\mathbf {P}_{ij}\) and \(d\mathbf {P}_{ij}\), both \(N \times N\). Materializing either one is exactly the quadratic memory cost the forward pass went to such lengths to avoid, so the backward pass has to be able to produce those entries on demand.

Insight. Both are recoverable from the \(N \times d\) tensors already resident in memory. The forward pass saved \(\mathbf {L}\), so \[\mathbf {P}_{ij} = \frac {\exp \left (\mathbf {Q}_{i} \cdot \mathbf {K}_{j}\right )}{\mathbf {L}_{i}},\] and \(d\mathbf {P}\) is just an inner product of two rows, \[d\mathbf {P}_{ij} = \sum _{k} d\mathbf {O}_{ik} \mathbf {V}_{jk} = d\mathbf {O}_{i} \cdot \mathbf {V}_j.\] Neither ever requires an \(N \times N\) intermediate.

Substituting both into the previous section leaves \(d\mathbf {Q}\) and \(d\mathbf {K}\) in terms of \(\mathbf {Q}\), \(\mathbf {K}\), \(\mathbf {V}\), \(d\mathbf {O}\), \(\mathbf {L}\), and \(\mathbf {D}\) alone:

\[ \begin {align*} d\mathbf {Q}_{i} &= \sum _{j} \frac {\exp \left (\mathbf {Q}_{i} \cdot \mathbf {K}_{j}\right )}{\mathbf {L}_{i}} \left (d\mathbf {O}_{i} \cdot \mathbf {V}_j - \mathbf {D}_i\right ) \mathbf {K}_{j}, \\ d\mathbf {K}_{j} &= \sum _{i} \frac {\exp \left (\mathbf {Q}_{i} \cdot \mathbf {K}_{j}\right )}{\mathbf {L}_{i}} \left (d\mathbf {O}_{i} \cdot \mathbf {V}_j - \mathbf {D}_i\right ) \mathbf {Q}_{i}. .\end {align*} \]

Getting \(\mathbf {D}\) for free

  • August 3, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

One problem survives. \(\mathbf {D}_i = \mathbf {P}_i \cdot d\mathbf {P}_i\) is a dot product over a full row, so computing it inside the streaming loop would mean a reduction over all \(j\) before any tile of \(d\mathbf {Q}_i\) could be finished. This is the same global dependency the online softmax was designed to break.

The way out is that the row sum has already been computed once, in the forward pass. Expanding and pulling \(d\mathbf {O}_i\) out of the sum:

\[ \begin {align*} \mathbf {D}_i &= \mathbf {P}_{i} \cdot d\mathbf {P}_{i} \\ &= \sum _{j} \frac {\exp \left (\mathbf {Q}_{i} \cdot \mathbf {K}_{j}\right )}{\mathbf {L}_{i}} d\mathbf {P}_{ij} \\ &= \sum _{j} \frac {\exp \left (\mathbf {Q}_{i} \cdot \mathbf {K}_{j}\right )}{\mathbf {L}_{i}} \left (d\mathbf {O}_{i} \cdot \mathbf {V}_{j}\right ) \\ &= d\mathbf {O}_{i} \cdot \sum _{j} \frac {\exp \left (\mathbf {Q}_{i} \cdot \mathbf {K}_{j}\right )}{\mathbf {L}_{i}} \mathbf {V}_{j} \\ &= d\mathbf {O}_{i} \cdot \mathbf {O}_{i} .\end {align*} \]

The inner sum is precisely the definition of \(\mathbf {O}_i\). So \(\mathbf {D}\) is a single elementwise product of \(d\mathbf {O}\) and \(\mathbf {O}\) summed along the head dimension — one \(O(Nd)\) pass over tensors we already have, done once before the backward loop begins.

Summary

  • May 27, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

Forward pass. Store \(\mathbf {O}\) and the softmax denominators \(\mathbf {L}\), both \(O(Nd)\).

Between the passes. Receive \(d\mathbf {O}\) from the layer above (automatic in JAX), then precompute \(\mathbf {D}_i = d\mathbf {O}_i \cdot \mathbf {O}_i\) in \(O(N)\) memory.

Backward pass. Stream over tiles, recomputing \(\mathbf {P}_{ij}\) from \(\mathbf {Q}, \mathbf {K}, \mathbf {L}\) and \(d\mathbf {P}_{ij}\) from \(d\mathbf {O}, \mathbf {V}\) as needed:

  1. \(d\mathbf {V}_j = \sum _i \mathbf {P}_{ij} d\mathbf {O}_i\), accumulated over query tiles.
  2. \(d\mathbf {Q}_i = \sum _j \mathbf {P}_{ij}(d\mathbf {O}_i \cdot \mathbf {V}_j - \mathbf {D}_i)\mathbf {K}_j\), accumulated over key tiles.
  3. \(d\mathbf {K}_j = \sum _i \mathbf {P}_{ij}(d\mathbf {O}_i \cdot \mathbf {V}_j - \mathbf {D}_i)\mathbf {Q}_i\), accumulated over query tiles.

Each accumulator is \(O(d)\) per row or column, so the whole backward pass stays linear in \(N\).

Card. The running max makes the chunk merge exact [6UFW]

  • August 18, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

In flash attention, what running statistics travel between KV chunks, and how are two chunks merged?

Answer Each query block carries three: \(M\), the running maximum of \(q \cdot k\); \(L\), the running softmax denominator; and \(O\), the running output. Merging chunks with local maxima \(M^1, M^2\) and sums \(L^1, L^2\) rescales each to the shared maximum: \[L = e^{M^1 - \max (M^1, M^2)}L^1 + e^{M^2 - \max (M^1, M^2)}L^2\] This is exact, not an approximation. It is only \(\sum _i e^{a_i + b} = e^b \sum _i e^{a_i}\): pulling a constant out of a sum of exponentials. The maximum is subtracted for numerical stability and put back by the same identity — see Online Softmax for the one-pass version of the argument. The payoff is memory, not FLOPs. The \([B,T,S,N]\) attention matrix is never materialised, so memory is \(O(1)\) in the number of chunks while the FLOP count stays quadratic. The query block sits in VMEM and only the KV chunks stream in, which is also what raises the arithmetic intensity.

ASIC accelerators [OGCRS]

  • May 24, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

Application-Specific Integrated Circuits fuse multiple operations into hardware that a general-purpose pipeline would have to schedule sequentially. The motivating intuition: if you frequently multiply-accumulate, the multiply and the add each traverse the entire pipeline separately. A dedicated multiply-accumulate ALU does both in one cycle.

The cost-of-operation gap is large — 32-bit vs 8-bit addition has roughly an order of magnitude difference in energy per op. ASICs win by matching width to need.

TPU Architecture [NZZ7]

  • March 24, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

TPU specs [676P]

  • August 10, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

Per-chip and per-pod numbers for each generation of TPU, from the Scaling Book. Pod size is the ICI topology of a full slice; host size is the chips hanging off a single CPU host.

Model Pod size Host size HBM/chip HBM BW/chip (bytes/s) FLOPs/s/chip (bf16) FLOPs/s/chip (int8)
TPU v3 \(32 \times 32\) \(4 \times 2\) 32GB \(9.0e11\) \(1.4e14\) \(1.4e14\)
TPU v4p \(16 \times 16 \times 16\) \(2 \times 2 \times 1\) 32GB \(1.2e12\) \(2.75e14\) \(2.75e14\)
TPU v5p \(16 \times 20 \times 28\) \(2 \times 2 \times 1\) 96GB \(2.8e12\) \(4.59e14\) \(9.18e14\)
TPU v5e \(16 \times 16\) \(4 \times 2\) 16GB \(8.2e11\) \(1.97e14\) \(3.94e14\)
TPU v6e \(16 \times 16\) \(4 \times 2\) 32GB \(1.6e12\) \(9.20e14\) \(1.84e15\)
TPU7x \(4 \times 4 \times 576\) \(2 \times 2 \times 1\) 192GB \(7.4e12\) \(2.30e15\) \(4.61e15\)
Remark. The int8 column only doubles from v5p onward — v3 and v4p run int8 through the MXU at the same rate as bf16, so quantizing there saves memory traffic but buys no extra OPs/s. The ratio of a FLOPs/s column to the HBM bandwidth column is the roofline ridge point: on v5e, \(3.94e14 / 8.2e11 \approx 480\), i.e. batch \(240\) in the \(2B\) arithmetic-intensity approximation.

Interconnect bandwidth is quoted per link, not per chip — multiply by the number of neighbors a chip has in the topology above to get its aggregate off-chip bandwidth.

Model ICI BW/link (one-way, bytes/s) ICI BW/link (bidi, bytes/s)
TPU v3 \(1.0e11\) \(2.0e11\)
TPU v4p \(4.5e10\) \(9.0e10\)
TPU v5p \(9.0e10\) \(1.8e11\)
TPU v5e \(4.5e10\) \(9.0e10\)
TPU v6e \(9.0e10\) \(1.8e11\)
TPU7x \(9.0e10\) \(1.8e11\)
Remark. The bidi column is exactly \(2 \times \) the one-way column in every row, so it carries no extra information — it only names whether you are counting both directions of the link. Which one belongs in a cost model depends on the collective: a ring all-reduce drives both directions at once, a one-directional shift does not. Note also that v3 has the highest per-link bandwidth in the table but the smallest neighbor count, since a \(32 \times 32\) pod is a 2D torus — four neighbors per chip rather than the six a 3D torus gives.

Definition. TensorCore (TPU) [OGCRQ]

  • May 22, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios
  • Vector register file each register is 8x128 vector registers with 8 horizontal lanes and 128 vertical lanes. There are typically 64 of these registers.

Definition. Vector Processing Unit [OGCRN]

  • May 22, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

A core component of the TPU architecture responsible for elementwise operations.

  • 2D SIMD execution, where each of 1024 sites execute same program in lockstep.
  • Each site contains 4 ALUs, enabling 4096 FLOPs.
  • Fed a 8x128 Vector Register in one cycle.

Card. The VPU is thirty times smaller than the MXU [JFWY]

  • August 10, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

Vector Processing Unit: what is its shape and throughput relative to the Matrix Multiply Unit (MXU), and which reductions are cheap?

Answer Shape \((8\ \text {sublanes}, 128\ \text {lanes})\), with 4 independent ALUs per position and most ops at 1/cycle: \[8 \times 128 \times 4 \times 1.75\mathrm {e}9 \approx 7\mathrm {e}12 \text { FLOPs/s}\] on v5p — about \(30\times \) less than the ~\(2e14\) MXU FLOPs/s per core. VPU work is fp32. Reductions along the sublane axis (the 8) are cheap: an intra-lane shuffle by 4/2/1 plus three pairwise adds. Cross-lane reductions need the separate XLU, which is slow and expensive. Control is skewed the other way: a single scalar core fetches and dispatches everything and can issue only one DMA request per cycle. Efficient, but it blocks data-dependent vectorization.

Definition. Matrix Multiply Unit (MXU) [OGCRP]

  • May 22, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

A core component of the TPU architecture responsible for performing matrix multiplication via a weight stationary Systolic array.

  • \(128 \times 128\) — 16,384 multiply accumulate units, each multiplying and adding in one cycle. v6e/Trillium widens the array to \(256 \times 256\), i.e. 65,536.
  • The native op is one bf16[8,128] @ bf16[128,128] -> f32[8,128] every 8 cycles, or about \(5e13\) bf16 FLOPs/s per MXU at 1.5 GHz. A v5e chip has enough MXUs to reach ~\(2e14\).
Remark. The side length is fixed in hardware, so every dimension has to be tiled down to it and any axis shorter than it is padded up to it, wasting the FLOPs spent on the padding. The order is
  1. Tiling the matrix to load from HBM to VMEM.
  2. Compiler tiles from VMEM to \(128 \times 128\) tiles to load into the MXU.

Card. Why the MXU pads everything to 128 [HPSO]

  • August 10, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

What is the native op of one Matrix Multiply Unit (MXU), and why does that force padding to 128?

Answer One bf16[8,128] @ bf16[128,128] -> f32[8,128] every 8 cycles, on a \(128 \times 128\) systolic array — \(256 \times 256\) on v6e/Trillium. The array's side length is fixed in hardware, so any matrix axis shorter than 128 (256 on v6e) is padded up to it, and the FLOPs spent on the padding are simply wasted. With 2–4 MXUs per core, tiling dimensions want to exceed \(128 \times \) the MXU count. Scale: roughly \(5e13\) bf16 FLOPs/s per MXU at 1.5 GHz, so about \(2e14\) per v5e chip. int8 runs ~\(2\times \) faster, int4 ~\(4\times \).

Processing in Memory for ML [2BGU]

  • April 6, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

Notes on guest lecture by Yufeng Gu titled Architecture and System Co-Design for Scalable Large Language Model Inference

TFLOPs increasing much faster than DRAM bandwidth -> Hardware scaling is hitting the memory wall.

Data center power consumption also increasing \(\approx \) 10% a year.

GPUs are under low utilization for LLM inference

  • Prefix stage: parallel
  • Decoding stage: sequential -> bottleneck!

As batch size increases, the KV-cache dominates memory usage.

  • KV cache size grows with context length.
  • Tradeoff between context length and batch size.
Remark. Unlike fully-connected cannot batch self-attention because it depends on the individual prompts.

Recall. operational intensity is \[\frac {\text {compute throughput}}{\text {memory bandwidth}}\]

Inference much lower operational intensity than GEMM!

  • Inference only doing matrix \(\times \) row
  • If embedding dim is \(D\), then this is only \(D\) ops / byte.

Processing in memory (PIM) enables faster memory bandwidth.

Problem. Has lower memory capacity (fewer GB) due to added processing units (PU).
Solution.Use Compute eXpress Link (CXL) to do memory expansion to get high memory bandwidth + expend memory capacity.
Remark. Put high use operations i.e. vector multiplication, element-wise multiplication in PIM module (99% usage). Put more complicated operations on PNM accelerator. TODO: ISAs for each specified on slides (not available yet).
Remark. CENT supports inter and intra-device communication via connecting communication controller to shared buffer and CXL port.

Communcation primitives. multicast and gather

  • Multicast: send to all CXL devices.
  • Gather: receive data sequentially from all CXL devices.
  • Multicsat-gather -> tensor parallel.

Peer-to-peer: can also support pipeline parallelism.

Remark. For fast communication, use tensor parallelism i.e. if connected via NVLink. If slower communication use pipeline parallelism. Can mix.
Remark. Longer context -> better performance for PIM (TODO: why?). HBM + PIM does not scale. Cannot arbitrarily add PIM.

Definition. Full fence [S80U]

  • May 24, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

A Memory fence across which no memory operation may move in either direction. Prior accesses must become globally visible before any subsequent access may issue. x86's mfence is the canonical example — the hammer that drains the Store buffer and serializes all prior memory operations against all subsequent ones.

Full fences are the default ordering primitive under Sequential consistency — every memory operation behaves as if a full fence sat on either side. They are also the only fence one needs to reason about correctness, which is why they are the building block for the half-fences of Release consistency.

Definition. Half fence [S5D0]

  • May 24, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

A Memory fence that constrains motion in only one direction, splitting the symmetric guarantee of a Full fence into two cheaper primitives:

  • Acquire — operations after the fence may not move above it. Used at the entry to a critical section: subsequent reads and writes cannot be hoisted before the lock is held.
  • Release — operations before the fence may not move below it. Used at the exit of a critical section: prior writes cannot be deferred past the unlock.

The asymmetry is exactly the freedom one wants around a critical section: expanding the section is fine — work may sink into it (past acquire) or rise into it (before release) — but work may not leak out of it. This is the basis of Release consistency and the reason C++ std::atomic exposes memory_order_acquire / memory_order_release as its core primitives.

Definition. Relaxed memory order [WT44]

  • May 24, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

A Relaxed consistency relaxation in which any pair of memory operations may be reordered. RMO is the most permissive end of the consistency spectrum; the programmer recovers ordering only through explicit Memory fence instructions.

Each stronger reordering still has to be justified per case:

  • Load → store — no performance gain to reorder; leave alone.
  • Store → store — keep ordering with a slightly larger Store buffer.
  • Load → load — speculate the second load while waiting for the first; the reorder is invisible if the speculation is verified.

Because every fence is expensive under RMO, the natural next move is to weaken the fences themselves into half-fences, which is what Release consistency does.

Definition. Release consistency [ZWHV]

  • May 24, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

A Relaxed consistency discipline that recovers data-race freedom (see Data race) under Relaxed memory order not by issuing fewer fences, but by issuing weaker ones. The full-fence cost of Sequential consistency is replaced by a pair of half-fences placed exactly at the boundaries of critical sections — acquire on entry, release on exit.

The intuition is that correctness around a critical section only requires that work cannot leak out of it; work is free to sink into it. Half-fences encode exactly this asymmetry, which is why they are the right primitive for lock-based and lock-free synchronization alike.

Definition. Full fence [S80U]

  • May 24, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

A Memory fence across which no memory operation may move in either direction. Prior accesses must become globally visible before any subsequent access may issue. x86's mfence is the canonical example — the hammer that drains the Store buffer and serializes all prior memory operations against all subsequent ones.

Full fences are the default ordering primitive under Sequential consistency — every memory operation behaves as if a full fence sat on either side. They are also the only fence one needs to reason about correctness, which is why they are the building block for the half-fences of Release consistency.

Definition. Half fence [S5D0]

  • May 24, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

A Memory fence that constrains motion in only one direction, splitting the symmetric guarantee of a Full fence into two cheaper primitives:

  • Acquire — operations after the fence may not move above it. Used at the entry to a critical section: subsequent reads and writes cannot be hoisted before the lock is held.
  • Release — operations before the fence may not move below it. Used at the exit of a critical section: prior writes cannot be deferred past the unlock.

The asymmetry is exactly the freedom one wants around a critical section: expanding the section is fine — work may sink into it (past acquire) or rise into it (before release) — but work may not leak out of it. This is the basis of Release consistency and the reason C++ std::atomic exposes memory_order_acquire / memory_order_release as its core primitives.

C++ std::atomic compiles to half-fences in the right places, which is why it is the standard primitive for portable lock-free code.

Definition. Total store order [VH8Y]

  • May 24, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

A Relaxed consistency relaxation in which loads may be hoisted above prior stores, but no other reorderings are permitted. The motivation: a store can sit in the Store buffer waiting for cache, while subsequent loads — which do not touch the buffered address — proceed without stalling.

Same-core reads of a still-buffered store get the right value through Store-to-load forwarding; cross-core reads see the old value until the buffer drains. This asymmetry is the entire point of TSO's relaxation: the store buffer hides latency from the issuing thread without forcing other threads to wait. x86 implements TSO.

Remark. Under TSO, Dekker's algorithm is still broken without Memory fence — the classic example where TSO is too weak for naive software synchronization.
Remark. The IBM 370 variant is TSO without Store-to-load forwarding — it preserves global store atomicity at the cost of same-core stall-on-self-read.

Card. The merge under M is the visibility point [JC0I]

  • August 9, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

What is a store's global visibility point, and what does that imply for Total store order?

Answer The instant the data is merged into the L1D line while holding M. Before that, the value lives only in the Store buffer — forwardable to this core through Store-to-load forwarding, invisible to every other. That asymmetry is exactly why TSO permits store\(\to \)load reordering.

Data parallelism [QPFO]

  • May 22, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

A form of parallelism where the model is replicated across multiple devices and performed on different data.

  • Data sharding: data is split across multiple devices i.e. 32 samples and 8 devices results in 4 unique samples per device.
  • Parameter replication: on each device, we need to replcicate the model parameters to run the forward pass for the unique samples.
  • Gradient aggregation: backward pass we need to perform an all-reduce to sum and average the gradients across devices. This is automatically done by @nnx.jit.

TPU Ironwood [ZYB7]

  • May 22, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

The newest generation TPU architecture.

Scaling Ironwood

  • May 22, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

Torus Cube:

  • 64 ironwood chips
  • Each chip connects to 6 neighbors via high-speed Inter-Chip Interconnect
  • Form a 3d torus, providing three axes for parallel bandwidth.

Optical Circuit Switching:

  • Multiple cubes are linked by an OCS network to build pods.
  • If a cube fails, the OCS optically bypasses and swaps in a spare.
  • OCS allows for slices without system shutdown (?)

Tensor Parallelism [A7PN]

  • May 22, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

A form of parallelism that splits the actual weights of the model across devices.

  • Large weight matrices split across devices. Can train larger models that exceed memory of single device.
  • Devices exchange partial activations to compute layer outputs.

XLA Compilation [M74N]

  • May 22, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

Overview.

  • Dispatch / Cache: caches compilation based on input argument signatures i.e. shapes, dtypes, sharding. If shapes change will need to recompile.
  • Lowering: Python -> jaxpr -> StableHLO. This stage is a translation, not an optimization — no Operator fusion happens here. See chlo desugars, stablehlo is stable, mhlo is internal for the dialects involved and Three calls, three IR levels for how to print each level.
  • XLA: StableHLO is converted to HLO, and the optimizing passes — simplification, layout assignment, fusion, collective scheduling, memory assignment — run there. Read after_optimizations, not before_optimizations, for anything performance-related (Only after_optimizations matches the profile).
  • TPU specific: Further reduced to LLO IR, then very large instruction word (VLIW) scheduling to map dot products to Matrix Multiply Unit (MXU).
Remark. The Python source is thrown away as soon as it is traced into a jaxpr, and the jaxpr in turn is thrown away once it is lowered. What XLA ingests is StableHLO, which it converts to HLO before optimizing; HLO is XLA's internal representation, not its input format. The only thread back to the Python you wrote is the metadata carried on each instruction (op_name is the trace path back to Python).

Lifecycle of a JAX program [NR79]

  • August 7, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

We have the following compilation pipeline

  1. Tracing: Python / JAX -> jaxpr
    • jax.make_jaxpr(fun)(*args)
    • Abstract execution. JAX executes python code using abstract tracer objects instead of real arrays.
    • Every operation and its intermediate result is recorded into jaxpr.
    • Sequence used to construct a grap, which the XLA compiler will later optimize.
    • Python code is executed once during tracing but excluded from final graph.
    • Each JAX primitive registers functions for
      • Lowering to StableHLO
      • How it is transformed under grad and vmap.
  2. Lowering: Jaxpr -> StableHLO
    • fn_lowered = jax.jit(fun).lower(*args)
    • stable_hlo = fn_lowered.as_text()
    • fn_lowered.compiler_ir(dialect='stablehlo') for the MLIR module rather than its text. There is no 'hlo' dialect to ask for here — HLO is produced inside XLA, one step later (chlo desugars, stablehlo is stable, mhlo is internal), and you reach it through .compile().as_text() (Three calls, three IR levels).
    • Multiple ML frameworks lower to StableHLO.
      • Hardware agnostic.
      • Backwards compatible.
  3. Compile: HLO -> Optimized HLO -> LLO IR -> VLIW -> Executables
    • compiled = fn_lowered.compile()
    • compiled.runtime_executable() returns a LoadedExecutable.
    • Useful(?) compiled.cost_analysis().
    • HLO:
      • Input for XLA compiler.
      • Directed acyclic graph of copmutational operations.
      • All array dimensions are known at compile time.
      • Limited opcodes i.e. Add, Multiply, Transpose, Dot, etc.

XLA Shapes and Memory Layout.

  • Every data type defined by data type and fixed dimensions, determined at compile time.
  • Minor-to-major order i.e. fastest changing to slowesting changin.
  • Tiling: arrays are split into smaller blocks to fit into VREG. Want to arrange data to efficiently fit VREG.

Execution.

  • Move tensors from CPU to HBM. Sharding is taken care of by PJIT if on TPU pod.
  • Async: Immediately returns a Future JAX array while the hardware executes VLIW microcode asynchronously.
  • Buffer management: Returns pointer to TPU memory. All handled lazily. Not copied back to CPU until jax.block_until_ready().

Getting the dumps

  • May 22, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

Half of reading compiler output is arranging to read the right compiler output. The recurring mistake is answering a performance question from before_optimizations, which describes a program that never ran.

Card. Three calls, three IR levels [AGEG]

  • August 22, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

How do you print each IR level for a JAX function f?

Answer
  1. jaxpr — jax.make_jaxpr(f)(x).
  2. StableHLO, pre-XLA — jax.jit(f).lower(x).as_text(), or .compiler_ir(dialect='stablehlo').
  3. Optimized HLO, post-XLA passes and matching the profile — jax.jit(f).lower(x).compile().as_text().
The three answer genuinely different questions, and reaching for the wrong one wastes an afternoon (Lifecycle of a JAX program):
  • The jaxpr says what tracing captured — so it answers "why is this constant baked in", "why is there a convert_element_type here" (A weak type adopts the other operand's dtype), "did my Python branch get traced at all".
  • The StableHLO says what JAX handed to XLA — the boundary where a JAX bug becomes an XLA bug.
  • The optimized HLO says what XLA built — fusions, layouts, collectives (Only after_optimizations matches the profile).

Card. Only after_optimizations matches the profile [BQUG]

  • August 22, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

What is the difference between the before_optimizations and after_optimizations HLO files in an XLA dump?

Answer before_optimizations — the HLO as imported from StableHLO. Shapes carry no meaningful layouts yet (The layout is minor-to-major), nothing is fused, and there is roughly one instruction per source operation. Read it when you want to know what JAX asked for. after_optimizations — past simplification, layout assignment, Operator fusion, collective scheduling, and memory assignment. Read it when you want to know what runs. Only the second one corresponds to the kernels in a profile, because the fusion names in the profile are the fusion instruction names here (A fusion op is a kernel launch boundary). A performance question answered from before_optimizations is answered about a program that never executed — the op you are worried about may have been fused away, folded, or duplicated (The dump filename encodes the stage).

Card. Per-pass dumps find the pass that broke it [8U47]

  • August 22, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

What does XLA_FLAGS=--xla_dump_to=/tmp/dump give you, and how do you get per-pass IR?

Answer A directory of per-module files: pre- and post-optimization HLO text (Only after_optimizations matches the profile), the buffer assignment, and on GPU the generated PTX and LLVM IR (The dump filename encodes the stage). Add --xla_dump_hlo_pass_re=.* to dump the HLO before and after every pass matching the regex. That is how you find which pass introduced a copy or broke a fusion — bisect the pass list rather than staring at the endpoints. Narrow the regex once you have a suspect, since .* on a real model produces a great many files. --xla_dump_hlo_as_html and --xla_dump_hlo_as_dot give graph views, which are far easier than text for fusion structure (A fusion op is a kernel launch boundary) — a flat instruction list hides exactly the thing you are looking at. The MLIR side has the same facility in --mlir-print-ir-after-all (Print generic, print locations, disable threading).

Card. The dump filename encodes the stage [JFMQ]

  • August 22, 2026
  • Kellen Kanarios

Reading an XLA dump directory: what is in module_0001.jit_f.before_optimizations.txt versus the after_optimizations and sm_XX files?

Answer The filename encodes module index, entry name, and pipeline stage. Read them in this order:
  1. before_optimizations — one-to-one with your StableHLO. Use it to confirm JAX emitted what you meant.
  2. after_optimizations — fused, laid out, scheduled. Map profile kernels to the fusion names here (Only after_optimizations matches the profile).
  3. Backend artifacts — PTX and LLVM IR on GPU, Mosaic or LLO on TPU. What actually ran.
Each module index is a separate compilation, so a program with several jit boundaries, or one that retraced on a new input shape, produces several sets. When a dump directory has more modules than you expected, that count is the finding — it means recompilation you did not intend (XLA Compilation).
