We expand this as \[\begin {align*} \nabla _{\theta }v_{\pi _{\theta }}(s_{0}) &= \nabla _{\theta } \left (\sum _{a} \pi (a \mid s_{0}) Q_{\pi _{\theta }}(s_{0}, a)\right ) \\ &= \sum _{a} \nabla _{\theta } \pi _{\theta }(a \mid s_{0}) Q_{\pi _{\theta }}(s_{0}, a) + \pi _{\theta }(a \mid s_{0})\underbrace {\nabla _{\theta }Q_{\pi _{\theta }}(s_{0}, a)}_{\text {problem}} .\end {align*}\] The gradient \(\nabla _{\theta }Q_{\pi _{\theta }}(s, a)\) implicitly relies on \(\theta \). Therefore, we must unroll it i.e. \[\begin {align*} \nabla _{\theta } Q_{\pi _{\theta }}(s_{0},a) &= \nabla _{\theta } \left [\sum _{r} p(r \mid s_{0}, a) r + \gamma \sum _{s} p(s \mid s_{0}, a) \sum _{a'} \pi (a' \mid s) Q_{\pi _{\theta }}(s, a')\right ] \\ &= \gamma \sum _{s} p(s \mid s_{0}, a) \nabla _{\theta } \left (\sum _{a'} \pi (a' \mid s) Q_{\pi _{\theta }}(s, a')\right ) \\ &= \gamma \sum _{s} p(s \mid s_{0}, a) \left [\sum _{a'} \nabla _{\theta } \pi (a' \mid s) Q_{\pi _{\theta }}(s, a') + \pi (a' \mid s) \nabla _{\theta } Q_{\pi _{\theta }}(s, a')\right ] .\end {align*}\] We define \(p_{\pi }^{k}(s_{0} \to s)\) to be the probability of transitioning from \(s_{0}\) to \(s\) in \(k\) steps under policy \(\pi \). Then continuously unrolling we observe that \[\begin {align*} \nabla _{\theta }v_{\pi _{\theta }}(s_{0}) &= \sum _{k}^{\infty } \sum _{a} \sum _{s} \gamma ^{k} p_{\pi _{\theta }}^k(s_{0} \to s) \nabla _{\theta } \pi _{\theta }(a \mid s) Q_{\pi _{\theta }}(s, a) \\ &= \sum _{s} \sum _{a} \nabla _{\theta } \pi _{\theta }(a \mid s) Q_{\pi _{\theta }}(s, a) \underbrace {\sum _{k}^{\infty } \gamma ^{k} p_{\pi _{\theta }}^k(s_{0} \to s)}_{M_{\pi _{\theta }}(s)} ,\end {align*}\] where we introduce \(M_{\pi _{\theta }}(s)\) to be the unnormalized state occupancy measure. We want this as an expectation we can estimate with samples. To do this, we simply multiply and divide by the normalizing constant i.e. for \(m_{\pi _{\theta }}(s) = \frac {M_{\pi _{\theta }}(s)}{\sum _{s'} M_{\pi _{\theta }}(s')}\) \[\begin {align*} &= \left (\sum _{s'} M_{\pi _{\theta }}(s')\right )\sum _{s} \left (\sum _{a} \nabla _{\theta } \pi _{\theta }(a \mid s) Q_{\pi _{\theta }}(s, a)\right ) m_{\pi _{\theta }}(s) \\ &\propto \mathbb {E}_{m_{\pi _{\theta }}(s)} \left [\sum _{a} \nabla _{\theta } \pi _{\theta }(a \mid s) Q_{\pi _{\theta }}(s, a)\right ] .\end {align*}\] Now this in itself is a policy gradient, but it is a batched policy gradient in the sense that it requires summing over all \(a\). To get around this, we use the log trick. Namely, \[\begin {align*} \sum _{a} \nabla _{\theta } \pi _{\theta }(a \mid s) Q_{\pi _{\theta }}(s, a) &= \sum _{a} \nabla _{\theta } \pi _{\theta }(a \mid s) Q_{\pi _{\theta }}(s, a) \frac {\pi _{\theta }(a \mid s)}{\pi _{\theta }(a \mid s)} \\ &= \sum _{a} \nabla _{\theta } \log \pi _{\theta }(a \mid s) Q_{\pi _{\theta }}(s, a) \pi _{\theta }(a \mid s) \\ &= \mathbb {E}_{\pi (a \mid s)} \left [\nabla _{\theta } \log \pi _{\theta }(a \mid s) Q_{\pi _{\theta }}(s', a)\right ] .\end {align*}\] Putting it all together, \[ \nabla _{\theta }v_{\pi _{\theta }}(s_{0}) = \mathbb {E}_{m_{\pi _{\theta }}(s), \pi (a \mid s)} \left [\nabla _{\theta } \log \pi _{\theta }(a \mid s) Q_{\pi _{\theta }}(s, a)\right ] \]

    Limited Direct Execution [VE8C]

    • July 19, 2025
    • Kellen Kanarios

    The OS lets user code run directly on the CPU for speed, but with hardware-enforced limits that prevent a buggy or malicious program from compromising the rest of the system. Two questions motivate the mechanism:

    Question. How do we make sure a program doesn't do what we don't want it to do? and how do we enable time-sharing?

    The first question is answered by hardware User mode vs kernel mode enforced via the Trap table, with a controlled Syscall mechanism as the only path from one to the other. The second is answered by periodic timer interrupts that trap to the OS, which performs a Context switch and runs the scheduler.

    The whole stack is bootstrapped during the Boot sequence, when the kernel installs the trap table and starts the timer before handing control to user space.

    User mode vs kernel mode [QUQC]

    • May 12, 2026
    • Kellen Kanarios

    Two privilege levels supported by the CPU. User mode restricts the running process to a limited set of instructions and a limited view of memory — usually just its own address space. Kernel mode runs the OS with full access to all instructions and all of physical memory.

    Switching between modes is mediated by hardware via a Trap table populated at boot. The OS sets up the table; the CPU enforces it. A process cannot promote itself to kernel mode arbitrarily — it must invoke a Syscall mechanism, which traps to a fixed entry point in the OS.

    Remark. Kernel mode is dangerous because the address space is effectively the entire machine. The mode bit + the trap table together are what makes it safe to time-share a CPU between mutually distrusting programs.

    Trap table [0NVY]

    • May 12, 2026
    • Kellen Kanarios

    A hardware-readable table installed by the OS at boot that maps each kind of exceptional control-flow event (syscall, interrupt, page fault, illegal instruction, ...) to the address of an OS handler. When the CPU takes a trap, it consults this table to decide where to jump, switches into kernel mode, and runs the handler.

    The table is what makes it safe to expose privileged operations to user mode: user code never gets to pick the destination of a mode-switch, only the trap number. The OS controls every entry point, the CPU enforces the indirection.

    Remark. Installing the trap table is itself a privileged operation. It happens once, early in boot, before any user process exists.

    Syscall mechanism [A5S6]

    • May 12, 2026
    • Kellen Kanarios

    A syscall is a user-mode-initiated request for a privileged service from the kernel. Because user code cannot jump into kernel code directly, the mechanism is built around a single trap instruction plus a pre-agreed register convention identifying which service to perform.

    The end-to-end sequence:

    1. User code places the syscall number in a pre-defined register and invokes the trap instruction.
    2. Hardware saves enough state to resume the process and switches to kernel mode.
    3. Hardware jumps to the OS-installed handler via the Trap table.
    4. The handler reads the syscall number from the agreed register and dispatches to the corresponding OS routine.
    5. The OS validates the request, performs the work, and arranges return values per the calling convention.
    6. The OS restores user state and returns the process to user mode.
    Remark. Because the register convention is fixed by ABI, the user-mode side of a syscall is typically hand-written in assembly within libc.
    Remark. Interrupts work via a similar trap-handler mechanism, but are initiated by hardware (timer, device) rather than user code.
    Remark. The kernel must validate any pointers or arguments the user supplies — user code cannot be trusted not to ask the kernel to read kernel memory on its behalf.

    Context switch [OKCI]

    • May 12, 2026
    • Kellen Kanarios

    The operation of saving the full execution state of one process (or thread) and restoring another's so the CPU can resume it as if it had never been interrupted. On a trap into the kernel, the hardware stashes the user-visible state (PC, condition codes, stack pointer) into a known location, and the OS saves the remaining general-purpose registers as part of the switching code.

    Two flavors of state are involved:

    1. User registers: the current program's context (general-purpose registers, stack vars).
    2. Kernel registers: meta-information used to resume the trap correctly (PC at trap, syscall number, etc.).

    Context switches are not free — they incur the cost of cache and TLB pollution in addition to the direct cost of saving/restoring state. This is the cost amortized by larger scheduling quanta and a recurring concern for any Concurrency system.

    Boot sequence [XSFO]

    • May 12, 2026
    • Kellen Kanarios

    The fixed series of steps a machine performs from power-on until a usable operating system is running. Each stage runs from a known location and hands off control to the next.

    1. Power signal resets the CPU to a known state.
    2. The CPU fetches from a hard-wired address — the BIOS (or UEFI firmware). The BIOS runs basic hardware checks (POST).
    3. The BIOS loads and jumps to the bootloader (e.g. GRUB) from a known location on disk.
    4. The bootloader places the kernel image at the correct address and jumps to its entry point.
    5. The kernel performs early setup: installs the Trap table (a special privileged instruction), starts the timer interrupt, sets up memory management, and finally enters user space.
    Remark. The hardware is hard-wired only to find the BIOS. Everything past that is software the user can replace, which is why dual-booting and custom bootloaders work.

    Reference. Motion-Planning via Contrastive Reinforcement Learning and MCTS [kanariosMotionPlanningContrastiveReinforcement2025]

    • July 18, 2025

    • Kellen Kanarios, Lei Ying

    • Slides
    • OpenReview
    • Poster
    @article{kanariosMotionPlanningContrastiveReinforcement2025,
 title = {Motion-{{Planning}} via {{Contrastive Reinforcement Learning}} and {{Monte-Carlo Tree Search}}},
 author = {Kanarios, Kellen and Ying, Lei},
 year = {2025},
 file = {/home/kellen/Downloads/papers/Motion-Planning via Contrastive Reinforcement Learning and Monte-Carlo Tree Search - Kanarios and Ying.pdf},
 langid = {english},
 abstract = {We consider the generalized movers' problem i.e. finding any path that moves an object to a desired goal while avoiding collisions. Even relaxing optimality requirements, the any-path problem is computationally challenging. Namely, exponential in the degrees of freedom of the object. Due to the curse of dimensionality, applying traditional search algorithms to the discretized state space becomes infeasible as the state space grows. This motivated the use of sampling-based methods. These sampling-based methods are tabula rasa and require complete re-learning on each problem instance. Existing learning-based methods that attempt to leverage shared structure aim to handle arbitrary changes in the environment. Often, this still requires a significant number of samples and / or expert demonstrations. In practice, many robotics applications or UAV routing do not need to handle these pathological cases, where the environment undergoes drastic change. Rather, they must only be able to avoid a minor mismatch with the training environment while their route remains largely unchanged. We allow pre-training in an obstacle free environment and show that combining contrastive reinforcement learning with classical game-inspired search algorithms enables zero shot performance to unseen obstacles.}
}

    Normalizing Flows [B9J9]

    • July 15, 2025

    Brief notes on Variational Inference with Normalizing Flows to motivate flow matching.

    Goal. We are concerned with the problem of density estimation. Given a dataset \(\mathcal {X}\), consisting of samples \(\mathbf {x}_i \sim p(\mathbf {x})\), we want to learn \(p(\mathbf {x})\).

    One popular way to do this is via variational inference. As a brief recap, in variational inference, we assume that there is actually a joint distribution \(p(\mathbf {x}, \mathbf {z})\), where \(\mathbf {z}\) is a latent variable. We then find \(p(\mathbf {x})\) by maximizing the log-likelihood \(\log \int p(\mathbf {x} \mid \mathbf {z}) \mathrm {d}\mathbf {z}\)

    For an example of this, see my post on expectation maximization. In that post, we utilize the ELBO to learn a latent variable model \(q_{\phi }(\mathbf {z} | \mathbf {x})\). As discussed in my post on ELBO, in order to learn \(p(\mathbf {x})\), we must have that \(p(\mathbf {z} | \mathbf {x})\) is in the family \(q_{\phi }\). However, \(q_ {\phi }\) is usually a Gaussian parametrized by \(\phi \), so that we can easily learn \(\phi \). In this case, it is very unlikely that \(p(\mathbf {z} \mid x)\) lies in the family of \(q_{\phi }\) and therefore we have no hope of learning the true \(p(\mathbf {x})\).

    Card. GQA saves cache, not projection FLOPs [59OV]

    • August 18, 2026
    • Kellen Kanarios

    Per layer, what do the QKVO projections cost in parameters and training FLOPs under Group Query Attention with \(N\) query heads, \(K\) key/value heads, and head dimension \(H\)?

    Answer Parameters: \(2D(N+K)H\), from \(W_Q[D,N,H]\) and \(W_O[N,H,D]\) at \(DNH\) each, plus \(W_K, W_V[D,K,H]\) at \(DKH\) each. Training FLOPs: \(12BTD(N+K)H\) — each projection is \(6BTD \cdot (\text {heads}) \cdot H\). The variants are one knob. \(K = N\) is plain multi-head attention; \(K = 1\) is MQA; \(1 < K < N\) with \(K \mid N\) is grouped-query, with group size \(G = N/K\). Read the formula for what shrinking \(K\) actually buys. It touches only the \(K\) term, so the projection cost falls from \(2N\) to \(N + K\) — at most a factor of two, and usually far less. That is not why anyone uses GQA. The payoff is the KV-cache, which scales with \(K\) alone and is the binding constraint at generation time.

    Definition. KV-cache [TJLA]

    • July 14, 2025
    • Kellen Kanarios

    The keys and values of every token seen so far, held in memory across decoding steps so that each is projected once rather than once per step. Attention at step \(t\) needs \(k_j\) and \(v_j\) for every \(j \le t\), and each of those is a function of token \(j\) and the weights alone — nothing about it depends on \(t\). So it is computable once and never again, and the only real question is whether you will spend memory to avoid recomputing it.

    The cost of not spending it is quadratic, which is easy to miss because per step it looks merely linear: admitting token \(t\) means rebuilding \(t+1\) key–value pairs, so a sequence of \(S\) tokens costs \(\sum _{t=1}^{S} t = S(S+1)/2\) projections rather than \(S\). The query is the asymmetry that makes the trade available at all — only the newest position needs one, so \(q_t\) is a single row either way, and decoding is a matrix–vector product against a \(K\) and \(V\) that grow by one row a step.

    Notation. Following the scaling book: \(S\) is the KV sequence length, \(K\) the number of key/value heads, \(H\) the head dimension, \(L\) the layers, \(B\) the batch. The clash between \(K\) as a matrix and \(K\) as a head count is unfortunate and universal.

    What the cache costs is memory, and the shape of that cost is the reason it governs inference planning. Each token contributes a key and a value in every layer, so a batch holds

    \[2 \cdot B \cdot S \cdot L \cdot K \cdot H \cdot \mathrm {bytes}\]

    which is linear in the sequence length and — unlike the weights — per sequence, so it cannot be amortised over the batch. Context length and batch size are therefore drawn from the same High bandwidth memory budget, and past a certain context the cache dominates residency outright, which is Processing in Memory for ML's framing of the memory wall.

    It also decides what decoding is bound by. At step \(t\) the model streams the entire cache through the Matrix Multiply Unit (MXU) to do \(O(S)\) multiply-accumulates against a single query row, so the Arithmetic intensity is roughly one FLOP per byte read — far below the ridge point of any accelerator, and flat in \(S\). Decoding is bandwidth-bound, and the cache is what it is bound by.

    Every fix for that attacks a factor in the expression above rather than the idea of caching. MQA sets \(K = 1\) and shares one key/value head across all query heads; Group Query Attention sets it to a group count and interpolates; Sliding Window Attention bounds \(S\) instead by refusing to attend past a window. The FLOPs are unchanged in all three — what changes is how many bytes have to move to supply them.

    Card. The KV cache scales with K, and is per-sequence [J65M]

    • August 18, 2026
    • Kellen Kanarios

    How large is a KV-cache, and which dimension actually drives it?

    Answer The cache has shape \([2, S, L, K, H]\) per sequence — the leading 2 is keys and values — so in int8 it is \(2SLKH\) bytes. Worked: \(S = 8\mathrm {k}\), \(L = 64\), \(KH = D = 8192\) gives \(2 \cdot 8192 \cdot 64 \cdot 8192 \approx 8\) GiB for a single sequence. Two things in that expression decide inference planning. It scales with \(K\), the number of key/value heads, and not with the \(N\) query heads — which is the whole argument for Group Query Attention and MQA at \(K \ll N\). And it is per sequence, so unlike the weights it cannot be amortised over the batch: it competes with batch size for the same High bandwidth memory budget, and generation is bandwidth-bound on streaming it.

    POTW: Fast Transformer Decoding: One Write-Head is All You Need [W4YP]

    • July 14, 2025
    • Kellen Kanarios

    Notes on the paper Fast Transformer Decoding: One Write-Head is All You Need.

    For,

    • \(b\) batch dimension,
    • \(n\) sequence length,
    • \(d\) hidden dimension,
    • \(h\) number of heads.
    The total FLOPS for attention are roughly \(bnd^2\). This comes from
    1. \(3nd^2\) FLOPS to compute \(Q = XW_Q, K = XW_K, V = XW_V\).
    2. Need to do this \(b\) times for each input in batch.
    and the total memory accesses are roughly \(\underbrace {bnd}_{X} + \underbrace {bhn^2}_{\text {softmax}} + \underbrace {d^2}_{\text {projection}}\). This gives high arithmetic intensity \[O\left (\left (\frac {h}{d} + \frac {1}{bn}\right )^{-1}\right )\]

    However, if we do incremental inference then we must multiply our total number of memory accesses by \(n\) i.e. \(bn^2d + nd^2\). This gives arithmetic intensity \[O\left (\left (\frac {n}{d} + \frac {1}{b}\right )^{-1}\right ),\] which requires large batch and short sequence length.

    Remark. I believe we just ignore the softmax memory contribution in the inference case because it does not scale with \(n\) anymore as we are computing the logits just for the next token. Therefore, it becomes a \(\frac {d}{h}\) term, which we can safely ignore?

    The key is that the \(\frac {n}{d}\) term comes from the \(bn^2d\) term, where we are loading \(h\) \((b \times n \times d / h)\) \(K\) and \(V\) matrices \(n\) times. Thus, we can improve the \(\frac {n}{d}\) term by a factor of \(h\) by simply not using a different \(K\) and \(V\) matrix for each head. This is the entire idea behind MQA.

    Remark. Similar to the KV-cache, we still can use \(h\) \(Q\) matrices because we do not need to load \(n\) of them into memory because only the last one matters for inference.

    Definition. Softmax [C00V]

    • July 14, 2025
    • Kellen Kanarios

    The softmax function \(\mathrm {softmax}: \mathbb {R}^d \to \mathbb {R}^d\) is defined by \[\mathrm {softmax}(\mathbf {x})_i = \frac {e^{x_i}}{\sum _{j = 1}^{d} e^{x_j}}\]

    Claim. The Jacobian of the softmax function for \(\mathbf {y} = \mathrm {softmax}(\mathbf {x})\) is given by \[ \begin {align*} \frac {\partial y_i}{\partial x_j} = y_i(\delta _{ij} - y_j), \end {align*} \] or, in matrix form, \[ \begin {align*} J = \mathrm {diag}(\mathbf {y}) - \mathbf {y}\mathbf {y}^\top . \end {align*} \]
    Proof. Write \(y_i = e^{x_i} / S\) with \(S = \sum _{k=1}^{d} e^{x_k}\), so that \(\partial S / \partial x_j = e^{x_j}\). By the quotient rule, \[ \begin {align*} \frac {\partial y_i}{\partial x_j} &= \frac {\delta _{ij} e^{x_i} S - e^{x_i} e^{x_j}}{S^2} \\ &= \delta _{ij}\frac {e^{x_i}}{S} - \frac {e^{x_i}}{S}\frac {e^{x_j}}{S} \\ &= \delta _{ij} y_i - y_i y_j \\ &= y_i(\delta _{ij} - y_j). \end {align*} \] Collecting these entries into a matrix, the diagonal contributes \(y_i\) along \(\mathrm {diag}(\mathbf {y})\) and the \(-y_i y_j\) term is the outer product \(\mathbf {y}\mathbf {y}^\top \), giving \(J = \mathrm {diag}(\mathbf {y}) - \mathbf {y}\mathbf {y}^\top \).

    Hyperparameter Rules (CS336) [9VZH]

    • July 14, 2025
    • Kellen Kanarios

    Rule 1. \(d_{\text {ff}} = d_{\text {model}}\)

    • \(d_{\text {model}}\) is the input dimension
    • \(d_{\text {ff}}\) is the hidden dimension

    Exception 1. in the case of GLUs, we recall that to account for extra parameters we scale \(\frac {2}{3}\). Therefore, \(d_{\text {ff}} = \frac {8}{3}d_{\text {model}}\).

    Exception 2. In T5, they use \(d_{\text {ff}} = 64d_{\text {model}}\). The logic for this was that we could maximize the MFU by increasing matrix size. Ended up going back to small \(d_{\text {model}}\).

    Rule 2. \(d_{\text {head}} = d_{\text {model}} / \text {num heads}\)

    • I believe the \(d_{\text {head}}\) is the output dim of each head.
    • This just says the total output dim for \(n\) heads is the same as if we did one head.
    • Means there is something important about splitting up the heads.

    Rule 3. Aspect ratio = \(\frac {d_{\text {model}}}{n_{\text {layer}}} \approx 100-200\)

    • Pipeline dependent: if network speed is fast than parallelizing is easier and shallow networks are better.
    • If poor network speed then pipeline parallel might be more viable and deeper networks would be more parallelizable.

    Rule 4. Vocab size

    • For single language models, vocab size is typically \(30-50k\)
    • For multi language models, vocab size is typically \(100-250k\)

    Definition. Rotation matrix [10H9]

    • July 14, 2025
    • Kellen Kanarios

    A rotation matrix is a linear transformation that rotates a vector \(v\) by an angle \(\theta \) via the transformation \[\mathbf {R} = \begin {bmatrix} \cos \theta & - \sin \theta \\ \sin \theta & \cos \theta \end {bmatrix} \]

    The transformation can be easily understood by noting where it maps the basis vectors. Namely, \[\mathbf {R} \mathbf {e}_1 = \begin {bmatrix} \cos \theta \\ \sin \theta \end {bmatrix}, \quad \mathbf {R} \mathbf {e}_2 = \begin {bmatrix} -\sin \theta \\ \cos \theta \end {bmatrix}\]

    Definition. Field [X9AO]

    • July 14, 2025
    • Kellen Kanarios

    A field is a set \(F\) together with two binary operations on \(F\): \(+\) and \(\cdot \), where a binary operation is a mapping \(F \times F \to F\). These operations are defined by the following axioms

    • Associativity of addition and multiplication: \(a + (b + c) = (a + b) + c\), and \(a \cdot (b \cdot c) = (a \cdot b) \cdot c\).
    • Commutativity of addition and multiplication: \(a + b = b + a\), and \(a \cdot b = b \cdot a\).
    • Additive and multiplicative identity: there exist two distinct elements 0 and 1 in \(F\) such that \(a + 0 = a\) and \(a \cdot 1 = a\).
    • Additive inverses: for every \(a\) in \(F\), there exists an element in \(F\), denoted \(-a\), called the additive inverse of a, such that \(a + (-a) = 0\).
    • Multiplicative inverses: for every \(a \neq 0\) in \(F\), there exists an element in \(F\), denoted by \(a^{-1}\) or \(1/a\), called the multiplicative inverse of \(a\), such that \(a \cdot a^{-1} = 1\).
    • Distributivity of multiplication over addition: \(a \cdot (b + c) = (a \cdot b) + (a \cdot c)\).

    Definition. Inner Product [B1RI]

    • July 14, 2025
    • Kellen Kanarios

    Given a vector space \(V\) and a field \(F\). An inner product is a map \[\langle \cdot , \cdot \rangle : V \times V \to F\] that satisfies the following three properties:

    • Conjugate symmetry: \(\langle \mathbf {x}, \mathbf {y} \rangle = \overline {\langle \mathbf {y}, \mathbf {x}\rangle }\)
    • Linearity in the first argument: \(\langle a\mathbf {x} + b\mathbf {y}, \mathbf {z} \rangle = a\langle \mathbf {x}, \mathbf {z} \rangle + b \langle \mathbf {y}, \mathbf {z} \rangle \)
    • Positive-definiteness: If \(\mathbf {x}\) is not zero, then \(\langle \mathbf {x}, \mathbf {x} \rangle > 0\)

    Rotary Position Embeddings (ROPE) [TOD6]

    • July 14, 2025
    • Kellen Kanarios
    Notation. For this section, our notion of an embedding is a function \(f\) that takes a token and a position i.e. \(f(x, i)\) is the embedding of token \(x\), occurring at position \(i\).
    Insight. The inner product of two embeddings should only need relative positioning i.e. for any two \(\mathbf {x}\), \(\mathbf {y}\) with positions \(i\) and \(j\) respectively, there should exist some \(g\), such that \[\langle f(\mathbf {x}, i), f(\mathbf {y}, j) \rangle = g(\mathbf {x}, \mathbf {y}, i - j)\] Namely, this can be written as a function of just the relative positioning between the embeddings.

    The simplest transformation that only preserves this relative information are rotations.

    However, rotations are only easily defined for \(\mathbb {R}^2\). To get around this, they simply partition their input 2d slices and apply the rotation via \[\mathrm {ROT} = \begin {bmatrix} \cos m \theta _{1} & - \sin m \theta _{1} & & & \\ \sin m \theta _{1} & \cos m \theta _{1} & & & \\ & & \cos m \theta _{2} & -\sin m \theta _{2} & \\ & & \sin m \theta _{2} & \cos m \theta _{2} & \\ & & & & \ddots \end {bmatrix} \]

    Remark. The \(\theta _i\)'s are fixed and chosen according to some schedule to capture different "frequencies".

    The embedding are used by appling them to the query and key matrices separately i.e. \[W_K = \mathrm {ROT}(W_K), \quad W_Q = \mathrm {ROT}(W_Q)\] These are then what is used in self-attention.

    Definition. Gated Linear Unit (GLU) [K2N7]

    • July 14, 2025
    • Kellen Kanarios

    A gated linear unit is an activation function combined with an elementwise multiplication i.e.

    • \(\mathrm {ReGLU} = \mathrm {ReLU}(\mathbf {x}) \otimes \mathbf {V} \mathbf {x},\)
    • \(\mathrm {SwiGLU} = \mathrm {Swish}(\mathbf {x}) \otimes \mathbf {V} \mathbf {x},\)
    where \(\mathrm {ReLU}\) is the ReLU activation and \(\mathrm {Swish}\) is the Swish activation respectively.

    Remark. The matrix \(\mathbf {V}\) introduces additional learnable parameters. Therefore, an architecture that uses gating typically reduces their other parameters by a factor of \(\frac {2}{3}\).

    Card. Gating splits the up-projection in two [Y4Y8]

    • August 18, 2026
    • Kellen Kanarios

    For one Transformer layer with a gated MLP, what are the parameter count and training FLOPs — and why is the coefficient three rather than two?

    Answer Parameters: \(3DF\), from \(W_{in1}[D,F]\), \(W_{in2}[D,F]\), \(W_{out}[F,D]\). Training FLOPs: \(18BTDF\) — three matmuls at \(6BTDF\) each, by the \(6NPM\) rule. Where the third matrix comes from. A Gated Linear Unit (GLU) splits the up-projection into two matrices whose outputs are multiplied elementwise, \(\sigma (AW_{in1}) \odot (AW_{in2})\), so one of them acts as a gate on the other. LLaMA, DeepSeek and most current models do this. A non-gated MLP has a single \(W_{in}\) and so \(2DF\) params — and typically scales \(D\) and \(F\) up to compensate, which is why the two families cost about the same at equal quality. The gate itself is \(O(BTF)\) — elementwise, no contraction, and negligible against \(BTDF\).

    Definition. Sigmoid [NNDS]

    • July 14, 2025
    • Kellen Kanarios

    The sigmoid function is given by \[s(\mathbf {x}) = \frac {1}{1 + e^{-x}}\]

    Definition. Swish Activation [OZD8]

    • July 14, 2025
    • Kellen Kanarios

    The Swish activation is given by \[\mathrm {Swish}(\mathbf {x}) : \mathbb {R}^d \to \mathbb {R}^d, \quad \mathbf {x} \mapsto \mathbf {x} s(\mathbf {x}),\] where \(s : \mathbb {R}^d \to \mathbb {R}^d\) is the sigmoid function.

    Definition. Gaussian Error Linear Unit (GELU) [5SPM]

    • July 14, 2025
    • Kellen Kanarios

    The Gaussian Error Linear Unit (GELU) is a slight modification to the ReLU to account for the non-differentiability at \(0\). Namely, \[\mathrm {GELU}(\mathbf {x}) : \mathbb {R}^d \to \mathbb {R}^d, \quad \mathbf {x} \mapsto \mathbf {x} \cdot \psi (\mathbf {x}),\] where \(\psi (\mathbf {x}) = \mathrm {CDF}(\mathcal {N}(\mathbf {x}, \mathbf {I}))\)

    Definition. Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU) [BEA2]

    • July 14, 2025
    • Kellen Kanarios

    The rectified linear unit(ReLU) is defined as \[\mathrm {ReLU} : \mathbb {R}^d \to \mathbb {R}^d, \quad \mathbf {x} \mapsto \max (0, \mathbf {x}),\] where the \(\max \) is done elementwise i.e. \(\mathrm {ReLU}(\mathbf {x})_i = \max (0, x_i)\) This provides "nice" gradients, making it common when training neural networks.

    Definition. RMS Norm [1XNO]

    • July 14, 2025
    • Kellen Kanarios

    The RMS norm is simply the layer norm without the added bias term and centering i.e. \[\mathrm {RMSNorm}: \mathbb {R}^d \to \mathbb {R}^d, \quad \mathbf {x} \mapsto \frac {\mathbf {x}}{\sqrt {\mathrm {Var}[\mathbf {x}_i] + \epsilon }}*\gamma .\] This is used to spare memory movement of layernorm, where the bias term \(\beta \in \mathbb {R}^d\) and has been found to be empirically almost if not as good.

    Definition. Layer Normalization [LVV4]

    • July 14, 2025
    • Kellen Kanarios

    While training a neural network, a common stabilization trick is to apply a normalization to the output. This is done via \[\mathrm {LN}: \mathbb {R}^d \to \mathbb {R}^d, \quad \mathbf {x} \mapsto \frac {\mathbf {x} - \mathbb {E}[\mathbf {x}_i]}{\sqrt {\mathrm {Var}[\mathbf {x}_i] + \epsilon }}*\gamma + \beta ,\] Here \(\mathbf {x}\) is the output of a layer i.e. \(\mathbf {x}^{\ell } = W^{\ell } f(\mathbf {x}^{\ell - 1})\). The purpose of this is to stabilize weight changes in previous layers and their affect on later layers.

    Remark. Batch normalization is the same idea, where the expectation is taken over the samples \(\mathbf {x}^{(i)}\) rather than the components of one sample \(\mathbf {x}_i\). This gives layer normalization the added benefit of being viable for one sample and inference.

    Norms [7JRP]

    • July 16, 2026
    • Kellen Kanarios

    Pre-norm vs. Post-norm. The first architecture variation discussed is when to apply the layer norm. As can be seen in the figure below, rather than apply the layer norm in the residual stream. They instead place it before the FFN and MHA layers.

    They actually found that adding layer normalization before and after the MHA and FFN works the best. This is known as double norm.

    RMSNorm vs. LayerNorm. Another useful trick is to use the RMSNorm instead of LayerNorm.

    Definition. RMS Norm [1XNO]

    • July 14, 2025
    • Kellen Kanarios

    The RMS norm is simply the layer norm without the added bias term and centering i.e. \[\mathrm {RMSNorm}: \mathbb {R}^d \to \mathbb {R}^d, \quad \mathbf {x} \mapsto \frac {\mathbf {x}}{\sqrt {\mathrm {Var}[\mathbf {x}_i] + \epsilon }}*\gamma .\] This is used to spare memory movement of layernorm, where the bias term \(\beta \in \mathbb {R}^d\) and has been found to be empirically almost if not as good.

    One might wonder if matrix multiplies are the only thing that matters what can such a small change really accomplish.

    • Due to memory movement, despite being .17% of FLOPS, provided 25% speedup in runtime!!
    Remark. Most people apparently just drop the bias term and keep the centering i.e. subtracting the mean. This makes sense because computing the mean does not require loading any additional information back to memory.

    Computing FFN and MHA in parallel is free speedup [ZAR4]

    • July 16, 2026
    • Kellen Kanarios

    Another small trick is to parallelize computation. Traditionally, one computes the \(\mathrm {MHA}\) output and then passes this to the \(\mathrm {FFN}\) i.e. \[\mathbf {y} = \mathbf {x} + \mathrm {FFN}(\mathrm {LN}(\mathbf {x} + \mathrm {MHA}(\mathrm {LN}(\mathbf {x})))).\] However, this requires waiting for the \(\mathrm {MHA}\) to complete before performing the \(\mathrm {FFN}\) computation. It has been found that performing these in parallel does not cause any severe degradation in performance. Explicitly, instead they do \[\mathbf {y} = \mathbf {x} + \mathrm {FFN}(\mathrm {LN}(\mathbf {x})) + \mathrm {MHA}(\mathrm {LN}(\mathbf {x}))\]

    Question. What is the role of weight decay in training large models? [U52K]

    • July 16, 2026
    • Kellen Kanarios

    Since there is so much data, it is not feasible to train your model for multiple epochs. This is actually nice in the sense that we do not have to worry about overfitting and performing regularization.

    However, many of the large models are still trained with weight decay. Tatsu claims that this is not to do with regularization but actually due to some weird interaction with the learning rate schedule. I am not sure I entirely understood this part.

    Definition. Flow Matching Loss [LRL4]

    • July 9, 2025
    • Kellen Kanarios

    Given an initial noise distribution \(p\), a desired data distribution \(q\), a probability density path \(p_t\), such that \(p_{0} = p\) and \(p_{1} =q\), and a vector field \(u_t\) that generates \(p_t\). We define the flow matching loss \(\mathcal {L}_{\mathrm {FM}}\) as \[\mathcal {L}_{\mathrm {FM}}(\theta ) \coloneqq \mathbb {E}_{t, p_t(x)} \|v_t(x; \theta ) - u_t\|\]

    Definition. Smooth Manifold [0073]

    • April 14, 2025
    • Kellen Kanarios

    We say \( \mathcal {M}\subseteq \mathbb {R}^{n} \) is an embedded smooth submanifold of codimension \( k \) if there exists a smooth function \( g:\mathbb {R}^{n}\mapsto \mathbb {R}^{k} \), such that \[ \mathcal {M}\equiv \left \{\boldsymbol {x}\in \mathbb {R}^{n}\mid g(\boldsymbol {x})=\boldsymbol {0}\right \}, \] \[ \mathrm {D}g(\boldsymbol {x}):\mathbb {R}^{n}\mapsto \mathbb {R}^{k}\text { has rank }k,\ \forall \boldsymbol {x}\in \mathcal {M}. \]

    Definition. Riemannian Manifold [0072]

    • April 14, 2025
    • Kellen Kanarios

    A Riemannian manifold \( (\mathcal {M},\langle \cdot ,\cdot \rangle ) \) is a smooth manifold \( \mathcal {M} \) equipped with positive-definite inner product \( \langle \cdot ,\cdot \rangle \) on the tangent space \( \mathrm {T}_{\pmb {x}}\mathcal {M} \) at each point \( \pmb {x}\in \mathcal {M} \).

    Definition. Tangent Space [0075]

    • April 14, 2025
    • Kellen Kanarios

    The tangent space \( \mathrm {T}_{\pmb {x}}\mathcal {M} \) at a point \( \pmb {x}\in \mathcal {M} \) is defined as \[T_x \mathcal {M} = \ker Dg(\mathbf {x})\] which is a linear subspace of \( \mathbb {R}^{n} \).

    Definition. Tangent Bundle [0074]

    • April 14, 2025
    • Kellen Kanarios

    The tangent bundle of \( {\cal M} \) is the disjoint union of all tangent spaces: \[ {\rm T}{\cal M}\ =\ \{(\mathbf {x},\mathbf {v})\ \mid \ \mathbf {x}\in {\cal M},\ {\rm and}\ \mathbf {v}\in {\rm T}_{\mathbf {x}}{\cal M}\} \]

    Definition. Retraction [0076]

    • April 14, 2025
    • Kellen Kanarios

    A retraction is a smooth map \( R:\mathrm {T}\mathcal {M}\mapsto \mathcal {M} \) such that if \( h(t)=R(\mathbf {x},t\mathbf {v})=R_{\mathbf {x}}(t\mathbf {v}) \), then \( h(0)=\mathbf {x} \) and \( h^{\prime }(0)=\mathbf {v} \).

    Definition. Riemannian Metric [0079]

    • April 14, 2025
    • Kellen Kanarios

    A choice of inner product \(\langle \cdot , \cdot \rangle _x\) for each tangent space \(\mathrm {T}_x \mathcal {M}\) defines a Riemannian metric on \(\mathcal {M}\).

    Claim. Riemmanian Metric [0078]

    • April 14, 2025
    • Kellen Kanarios

    \( \langle \cdot ,\cdot \rangle _{\textbf {x}} \) defines a Riemmanian Metric on \( \mathcal {M} \) if for any two smooth vector fields \(\mathbf {V}\) and \(\mathbf {W}\), the function \( \textbf {x}\mapsto \left \langle \mathbf {V}(\textbf {x}),\mathbf {W}(\textbf {x})\right \rangle _{\textbf {x}} \) is smooth.

    Definition. Riemannian Gradient [0077]

    • April 14, 2025
    • Kellen Kanarios

    Let \( f:\mathcal {M}\mapsto \mathbb {R} \) be smooth on the Riemannian manifold \( \mathcal {M} \). The Riemannian gradient \( \,\operatorname {grad}f(\boldsymbol {x})\, \) of \( f \) at \( \boldsymbol {x}\in \mathcal {M} \) is the unique tangent vector at \( \boldsymbol {x} \) such that \[ \mathrm {D}f(\boldsymbol {x})[\boldsymbol {v}]\ =\ \langle \operatorname {grad}f(\boldsymbol {x}),\boldsymbol {v}\rangle _{\boldsymbol {x}}\,,\quad \forall \,\boldsymbol {v}\in \mathrm {T}_{\boldsymbol {x}}\mathcal {M}. \] By extending the definition of \( f \) to the ambient Euclidean space \( \mathbb {R}^{n} \), we can show that \[\mathrm {grad} f(\mathbf {x}) = \mathcal {P}_{T_x \mathcal {M}}(\nabla f(\mathbf {x}))\] where \( {\mathcal {P}}_{\mathrm {T}_{\mathbf {x}}\mathcal {M}}\) is the orthogonal projector from \(\mathbb {R}^n\) to \(T_x \mathcal {M}\)

    Definition. Riemannian Hessian [007A]

    • April 14, 2025
    • Kellen Kanarios

    Let \( f:{\cal M}\mapsto \mathbb {R} \) be smooth on the Riemannian Manifold \( {\cal M} \). The Riemannian Hessian \( {\rm Hess}\,f(\mathbf {x}):{\rm T}_{\mathbf {x}}{\cal M}\mapsto {\rm T}_{\mathbf {x}}{\cal M} \) of \( f \) at \( \mathbf {x}\in {\cal M} \) is a mapping from \( {\rm T}_{\mathbf {x}}{\cal M} \) to \( {\rm T}_{\mathbf {x}}{\cal M} \) with \[ {\rm Hess}\,f(\mathbf {x})[\mathbf {v}]\ :=\ \widetilde {\nabla }_{\mathbf {v}}\,{\rm grad}\,f(\mathbf {x}). \]

    • Here, \(\tilde {\nabla }\) is the Riemannian connection.
    • On a Riemannian submanifold embedded in \(\mathbb {R}^n\) \[\tilde {\nabla }_{\mathbf {u}} V = \mathcal {P}_{T_{\mathbf {x}} \mathcal {M}}(\mathrm {D}V(\mathbf {x})[\mathbf {u}])\] and \[\mathrm {Hess}\,f(\mathbf {x})[\mathbf {v}]\ =\ {\mathcal {P}}_{\mathrm {T}_{\mathbf {x}}{\mathcal {M}}}\,(\mathrm {D}\,\mathrm {grad}\,f(\mathbf {x})[\mathbf {v}])\]

    Definition. Riemannian Gradient Descent [007B]

    • April 14, 2025
    • Kellen Kanarios

    For \(f : \mathcal {M} \mapsto \mathbb {R}\), \[ x_{k+1}\ =\ R_{{\mathbf {x}}_{k}}(-\tau _{k}\operatorname {grad}f({\mathbf {x}}_{k})) \]

    Can do backtracking line search i.e. while \[f(R_{x_{k}}(-\tau \,{\rm grad}\,f(\mathbf {x}_{k}))) > f(\mathbf {x}_{k}) - c_{1}\tau \, | |{\rm grad}\,f(\mathbf {x}_{k})| |_{2}^{2} \] do \[ \tau \ \leftarrow \ \alpha \cdot \tau \]

    Newton and Quasi-Newton Method [DERA]

    • July 6, 2025
    • Kellen Kanarios

    Newton's Method [004V]

    • February 3, 2025
    • Kellen Kanarios

    Consider second-order taylor approximation of \(f\) \[ f(\mathbf {x}_{k}+\mathbf {d})\ \approx \ \underbrace {f(\mathbf {x}_{k})+\mathbf {d}^{\top }\nabla f(\mathbf {x}_{k})+{\frac {1}{2}}\mathbf {d}^{\top }\nabla ^{2}f(\mathbf {x}_{k})\mathbf {d}}_{Q_k( \mathbf {d})}\] Then setting \(\nabla Q_k( \mathbf {d})\) and solving for \(\mathbf {d}\), we get \[ \nabla f( \mathbf {x}_k) + \frac {1}{2}\nabla ^2 f( \mathbf {x}_k) \mathbf {d} = 0 \] Thus, take Newton's direction \[\mathbf {d}_{k}^{N}=-\left (\nabla ^{2}f(\mathbf {x}_{k})\right )^{-1}\nabla f(\mathbf {x}_{k}).\]

    Remark. Some notes
    • Fast convergence. Newton's method usually has local quadratic convergence.
    • Expensive. requires storing and inverting \(\nabla ^2 f( \mathbf {x})\).
    • Unstable. \(\nabla ^2 f \succ 0\) might not hold for general nonlinear problems.

    Quasi-Newton's Method [004W]

    • February 3, 2025
    • Kellen Kanarios

    Get around computing and inverting hessian by using a surrogate i.e. \[\mathbf {d}_{k}^{QN}=-\underbrace {\mathbf {H}_k}_{\text {surrogate for } \left (\nabla ^{2}f(\mathbf {x}_{k})\right )^{-1}} \nabla f(\mathbf {x}_{k}).\] Want \[{\mathbf {H}}_{k+1}^{-1}\cdot \underbrace {({\mathbf {x}}_{k+1}-{\mathbf {x}}_{k})}_{{\mathbf {s}}_{k}}\;=\;\underbrace {\nabla f({\mathbf {x}}_{k+1})-\nabla f({\mathbf {x}}_{k})}_{{\mathbf {y}}_{k}}\] BFGS rank-2 update: \[{\mathbf {H}}_{k+1}\ =\ {\mathbf {H}}_{k}+{\frac {\left ({\mathbf {s}}_{k}^{\top }{\mathbf {y}}_{k}+{\mathbf {y}}_{k}^{\top }{\mathbf {H}}_{k}{\mathbf {y}}_{k}\right ){\mathbf {s}}_{k}{\mathbf {s}}_{k}^{\top }}{\left ({\mathbf {s}}_{k}^{\top }{\mathbf {y}}_{k}\right )^{2}}}-{\frac {{\mathbf {H}}_{k}{\mathbf {y}}_{k}{\mathbf {s}}_{k}^{\top }+{\mathbf {s}}_{k}{\mathbf {y}}_{k}^{\top }{\mathbf {H}}_{k}}{{\mathbf {s}}_{k}^{\top }{\mathbf {y}}_{k}}}\]

    How function properties affect convergence [DER9]

    Theorem. Linear convergence for strong convexity [004U]

    • February 3, 2025
    • Kellen Kanarios

    Let \(f:\mathbb {R}^{n}\mapsto \mathbb {R}\) be smooth and \(\mu \)-strongly convex, and suppose its gradient \(\nabla f(\mathbf {x})\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz. Choose a fixed step size \(\tau _{k}\equiv \tau =\frac {2}{\mu +L}\), then \[\left ||\mathbf {x}_{k}-\mathbf {x}_{\star }\right ||_{2}\ \leq \ \left (\frac {\kappa -1}{\kappa +1}\right )^{k}\left ||\mathbf {x}_{0}-\mathbf {x}_{\star }\right ||_{2},\] where \(\kappa =\frac {L}{\mu }\) is the condition number, and \(\mathbf {x}_{\star }\) is the minimizer.

    Remark. Strong convexity is a sufficient but not necessary condition for linear convergene of gradient descent.

    Definition. Exact Linesearch [004Q]

    • February 3, 2025
    • Kellen Kanarios

    For \[x_{k+1}\ =\ x_{k}\ -\ \tau _{k}\cdot \nabla f(x_{k})\] Choose step size by solving \[\tau _{k}\;=\;\arg \operatorname *{min}_{t\geq 0}\;f({\mathbf {x}}_{k}-t\cdot \nabla f({\mathbf {x}}_{k}))\]

    Remark. Way to computationally expensive to use in practice.

    Definition. Armijo Condition [004R]

    • February 3, 2025
    • Kellen Kanarios

    For some \(c_1 \in (0,1)\), \[f( \mathbf {x}_k + \tau _k \cdot \mathbf {d}_k) < f( \mathbf {x}_k) + c_1 \cdot \tau _k \cdot \mathbf {d}_{k}^{\top } \nabla f(\mathbf {x}_k)\]

    Definition. Wolfe condition [004S]

    • February 3, 2025
    • Kellen Kanarios

    For some \(0 < c_1 < c_2 < 1\), \[f(\mathbf {x}_{k}+\tau _{k}\cdot \mathbf {d}_{k})\ <\ f(\mathbf {x}_{k})+c_{1}\cdot \tau _{k}\cdot \mathbf {d}_{k}^{\intercal }\nabla f(\mathbf {x}_{k})\] \[d_{k}^{\top }\nabla f({\mathbf {x}}_{k}+\tau _{k}{\mathbf {d}}_{k})\ \geq \ c_{2}{\mathbf {d}}_{k}^{\top }\nabla f({\mathbf {x}}_{k})\]

    Remark. Wolfe condition requires evaluating gradient of function each update to \(\tau _k\). However, Armijo Condition only requires evaluating gradient once. Therefore, it is primarily used in practice.
    Remark. Backtracking is not used in optimizing DNNs because even function evaluation is very expensive.

    Theorem. Convergence of GD with backtracking [004T]

    • February 3, 2025
    • Kellen Kanarios

    Let the function \(f(\pmb {x})\) be \(\mu \)-strongly convex and \(L\)-smooth. With backtracking linesearch, the GD method converges with \[f(\pmb {x}_k)-f(\pmb {x}_\star )\ \le \ \left (1-\min \left \{2c_1\mu ,\dfrac {2\alpha c_1\mu }{L}\right \}\right )^k(f(\pmb {x}_0)-f(\pmb {x}_\star ))\] where \(\pmb {x}_\star \) is the unique minimizer.

    Accelerated Gradient Descent [DER7]

    • July 6, 2025
    • Kellen Kanarios

    Nesterov's Method [004O]

    • February 3, 2025
    • Kellen Kanarios

    Generate two sequences \(\{\mathbf {x}_{k}\}_{k\geq 1}{\mathrm {~and~}}\{\mathbf {p}_{k}\}_{k\geq 1}\) \[ \begin {align*} {\mathbf {\mathit {p}}}_{k+1}\ &=\ {\mathbf {\mathit {x}}}_{k}\ +\ \beta _{k}\cdot ({\mathbf {\mathit {x}}}_{k}-{\mathbf {\mathit {x}}}_{k-1}), \\ x_{k+1} &= p_{k+1}-\alpha \nabla f(p_{k+1}) \end {align*} \]

    • Not a descent method.
    • With properly chosen \(\alpha \) and \(\beta \) can achieve optimal convergence rate \(O(1/k^2)\)

    Theorem. Convergence of accelerated GD [004P]

    • February 3, 2025
    • Kellen Kanarios

    Suppose \(f:\mathbb {R}^{n}\mapsto \mathbb {R}\) is convex and smooth with its gradient \(L\)-Lipschitz. The iterates \(\{\mathbf {x}_{k}\}_{k\geq 1}\) generated by the accelerated GD method satisfy \[f(\mathbf {x}_{k})-f(\mathbf {x}_{\star })\ \leq \ \frac {L}{2(k+1)^{2}}\ ||\mathbf {x}_{0}-\mathbf {x}_{\star }||_{2}^{2}\ =\ O(\frac {1}{k^{2}}).\] Moreover, as \(k\to +\infty \), then \(\mathbf {x}_{k}\to \mathbf {x}_{\star }\).

    Convergence of Gradient Descent [DER6]

    • July 6, 2025
    • Kellen Kanarios

    Lemma. Sufficient Value [004L]

    • February 3, 2025
    • Kellen Kanarios

    With step size \(\tau _{k}=1/L\,,\) the gradient descent iterates \(\{\mathbf {x}_{k}\}_{k\geq 1}\) generated by \[\mathbf {x}_{k+1}\ =\ \mathbf {x}_{k}\ -\ \tau _{k}\cdot \nabla f(\mathbf {x}_{k})\] satisfy the following: \[f(\mathbf {x}_{k+1})\ \leq \ f(\mathbf {x}_{k})\ -\ \frac {1}{2L}\,||\nabla f(\mathbf {x}_{k})||_{2}^{2}\] \[<\ f(\mathbf {x}_{k})\quad (||\nabla f(\mathbf {x}_{k})||_{2}\neq 0)\]

    Proof. Because \(\nabla f\) is Lipschitz, by 1st-order Taylor approximation \[f(\mathbf {x}^{\prime })\leq f(\mathbf {x})+\langle \nabla f(\mathbf {x}),\mathbf {x}^{\prime }-\mathbf {x}\rangle +\frac {L}{2}\left ||\mathbf {x}^{\prime }-\mathbf {x}\right ||_{2}^{2},\quad \forall \ \mathbf {x}^{\prime },\mathbf {x}\] Now take \(\mathbf {x}' = \mathbf {x} - \tau \nabla f( \mathbf {x})\). Then \[ \begin {align*} f(\mathbf {x}^{\prime }) &\leq f(\mathbf {x})+ \tau ||\nabla f( \mathbf {x} )||_2^2 + \frac {\tau ^2 L}{2} ||\nabla f( \mathbf {x})||_2^2 \\ &= f( \mathbf {x}) - \tau (1 - \frac {\tau L}{2})||\nabla f( \mathbf {x})||_2^2 \end {align*} \] Take \(\tau = \frac {1}{L}\), such that \[ \begin {align*} f( \mathbf {x}) - \tau (1 - \frac {\tau L}{2})||\nabla f( \mathbf {x})||_2^2 &= f( \mathbf {x}) - \frac {1}{2L}||\nabla f( \mathbf {x})||_2^2 \end {align*} \]

    Theorem. Sublinear convergence of GD [004M]

    • February 3, 2025
    • Kellen Kanarios

    Suppose \(f:\mathbb {R}^{n}\mapsto \mathbb {R}\) is convex and smooth with its gradient \(L\)-Lipschitz. If we run GD for \(k\) iterations with a fixed step size \(\tau =1/L\), it will yield a sequence \(\left \{\mathbf {x}_{k}\right \}_{k\geq 1}\) such that \[f(\mathbf {x}_{k})-f(\mathbf {x}_{\star })\ \leq \ \frac {L}{2k}\left ||\mathbf {x}_{0}-\mathbf {x}_{\star }\right ||_{2}^{2}\ =\ O(\frac {1}{k}),\] Moreover, as \(k\to +\infty \), then \(\mathbf {x}_{k}\to \mathbf {x}_{\star }\).

    Proof. Given \(f\) is convex and smooth, and \(\mathbf {x}_*\) is an optimal solution, then \[f(\mathbf {x}_{\star })\geq f(\mathbf {x})+\nabla f(\mathbf {x})^{\top }(\mathbf {x}_{\star }-\mathbf {x})\] Flipping the inequality yields \[f(\mathbf {x})\leq f(\mathbf {x}_{\star })+\nabla f(\mathbf {x})^{\top }(\mathbf {x}-\mathbf {x}_{\star })\] By previous lemma, taking \(\mathbf {x}' = \mathbf {x} - \frac {1}{L} \nabla f( \mathbf {x})\) yields \[f(\mathbf {x}^{\prime })\leq f(\mathbf {x})-{\frac {1}{2L}}\left ||\nabla f(\mathbf {x})\right ||_{2}^{2}\] such that \[f(\mathbf {x}^{\prime })\leq f(\mathbf {x}_{\star })+\nabla f(\mathbf {x})^{\top }(\mathbf {x}-\mathbf {x}_{\star })-{\frac {1}{2L}}\left ||\nabla f(\mathbf {x})\right ||_{2}^{2}\] Equivalently, \[f(\mathbf {x}^{\prime })-f(\mathbf {x}_{\star })\leq {\frac {L}{2}}\left [{\frac {2}{L}}\nabla f(\mathbf {x})^{\top }(\mathbf {x}-\mathbf {x}_{\star })-{\frac {1}{L^{2}}}\left ||\nabla f(\mathbf {x})\right ||_{2}^{2}\right ]\] Completing the square, \[ \begin {align*} f(\mathbf {x}^{\prime })-f(\mathbf {x}_{\star })&\leq \frac {L}{2}\left [\frac {2}{L}\nabla f(\mathbf {x})^{\top }(\mathbf {x}-\mathbf {x}_{\star })-\frac {1}{L^{2}}\left ||\nabla f(\mathbf {x})\right ||_{2}^{2}\right ] \\ &=\frac {L}{2}\left [\left ||\mathbf {x}-\mathbf {x}_{\star }\right ||_{2}^{2}-\left ||\mathbf {x}-\frac {1}{L}\nabla f(\mathbf {x})-\mathbf {x}_{\star }\right ||_{2}^{2}\right ] \\ &=\frac {L}{2}\left [\left ||\mathbf {x}-\mathbf {x}_{\star }\right ||_{2}^{2}-\left ||\mathbf {x}^{\prime }-\mathbf {x}_{\star }\right ||_{2}^{2}\right ] \end {align*} \] Let \(\mathbf {x}_{k}=\mathbf {x}_{k-1}-\frac {1}{L}\nabla f(\mathbf {x}_{k-1})\), then we have \[ \begin {align*} \sum _{i=1}^{k}\left (f(\mathbf {x}_{i})-f(\mathbf {x}_{\star })\right ) &\leq \frac {L}{2}\sum _{i=1}^{k}\left [\left ||\mathbf {x}_{i-1}-\mathbf {x}_{\star }\right ||_{2}^{2}-\left ||\mathbf {x}_{i}-\mathbf {x}_{\star }\right ||_{2}^{2}\right ] \\ &=\frac {L}{2}\left [\left ||\mathbf {x}_{0}-\mathbf {x}_{\star }\right ||_{2}^{2}-\left ||\mathbf {x}_{k}-\mathbf {x}_{0}\right ||_{2}^{2}\right ] \\ &\leq \frac {L}{2}\left ||\mathbf {x}_{0}-\mathbf {x}_{\star }\right ||_{2}^{2} \end {align*} \] Therefore, given \(f(\mathbf {x}_{k})-f(\mathbf {x}_{\star })\leq f(\mathbf {x}_{i})-f(\mathbf {x}_{*}) \text { for } \forall i\leq k\,,\) \[k\left (f(\mathbf {x}_{k})-f(\mathbf {x}_{\star })\right )\leq \sum _{i=1}^{k}\left (f(\mathbf {x}_{i})-f(\mathbf {x}_{\star })\right )\leq \frac {L}{2}\left ||\mathbf {x}_{0}-\mathbf {x}_{\star }\right ||_{2}^{2}\]

    Theorem. Suboptimality of Gradient Descent [004N]

    • February 3, 2025
    • Kellen Kanarios

    Suppose the iterates \(\{\mathbf {x}_{i}\}_{i\geq 0}\) is generated from a black-box model: \[\mathbf {x}_{k+1}\ =\ \mathcal {F}_{k}\left (\left \{\mathbf {x}_{i}\right \}_{i=0}^{k},\ \left \{f(\mathbf {x}_{i})\right \}_{i=0}^{k},\ \left \{\nabla f(\mathbf {x}_{i})\right \}_{i=0}^{k}\right )\]

    For every positive \(L\) and \(R\), there exists a convex differentiable \(f\) with \(\nabla f\) \(L\)-Lipschitz, and an initial point \(\mathbf {x}_{0}\) satisfying \(||\mathbf {x}_{0}-\mathbf {x}_{\star }||_{2}\leq R\), such that \[f(\mathbf {x}_{k})-f(\mathbf {x}_{\star })\ \geq \ c\frac {LR}{k^{2}}\ =\ \Omega (\frac {1}{k^{2}}),\] where \(\ c>0\) is some numerical constant.

    Rate of Convergence [DER5]

    • July 6, 2025
    • Kellen Kanarios

    Want to find \[\operatorname *{min}_{\mathbf {x}}\ f(\mathbf {x}),\quad \text {s.t.}\quad \mathbf {x}\ \in \ \mathcal {C}.\] Solve the problem via iterative methods of optimization, which produce a sequence of points \[\mathbf {x}_{1},\ \mathbf {x}_{2},\ \cdots ,\mathbf {x}_{k},\cdots \] starting from an initialization \(\mathbf {x}_{0}\).

    Definition. First-order convergence [003R]

    • January 27, 2025
    • Kellen Kanarios

    First-order function value convergence \[||\nabla f(\mathbf {x}_k)||_2 \; \leq \; \varepsilon .\]

    • For convex functions, this also means convergence to the global minimizer
    • For nonconvex functions, this only means convergence to a Stationary point (e.g., a local minimizer or a saddle point).

    Definition. \(Q\)-convergence [003Q]

    • January 27, 2025
    • Kellen Kanarios

    We say the \(Q\)-convergence is of order \((p \geq 1)\) and with factor \((\gamma > 0)\), if \(\exists k_{0}\), such that \(\forall k\geq k_{0}\): \[\boxed {\min _{\mathbf {x_{*}}\in \mathcal {X}}||\mathbf {x_{k}}-\mathbf {x_{*}}||_{2}\ \leq \ \gamma \cdot \left (\min _{\mathbf {x_{*}}\in \mathcal {X}}||\mathbf {x_{k-1}}-\mathbf {x_{*}}||_{2}\right )^{p}.}\]

    Definition. \(R\)-convergence [003S]

    • January 27, 2025
    • Kellen Kanarios

    We say the \(R\)-convergence is of order \(p\;(\geq 1)\), \[\min _{\mathbf {x}_{*}\in \mathcal {X}}||\mathbf {x}_{k}-\mathbf {x}_{*}||_{2}\;\leq \;\rho _{k},\] if the sequence \(\{\rho _{k}\}_{k\geq 1}\) is \(Q\)-convergence of the order \(p\).

    Constrained Optimality [DER4]

    • July 6, 2025
    • Kellen Kanarios

    Consider a smooth contained problem with \[\min _{\mathbf {x}}f(\mathbf {x}),\quad \text {s.t.} \quad r_{i}(\mathbf {x})\ =\ 0,\ 1\leq i\leq p,\] \[h_{j}(\mathbf {x})\ \leq \ 0,\ 1\leq j\leq q.\] Consider its Lagrangian function \[\mathscr {L}(\mathbf {x},\mathbf {u},\mathbf {v})\ =\ f(\mathbf {x})+\sum _{i=1}^{p}u_{i}\cdot r_{i}(\mathbf {x})+\sum _{j=1}^{q}v_{j}\cdot h_{j}(\mathbf {x}).\]

    Definition. KKT Conditions [4IPN]

    • Kellen Kanarios
    • Stationary \[\nabla _{\mathbf {x}}{\mathcal {L}}(\mathbf {x_*},\mathbf {u_*},\mathbf {v_*})\;=\;\mathbf {0}\]
    • Primal Feasibility: \[\begin {array}{l}{{r_{i}(x_{\star })\ =\ 0,\ 1\leq i\leq p,}}\\ {{h_{j}(x_{\star })\ \leq \ 0,\ 1\leq j\leq q.}}\end {array}\]
    • Dual Feasibility: \[v_{\star }\geq 0.\]
    • Complimentary slackness: \[h_{j}(x_{\star })\cdot v_{\star j}\ =\ 0,\quad \forall \ 1\leq j\leq q.\]

    Optimality Conditions [DER3]

    • July 6, 2025
    • Kellen Kanarios

    Local conditions that a minimizer of a (not necessarily convex) \(f\) must satisfy, phrased in terms of its gradient and Hessian at the candidate point. They pin an optimum down to a stationary point and then use curvature to separate minima from maxima and saddles.

    Definition. Stationary point [003P]

    • January 27, 2025
    • Kellen Kanarios

    A point \(\mathbf {x_{\star }}\) is a stationary point of \(f(\cdot )\), if \[\nabla f(\mathbf {x_{\star }})\ =\ \mathbf {0}.\] Here, \(\mathbf {x_{\star }}\) is also known as a critical point.

    Theorem. First-order optimality condition [I6DT]

    • July 11, 2026
    • Kellen Kanarios

    If \(\mathbf {x_\star }\) is a local minimizer of \(f:\mathbb {R}^n\to \mathbb {R}\) and \(f\) is continuously differentiable in an open neighborhood of \(\mathbf {x_\star }\), then \(\mathbf {x_\star }\) is a stationary point: \[\nabla f(\mathbf {x_\star })\ =\ \mathbf {0}.\]

    This is only necessary: a stationary point may be a maximizer or saddle, which is what the second-order conditions disambiguate. Under convexity it becomes sufficient as well — a stationary point of a convex function is a global minimizer.

    Theorem. Second-order optimality conditions [U3L4]

    • July 11, 2026
    • Kellen Kanarios

    Let \(f:\mathbb {R}^n\to \mathbb {R}\) be twice continuously differentiable in an open neighborhood of \(\mathbf {x_\star }\).

    Necessary. If \(\mathbf {x_\star }\) is a local minimizer, then \[(i)\ \nabla f(\mathbf {x_\star })=\mathbf {0};\qquad (ii)\ \nabla ^2 f(\mathbf {x_\star })\succeq \mathbf {0}.\] That is, it is a stationary point whose Hessian is positive semidefinite.

    Sufficient. If instead \(\nabla f(\mathbf {x_\star })=\mathbf {0}\) and \(\nabla ^2 f(\mathbf {x_\star })\succ \mathbf {0}\) (Hessian strictly positive definite), then \(\mathbf {x_\star }\) is a strict local minimizer. The gap between \(\succeq \) and \(\succ \) is exactly the ambiguity the first-order condition alone cannot resolve.

    Remark. Let \(f:\mathbb {R}^{n}\mapsto \mathbb {R}\) be a convex function, then
    • A local minimizer of \(f\) is also its global minimizer. If \(f\) is strictly convex, the global minimizer is unique
    • A point is a global minimizer of \(f\) iff \[\mathbf {0}\ \in \ \partial f(\mathbf {x_{\star }}).\]
    If \(f\in \mathcal {C}^{1}\), then \(\nabla f(\mathbf {x_{\star }})=\mathbf {0}\) implies that \(\mathbf {x_{\star }}\) is a global minimizer.

    Constrained Optimality [DER4]

    • July 6, 2025
    • Kellen Kanarios

    Consider a smooth contained problem with \[\min _{\mathbf {x}}f(\mathbf {x}),\quad \text {s.t.} \quad r_{i}(\mathbf {x})\ =\ 0,\ 1\leq i\leq p,\] \[h_{j}(\mathbf {x})\ \leq \ 0,\ 1\leq j\leq q.\] Consider its Lagrangian function \[\mathscr {L}(\mathbf {x},\mathbf {u},\mathbf {v})\ =\ f(\mathbf {x})+\sum _{i=1}^{p}u_{i}\cdot r_{i}(\mathbf {x})+\sum _{j=1}^{q}v_{j}\cdot h_{j}(\mathbf {x}).\]

    Definition. KKT Conditions [4IPN]

    • Kellen Kanarios
    • Stationary \[\nabla _{\mathbf {x}}{\mathcal {L}}(\mathbf {x_*},\mathbf {u_*},\mathbf {v_*})\;=\;\mathbf {0}\]
    • Primal Feasibility: \[\begin {array}{l}{{r_{i}(x_{\star })\ =\ 0,\ 1\leq i\leq p,}}\\ {{h_{j}(x_{\star })\ \leq \ 0,\ 1\leq j\leq q.}}\end {array}\]
    • Dual Feasibility: \[v_{\star }\geq 0.\]
    • Complimentary slackness: \[h_{j}(x_{\star })\cdot v_{\star j}\ =\ 0,\quad \forall \ 1\leq j\leq q.\]

    Taylor Expansion and Lipschitz Functions [DER2]

    • July 6, 2025
    • Kellen Kanarios

    Definition. Lipschitz Continous [003J]

    • January 27, 2025
    • Kellen Kanarios

    Suppose that

    • \(f:\mathcal {X}\mapsto \mathcal {Y}\) with \(\mathcal {X}\) and \(\mathcal {Y}\) being open sets;
    • \(||\cdot ||_{\mathcal {X}}\) and \(||\cdot ||_{\mathcal {Y}}\) are norms on \(\mathcal {X}\) and \(\mathcal {Y}\), respectively.
    \(f(\cdot )\) is Lipschitz continuous over \(\mathcal {X}\) if \(\exists L<\infty \,,\) such that \[||f(\boldsymbol {y})-f(\boldsymbol {x})||_{\mathcal {Y}}\ \leq \ L(\boldsymbol {x})\,||\boldsymbol {y}-\boldsymbol {x}||_{\mathcal {X}}\,,\quad \forall \boldsymbol {x},\ \boldsymbol {y}\in \mathcal {X}.\]

    Definition. Smooth Function [003K]

    • January 27, 2025
    • Kellen Kanarios

    A differentiable function \(f(\mathbf {x})\) is called smooth iff it has a Lipschitz continuous gradient, i.e., iff \(L< \infty \) such that \[||\nabla f(\mathbf {x})-\nabla f(\mathbf {z}) ||_{2}\ \leq L ||\mathbf {x}-\mathbf {z} ||_{2},\quad \forall \mathbf {x},\ \mathbf {z}\in \mathbb {R}^{n}\]

    Theorem. Mean Value Theorem I [003L]

    • January 27, 2025
    • Kellen Kanarios

    Let \(f:\mathbb {R}^{n}\mapsto \mathbb {R}\) be continuously differentiable. For any fixed \(\mathbf {x}\) and \(\mathbf {y}\), we have \[\,f(\mathbf {y})\,=\,f(\mathbf {x})\,+\,\langle \nabla f(\mathbf {z}(t_{L})),\mathbf {y}-\mathbf {x}\rangle \,\] for some \(\mathbf {z}(t_{L})=(1-t_{L})\cdot \mathbf {x}+t_{L}\cdot \mathbf {y}\) with \(t_{L}\in (0,1)\,\).

    Remark.
    • If \(f:\mathbb {R}^n\mapsto \mathbb {R}\) is continuously differentiable, \[\begin {aligned} |f(\pmb {x})-f(\pmb {y})| &\leq & \sup _{\pmb {z} \in \mathbb {R}^n} ||\nabla f(\pmb {z})||_2 \, ||\pmb {x}-\pmb {y}||_2 \end {aligned}\] so that the Lipschitz constant of \(f\) is \(\sup _{\pmb {z} \in \mathbb {R}^n} ||\nabla f(\pmb {z})||_2\).
    • If \(f:\mathbb {R}^{n}\mapsto \mathbb {R}\) is twice continuously differentiable, \[||\nabla f(\boldsymbol {x})-\nabla f(\boldsymbol {y})||_{2}\ \leq \ \sup _{\boldsymbol {z}\in \mathbb {R}^{n}}||\nabla ^{2}f(\boldsymbol {z})||_{2}\,||\boldsymbol {x}-\boldsymbol {y}||_{2}\] so that the Lipschitz constant of \(\nabla f\) is \(\sup _{\boldsymbol {z}\in \mathbb {R}^{n}}||\nabla ^{2}f(\boldsymbol {z})||_{2}\)

    Theorem. Mean Value Theorem II [003M]

    • January 27, 2025
    • Kellen Kanarios

    Let \(f:\mathbb {R}^{n}\mapsto \mathbb {R}\) be twice continuously differentiable. For any fixed \(\mathbf {x}\) and \(\mathbf {y}\), we have \[\nabla f(\mathbf {y})\;=\;\nabla f(\mathbf {x})\,+\,\int _{0}^{1}\nabla ^{2}f(\mathbf {z}(t))\cdot (\mathbf {y}-\mathbf {x})dt\] for some \(\mathbf {z}(t)=(1-t)\mathbf {x}+t\mathbf {y}\) with \(t\in (0,1)\,,\) and that \[\boxed {f(\mathbf {y})\;=\;f(\mathbf {x})+(\nabla f(\mathbf {x}),\mathbf {y}-\mathbf {x})+\frac {1}{2}(\mathbf {y}-\mathbf {x})^{\top }\nabla ^{2}f(\mathbf {z}(t_{Q}))(\mathbf {y}-\mathbf {x})}\] for some \(t_{Q}\in (0,1)\,.\)

    Theorem. First-order approximation [003N]

    • January 27, 2025
    • Kellen Kanarios

    Let \(f:\mathbb {R}^{n}\to \mathbb {R}\) be continuously differentiable, and \(\nabla f(\mathbf {x})\) is \(\gamma _{L}(\mathbf {x}_{0})\)-Lipschitz continuous at \(\mathbf {x}_{0}\), then \[\left |f(\mathbf {x})-\widehat {f_{L}}(\mathbf {x};\mathbf {x}_{0})\right |\ \leq \ \frac {\gamma _{L}(\mathbf {x}_{0})}{2}\,||\mathbf {x}-\mathbf {x}_{0}||_{2}^{2}\,,\] where we define \[\widehat {f_{L}}(\mathbf {x};\mathbf {x}_{0})\ :=\ f(\mathbf {x}_{0})\ +\ \langle \nabla f(\mathbf {x}_{0}),\mathbf {x}-\mathbf {x}_{0}\rangle \,.\]

    Theorem. Second-order approximation [003O]

    • January 27, 2025
    • Kellen Kanarios

    Let \(f:\mathbb {R}^{n}\to \mathbb {R}\) be twice continuously differentiable, and suppose \(\nabla ^{2}f(\mathbf {x})\) is \(\gamma _{Q}(\mathbf {x}_{0})\)-Lipschitz continuous at \(\mathbf {x}_{0}\), then \[\left |f(\mathbf {x})-\widehat {f}_{Q}(\mathbf {x};\mathbf {x}_{0})\right |\ \leq \ \frac {\gamma _{Q}(\mathbf {x}_{0})}{6}\left ||\mathbf {x}-\mathbf {x}_{0}\right ||_{2}^{3},\] where we define \[\widehat {f}_{Q}(\mathbf {x};\mathbf {x}_{0}):=f(\mathbf {x}_{0})+\langle \nabla f(\mathbf {x}_{0}),\mathbf {x}-\mathbf {x}_{0}\rangle \] \[+\frac {1}{2}(\mathbf {x}-\mathbf {x}_{0})^{\top }\nabla ^{2}f(\mathbf {x}_{0})(\mathbf {x}-\mathbf {x}_{0}).\]

    Basic Matrix Analysis [DER1]

    • July 6, 2025
    • Kellen Kanarios

    A hub for the linear-algebra facts that recur throughout the optimization notes — inner products and traces, positive-definiteness, and the family of matrix norms built on the singular values.

    Definition. Matrix inner product [WWMR]

    • July 11, 2026
    • Kellen Kanarios

    The inner product on \(\mathbb {R}^{m\times n}\), obtained by treating a matrix as a long vector and summing the entrywise products: \[\langle \mathbf {X},\mathbf {Z}\rangle \ :=\ \sum _{i=1}^{m}\sum _{j=1}^{n}X_{ij}Z_{ij},\] the direct generalization of the vector case \(\langle \mathbf {x},\mathbf {z}\rangle =\sum _i x_i z_i\). It is the inner product whose induced norm is the Frobenius norm, \(\|\mathbf {X}\|_F=\sqrt {\langle \mathbf {X},\mathbf {X}\rangle }\).

    It has a compact trace form (see Matrix trace): \[\langle \mathbf {X},\mathbf {Z}\rangle \ =\ \mathrm {tr}(\mathbf {X}^{\top }\mathbf {Z})\ =\ \mathrm {tr}(\mathbf {X}\mathbf {Z}^{\top }).\]

    Definition. Matrix trace [PDX6]

    • July 11, 2026
    • Kellen Kanarios

    For a square matrix \(\mathbf {M}\in \mathbb {R}^{n\times n}\), the trace is the sum of its diagonal entries: \[\mathrm {tr}(\mathbf {M}):=\sum _{i=1}^{n}M_{ii}.\]

    Two identities make it the workhorse of matrix calculus. It is invariant under cyclic permutation of a product, \[\mathrm {tr}(\mathbf {A}\mathbf {B})=\mathrm {tr}(\mathbf {B}\mathbf {A}),\qquad \mathrm {tr}(\mathbf {A}_{1}\mathbf {A}_{2}\cdots \mathbf {A}_{n})=\mathrm {tr}(\mathbf {A}_{\pi (1)}\cdots \mathbf {A}_{\pi (n)})\] for any cyclic permutation \(\pi \) of \(\{1,\dots ,n\}\); and it computes the matrix inner product, \[\langle \mathbf {X},\mathbf {Z}\rangle =\mathrm {tr}(\mathbf {X}^{\top }\mathbf {Z})=\mathrm {tr}(\mathbf {X}\mathbf {Z}^{\top }).\]

    Definition. Positive (semi)definiteness [003A]

    • January 26, 2025
    • Kellen Kanarios

    A symmetric matrix \(\mathbf {A}\in \mathbb {R}^{n\times n}\) is positive definite if \(\mathbf {x}^{\top }\mathbf {A}\mathbf {x}>0\) for all nonzero \(\mathbf {x}\in \mathbb {R}^{n}\). It is positive semidefinite (p.s.d.) if \(\mathbf {x}^{\top }\mathbf {A}\mathbf {x}\geq 0\) for all \(\mathbf {x}\in \mathbb {R}^{n}\).

    Fact. Singular Value Decomposition [003B]

    • January 26, 2025
    • Kellen Kanarios

    Let \(\mathbf {A}\in \mathbb {R}^{m\times n}\) with \(\operatorname {rank}(\mathbf {A})=r\). There exist \(\sigma _{1}\geq \sigma _{2}\geq \cdots \geq \sigma _{r}>0\), and matrices \[\mathbf {U}\in \mathbb {R}^{m\times r},\ \mathbf {V}\in \mathbb {R}^{n\times r},\] with orthonormal columns \((\mathbf {U}^{\top }\mathbf {U}=\mathbf {I},\ \mathbf {V}^{\top }\mathbf {V}=\mathbf {I})\) such that \[\mathbf {A}\ =\ \mathbf {U}\mathbf {\Sigma }\mathbf {V}^{\top }\ =\ \sum _{i=1}^{r}\sigma _{i}\mathbf {u}_{i}\mathbf {v}_{i}^{\top }\,,\quad \mathbf {\Sigma }\ =\ \operatorname {diag}\left (\sigma _{1},\cdots ,\sigma _{r}\right ).\]

    Relationship between eigen decomposition and SVD

    • The columns of \(\boldsymbol {V}\) are eigenvectors of \(\boldsymbol {A}^T\boldsymbol {A}\)
    • The columns of \(\boldsymbol {U}\) are eigenvectors of \(\boldsymbol {A}\boldsymbol {A}^T\)
    • \({{\sigma _{i}({\mathbf {A}})}}={\sqrt {\lambda _{i}({{{\mathbf {A}}{\mathbf {A}}^{\mathsf {T}}}})}}={\sqrt {\lambda _{i}({\mathbf {A}}^{\mathsf {T}}{\mathbf {A}})}}\)

    Theorem. Best rank-\(r\) approximation [003C]

    • January 26, 2025
    • Kellen Kanarios

    Let \(\mathbf {A}\in \mathbb {R}^{m\times n}\) with SVD, \(\mathbf {A}=\sum _{i=1}^{\min \{m,n\}}\sigma _{i}\mathbf {u}_{i}\mathbf {v}_{i}^{\top }\). Then an optimal solution to the best rank-\(r\) approximation problem \[\min _{\mathbf {X}}||\mathbf {X}-\mathbf {A}||_{2}\,,\quad \text {s.t.}\quad \text {rank}(\mathbf {X})\ \leq \ r\] is the truncated SVD of the following form \[\boxed {\widehat {\mathbf {A}}_{r}\ =\ \sum _{i=1}^{r}\sigma _{i}\mathbf {u}_{i}\mathbf {v}_{i}^{\top }}\,,\ \ \text {if}\ \ \sigma _{r}>\sigma _{r+1}\,,\,\text {it is unique.}\]

    Proof. Suppose \(m \geq n\), then we observe that \[\left |\left |{\widehat {\mathbf {A}}}_{r}-{\mathbf {A}}\right |\right |_{2}\;=\;\left |\left |\sum _{i=r+1}^{n}\sigma _{i}\mathbf {u}_{i}\mathbf {v}_{i}^{\mathsf {T}}\right |\right |_{2} \leq \sigma _{r+1}\] Second, to prove our result, we want to show that \[\left |\left |\mathbf {B}_{r}-\mathbf {A}\right |\right |_{2}\ \geq \ \sigma _{r+1},\quad \forall \mathbf {B}_{r}\ \text {with}\ \mathrm {rank}(\mathbf {B}_{r})=r.\] We suppose \(\ \mathbf {B}_{r}=\widetilde {\mathbf {U}}\widetilde {\mathbf {V}}^{\top },\quad \widetilde {\mathbf {U}}\in \mathbb {R}^{m\times r},\ \widetilde {\mathbf {V}}\in \mathbb {R}^{n\times r}.\) Note \[ \begin {align*} ||\mathbf {B}_r - A||_2^2 &= \sup _{||\boldsymbol {z}||_2 \leq 1} ||(\mathbf {B}_r - \mathbf {A})\mathbf {z}||_2^2 \\ &\geq ||(\mathbf {B}_r - \mathbf {A})\mathbf {w}||_2^2 \end {align*} \] Since \(\widetilde {V}\) has \(r\) columns, then there must be a nontrivial linear combination of the first \(r{+}1\) columns of \(V\), i.e., \[\mathbf {w}=\gamma _{1}\mathbf {v}_{1}+\cdots +\gamma _{r+1}\mathbf {v}_{r+1}\] such that \(\widetilde {V}^{\top }\mathbf {w}=\mathbf {0}\,.\) Wlog, we can scale \(\left |\left |\mathbf {w}\right |\right |_{2}=1\) and \(\,\sum _{i=1}^{r+1}\gamma _{i}^{2}=1\) Then \[||\mathbf {A}-\mathbf {B}_{k}||_{2}^{2}\geq ||(\mathbf {A}-\mathbf {B}_{k})\,\mathbf {w}||_{2}^{2}=||\mathbf {A}\mathbf {w}||_{2}^{2}=\gamma _{1}^{2}\sigma _{1}^{2}+\cdots +\gamma _{r+1}^{2}\sigma _{r+1}^{2}\geq \sigma _{r+1}^{2}.\]

    Definition. Matrix Operator Norm [003G]

    • January 27, 2025
    • Kellen Kanarios

    Let \(\mathbf {A}\in \mathbb {R}^{m\times n}\). If \(\left |\left |\cdot \right |\right |_{a}\) and \(\left |\left |\cdot \right |\right |_{b}\) are norms on \(\mathbb {R}^{n}\) and \(\mathbb {R}^{m}\), we have \[\left |\left |\mathbf {A}\right |\right |_{a\to b}\ :=\ \sup _{\left |\left |\mathbf {x}\right |\right |_{a}\leq 1}\left |\left |\mathbf {A}\mathbf {x}\right |\right |_{b}.\] It satisfies the three criteria for norm, and is submultiplicative \[||\boldsymbol {A}\boldsymbol {B}||_{a\to b}\ \leq \ ||\boldsymbol {A}||_{a\to b}\cdot ||\boldsymbol {B}||_{a\to b};\]. \[||{\cal A}||_{2\to 2}\;=\;\sigma _{1}({\cal A})\;\;(\mathrm {{spectral\ norm}},\;\mathrm {{write\ as}}\;||{\cal A}||\;\;);\;\] \[\begin {array}{l}{{||{\boldsymbol {A}}||_{1\to b}\ =\ \operatorname *{max}_{j=1,\cdots ,n}||{\boldsymbol {A e}}_{j}||_{b}}}\\ {{||{\boldsymbol {A}}||_{a\to \infty }\ =\ \operatorname *{max}_{i=1,\cdots ,m}||{\boldsymbol {e}}_{i}^{*}{\boldsymbol {A}}||_{b}^{*}\,,\ \ ||{\boldsymbol {v}}||_{b}^{*}\ :=\ \operatorname *{sup}_{||{\boldsymbol {u}}||_{b}\leq 1}\langle {\boldsymbol {u}},{\boldsymbol {v}}\rangle \,,}}\end {array}\]

    Definition. Unitary Invariant Matrix Norm [003H]

    • January 27, 2025
    • Kellen Kanarios

    Let \(\mathbf {A}\in \mathbb {R}^{m\times n}.\) We say the matrix norm is unitary invariant if \[\left ||\mathbf {A}\right ||_{\sharp }\ =\ \left ||\mathbf {PAQ}\right ||_{\sharp },\quad \forall \ \mathbf {P}\in O(m),\ \mathbf {Q}\in O(n).\]

    The two most common examples are both unitary invariant because they depend on \(\mathbf {A}\) only through its singular values: the Spectral norm (\(\|\sigma (\mathbf {A})\|_\infty \)) and the Frobenius norm (\(\|\sigma (\mathbf {A})\|_2\)).

    Definition. Spectral norm [3U43]

    • July 11, 2026
    • Kellen Kanarios

    The operator norm of a matrix induced by the Euclidean norm on both sides, \(\|\mathbf {A}\|_{2\to 2}\), usually written just \(\|\mathbf {A}\|\). It equals the largest singular value, \[\|\mathbf {A}\|\ =\ \sup _{\|\mathbf {x}\|_2\leq 1}\|\mathbf {A}\mathbf {x}\|_2\ =\ \sigma _1(\mathbf {A}),\] i.e. the most any unit vector can be stretched by \(\mathbf {A}\). As a Schatten norm it is the \(p=\infty \) case, \(\|\mathbf {A}\|_{\mathrm {S}_\infty }=\|\sigma (\mathbf {A})\|_\infty \), sitting opposite the Frobenius norm (\(p=2\)) in that family.

    Definition. Frobenius norm [4M9J]

    • July 11, 2026
    • Kellen Kanarios

    The entrywise Euclidean norm of a matrix — treat \(\mathbf {A}\) as a long vector and take its 2-norm: \[\|\mathbf {A}\|_F\ =\ \sqrt {\sum _{i,j}A_{ij}^2}\ =\ \sqrt {\langle \mathbf {A},\mathbf {A}\rangle }\ =\ \sqrt {\mathrm {tr}(\mathbf {A}^{\top }\mathbf {A})}.\] It is the norm induced by the matrix inner product, and in terms of singular values it is the \(p=2\) Schatten norm, \(\|\mathbf {A}\|_F=\sqrt {\sum _i\sigma _i^2(\mathbf {A})}\) — the Euclidean length of the singular-value vector, dual in that family to the spectral norm (\(p=\infty \)).

    Definition. Schatten \(p\)-norm [003I]

    • January 27, 2025
    • Kellen Kanarios

    Let \(\mathbf {A}\in \mathbb {R}^{m\times n}\). For any \(p \in [1,+\infty ]\), the function \[\left ||\mathbf {A}|\right |_{\mathrm {S}_{p}}\,:=\,\left ||\mathbf {\sigma }(\mathbf {A})|\right |_{p}\] is a norm on \(\,\mathbb {R}^{m\times n}\).

    Operations that preserve convexity [DER0]

    • July 6, 2025
    • Kellen Kanarios

    The following operations preserve convexity

    • Nonnegative weighted sums. if \(f_1, \ldots , f_n\) are convex and \(\alpha _1, \ldots , \alpha _n > 0\) then we have \(f(\boldsymbol {x}) = \sum _{i = 1}^{n} \alpha _i f_i(\boldsymbol {x})\) is convex
    • Pointwise maximum. if \(f_1, \ldots , f_n\) are convex then \(f(\boldsymbol {x}) = \max _i \{f_i(\boldsymbol {x})\}\) is convex

    Low Precision Data Types [DEQV]

    • July 3, 2025
    • Kellen Kanarios

    float16: here, we decrease both the fraction and exponent bits. Importantly, there are only \(5\) exponent bits making the effective range \((2^{-6}, 2^{6})\). The dynamic range for small numbers is pretty bad. This can cause small numbers to "die" effectively killing these neurons for the remainder of learning due to backpropagation.

    bfloat16: to fix the problems with float16, they instead keep \(8\) exponent bits and reduce the fraction bits to \(7\). This maintains the same dynamic range as float32 while still only using \(16\) bits.

    fp8: Two variants

    1. E4M3: has 4 exponent bits and 3 mantissa bits
    2. E5M2: has 5 exponent bits and 2 mantissa bits
    Requires modern Hopper Architecture i.e. H100 to perform operations. Also supported by TPUs.

    Tensor Memory. Tensors are stored as a floating point number. Memory is determined by (i) number of values in tensor and (ii) data type of each value.

    Low Precision Data Types [DEQV]

    • July 3, 2025
    • Kellen Kanarios

    float16: here, we decrease both the fraction and exponent bits. Importantly, there are only \(5\) exponent bits making the effective range \((2^{-6}, 2^{6})\). The dynamic range for small numbers is pretty bad. This can cause small numbers to "die" effectively killing these neurons for the remainder of learning due to backpropagation.

    bfloat16: to fix the problems with float16, they instead keep \(8\) exponent bits and reduce the fraction bits to \(7\). This maintains the same dynamic range as float32 while still only using \(16\) bits.

    fp8: Two variants

    1. E4M3: has 4 exponent bits and 3 mantissa bits
    2. E5M2: has 5 exponent bits and 2 mantissa bits
    Requires modern Hopper Architecture i.e. H100 to perform operations. Also supported by TPUs.

    Training Implications.

    1. float32 training works but requires lots of memory
    2. Using lower precision data types allows you to train larger models due to lower memory requirements, but can cause instability
    3. To optimize this tradeoff, use mixed-precision training.

    Torch Tensors [DYIV]

    • July 3, 2025
    • Kellen Kanarios

    In pytorch, tensors are contiguous blocks of memory, where their shape is controlled by strides. A stride basically just refers to how far you have to jump in physical memory to correspond to incrementing the logical index i.e. in a (2, 3) matrix each row requires jumping \(3\) spots in physical memory. Thus, stride[1] = 3.

    Remark. Calling .view((m, n)) just changes the stride but does not modify the physical memory. If you call .view that results in a non-contiguous view, then you cannot call .view again because it assumes contiguous indexing to properly adjust the strides. To deal with this, they have .contiguous() and .reshape() is basically .contiguous().view().
    Remark. All elementwise operations make a copy i.e. x + y. A useful function for masked attention is triu().

    Einops

    • July 3, 2025
    • Kellen Kanarios
     Einops is a useful python library to keep track of high-dimensional matrix operations i.e. matmuls over batch_size, seqlen, etc. High level overview
    • Initialize like X[float.tensor, "batch seq hidden"] = torch.tensor((2, 3, 4))
    • Can perform matmul with named dims like
      • z = einsum(x, y, "batch seq1 hidden, batch seq2 hidden -> batch seq1 seq2")
    • reduce: x = reduce(x, "x y z -> x y 1") is just like mean(x, axis=-1)
    • rearrange: x = rearrange(x, "... (heads hidden1) -> ... heads hidden 1")

    Conditioning Trick FM [008F]

    • July 2, 2025

    Given data distribution \(q(x)\), we define an approximation \(p(x)\) with the form \[p(x) = \int p(x \mid x_1) q(x_1) \mathrm {d}x_{1}\] In order to ensure \(p(x) \approx q(x)\), we pick \(p(x \mid x_{1})\) that concentrates around \(x_{1}\) i.e. \(p(x \mid x_{1}) \sim N(x \mid x_{1}, \sigma ^2 I)\) for small \(\sigma \).

    Normalizing Flows [B9J9]

    • July 15, 2025

    Brief notes on Variational Inference with Normalizing Flows to motivate flow matching.

    Goal. We are concerned with the problem of density estimation. Given a dataset \(\mathcal {X}\), consisting of samples \(\mathbf {x}_i \sim p(\mathbf {x})\), we want to learn \(p(\mathbf {x})\).

    One popular way to do this is via variational inference. As a brief recap, in variational inference, we assume that there is actually a joint distribution \(p(\mathbf {x}, \mathbf {z})\), where \(\mathbf {z}\) is a latent variable. We then find \(p(\mathbf {x})\) by maximizing the log-likelihood \(\log \int p(\mathbf {x} \mid \mathbf {z}) \mathrm {d}\mathbf {z}\)

    For an example of this, see my post on expectation maximization. In that post, we utilize the ELBO to learn a latent variable model \(q_{\phi }(\mathbf {z} | \mathbf {x})\). As discussed in my post on ELBO, in order to learn \(p(\mathbf {x})\), we must have that \(p(\mathbf {z} | \mathbf {x})\) is in the family \(q_{\phi }\). However, \(q_ {\phi }\) is usually a Gaussian parametrized by \(\phi \), so that we can easily learn \(\phi \). In this case, it is very unlikely that \(p(\mathbf {z} \mid x)\) lies in the family of \(q_{\phi }\) and therefore we have no hope of learning the true \(p(\mathbf {x})\).

    Definition. Time-dependent vector field [008C]

    • July 1, 2025

    We define a time-dependent vector field as a map \(v: [0,1] \times \mathbb {R}^d \to \mathbb {R}^d\)

    Definition. Flow [008D]

    • July 1, 2025
    • Kellen Kanarios

    Give a vector field \(v_t\) one can construct a time-dependent diffeomorphic map called a flow \(\phi : [0,1] \times \mathbb {R}^d \to \mathbb {R}^d\) defined via the ordinary differential equation \[\begin {align*} \frac {\mathrm {d}}{\mathrm {d}t} \phi _t(x) &= v_t(\phi _t(x)) \\ \phi _{0}(x) &= x .\end {align*}\]

    Remark. Modeling a vector field via a neural network i.e. \(v_t(x; \theta )\) implicitly defines a deep parametric model of the flow \(\phi _t(x)\) via solving the ODE or an approximation, such as \[\phi _{t + \Delta t}(x) \approx \phi _t(x) + \Delta t \cdot v_t(\phi _t(x); \theta )\] Obviously, accuracy will be dependent on the step size \(\Delta t\).

    Definition. Generated probability paths [008E]

    • Kellen Kanarios

    We say that a vector field generates a probability density path if the flow of \(v_t\) satisfies \[p_t = [\phi _t]_* p_{0},\] where \[[\phi _t]_*p_{0}(x) = p_{0}(\phi _t^{-1}(x)) \det \left [ \frac {\partial \phi _t^{-1} }{\partial x}(x) \right ]. \]

    A vector field generates a probability density path if it satisfies the continuity equation.

    Definition. Flow Matching Loss [LRL4]

    • July 9, 2025
    • Kellen Kanarios

    Given an initial noise distribution \(p\), a desired data distribution \(q\), a probability density path \(p_t\), such that \(p_{0} = p\) and \(p_{1} =q\), and a vector field \(u_t\) that generates \(p_t\). We define the flow matching loss \(\mathcal {L}_{\mathrm {FM}}\) as \[\mathcal {L}_{\mathrm {FM}}(\theta ) \coloneqq \mathbb {E}_{t, p_t(x)} \|v_t(x; \theta ) - u_t\|\]

    Flow Matching vs. Diffusion [TGWF]
