      Definition. Latent Variable [0083]

      • June 30, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      Given a joint distribution \(p(X,Z)\) for two random variables \(X\) and \(Z\). We call a random variable a latent random variable if we have a dataset \(\mathcal {D}\) that only consists of realizations of \(X\).

      Evidence Lower Bound [0082]

      • June 30, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios
      • 5 min read

      Setup. We are given a joint distribution \(p(X, Z; \theta )\), where \(X\) and \(Z\) are random variables with their joint parametrized by \(\theta \). We are also given a dataset \(\mathcal {D}\) containing realizations of only \(X\) i.e. \(Z\) is a latent random variable.

      Goal. We want to learn \(p(x; \theta )\).

      However, \[p(x; \theta ) = \int p(x, z; \theta ) \mathrm {d}z = \int p(x | z; \theta )p(z) \mathrm {d}z,\] which is computationally intractable for most continuous \(Z\).

      Question. Can we update \(\theta \) for a given realization of \(x\) and \(z\)?
      Answer.Yes!!!

      Motivation. Suppose we had some \(q(z)\) that we could sample realizations of \(Z\) from. Then we want to find some reasonable \(\ell _{\theta }\), such that \[\theta ^* \approx \arg \max _{\theta } \mathbb {E}_{x, \sim p(x; \theta ^*), z \sim q(z)}[\ell _{\theta }(X, Z)]\]

      Remark. \(q(z)\) can potentially (and will) depend on the sample \(x_i\). This is OK because we are given \(x_i\)'s, which we can then just pass to \(q\) to get the corresponding \(z_i\).
      Why is this the case? Because then (for well-behaved \(\ell _{\theta }\)) \[\theta _{t + 1} = \theta _{t} - \alpha \nabla _{\theta _{t}}\ell _{\theta _{t}}(x_i, z_i) \to \theta ^*\] i.e. SGD is a reasonable thing to do, where the gradient is for a single sample of \(x_i\) and \(z_i\) which we have readily available from our dataset \(\mathcal {D}\) and our distribution \(q\) that we can sample from. This idea comes up a lot in optimization, such as the \(\log \) trick in the original policy gradient.

      Similar to the \(\log \) trick, the Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO) comes from a simple multiply and divide trick. Namely, \[\begin {align*} \log p(x; \theta ) &= \log \int p(x, z; \theta ) \mathrm {d}z \\ &= \log \int p(x, z; \theta ) \frac {q(z)}{q(z)} \mathrm {d}z \\ &= \log \mathbb {E}_{z \sim q(z)} \frac {p(x, Z; \theta )}{q(z)} \\ &\geq \mathbb {E}_{z \sim q(z)} \log \frac {p(x, Z; \theta )}{q(z)} .\end {align*}\] The last inequality follows directly from Jensen's Inequality. However, note that this is only a lower bound and therefore not exactly what we want. For example, if we were to pick \(q \sim N(0, 1)\) and then optimize the ELBO for \(\theta \) we would not necessarily find a good \(\theta \) for the likelihood \(\log p(x; \theta )\). Luckily, we can actually get the difference \(\log p(x; \theta ) - \)ELBO in closed form! Namely, \[\begin {align*} \log p(x; \theta ) - \mathrm {ELBO} &= \log p(x; \theta ) - \mathbb {E}_{z \sim q(z)} \log \frac {p(x, Z; \theta )}{q(z)} \\ &= \int \left (\log p(x; \theta ) - \log \frac {p(x, z; \theta )}{q(z)}\right )q(z) \\ &= \int \left (\log \frac {p(x; \theta )q(z)}{p(x, z; \theta )}\right )q(z) \\ &= \int \left (\log \frac {p(x; \theta )q(z)}{p(z | x; \theta )p(x; \theta )}\right )q(z) \\ &= \int \left (\log \frac {q(z)}{p(z | x; \theta )}\right )q(z) \\ &= \mathrm {KL}\big (q(z) \mid \mid p(z | x; \theta )\big ) .\end {align*}\] Thus, to tighten the lower bound we can optimize \(q_{\phi }(z)\) to try to match \(p(z | x; \theta )\). As a sanity check, lets make sure these match when \(q(z) = p(z \mid x; \theta )\). \[\begin {align*} \mathbb {E}_{z \sim q(z)} \log \frac {p(x, Z; \theta )}{q(z)} &= \int \log \frac {p(x, z; \theta )}{q(z)}\mathrm {d}z \\ &= \int \log \frac {p(x; \theta )p(z \mid x; \theta )}{p(z \mid x; \theta )}\mathrm {d}z \\ &= \int \log p(x; \theta )\mathrm {d}z \\ &= \log (x; \theta ) .\end {align*}\] You may be wondering how we use this algorithmically to find \(\theta ^*\)? This will be the main idea of expectation maximization. Feel free to check it out!

      Diversity is All You Need [0080]

      • June 30, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      The talk starts discussing Ben's amazing paper DIAYN. An idea that has become incredibly popular in unsupervised / self-supervised RL is learning conditional policies. In All things contrastive reinforcement learning, the learn a goal-conditioned policy and value function i.e. \[\pi _{\theta }(s \mid g), \quad Q_{\psi }(s, a, g)\] However, we are not limited to goals. In successor-feature-based frameworks, one learns a task vector \(\mathbf {w}\) such that \[r(s, a) = \phi (s,a) \cdot \mathbf {w},\] where \(\phi \) is a lower dimensional representation. To learn the task vector (assuming you have \(\phi \) which is a whole other issue), you can recover \(\mathbf {w}\) by solving the linear regression \[\min _{\psi } \|r(s,a) - \phi (s,a) \cdot \mathbf {w}_{\psi }\|^{2} \] One can then learn a task conditioned policy \(\pi _{\theta }(s \mid \mathbf {w})\). This is precisely the idea in USFA.

      Getting back to DIAYN (get used to these tangents), instead of a task or goal, they condition on a skill \(\mathbf {z}\). However, unlike a goal which is just a state in the environment, or a task which can be learned via regression as above, it is unclear how to learn this "skill" \(\mathbf {z}\).

      In this paper, they consider a skill as something distinguishable by a third party. What does this mean:

      Remark. If you have a skill, then a discriminator observing you perform your skill should be able to tell you which skill you performed.

      Crucially, the discriminator does not know which actions you took when performing this skill. Namely, they must be able to identify the skill purely based on the states you visited when performing that skill. Mathematically, this can be roughly translated as maximizing the mutual information \(I^{\pi }(\mathbf {z}; \tau )\), where \(\tau \) is a trajectory of states \((s_0, s_1, \ldots , s_T) \sim \pi \) visited by your policy \(\pi \). Using our previous knowledge of mutual information, we can rewrite this as \[I^{\pi }(\mathbf {z}, \tau ) = H(\mathbf {z}) - H(\mathbf {z} \mid \tau ),\] where \(H\) is the entropy. Since \(H(\mathbf {z})\) is a constant, this is essentially, \[\min _{\mathbf {z}} H(\mathbf {z} \mid \tau )\] which very intuitively corresponds to the notion that \(\mathbf {z}\) should be able to be predicted by \(\tau \). Formally, this is captured by the fact that the entropy is minimized i.e. \(0\) when \(\mathbf {z} = f(\tau )\) for some invertible \(f\).

      Remark. Recall that entropy is actually defined on the PDF of a random variable \(X\). Therefore, minimizing the entropy over \(\mathbf {z}\) is actually finding a distribution \(p(\mathbf {z})\).
      To learn the distribution \(p(\mathbf {z})\), they utilize the ELBO.

      TPE Processes Intro [007V]

      • June 23, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      The process abstraction, what the OS has to support to maintain it, and the data structure that holds it together.

      Process [FCHM]

      • May 12, 2026
      • Kellen Kanarios

      A running program, plus all the state the OS needs to pause it and resume it later. A process consists of:

      1. Memory: an Address space holding the program's code, stack, and heap.
      2. Registers: general-purpose registers carrying current computation, plus special-purpose registers:
        • Program counter (PC): the next instruction to run.
        • Stack pointer and frame pointer: where the process sits on its stack.

      A process moves between three states:

      • running: currently on a CPU.
      • ready: runnable, waiting for the Scheduling to give it a CPU.
      • blocked: waiting on I/O or another event, not runnable.
      Remark. Threads (see Concurrency Intro) share an address space within a process but each have their own PC, register set, and stack.

      Process API [JJ45]

      • May 12, 2026
      • Kellen Kanarios

      The minimum operations any OS must expose for working with Processes:

      1. Create: load a program from disk, set up its address space (stack, heap, code), and jump to main. The OS also initializes argc/argv.
      2. Destroy: kill a misbehaving or unwanted process.
      3. Wait: block until another process completes — useful for ordering dependent work.
      4. Miscellaneous control: e.g. suspend / resume.
      5. Status: report on running processes.
      Remark. The stack is allocated up front. The heap starts small and grows via malloc, which calls into the OS (brk/sbrk) when it runs out of headroom.

      On Unix, the concrete realization of this API uses fork(), wait(), and exec() — covered separately.

      Process control block [JE53]

      • May 12, 2026
      • Kellen Kanarios

      The kernel-side data structure holding all per-process state. There is one PCB per Process, threaded together into the process list. The PCB is what the OS reads and writes during a Context switch: the saved register set lives here, as does the process state, the open files, the parent pointer, and so on.

      An example from xv6:

      // the registers xv6 will save and restore
// to stop and subsequently restart a process
struct context {
  int eip;
  int esp;
  int ebx;
  int ecx;
  int edx;
  int esi;
  int edi;
  int ebp;
};
// the different states a process can be in
enum proc_state { UNUSED, EMBRYO, SLEEPING, RUNNABLE, RUNNING, ZOMBIE };
// the information xv6 tracks about each process
// including its register context and state
struct proc {
  char *mem;                 // Start of process memory
  uint sz;                   // Size of process memory
  char *kstack;              // Bottom of kernel stack for this process
  enum proc_state state;     // Process state
  int pid;                   // Process ID
  struct proc *parent;       // Parent process
  void *chan;                // If non-zero, sleeping on chan
  int killed;                // If non-zero, have been killed
  struct file *ofile[NOFILE]; // Open files
  struct inode *cwd;         // Current directory
  struct context context;    // Switch here to run process
  struct trapframe *tf;      // Trap frame for the current interrupt
};
      Remark. Threads need an analogous thread control block; see Concurrency Intro.

      Worked exercises for this chapter are parked separately in Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces: Exercises under the Processes Intro section.

      Definition. Differential Entropy [007C]

      • April 22, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      The differential entropy \( h(X) \) of a continuous random variable \( X \) with density \( f(x) \) is defined as \[ h(X)=-\int _{S}f(x)\log f(x)\,dx, \] where \( S \) is the support set of the random variable.

      Definition. Discrete Approximation of Differential Entropy [007G]

      • April 22, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      For, \[ p_{i}=\int _{i\,\Delta }^{(i+1)\,\Delta }f(x)\,d x=f(x_{i})\Delta \,. \] We define the discrete approximation of the differential entropy as \[\begin {align*} H(X^{\Delta })&\coloneqq -\sum _{-\infty }^{\infty }p_{i}\log p_{i} \\ &=-\sum _{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x_{i})\Delta \log (f(x_{i})\Delta ) \\ &=-\sum \Delta f(x_{i})\log f(x_{i})-\sum f(x_{i})\Delta \log \Delta \\ &=-\sum \Delta f(x_{i})\log f(x_{i})-\log \Delta , .\end {align*}\]

      Definition. Information dimension [007H]

      • April 22, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      Let \( X \) be any real valued random variable, and let \( X^{(1/n)} \) denote the discretization of \( X \) with parameter \( \Delta =1/n \). Then, the information dimension associated with \( X \) is defined as \[ d=\lim _{n\to \infty }\frac {H(X^{(1/n)})}{\log n}, \]

      Definition. Multivariate Normal Distribution [007I]

      • April 22, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      The multivariate normal distribution is defined by the density function \[f(\mathbf {x}) = (2\pi )^{-k/2}\operatorname *{det}(\mathbf {\Sigma })^{-1/2}\ \exp \left (-\frac {1}{2}(\mathbf {x}-{\boldsymbol {\mu }})^{\mathrm {{T}}}{\boldsymbol {\Sigma }}^{-1}\big (\mathbf {x}-{\boldsymbol {\mu }}\big )\right )\] where \( \mathbf {\Sigma } \) is the covariance matrix \[\mathbf {\Sigma }_{i,j} = \mathbb {E}[(X_i - \mu _i)(X_j - \mu _j)^{\top }]\]and \( \boldsymbol {\mu } \) is the mean vector \[\mathbf {\mu } = (\mathbb {E}[X_1], \ldots , \mathbb {E}[X_n])\].

      Theorem. Properties of the typical set for continuous variables [007F]

      • April 22, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      The typical set \( A_{\epsilon }^{(n)} \) has the following properties:

      1. \( \Pr \left (A_{\epsilon }^{(n)}\right )>1-\epsilon \) for \( n \) sufficiently large.
      2. \( \mathrm {Vol}\left (A_{\epsilon }^{(n)}\right )\leq 2^{n(h(X)+\epsilon )} \) for all \( n \).
      3. \( \mathrm {Vol}\left (A_{\epsilon }^{(n)}\right )\geq (1-\epsilon )2^{n(h(X)-\epsilon )} \) for \( n \) sufficiently large.

      Definition. Typical Set for Continuous Random Variables [007E]

      • April 22, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      For \( \epsilon >0 \) and any \( n \), we define the typical set \( A_{\epsilon }^{(n)} \) with respect to \( f(x) \) as follows: \[ A_{\epsilon }^{(n)}=\left \{(x_{1},x_{2},\ldots ,x_{n})\in S^{n}:\left |-\frac {1}{n}\log f(x_{1},x_{2},\ldots ,x_{n})-h(X)\right |\leq \epsilon \right \}, \] where \( f(x_{1},x_{2},\ldots ,x_{n})=\prod _{i=1}^{n}f(x_{i}) \).

      Definition. Volume of set [007D]

      • April 22, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      The volume Vol(\( A \)) of a set \( A\subset \mathcal {R}^{n} \) is defined as \[ \text {Vol}(A)=\int _{A}dx_{1}\,dx_{2}\,\cdots \,dx_{n}. \]

      Definition. Retraction [0076]

      • April 14, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      A retraction is a smooth map \( R:\mathrm {T}\mathcal {M}\mapsto \mathcal {M} \) such that if \( h(t)=R(\mathbf {x},t\mathbf {v})=R_{\mathbf {x}}(t\mathbf {v}) \), then \( h(0)=\mathbf {x} \) and \( h^{\prime }(0)=\mathbf {v} \).

      Definition. Riemannian Gradient [0077]

      • April 14, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      Let \( f:\mathcal {M}\mapsto \mathbb {R} \) be smooth on the Riemannian manifold \( \mathcal {M} \). The Riemannian gradient \( \,\operatorname {grad}f(\boldsymbol {x})\, \) of \( f \) at \( \boldsymbol {x}\in \mathcal {M} \) is the unique tangent vector at \( \boldsymbol {x} \) such that \[ \mathrm {D}f(\boldsymbol {x})[\boldsymbol {v}]\ =\ \langle \operatorname {grad}f(\boldsymbol {x}),\boldsymbol {v}\rangle _{\boldsymbol {x}}\,,\quad \forall \,\boldsymbol {v}\in \mathrm {T}_{\boldsymbol {x}}\mathcal {M}. \] By extending the definition of \( f \) to the ambient Euclidean space \( \mathbb {R}^{n} \), we can show that \[\mathrm {grad} f(\mathbf {x}) = \mathcal {P}_{T_x \mathcal {M}}(\nabla f(\mathbf {x}))\] where \( {\mathcal {P}}_{\mathrm {T}_{\mathbf {x}}\mathcal {M}}\) is the orthogonal projector from \(\mathbb {R}^n\) to \(T_x \mathcal {M}\)

      Definition. Riemannian Gradient Descent [007B]

      • April 14, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      For \(f : \mathcal {M} \mapsto \mathbb {R}\), \[ x_{k+1}\ =\ R_{{\mathbf {x}}_{k}}(-\tau _{k}\operatorname {grad}f({\mathbf {x}}_{k})) \]

      Can do backtracking line search i.e. while \[f(R_{x_{k}}(-\tau \,{\rm grad}\,f(\mathbf {x}_{k}))) > f(\mathbf {x}_{k}) - c_{1}\tau \, | |{\rm grad}\,f(\mathbf {x}_{k})| |_{2}^{2} \] do \[ \tau \ \leftarrow \ \alpha \cdot \tau \]

      Definition. Riemannian Hessian [007A]

      • April 14, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      Let \( f:{\cal M}\mapsto \mathbb {R} \) be smooth on the Riemannian Manifold \( {\cal M} \). The Riemannian Hessian \( {\rm Hess}\,f(\mathbf {x}):{\rm T}_{\mathbf {x}}{\cal M}\mapsto {\rm T}_{\mathbf {x}}{\cal M} \) of \( f \) at \( \mathbf {x}\in {\cal M} \) is a mapping from \( {\rm T}_{\mathbf {x}}{\cal M} \) to \( {\rm T}_{\mathbf {x}}{\cal M} \) with \[ {\rm Hess}\,f(\mathbf {x})[\mathbf {v}]\ :=\ \widetilde {\nabla }_{\mathbf {v}}\,{\rm grad}\,f(\mathbf {x}). \]

      • Here, \(\tilde {\nabla }\) is the Riemannian connection.
      • On a Riemannian submanifold embedded in \(\mathbb {R}^n\) \[\tilde {\nabla }_{\mathbf {u}} V = \mathcal {P}_{T_{\mathbf {x}} \mathcal {M}}(\mathrm {D}V(\mathbf {x})[\mathbf {u}])\] and \[\mathrm {Hess}\,f(\mathbf {x})[\mathbf {v}]\ =\ {\mathcal {P}}_{\mathrm {T}_{\mathbf {x}}{\mathcal {M}}}\,(\mathrm {D}\,\mathrm {grad}\,f(\mathbf {x})[\mathbf {v}])\]

      Definition. Riemannian Manifold [0072]

      • April 14, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      A Riemannian manifold \( (\mathcal {M},\langle \cdot ,\cdot \rangle ) \) is a smooth manifold \( \mathcal {M} \) equipped with positive-definite inner product \( \langle \cdot ,\cdot \rangle \) on the tangent space \( \mathrm {T}_{\pmb {x}}\mathcal {M} \) at each point \( \pmb {x}\in \mathcal {M} \).

      Definition. Riemannian Metric [0079]

      • April 14, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      A choice of inner product \(\langle \cdot , \cdot \rangle _x\) for each tangent space \(\mathrm {T}_x \mathcal {M}\) defines a Riemannian metric on \(\mathcal {M}\).

      Claim. Riemmanian Metric [0078]

      • April 14, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      \( \langle \cdot ,\cdot \rangle _{\textbf {x}} \) defines a Riemmanian Metric on \( \mathcal {M} \) if for any two smooth vector fields \(\mathbf {V}\) and \(\mathbf {W}\), the function \( \textbf {x}\mapsto \left \langle \mathbf {V}(\textbf {x}),\mathbf {W}(\textbf {x})\right \rangle _{\textbf {x}} \) is smooth.

      Definition. Smooth Manifold [0073]

      • April 14, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      We say \( \mathcal {M}\subseteq \mathbb {R}^{n} \) is an embedded smooth submanifold of codimension \( k \) if there exists a smooth function \( g:\mathbb {R}^{n}\mapsto \mathbb {R}^{k} \), such that \[ \mathcal {M}\equiv \left \{\boldsymbol {x}\in \mathbb {R}^{n}\mid g(\boldsymbol {x})=\boldsymbol {0}\right \}, \] \[ \mathrm {D}g(\boldsymbol {x}):\mathbb {R}^{n}\mapsto \mathbb {R}^{k}\text { has rank }k,\ \forall \boldsymbol {x}\in \mathcal {M}. \]

      Definition. Tangent Bundle [0074]

      • April 14, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      The tangent bundle of \( {\cal M} \) is the disjoint union of all tangent spaces: \[ {\rm T}{\cal M}\ =\ \{(\mathbf {x},\mathbf {v})\ \mid \ \mathbf {x}\in {\cal M},\ {\rm and}\ \mathbf {v}\in {\rm T}_{\mathbf {x}}{\cal M}\} \]

      Definition. Tangent Space [0075]

      • April 14, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      The tangent space \( \mathrm {T}_{\pmb {x}}\mathcal {M} \) at a point \( \pmb {x}\in \mathcal {M} \) is defined as \[T_x \mathcal {M} = \ker Dg(\mathbf {x})\] which is a linear subspace of \( \mathbb {R}^{n} \).

      Definition. Encoder [0071]

      • April 12, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      An encoder (with feedback) with parameter \( (n,\Theta ) \) for a channel is a vector of mappings \( e_{i} \) for \( i=1,2,\ldots ,n \), where \[ e_{i}:\{1,2,\ldots ,\Theta \}\times \mathcal {Y}^{i-1}\to \mathcal {X}. \]

      Definition. General definition of channel [0070]

      • April 12, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      A channel (with memory) is a sequence of conditional distributions:_ \[ P_{Y_{1}|X_{1}},P_{Y_{2}|Y_{1},X^{2}},P_{Y_{3}|Y^{2},X^{3}},\ldots ,P_{Y_{n}|Y^{n-1},X^{n}}, \] where \( P_{Y_{n}|Y^{n-1},X^{n}} \) is a collection of distributions on \( \mathcal {Y} \) one for every \( (y^{n-1},x^{n})\in \mathcal {Y}^{n-1}\times \mathcal {X}^{n} \).

      import os
HLO_PATH, MOSAIC_PATH, LLO_PATH = "/tmp/hlo", "/tmp/mosaic", "/tmp/llo"

os.environ["XLA_FLAGS"] = (
    f"--xla_dump_hlo_as_text "
    f"--xla_dump_to={HLO_PATH} "
    f"--xla_dump_hlo_pass_re=.* "
)
os.environ["LIBTPU_INIT_ARGS"] = (
    f"--xla_jf_dump_to={LLO_PATH} "
    f"--xla_jf_dump_llo_text=true "
    f"--xla_jf_dump_hlo_text=true "
    f"--xla_jf_dump_llo_static_gaps=true "
    f"--xla_jf_emit_annotations=true "
    f"--xla_jf_debug_level=2 "
    f"--xla_mosaic_dump_to={MOSAIC_PATH} "
    f"--xla_mosaic_enable_dump_debug_info=true "
    f"--xla_mosaic_enable_llo_source_annotations=true"
)

      To understand these flags, one first needs to understand the Pallas lowering pipeline.

      XLA Compilation [M74N]

      • May 22, 2026
      • Kellen Kanarios

      Overview.

      • Dispatch / Cache: caches compilation based on input argument signatures i.e. shapes, dtypes, sharding. If shapes change will need to recompile.
      • Lowering: Python -> jaxpr -> StableHLO. This stage is a translation, not an optimization — no Operator fusion happens here. See chlo desugars, stablehlo is stable, mhlo is internal for the dialects involved and Three calls, three IR levels for how to print each level.
      • XLA: StableHLO is converted to HLO, and the optimizing passes — simplification, layout assignment, fusion, collective scheduling, memory assignment — run there. Read after_optimizations, not before_optimizations, for anything performance-related (Only after_optimizations matches the profile).
      • TPU specific: Further reduced to LLO IR, then very large instruction word (VLIW) scheduling to map dot products to Matrix Multiply Unit (MXU).
      Remark. The Python source is thrown away as soon as it is traced into a jaxpr, and the jaxpr in turn is thrown away once it is lowered. What XLA ingests is StableHLO, which it converts to HLO before optimizing; HLO is XLA's internal representation, not its input format. The only thread back to the Python you wrote is the metadata carried on each instruction (op_name is the trace path back to Python).

      Lifecycle of a JAX program [NR79]

      • August 7, 2026
      • Kellen Kanarios

      We have the following compilation pipeline

      1. Tracing: Python / JAX -> jaxpr
        • jax.make_jaxpr(fun)(*args)
        • Abstract execution. JAX executes python code using abstract tracer objects instead of real arrays.
        • Every operation and its intermediate result is recorded into jaxpr.
        • Sequence used to construct a grap, which the XLA compiler will later optimize.
        • Python code is executed once during tracing but excluded from final graph.
        • Each JAX primitive registers functions for
          • Lowering to StableHLO
          • How it is transformed under grad and vmap.
      2. Lowering: Jaxpr -> StableHLO
        • fn_lowered = jax.jit(fun).lower(*args)
        • stable_hlo = fn_lowered.as_text()
        • fn_lowered.compiler_ir(dialect='stablehlo') for the MLIR module rather than its text. There is no 'hlo' dialect to ask for here — HLO is produced inside XLA, one step later (chlo desugars, stablehlo is stable, mhlo is internal), and you reach it through .compile().as_text() (Three calls, three IR levels).
        • Multiple ML frameworks lower to StableHLO.
          • Hardware agnostic.
          • Backwards compatible.
      3. Compile: HLO -> Optimized HLO -> LLO IR -> VLIW -> Executables
        • compiled = fn_lowered.compile()
        • compiled.runtime_executable() returns a LoadedExecutable.
        • Useful(?) compiled.cost_analysis().
        • HLO:
          • Input for XLA compiler.
          • Directed acyclic graph of copmutational operations.
          • All array dimensions are known at compile time.
          • Limited opcodes i.e. Add, Multiply, Transpose, Dot, etc.

      XLA Shapes and Memory Layout.

      • Every data type defined by data type and fixed dimensions, determined at compile time.
      • Minor-to-major order i.e. fastest changing to slowesting changin.
      • Tiling: arrays are split into smaller blocks to fit into VREG. Want to arrange data to efficiently fit VREG.

      Execution.

      • Move tensors from CPU to HBM. Sharding is taken care of by PJIT if on TPU pod.
      • Async: Immediately returns a Future JAX array while the hardware executes VLIW microcode asynchronously.
      • Buffer management: Returns pointer to TPU memory. All handled lazily. Not copied back to CPU until jax.block_until_ready().

      Getting the dumps

      • May 22, 2026
      • Kellen Kanarios

      Half of reading compiler output is arranging to read the right compiler output. The recurring mistake is answering a performance question from before_optimizations, which describes a program that never ran.

      Card. Three calls, three IR levels [AGEG]

      • August 22, 2026
      • Kellen Kanarios

      How do you print each IR level for a JAX function f?

      Answer
      1. jaxpr — jax.make_jaxpr(f)(x).
      2. StableHLO, pre-XLA — jax.jit(f).lower(x).as_text(), or .compiler_ir(dialect='stablehlo').
      3. Optimized HLO, post-XLA passes and matching the profile — jax.jit(f).lower(x).compile().as_text().
      The three answer genuinely different questions, and reaching for the wrong one wastes an afternoon (Lifecycle of a JAX program):
      • The jaxpr says what tracing captured — so it answers "why is this constant baked in", "why is there a convert_element_type here" (A weak type adopts the other operand's dtype), "did my Python branch get traced at all".
      • The StableHLO says what JAX handed to XLA — the boundary where a JAX bug becomes an XLA bug.
      • The optimized HLO says what XLA built — fusions, layouts, collectives (Only after_optimizations matches the profile).

      Card. Only after_optimizations matches the profile [BQUG]

      • August 22, 2026
      • Kellen Kanarios

      What is the difference between the before_optimizations and after_optimizations HLO files in an XLA dump?

      Answer before_optimizations — the HLO as imported from StableHLO. Shapes carry no meaningful layouts yet (The layout is minor-to-major), nothing is fused, and there is roughly one instruction per source operation. Read it when you want to know what JAX asked for. after_optimizations — past simplification, layout assignment, Operator fusion, collective scheduling, and memory assignment. Read it when you want to know what runs. Only the second one corresponds to the kernels in a profile, because the fusion names in the profile are the fusion instruction names here (A fusion op is a kernel launch boundary). A performance question answered from before_optimizations is answered about a program that never executed — the op you are worried about may have been fused away, folded, or duplicated (The dump filename encodes the stage).

      Card. Per-pass dumps find the pass that broke it [8U47]

      • August 22, 2026
      • Kellen Kanarios

      What does XLA_FLAGS=--xla_dump_to=/tmp/dump give you, and how do you get per-pass IR?

      Answer A directory of per-module files: pre- and post-optimization HLO text (Only after_optimizations matches the profile), the buffer assignment, and on GPU the generated PTX and LLVM IR (The dump filename encodes the stage). Add --xla_dump_hlo_pass_re=.* to dump the HLO before and after every pass matching the regex. That is how you find which pass introduced a copy or broke a fusion — bisect the pass list rather than staring at the endpoints. Narrow the regex once you have a suspect, since .* on a real model produces a great many files. --xla_dump_hlo_as_html and --xla_dump_hlo_as_dot give graph views, which are far easier than text for fusion structure (A fusion op is a kernel launch boundary) — a flat instruction list hides exactly the thing you are looking at. The MLIR side has the same facility in --mlir-print-ir-after-all (Print generic, print locations, disable threading).

      Card. The dump filename encodes the stage [JFMQ]

      • August 22, 2026
      • Kellen Kanarios

      Reading an XLA dump directory: what is in module_0001.jit_f.before_optimizations.txt versus the after_optimizations and sm_XX files?

      Answer The filename encodes module index, entry name, and pipeline stage. Read them in this order:
      1. before_optimizations — one-to-one with your StableHLO. Use it to confirm JAX emitted what you meant.
      2. after_optimizations — fused, laid out, scheduled. Map profile kernels to the fusion names here (Only after_optimizations matches the profile).
      3. Backend artifacts — PTX and LLVM IR on GPU, Mosaic or LLO on TPU. What actually ran.
      Each module index is a separate compilation, so a program with several jit boundaries, or one that retraced on a new input shape, produces several sets. When a dump directory has more modules than you expected, that count is the finding — it means recompilation you did not intend (XLA Compilation).

      TLDR: Learned weighting of token embeddings. Essentially, learning which words to "attend" to in the input sequence. Have matrices \(\mathbf {Q} = \begin {bmatrix} \begin {bmatrix} \text {---} & \mathbf {q}^{(1)} & \text {---} \end {bmatrix} \\ \vdots \\ \begin {bmatrix} \text {---} & \mathbf {q}^{(n)} & \text {---} \end {bmatrix} \end {bmatrix} \in \mathbb {R}^{n \times d_q}\), \( \mathbf {K} = \begin {bmatrix} \begin {bmatrix} \text {---} & \mathbf {k}^{(1)} & \text {---} \end {bmatrix} \\ \vdots \\ \begin {bmatrix} \text {---} & \mathbf {k}^{(n)} & \text {---} \end {bmatrix} \end {bmatrix} \in \mathbb {R}^{n \times d_k} \) \( \mathbf {V} = \begin {bmatrix} \begin {bmatrix} \text {---} & \mathbf {v}^{(1)} & \text {---} \end {bmatrix} \\ \vdots \\ \begin {bmatrix} \text {---} & \mathbf {v}^{(n)} & \text {---} \end {bmatrix} \end {bmatrix} \in \mathbb {R}^{n \times d_v} \)

      Intuition 1. Convex re-weighting of input tokens. Note that \[ \begin {align*} \begin {bmatrix} p_1 & p_2 & p_3 \end {bmatrix} \begin {bmatrix} \begin {bmatrix} \text {---} & \mathbf {v}^{(1)} & \text {---} \end {bmatrix} \\ \begin {bmatrix} \text {---} & \mathbf {v}^{(2)} & \text {---} \end {bmatrix} \\ \begin {bmatrix} \text {---} & \mathbf {v}^{(3)} & \text {---} \end {bmatrix} \end {bmatrix} = p_1 \mathbf {v}^{(1)} + p_2 \mathbf {v}^{(2)} + p_3 \mathbf {v}^{(3)} \end {align*} \] \[ \begin {align*} \begin {bmatrix} p_{11} & 0 & 0 \\ p_{21} & p_{22} & 0 \\ p_{31} & p_{32} & p_{33} \end {bmatrix} \begin {bmatrix} \begin {bmatrix} \text {---} & \mathbf {v}^{(1)} & \text {---} \end {bmatrix} \\ \begin {bmatrix} \text {---} & \mathbf {v}^{(2)} & \text {---} \end {bmatrix} \\ \begin {bmatrix} \text {---} & \mathbf {v}^{(3)} & \text {---} \end {bmatrix} \end {bmatrix} = \begin {bmatrix} p_{11} \mathbf {v}^{(1)} \\ p_{21} \mathbf {v}^{(1)} + p_{22} \mathbf {v}^{(2)} \\ p_{31} \mathbf {v}^{(1)} + p_{32} \mathbf {v}^{(2)} + p_{33} \mathbf {v}^{(3)} \end {bmatrix} \end {align*} \] Intuition 2. Context dependent re-weighting. If \(\mathbf {p} = \mathbb {S}(\mathbf {Q} \mathbf {K}^T)\) then \[ \begin {align*} p_{ij} = \frac {\mathbf {q}^{(i)} \cdot \mathbf {k}^{(j)}}{\sum _{j} \mathbf {q}^{(i)} \cdot \mathbf {k}^{(j)}} \end {align*} \]

      Example. Suppose that \(\mathbf {x} = \text {I play with the ball}\). Then \[ \begin {align*} \mathbf {x}^{(5)} = \mathrm {Embed}(\text {``ball"}) \end {align*} \] A feasible query for "ball" would be a verb describing the action of the ball, so maybe \[ \begin {align*} W_q \mathbf {x}^{(5)} = \mathrm {Embed}(\text {``play"}) \end {align*} \] and a key for "play" would be what you are playing with like a ball, so \[ \begin {align*} W_k \mathbf {x}^{(2)} = \mathrm {Embed}(\text {``ball"}) \end {align*} \] i.e. \[ \begin {align*} \mathrm {Query}(\text {``quantum"}) \cdot \mathrm {Key}(\text {``mechanics"}) \approx ||\mathrm {Query}(\text {``quantum"})|| \cdot ||\mathrm {Key}(\text {``mechanics"})|| \end {align*} \]

      \[ \begin {align*} \left [\mathbb {S}(\mathbf {Q}\mathbf {K}^T)\right ]_{4} &= \mathbb {S}\left (\begin {bmatrix} \mathbf {q}^{(4)} \cdot \mathbf {k}^{(1)} & \mathbf {q}^{(4)} \cdot \mathbf {k}^{(2)} & \mathbf {q}^{(4)} \cdot \mathbf {k}^{(3)} & \mathbf {q}^{(4)} \cdot \mathbf {k}^{(4)} & \mathbf {q}^{(4)} \cdot \mathbf {k}^{(5)} & \mathbf {q}^{(4)} \cdot \mathbf {k}^{(6)} \end {bmatrix} \right ) \\ &= \begin {bmatrix} 0 & 0.2 & 0.3 & 0.5 & 0 & 0 \end {bmatrix} \end {align*} \] \[ \left [\mathbb {S}(\mathbf {Q}\mathbf {K}^T)\right ]_{4} \mathbf {V} = 0.2 \mathbf {v}^{(2)} + 0.3 \mathbf {v}^{(3)} + 0.5 \mathbf {v}^{(5)} \]

      Definition. Achievable rates [006U]

      • April 1, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      A rate \(R \geq 0\) is achievable if

      1. \(\lim _{n\to \infty } P_{e, \text {max}} = 0\)
      2. \(\lim _{n \to \infty } \frac {\log _{2}M_n}{n} = R\)

      Definition. Channel capacity [006V]

      • April 1, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      The channel capacity is the maximum achievable rate i.e. \[C = \sup \{R \geq 0 \mid R \text { is achievable}\} \]

      Definition. Channel coding problem [006S]

      • April 1, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      A code with parameter \((M, n)\) i.e. (number of messages, number of channel users) consists of an encoder decoder pair

      • \(e : [M] \to \mathcal {X}^n\)
      • \(f: \mathcal {Y}^n \to [M]\)
      • The rate is \(\log _{2}\frac {M}{n} = \) (log of the number of distinct pairs)/(number of channel users)
      • \(P_{e, \text {max}} = \max _{1 \leq i \leq m}\mathbb {P}(f(Y^n) \neq i \mid W = i)\) - worst case over all transmitted messages prob of error.
      • \(P_{e} = \frac {1}{M}\sum _{i = 1}^{M} \mathbb {P}(f(Y^n) \neq i \mid W = i)\) - average prob of error.

      Definition. Symmetric Channels [006Y]

      • April 1, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      A channel is symmetric if

These AI kernels follow well-defined data-flow patterns, such as moving tiles between DRAM and SRAM and performing a sequence of computations on those tiles. However, writing high-performance kernels remains complex despite the clarity of these patterns. Achieving peak performance requires careful, hardware-centric optimizations to fully leverage modern accelerators. While domain-specific compilers attempt to reduce the burden of writing high-performance kernels, they often struggle with usability and expressiveness gaps. In this paper, we present TileLang, a generalized tiled programming model for more efficient AI Kernel programming. TileLang decouples scheduling space (thread binding, layout, tensorize and pipeline) from dataflow, and encapsulated them as a set of customization annotations and primitives.       Definition. Fixed rate universal code [006K]

      • March 30, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      A sequence of fixed-rate source codes \( \{(e_{n},f_{n}):n \geq 1\} \) with parameters \( \{(n,2^{nR_{n}}):n \geq 1\} \) is said to be universal with rate \( R \) if the following are true:

      1. The limiting rate satisfies \( \lim _{n\to \infty }R_{n}\leq R \).
      2. For any distribution \( P \) over the alphabet \( \mathcal {X} \) with \( H(P)<R \), the probability of error, \( \mathbb {P}_{X^{n}\sim P^{n}} \left (f_{n}(e_{n}(X^{n})) \neq X^{n}\right )=0\).

      Lempel-Ziv Algorithm [006P]

      • March 30, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      The algorithm proceed as follows:

      1. Initalize the dictionary to an empty set
      2. Make one pass through the stream of data
      3. Add every new "phrase" to the dictionary
      4. Encode only the elements of the dictionary

      Definition. Minimax Redundancy [006N]

      • March 30, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      Let \( \mathcal {X} \) denote an alphabet of size \( m \), and let \( \mathcal {P}=\{P_{1},\ldots ,P_{k}\} \) denote a collection of \( k \) distinct distributions on \( \mathcal {X} \) (every \( P_{i} \) can be identified with a pmf in \( \Delta _{m} \)). Now, consider the following two-player game:

      • Player 1, representing adversary, chooses a distribution \(P\) from the set \(\mathcal {P}\)
      • Player 2, representing source coder, constructs a code according to the distribution \(Q \in \Delta _m\) without knowledge of \(P\)
      The goal of Player 2is to identify a \(Q\) that minimizes the worst-case redundancy \[{\mathcal {R}}^{*}\equiv {\mathcal {R}}^{*}({\mathcal {P}}):=\operatorname *{min}_{Q\in \Delta _{m}}\operatorname *{max}_{P\in {\mathcal {P}}}{\mathcal {R}}(P,Q)=\operatorname *{min}_{Q\in \Delta _{m}}\operatorname *{max}_{P\in {\mathcal {P}}}D_{\mathrm {KL}}(P\parallel Q).\]

      Proposition. Redundancy of a mismatched code is the KL divergence [006M]

      • March 30, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      Suppose \( X\sim Q \), but we encode it using an optimal code for \( P \). Then, the redundancy incurred is approximately equal to \( D_{KL}(Q\parallel P) \).

      Proof. We know that the optimal codeword for \( P \) has lengths approximately equal to \( \ell _{P}(x)\approx \log (1/p(x)) \), where \( p \) denotes the pmf of \( P \). Whereas the optimal codeword for \( Q \) assigns lengths \( \ell _{Q}(x)\approx \log (1/q(x)) \). Then, the redundancy is \[ \begin {align*} \mathcal {R}(Q,P)&=\mathbb {E}_{X\sim Q}[\ell _{P}(X)-\ell _{Q}(X)]\approx \mathbb {E}_{X\sim Q}[-\log (p(X))+\log (q(X))] \\ &=\mathbb {E}_{X\sim Q}\left [\log \left (\frac {q(X)}{p(X)}\right )\right ]=D_{\mathrm {KL}}(Q\parallel P) .\end {align*} \]

      Theorem. Redundancy-Capacity Theorem [006O]

      • March 30, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      \(\mathcal {R}^*(\mathcal {P}) = C(\mathcal {P}) \coloneqq \sup _{\pi \in \Delta _k} I(W; X)\), where \(I(W; X)\) is the mutual information between \(W \sim \mathbf {\pi } \) and the output \(X\), with \(X | (W = i) \sim P_i\). The optimal \(Q^*\) is \(Q_{\pi }^* = \sum _{i = 1}^{k} \pi _i^* P_i\).

      Theorem. The type-based fixed-rate code is universal [006L]

      • March 30, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      The code constructed above is a universal fixed-rate code, such that \( \lim _{n\to \infty }\mathbb {P}_{X^{n}\sim P^{n}}(f_{n}(e_{n}(X^{n}))\neq X^{n})=0 \) for all \( P \) with \( H(P)<R \).

      Definition. Optimal Bayesian Error Exponent [006I]

      • March 26, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      Consider a binary Bayesian hypothesis testing problem with prior distribution \( (\pi _{0},\pi _{1}) \). Then, we say that an exponent \( V>0 \) is achievable, if there exist a sequence of tests \( \{\Psi _{n}:n\geq 1\} \), with probability of errors \( \{p_{n}(\Psi _{n})=\pi _{0}\psi _{0}(\Psi _{n})+\pi _{1}\psi _{01}(\Psi _{n}):n\geq 1\} \), such that \[ \liminf _{n\to \infty }\frac {1}{n}\log \left (\frac {1}{p_{n}}\right )=\liminf _{n\to \infty }\frac {1}{n}\log \left (\frac {1}{\pi _{0}\psi _{10}(\Psi _{n})+\pi _{1}\psi _{01}(\Psi _{n})}\right )\geq V. \] The optimal Bayesian error exponent for binary hypothesis testing with distributions \( P_{0} \) and \( P_{1} \) is defined as \( V^{*}\equiv V^{*}(P_{0},P_{1})=\sup \{V>0:V\text {is achievable}\} \).

      Theorem. Optimal Bayesian Error Exponent [006J]

      • March 26, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      For any \( \lambda \in [0,1] \) let \( P_{\lambda } \) denote the distribution over \( \mathcal {X} \) such that \( P_{\lambda }(x)\propto P_{0}^{\lambda }(x)\times P_{1}^{\lambda -1}(x) \). Let \( \lambda ^{*}\in [0,1] \) denote the value at which \( D_{KL}(P_{\lambda ^{*}}\parallel P_{0})=D_{KL}(P_{\lambda ^{*}}\parallel P_{1}) \). Then, the optimal error exponent in the Bayesian hypothesis testing problem with distributions \( P_{0} \) and \( P_{1} \) satisfies: \[ V^{*}(P_{0},P_{1})=D_{KL}(P_{\lambda ^{*}}\parallel P_{0})=D_{KL}(P_{\lambda ^{*}}\parallel P_{1}). \]

      Proposition. Optimal Bayesian Test [006F]

      • March 26, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      Let \( X^{n}\stackrel {{i.i.d.}}{{\sim }}P_{X} \), and consider a binary hypothesis testing problem with \( H_{0}:P_{X}=P_{0} \) versus \( H_{1}:P_{X}=P_{1}. \) Let \( (\pi _{0},\pi _{1}) \) denote the prior distribution of the two hypotheses being true. Then, the Bayes optimal hypothesis test with uniform loss is defined as \[ \Psi _{D}^{*}(X^{n})=\operatorname *{argmin}_{\Psi }\pi _{0}\pi _{10}(\Psi )+\pi _{1}\pi _{01}(\Psi )=\begin {cases}1&\text { if }L(X^{n})>\pi _{0}/\pi _{1}\\ 0&\text {otherwise.}\end {cases}, \]

      Definition. Optimal Error Exponent in NP setting [006G]

      • March 26, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      We say that an error exponent \( V \) is achievable with type-1 error \( \alpha >0 \), if there exist a sequence of tests \( (\Psi _{n}) \) with errors \( (\alpha _{n},\beta _{n}) \), satisfying \[ \alpha _{n}\leq \alpha ,\quad \text {and}\quad -\frac {1}{n}\log \beta _{n}\geq V. \] Let \( V_{\alpha }:=\sup \{V:V\text { is achievable with type-1 error }\alpha \} \). The optimal error exponent is defined as \( V^{*}=\inf \{V_{\alpha }:\alpha >0\}=\lim _{\alpha \downarrow 0}V_{\alpha } \).

      Theorem. Stein's Lemma [006H]

      • March 26, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      For any \( \alpha >0 \), we have \( V_{\alpha }=D_{KL}(P_{0}\parallel P_{1}) \), which also implies that \( V^{*}=D_{KL}(P_{0}\parallel P_{1}) \). In other words, the relative entropy between \( P_{0} \) and \( P_{1} \) is the optimal type-II error exponent associated with a binary hypothesis testing problem with \( H_{0}:P_{X}=P_{0} \) and \( H_{1}:P_{X}=P_{1} \).

      Definition. Bayesian Framework [006D]

      • March 25, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      Assume we have prior distributions \((\pi _{0}, \pi _{1})\) over the two hypotheses and there exists costs \(C_{1|0}\), \(C_{0|1}\) associated with type I and type II error respectively. Then the Bayes optimal solution is the solution of \[ \operatorname *{min}_{P_{Z|X}}\pi _{0}C_{1|0}\mathbb {P}_{H_{0}}(Z=1)+\pi _{1}C_{0|1}\mathbb {P}_{H_{1}}(Z=0). \]

      • March 25, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      Let \( P\in \mathcal {P}_{n} \), and \( T(P) \) denote its type class. Then, the following bounds hold: \[ (n+1)^{-m}2^{nH(P)}\leq |T(P)|\leq 2^{nH(P)}. \]

      Definition. Huffman Code [005W]

      • March 25, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      Given \(x_1, \ldots x_m\) proceed as follows:

      1. Take two \(x_i, x_j\) with smallest \(p(x_i), p(x_j)\) append 0 and 1 to their respective codes.
      2. Combine them and treat them as a new value with \(p(x_i') = p(x_i) + p(x_j)\)
      3. Repeat

      Given \(x_1, \ldots x_m\) proceed as follows:

      1. Take two \(x_i, x_j\) with smallest \(p(x_i), p(x_j)\) append 0 and 1 to their respective codes.

      Theorem. Optimality of Huffman Code [0060]

      • March 25, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      Let \(X \sim P_X\) be an \(\mathcal {X}\)-valued random variable. Define \[L_H = \mathbb {E}_{X \sim P_X}[\ell _H(x)]\] and \[L^*(P_X) = \min _{\ell _1, \ldots , \ell _m} \sum _{i = 1}^{m} P_X(x_i) \ell _i.\] Then \(L_H = L^*(P_X)\).

      Remark. SFE satisfies \(L_H < H(X) + \frac {2}{n}\) i.e. it achieves the optimal rate as \(n \to \infty \). Huffman coding achieves optimality for all finite values \(n\).

      Definition. Hypothesis error [006B]

      • March 25, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      In any binary hypothesis testing problem, a test \( P_{Z|X|} \) can incur two types of errors: \[\begin {align*} \pi _{1|0}(P_{Z|X})&=\mathbb {P}_{H_{0}}\ (Z=1) \quad \text {(type-I error of false alarm rate)} \\ \pi _{01}(P_{Z|X})&=\mathbb {P}_{H_{1}}\ (Z=0) \quad \text {(type-II error or missed detection rate)} .\end {align*}\]

      Definition. Hypothesis test [006A]

      • March 25, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      A randomized hypothesis test is a channel which takes in the data \( X \) and outputs a \( \{0,1\} \) valued random variable \( Z \), where \( Z=i \) represents that the test declares that \( H_{i} \) is true, for \( i\in \{0,1\} \). \[ X\sim P\longrightarrow \boxed {P_{Z|X}}\longrightarrow Z \] In some cases, it is sufficient to focus on non-randomized or deterministic tests, for which \( P_{\mathbb {Z}|X=x} \) is a delta function. That is, for a given realization of \( X \), the output of the test is deterministic (it is equal to \( H_{0} \) or \( H_{1} \) with probability 1). Such deterministic tests can be equivalently represented by a function \( \Psi \), or a subset \( B \) of the domain \( X \): \[ \Psi (X)=\mathbf {1}_{B}(X)=\begin {cases}1,&\text {if}X\in B\\ 0,&\text {if}X\not \in B.\end {cases} \]

      Definition. Hypothesis testing problem [0069]

      • March 25, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      A binary hypothesis testing problem involves three components: the data \( X\sim P \), the null hypothesis class \( \mathcal {P}_{0} \), and the alternative distribution class \( \mathcal {P}_{1} \), and the goal is to use the data to decide between the null and alternative; that is, \[ \text {given}\ X\sim P,\quad \text {decide between}\quad H_{0}:P\in \mathcal {P}_{0},\quad \text {versus}\quad H_{1}:P\in \mathcal {P}_{1}. \] When \( {\cal P}_{0} \) and \( {\cal P}_{1} \) are singleton sets: that is \( {\cal P}_{0}=\{P_{0}\} \) and \( {\cal P}_{1}=\{P_{1}\} \) with known \( P_{0},P_{1} \), then the problem is called simple hypothesis testing, and this is what we will focus on mostly in this course: \[ \text {given}\ X\sim P,\quad \text {decide between} \quad H_{0}:P=P_{0},\quad \text {versus}\quad H_{1}:P=P_{1}. \]

      Definition. Minimax Optimal [006E]

      • March 25, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      Find a test that minimzes the maximum of the two errors i.e. \[ \operatorname *{min}_{P_{Z|X}}\operatorname *{max}\left \{\mathbb {P}_{H_{0}}(Z=1),\ \mathbb {P}_{H_{1}}(Z=0)\right \}=\operatorname *{min}_{P_{Z|X}}\operatorname *{max}\left \{\pi _{1|0}(P_{Z|X}),\ \pi _{0|1}(P_{Z|X})\right \}. \]

      Definition. Neyman-Pearson Framework [006C]

      • March 25, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      Given \(\alpha \in (0,1)\). The optimal hypothesis test in the Neyman-Pearson framework is one that satisfies \[\operatorname *{min}_{P_{Z\mid X}}\;\mathbb {P}_{H_{1}}\left (Z=0\right ),\quad \mathrm {subject\,to}\quad \mathbb {P}_{H_{0}}\left (Z=1\right )\leq \alpha .\]

      Theorem. Optimal NP Test [0068]

      • March 25, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      Consider a hypothesis testing problem with observations \( X^{n}\stackrel {\text {i.i.d.}}{\sim }P_{X} \), with the null \( H_{0} : P_{X} =P_{0} \) and alternative \( H_{1}:P_{X}=P_{1} \). Then, the optimal NP test with level \( \alpha \in (0,1] \) has the following structure: \[ \Psi _{NP}^{*}(X^{n})=\begin {cases}1,&\text { if }L(X^{n})>\tau \\ \gamma ,&\text { if }L(X^{n})=\tau \\ 0,&\text { if }L(X^{n})<\tau .\end {cases} \] In the above display, \( L(X^{n}) \) denotes the likelihood ratio \( p_{1}(X^{n})/p_{0}(X^{n}) \), and \( \gamma \in [0,1] \) and \( \tau \geq 0 \) are constants that ensure \( \pi _{1|0}(\Psi ^*_{NP})=\mathbb {P}_{H_{0}}(\Psi ^*_{NP}(X^{n})=1)=\alpha \). Namely, \[\tau = \inf \{\tau \mid \alpha \geq \mathbb {P}(L(X^n) > \tau )\}\] and \[\gamma = \frac {\alpha - \mathbb {P}(L(X^n) > \tau )}{\mathbb {P}(L(X^n) = \tau )}\]

      Theorem. Optimality of Huffman Code [0060]

      • March 25, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      Let \(X \sim P_X\) be an \(\mathcal {X}\)-valued random variable. Define \[L_H = \mathbb {E}_{X \sim P_X}[\ell _H(x)]\] and \[L^*(P_X) = \min _{\ell _1, \ldots , \ell _m} \sum _{i = 1}^{m} P_X(x_i) \ell _i.\] Then \(L_H = L^*(P_X)\).

      Theorem. Sanov's Theorem [0067]

      • March 25, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      Let \( X^{n}\sim Q^{n} \) (i.e., the \( X \)'s are drawn i.i.d. from \( Q \)), and \( E\subset \Delta _{m} \) denote a subset of pmfs over the finite alphabet \( X=\{a_{1},\ldots ,a_{m}\} \). Let \( Q^{n}(E) \) denote the probability \( \mathbb {P}_{X^{n}\sim Q^{n}}(\widehat {P}_{X^{n}}\in E) \). Then, we have \[ Q^{n}(E)\leq 2^{-nD_{\mathbb {E}}(P^{n} \parallel Q)}, \] where \( P^{*}=\inf _{P^{n}\in E}D_{\mathbb {E}}(P^{*}\mid Q) \) is the closest element of \( E \) to \( Q \) in terms of relative entropy. Furthermore, if \( E \) is the closure of its interior, we also have \[ \operatorname *{lim}_{n\to \infty }-{\frac {1}{n}}\log Q^{n}(E)=D_{K L}(P^{*}\parallel Q). \]

      Lemma. Sequence probability depends only on its type [0065]

      • March 25, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      Suppose \( X_{1},X_{2},\ldots ,X_{n}\stackrel {{i.i.d.}}{{\sim }}Q \) for an arbitrary distribution \( Q \) over the alphabet \( \mathcal {X} \). Then, we have \[ \mathbb {P}(X^{n}=x^{n}) \equiv Q^{n}(x^{n}) = 2^{-n(H(\widehat {P}_{x^{n}})+D_{2n}(\widehat {P}_{x^{n}})=Q)}. \] In other words, the probability that \( X^{n} \) takes a value \( x^{n} \) only depends on \( x^{n} \) through its type \( \widehat {P}_{x^{n}} \). Furthermore, types that are far away from \( Q \) in relative entropy are exponentially less probable than those that are close to \( Q \). An immediate consequence of this is that if \( Q\in \mathcal {P}_{n} \), and \( x^{n}\in T(Q) \), then \( Q^{n}(x^{n})=2^{-nH(Q)} \).

      Definition. Set of all types [005Y]

      • March 25, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      For any \( n\geq 1 \), let \( \mathcal {P}_{n} \) denote the set of all possible types over the alphabet \( \mathcal {X} \) with denominator \( n \). That is, \[ \mathcal {P}_{n}=\{\widehat {P}_{x^{n}}:x^{n}\in \mathcal {X}^{n}\}. \]

      Proposition. Size of a type class [0063]

      • March 25, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      Let \( P\in \mathcal {P}_{n} \) denote a type with denominator \( n \). Then, the type class associated with \( P \), defined as \( T(P)=\{x^{n}:\hat {P}_{x^n}=P\} \) satisfies \[ |T(P)|=\prod _{i=1}^{n}\binom {n-N_{i-1}}{N_{i}},\quad \text {where}\quad N_{0}=0,\text {and}\ N_{i}=n\times P(a_{i}), \] for all \( a_{i}\in \mathcal {X}=\{a_{1},\ldots ,a_{m}\} \).

      Proposition. The number of types is polynomial in \(n\) [0062]

      • March 25, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      Suppose \( |\mathcal {X}|=m \), and \( \mathcal {P}_{n} \) denotes the set of all distinct types that can be constructed using elements of \( \mathcal {X}^{n} \). Then, we have_ \[ |\mathcal {P}_{n}|=\binom {n+m-1}{m-1}\leq (n+1)^{m}. \]

      Remark. \(\mathcal {X}^n\) has exponentially many elements in \(n\). However, among the exponentially many elements they can only create polynomially many types in \(n\) for fixed \(m\).

      Theorem. The probability of a type class [0066]

      • March 25, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      Let \( X^{n}=(X_{1},\ldots ,X_{n})\stackrel {{i.i.d.}}{{\sim }}Q \) for an arbitrary distribution \( Q \) on \( \mathcal {X} \). Then, we have the following: \[ (n+1)^{-m}2^{-nD_{KL}(P|Q)}\leq Q^{n}(T(P))\leq 2^{-nD_{KL}(P|Q)}. \] In other words, the probability that \( X^{n}\stackrel {{i.i.d.}}{{\sim }}Q \) lies in the type class of \( P\in \mathcal {P}_{n} \) is \( \approx 2^{-nD_{KL}(P||Q)} \).

      Definition. Type classes [0061]

      • March 25, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      For any type \( P\in \mathcal {P}_{n} \), we can associate the type class \( T(P) \), defined as \[ T(P)=\{x^{n}:\tilde {P}_{x^{n}}=P\}. \]

      Definition. type or empirical distribution [005X]

      • March 25, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      The "type" \( \widehat {P}_{x^{n}} \) associated with \( x^{n}\in \mathcal {X}^{n} \) is the probability distribution on \( \mathcal {X} \) with pmf \( \widehat {\boldsymbol {p}}_{x^{n}} \), defined as \[ \widehat {\boldsymbol {p}}_{x^{n}}(a)=\frac {N(a|x^{n})}{n},\quad \text {where}\quad N(a|x^{n}):=\sum _{i=1}^{n}\mathbf {1}_{x_{i}=a}. \]

      Definition. Singularity of a code [005U]

      • March 24, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      If \(e\) is many-to-one then we say that \(e\) is singular. Similarly, if \(e\) is one-to-one then \(e\) is non-singular.

      Definition. Extensions and Unique Decodability [005M]

      • March 23, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      Given a code with \(n = 1\), we define its extension \(e^*\); that maps \(\mathcal {X}^* \to \{0,1\}^* \) by concatenation. That is \[e^*(x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots , x_m) = (e(x_{1}), e(x_{2}), \ldots , e(x_m))\] A code with encoder \(e\) is said to be uniquely decodable if \(e^*\) is non-singular.

      Theorem. Kraft's inequality [005O]

      • March 23, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      Let \(e: \mathcal {X} \to \{0,1\}^* \) denote a prefix-free code with lengths \(\ell _i = \ell (x_i)\) for \(x_i \in \mathcal {X}\). Suppose \(|\mathcal {X}| = m\). Then the following must be true: \[\sum _{i=1}^{m} 2^{-\ell _i} \leq 1\]

      Remark. The converse holds too: for any lengths \(\ell _i\) satisfying the inequality, one can construct a prefix-free code whose codewords have exactly those lengths.
      Remark. Surprisingly, the constraint is no weaker for the larger class of uniquely decodable codes — every uniquely decodable code must also satisfy the inequality (McMillan). So allowing non-prefix-free-but-decodable codes buys nothing in achievable lengths.

      Theorem. Optimal variable-rate source coding rate equals entropy [005S]

      • March 23, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      \(R_s = H(X)\)

      Definition. Rate of a variable-rate code [005L]

      • March 23, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      Let \(\ell (x^n)\) denote the number of bits in \(e(x^n)\), where \(e\) is the encoding function. Then, the rate is \[\frac {\mathbb {E}[\ell (X^n)]}{n}\]

      Shannon Fano Elias Code [005T]

      • March 23, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      Idea: map symbol \(x\) to interval in \((0,1)\) using the CDF of \(X\).

      • Assume \(x_{1} < x_{2} < \cdots < x_m\)
      • \(X \sim P_X\) is \(\mathcal {X}\)-valued r.v. with \(\mathbf {p}_X\)
      • CDF of \(X = F_X(x) \coloneqq \sum _{x_i \leq x} P(x_i)\)
      • Midpoint function: \(G(x) = \sum _{x_i < x} P_X(x) + \frac {P_X(x)}{2} = F_X(x) - \frac {P_X(x)}{2}\)
      • Codeword: \(e(x) = \left \lfloor G(x) \right \rfloor _{\ell (x)}=\) first \(\ell (x)\) bits of \(G(x)\)
      • \(\ell (x) = \left \lceil \log (\frac {1}{P_X(x)}) \right \rceil + 1\)

      Definition. Variable minimum rate [005R]

      • March 23, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      The minimum rate of variable rate source coding is \(R_s \coloneqq \inf \{R \mid R \text { is achievable}\} \)

      Definition. Variable rate achievability [005Q]

      • March 23, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      A nonnegative number \(R\) is said to be achievable if for all \(\epsilon > 0\), there exists an \(n(\epsilon )\) such that for all \(n \geq n(\epsilon )\), the following holds

      • There exists a variable rate code with \(\mathbb {E}[\ell (X^n)]/n = R\) and \(\mathbb {P}(X^n \neq f(e(X^n))) = 0\) for all \(n\).

      Definition. Variable rate code [005P]

      • March 23, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      A variable rate code with parameter \(n\) is a prefix-free code \(e : \mathcal {X}^n \to \{0, 1\}^* \), and a decoder \(f : \{0,1\}^* \to \mathcal {X}^n \)

      Definition. Variable-rate coding system [005K]

      • March 23, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      A coding system (variable rate) with parameter \(n\) and an encoder-decoder pair \((e,f)\), where \[e: \mathcal {X}^n \to \{0, 1\}^*, \quad \text {and} \quad f: \{0, 1\}^* \to \mathcal {X}^n\] We want the probability of error to be exactly zero; that is \(\mathbb {P}(X^n \neq f(e(X^n))) = 0\).

      Definition. instantaneous / prefix-free code [005N]

      • March 23, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      A code is said to be prefix-free or instantaneous if no codeword is a prefix of another.

      Rebuilding My (Neo)Vim Config From Scratch [005F]

      • March 4, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios
      • 8 min read

      I used LazyVim for a long time, but I kept hitting a wall: understanding how LazyVim did something was consistently harder than if I had just written the thing myself. So I gave myself one day to rebuild from scratch, with the modest goal of first-class support for \(\TeX \), Python, Forester, and C/C++. That one-day sprint is long past, and the config has kept evolving since; this note describes where it landed, not the frantic first pass. The through-line is that almost everything now leans on Neovim's own primitives instead of a framework, which is exactly the transparency I was missing.

      Remark. The whole config lives in my dotfiles. It is a thin init.lua that loads four modules (config.lazy, config.options, config.keymaps, and core.lsp), with the actual plugin specs under lua/plugins/ and per-server LSP tables under lsp/.

      Sane defaults

      • March 4, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      To my surprise, a lot of the behavior I had taken for granted turned out to be options LazyVim set internally. I was greeted on first launch by 8-space indents and a clipboard that would not survive a trip between terminal instances. So the first job was archaeology: I dug through LazyVim for every option I actually liked and copied them into config/options.lua. System clipboard, sensible folding via Treesitter (foldexpr = v:lua.vim.treesitter.foldexpr()), a global statusline, conceallevel for markup: the unglamorous foundation everything else sits on.

      Plugin management

      • March 4, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      The plugin manager is lazy.nvim, the de facto standard, and it genuinely just works. The bootstrap snippet from their docs clones it on first run, and after that every file under lua/plugins/ that returns a spec table is imported automatically. No central manifest to keep in sync; a new file is a new plugin.

      Native LSP, no framework

      • March 4, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      This is where the config diverged most sharply from where it started. The first pass used mason.nvim, mason-lspconfig, and nvim-lspconfig, the standard stack. All three are now gone. Neovim 0.11 ships a native LSP configuration API: vim.lsp.config defines a server and vim.lsp.enable turns it on, and any table returned from lsp/<name>.lua on the runtime path is picked up as that server's config. So core.lsp is just a list:

       vim.lsp.enable({ "forester", "texlab", "clangd", "basedpyright", "lua_ls", "ruff" })

      Each server then gets a plain Lua file in lsp/. No package manager, no bridge plugin translating between two config schemas. I install the servers themselves through my system package manager and let Neovim wire them up. It is dramatically less machinery for the same result, and when something breaks there is exactly one place to look.

      The Python setup is the clearest upgrade. I dropped pyright for basedpyright and split responsibilities: basedpyright does type checking and inlay hints, while ruff runs as its own language server handling import organization and diagnostics. In the LazyVim days I fought constantly with import resolution, hand-writing a function to locate each project's virtualenv and pin pythonPath to its interpreter. basedpyright resolves environments well enough on its own that the hack is gone. clangd, texlab, and lua_ls round out the set, each configured in its own file. texlab in particular carries a fair amount of custom command wiring for building, forward search into Zathura, and environment manipulation.

      A shared LspAttach autocommand in core.lsp binds the buffer-local LSP keymaps once, for every server: go-to-definition and friends route through fzf-lua pickers, and document highlighting, inlay-hint toggling, and native completion get enabled per-buffer based on what each client actually supports.

      Forester finally has a real language server

      • March 4, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      The original post described an ugly hack to get Forester completion. The forester.nvim plugin exposed a completion source, but only for nvim-cmp; blink.cmp (which I use; see below) needs a blink.compat shim, and that shim expected a plugin to be a source rather than to bury one inside a larger feature set. Getting reference completion working meant reading blink.compat internals and registering the source by hand.

      None of that survives, because Forester now ships an actual language server. My lsp/forester.lua just launches forester lsp and hands it the forest root. The one wrinkle worth recording: forester locates the forest by its process working directory and ignores the LSP rootUri, and Neovim does not spawn the server in root_dir by default. So the config resolves the nearest forest.toml and starts the RPC process with an explicit cwd; otherwise the server exits with status 1 whenever Neovim's cwd has no forest.toml (e.g. when I open a tree from $HOME). Reference completion, indispensable for writing this very blog, now flows through the standard LSP path with no shim in sight.

      Completion

      • March 4, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      Completion is blink.cmp, the successor that finally displaced nvim-cmp. Its sources are lsp, path, snippets, and omni, with LuaSnip as the snippet engine. Because I lean on native LSP, the on_attach handler calls vim.lsp.completion.enable with autotrigger, so the server's completions feed the picker directly.

      Layered on top is supermaven-nvim for AI ghost-text suggestions: accept-suggestion, accept-word, and clear bound to <C-l>, <C-j>, and <C-]>. It fills the role Copilot-style tools play elsewhere without getting in the way of the structured LSP and snippet completions.

      Snippets

      • March 4, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      Going all the way back to the Gilles Castel blog post, I have always wanted snippets that auto-expand. Under LazyVim I had settled for friendly-snippets on native Neovim snippets; rebuilding from scratch, I refused to compromise. The engine is LuaSnip, which blink.cmp supports natively, and I have to plug the luasnip-latex-snippets repo that ports the original UltiSnips math snippets over. My own snippets live in a small local plugin, custom-luasnip-snippets.nvim, vendored under lua/local/.

      The trick I had wanted for years and can finally do: load LaTeX math snippets while inside math environments in Forester. The snippet plugin runs with use_treesitter = true, so it inspects the Forester Treesitter grammar, finds the node types for math environments, and only expands the math snippets when the cursor is actually inside one. Writing \(\TeX \) inside a .tree file feels exactly like writing it in a .tex file.

      Formatting and linting

      • March 4, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      Formatting runs through conform.nvim on save. Python is handled by ruff_format followed by pyink, Lua by stylua. This replaced the old black + isort pairing, folding most of it into the same ruff that already runs as a language server. Formatting falls back to the LSP formatter when no dedicated tool is configured for a filetype.

      Fuzzy finding and forest integration

      • March 4, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      The fuzzy finder is fzf-lua, which replaced Telescope. File and grep pickers are scoped to a detected project root, which a small utils.root module (lifted from LazyVim) finds by walking LSP workspace folders, .git, and cwd. A dedicated tex override restricts live-grep to \(\TeX \) source files.

      The piece I am most fond of is forester-new, a local plugin that wires the editor into the forest's own note pipeline. It shells out to scripts/new so every tree gets the standard frontmatter and routing, then commands like :ForesterNew, :ForesterStub, :ForesterCitek, and :ForesterTransient handle the follow-through: creating a tree and inserting a \transclude, stubbing a concept and dropping a [[id]] link at the cursor, or, in visual mode, lifting a selection into a new tree and replacing it in place with the transclude. Stub-and-link without ever leaving the sentence, which is exactly the friction the forest workflow is supposed to remove.

      Anki

      • March 4, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      I originally built a whole in-editor Anki workflow on top of AnkiConnect and a vendored anki.nvim. That has since moved out of the editor and into the forest itself: cards are just \taxon{Card} trees, and scripts/anki-sync mirrors them into Anki, creating the note on first sync and updating in place thereafter. Writing a card is now the same as writing any other tree, snippets and all, and the sync is one command away. This is an example of a card.

      Reference. Temporal Difference Flows [farebrotherTemporalDifferenceFlows2025]

      • March, 2025

      • Jesse Farebrother, Matteo Pirotta, Andrea Tirinzoni, Rémi Munos, Alessandro Lazaric, Ahmed Touati

      • 10.48550/arXiv.2503.09817
      • https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.09817
      @misc{farebrotherTemporalDifferenceFlows2025,
 title = {Temporal {{Difference Flows}}},
 author = {Farebrother, Jesse and Pirotta, Matteo and Tirinzoni, Andrea and Munos, R{\'e}mi and Lazaric, Alessandro and Touati, Ahmed},
 year = {2025},
 doi = {10.48550/arXiv.2503.09817},

 keywords = {Computer Science - Artificial Intelligence,Computer Science - Machine Learning,Statistics - Machine Learning},
 archiveprefix = {arXiv},
 abstract = {Predictive models of the future are fundamental for an agent's ability to reason and plan. A common strategy learns a world model and unrolls it step-by-step at inference, where small errors can rapidly compound. Geometric Horizon Models (GHMs) offer a compelling alternative by directly making predictions of future states, avoiding cumulative inference errors. While GHMs can be conveniently learned by a generative analog to temporal difference (TD) learning, existing methods are negatively affected by bootstrapping predictions at train time and struggle to generate high-quality predictions at long horizons. This paper introduces Temporal Difference Flows (TD-Flow), which leverages the structure of a novel Bellman equation on probability paths alongside flow-matching techniques to learn accurate GHMs at over 5x the horizon length of prior methods. Theoretically, we establish a new convergence result and primarily attribute TD-Flow's efficacy to reduced gradient variance during training. We further show that similar arguments can be extended to diffusion-based methods. Empirically, we validate TD-Flow across a diverse set of domains on both generative metrics and downstream tasks including policy evaluation. Moreover, integrating TD-Flow with recent behavior foundation models for planning over pre-trained policies demonstrates substantial performance gains, underscoring its promise for long-horizon decision-making.},
 primaryclass = {cs},
 eprint = {2503.09817},
 month = {March}
}

      Optimization from a Deep Learning Perspective [005D]

      • February 24, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      Contrastive RL + Deepseek R1 [CRLR1]

      • February 12, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios
      • Slides

      Definition. Achievability [005A]

      • February 11, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      A positive real number \(R\) is said to be achievable if for all \(\epsilon > 0\) (perturbation parameter) there exists a block length \(N(\epsilon )\) such that \(\forall n > N(\epsilon )\) the following holds

      • There exists an \((n, \theta )\) coding system such that \(\frac {\log \theta }{n} < R + \epsilon \) and \(\mathbb {P}|\hat {X}^n \neq X^n| < \epsilon \).

      Alternatively, a positive real number \(R\) is said to be achievable if there exists a sequence of coding systems \((n, \theta )\) such that \(\lim _{n \to \infty } \frac {\log \theta }{n} \to R\) and \(\lim _{n \to \infty } \mathbb {P}|\hat {X}^n \neq X^n| \to 0\).

      Definition. Coding system [0059]

      • February 11, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      A coding system with parameters \((n, \theta )\) consist of an encoder and a decoder, where an encoder is a function \[ e: \mathcal {X}^n \to \{1, 2, \ldots , \theta \} \] and a decoder is a function \[f: \{1, 2, \ldots , \theta \} \to \mathcal {X}^n\]

      Theorem. Entropy as MRSC [005C]

      • February 11, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      \[R_s = H(P_X) = H(X) = -\sum _{x \in \mathcal {X}} P_X(x) \log P_X(x)\]

      Proof.

      First we will show that \(H(X)\) is achievable. Then we will have \(R_s \leq H(X)\) by definition. Idea: take \(\theta = 2^{n(H(X) + \epsilon )} + 1\). Give each element in typical set a unique index, everything else the same index. By properties of typical set, \(\mathbb {P}(\text {error}) < \epsilon \) for sufficiently large \(n\).

      For the other direction, suppose we have some \(R\) achievable. By definition, for all \(\epsilon > 0\), for all sufficiently large \(n\) there exists a Coding system with parameters \((n, \theta )\) such that \[ \begin {align*} \frac {\log \theta }{n} < R + \epsilon , \quad \mathbb {P}(\text {error}) < \epsilon \end {align*} \] Use Fano's Inequality to show this is not possible.

      Definition. Minimum rate of source coding [005B]

      • February 11, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      The minimum rate of source coding \(R_s\) is the infimum over all \(R\) such that \(R\) is achievable i.e. \[R_s \coloneqq \inf \{R \mid R \text { is achievable}\}\]

      Theorem. AEP Theorem [0054]

      • February 10, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      Let \(\{X_{n}:n\geq 1\}\) denote i.i.d. \(\mathcal {X}\)-valued r.v. with distribution \(P_{X}\). Then, \[ \begin {align*} \lim _{n\to \infty }-\frac {1}{n}\log p_{X^{n}}(X_{1},\ldots ,X_{n}) &= \lim _{n \to \infty } -\frac {1}{n} \log \prod _{i = 1}^{n} P_X(X_i) \\ &= \mathbb {E}_{X \sim p_X}[-\log p_X(X)] \\ &= H(X) \end {align*} \] Equivalently, for large \(n\) \[ \begin {align*} \left |-\frac {1}{n} \log p_{X^n}(X^n) - H(X)\right | \leq \epsilon \end {align*} \] with high probability.

      Theorem. Continuous Mapping Theorem [0053]

      • February 10, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      Let \(X_{n}\stackrel {{p}}{{\rightarrow }}X\), and \(f:\mathcal {X}\rightarrow \mathbb {R}\) denote a continuous function. Then, \[f(X_n) \stackrel {p}{\rightarrow } f(X)\]

      Theorem. Decomposition Theorem [0057]

      • February 10, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      If the state space \(S\) is finite, then \(S\) can be written as a disjoint union \(T\cup R_{1}\cup \cdots \cup R_{k}\), where \(T\) is a set of transient states and the \(R_{i},\ 1\leq i\leq k\), are closed irreducible sets of recurrent states.

      Corollary. High probability sets [0056]

      • February 10, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      Let \(B_{\epsilon }^{(n)}\subset \mathcal {X}^{n}\) be the smallest set with probability at least \(1-\epsilon \). Then, we must have \[\mathbb {P}(A_{\epsilon }^{(n)}\cap B_{\epsilon }^{(n)})\geq 1-2\epsilon \]

      Theorem. States in a finite closed irreducible set are recurrent [0058]

      • February 10, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      If \(C\) is a finite closed and irreducible set, then all states in \(C\) are recurrent.

      Proof. Let \(x \in C\). It suffices to show that \(\rho _{xx} = 1\). Recall that \[ \begin {align*} \rho _{xx} &= \mathbb {P}_{x}(T_x < \infty ) \\ &= \end {align*} \]

      Theorem. Weak Law of Large Numbers [0051]

      • February 10, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      \(\{X_{n}:n\geq 1\}\): a sequence of i.i.d. r.v.s. with mean \(\mu \), variance \(\sigma ^{2}\). Then, \[\frac {1}{n}\sum _{i=1}^{n}X_{i}\stackrel {{p}}{{\rightarrow }}\mu \]

      Proof. By Chebyshev's Inequality, \[ \begin {align*} \mathbb {P}(|\hat {X} - \mu | > a) \leq -\frac {\sigma ^2}{a^2} \end {align*} \] Since \(X_i\)'s are independent, \[\mathrm {Var}[\hat {X}] = \frac {1}{n^2} \sum _{i = 1}^{n} \mathrm {Var}[X_i]\] Therefore, \[ \begin {align*} \lim _{n \to \infty } \mathbb {P}(|\hat {X} - \mu | > a) \leq \lim _{n \to \infty }-\frac {\sigma ^2}{n a^2} \to 0 \end {align*} \]

      Corollary. Weak law of large numbers for functions [0052]

      • February 10, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      \(\{X_{n}:n\geq 1\}\): a sequence of i.i.d. r.v.s. with mean \(\mu \), variance \(\sigma ^{2}\). Let \(f:\mathcal {X}\rightarrow \mathbb {R}\) be any function, such that \(\mathrm {Var}(f(X))=\sigma _{f}^{2}<\infty \). Then, \[\frac {1}{n} \sum _{i = 1}^{n} f(X_i) \stackrel {p}{\rightarrow } \mathbb {E}[f(X)]\]

      \(\epsilon \)-typical set [0055]

      • February 10, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      Fix an \(\epsilon >0\). Then, an \(\epsilon \)-typical set with respect to the pmf \(p_{X}\), denoted by \(A_{\epsilon }^{(n)}\), is defined as \[\left \{X^n \in \mathcal {X}^n \mid \left |-\frac {1}{n} \log p_{X^n}(X^n) - H(X)\right | \leq \epsilon \right \}\] Alternatively, \[A_{\epsilon ^{(n)}} = \left \{X^n \in \mathcal {X}^n \mid 2^{-n(H(X) + \epsilon )} \leq p_{X^n}(X^n) \leq 2^{-n(H(X) - \epsilon )}\right \}\]

      Remark. We have the following important properties
      1. \(\mathbb {P}(A_{\epsilon }^{(n)})\geq 1-\epsilon {\text { for large enough }}n\)
      2. \(|A_{c}^{(n)}|\leq 2^{n(H(X)+\epsilon )}\)
      3. \(|A_{\epsilon }^{(n)}|\geq (1-\epsilon )2^{n(H(X)-\epsilon )}\;\text {for large enough }\;n\;,\)
      Together, this says that, depending on the entropy, the typical set can contain most of the probability despite being much smaller than the entire space.

      Theorem. Data Processing Inequality [004Z]

      • February 9, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      Suppose that \(U \to V \to W\). Then \(I(U; W) \leq I(U; V)\).

      Intuition. by data processing, we can never create new information about \(U\).

      Proof. Use chain rule to expand \(I(U; (V, W))\) in two ways i.e. \[ \begin {align*} I(U; (V, W)) = I(U; V) + I(U; W | V) = I(U; W) + I(U; V | W) \end {align*} \] Since \(U \to V \to W\) is a Markov chain, the conditional independence \((U \perp W) \mid V\) makes \(I(U; W | V) = 0\). Therefore, \[ \begin {align*} I(U; V) &= I(U; W) + I(U; V | W) \\ &\geq I(U; W) \end {align*} \]

      Fano's Inequality [0050]

      • February 9, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      Suppose that \(X \iff Y \iff \hat {X}\) and let \(p_e = \mathbb {P}(X \neq \hat {X})\). Then, we have \[ \begin {align*} H(p_e) + p_e \log (|\mathcal {X}| - 1) \geq H(X \mid \hat {X}) \geq H(X \mid Y) \end {align*} \]

      Theorem. Maximum Aposteriori Estimator [004Y]

      • February 9, 2025
      • Kellen Kanarios

      The optimal estimator \(g^* : \mathcal {Y} \to \mathcal {X}\) is \[ \begin {align*} g^*(y) = \arg \max _{x \in \mathcal {X}} P_{X | Y}(x | y) \end {align*} \]

      Proof. Recall that \[ \begin {align*} P_{e}(g) &= \sum _{x}\sum _y P_{XY}(x, y) \cdot \mathbf {1}_{x \neq g(y)} \\ &= \sum _{y} P_Y(y) \sum _{x} P_{X|Y}(x|y) \mathbf {1}_{x \neq g(y)} \\ &= \sum _{y} P_Y(y) (1 - P_{X|Y}(g(y)|y)) \\ \end {align*} \] To minimize this, we take \[ \begin {align*} g^*(y) = \arg \max _{x} P_{X|Y}(x | y) \end {align*} \] as desired.
