}

          Lemma. A \(\pi \)-system that is also a \(\lambda \)-system is a \(\sigma \)-field [001A]

          • November 26, 2024
          • Kellen Kanarios

          A class that is both a \(\pi \)-system and a \(\lambda \)-system is a \(\sigma \)-field.

          Axiom. Axiom of Choice [001H]

          • November 26, 2024
          • Kellen Kanarios

          The axiom of choice assumes the existence of a choice function \(f\), such that \[\forall X\left [\varnothing \not \in X\implies \exists f\colon X\to \bigcup _{A\in X}A\quad \forall A\in X\left (f(A)\in A\right )\right ]\,.\]

          Definition. Completeness of a measure [001F]

          • November 26, 2024
          • Kellen Kanarios

          A probability measure \((\Omega , \mathcal {F}, P)\) is complete if for \(A \subset B\) if \(P(B) = 0\) then \(P(A) = 0\).

          Theorem. Dynkin's \(\pi \text {-}\lambda \) [001B]

          • November 26, 2024
          • Kellen Kanarios

          f \(\mathscr {P}\) is a \(\pi \)-system and \(\mathscr {L}\) is a \(\lambda \)-system, then \(\mathscr {P}\subset \mathscr {L}\) implies \(\sigma (\mathscr {P})\subset \mathscr {L}\).

          Theorem. Halmo's Monotone Class Theorem [001E]

          • November 26, 2024
          • Kellen Kanarios

          If \(\mathscr {F}_{0}\) is a field and \(\mathscr {A}\) is a monotone class, then \(\mathscr {F}_{0}\subset \mathscr {A}\) implies \(\sigma (\mathscr {F}_{0})\subset \mathscr {A}\).

          Definition. Monotone Class [001D]

          • November 26, 2024
          • Kellen Kanarios

          A class \(\mathscr {M}\) of subsets of \(\Omega \) is monotone if it is closed under the formation of monotone unions and intersections:

          1. \(A_{1},A_{2},\ldots \in \mathscr {M}\) and \(A_{n}\uparrow A\) imply \(A\in \mathscr {M}\);
          2. \(A_{1},A_{2},\ \ldots \in \mathscr {M}\) and \(A_{n}\downarrow A\) imply \(A\in \mathscr {M}\).

          Theorem. Uniqueness of Extension [001C]

          • November 26, 2024
          • Kellen Kanarios

          Suppose that \(P_{1}\) and \(P_{2}\) are probability measures on \(\sigma (\mathscr {P})\), where \(\mathscr {P}\) is a \(\pi \)-system. If \(P_{1}\) and \(P_{2}\) agree on \(\mathscr {P}\), then they agree on \(\sigma (\mathscr {P})\).

          Proof. Take \(\mathscr {L}\) to be the class of sets such that \(A \in \mathscr {L} \implies P_1(A) = P_2(A)\). Since \(\mathscr {P}\) is a \(\pi \)-system, from Theorem 9, it is sufficient to show that \(\mathscr {L}\) is a \(\lambda \)-system. Since \(\Omega \in \mathscr {P}\), \(\Omega \in \mathscr {L}\). If \(A \in \mathscr {L}\), then \[P_1(A^c) = 1 - P_1(A) = 1 - P_2(A) = P_2(A^c).\] Therefore, \(A^c \in \mathscr {L}\). Finally, if \(A_1, A_2, \ldots \) disjoint then \[ P_1\left (\bigcup _{n = 1} A_n\right ) = \sum _{n = 1} P_1(A_n) = \sum _{n = 1}P_2 (A_n) = P_2\left (\bigcup _{n = 1}A_n\right ) \] Thus, \(\mathscr {L}\) is a \(\lambda \)-system. From Theorem 9, \(\sigma (\mathscr {P}) \subset \mathscr {L}\) and \(P_1\) and \(P_2\) agree on all of \(\sigma (\mathscr {P})\).

          Example. Vitali Sets [001G]

          • November 26, 2024
          • Kellen Kanarios

          If we consider \([0,1]\), then we can partition \([0, 1]\) into equivalent classes as \(x \sim y\) if \(x - y = r\) for some \(r \in \mathbb {Q} \cap [0, 1]\). Denote each of these as \(V_{r}\). By the Axiom of Choice, we can choose one representative from each \(V_r\). We call the set of these representatives \(V\). Therefore, we can write \([0, 1]\) as a countable union via \([0,1] = \bigcup _{r \in \mathbb {Q}} V + r\). For the Lebesgue measure \(\lambda \), each \(\lambda (V + r) = \lambda (V)\). Since each \(V + r\) is disjoint, we have \[\lambda \left (\bigcup _{r \in \mathbb {Q}} V + r\right ) = \sum _{r \in \mathbb {Q}} \lambda (V)\] If \(\lambda (V) = 0\), then \(\lambda ([0,1]) \leq \lambda (V) = 0\) which is a contradiction. Otherwise \(\lambda ([0,1]) = \sum _{r \in \mathbb {Q}} k = \infty \) for some \(k \in \mathbb {R}\). Thus, \(V\) is not Lebesgue measurable.

          Definition. \(\lambda \)-system [0019]

          • November 26, 2024
          • Kellen Kanarios

          A class \(\mathscr {L}\) is a \(\lambda \)-system if it contains \(\Omega \) and is closed under the formation of complements and of finite and countable disjoint unions:

          1. \(\Omega \in \mathscr {L}\);
          2. \(A\in \mathscr {L}\) implies \(A^{c}\in \mathscr {L}\);
          3. \(A_{1},A_{2},\ldots ,\in \mathscr {L}\) and \(A_{n}\cap A_{m}=\varnothing \) for \(m\neq n\) imply \(\bigcup _{n}A_{n}\in \mathscr {L}\).

          Definition. \(\pi \)-system [0018]

          • November 26, 2024
          • Kellen Kanarios

          A class \(\mathcal {P}\) of subsets of \(\Omega \) is a \(\pi \)-system if it is closed under the formation of finite intersections: \[A,B\in \mathcal {P} \implies A\cap B\in \mathcal {P}.\]

          Definition. Mean Square Value Error [0013]

          • November 24, 2024
          • Kellen Kanarios

          Since we are in the function approximation regime, we cannot perfectly compute the value of every state. Instead, we must prioritize which states are the most important to us. We can do this with a state distribution \(\mu (s)\). Then \[{\overline {{\mathrm {VE}}}}(\mathbf {w})\doteq \sum _{s\in S}\mu (s)\Big [v_{\pi }(s)-{\hat {v}}(s,\mathbf {w})\Big ]^{2}.\] The canonical choice for \(\mu \) is the on-policy distribution because this represents how much time is spent in each state and can be naturally approximated by Monte-carlo methods.

          Notebook: Reinforcement learning: An introduction [0012]

          • November 24, 2024
          • Kellen Kanarios

          This won't really be notes, my lab has begun taking a few undergrads who are not familiar with RL. I will be onboarding them by going through Reinforcement learning: An introduction. Specifically, I will be following the Richard Sutton flavor of RL through his CMPUT 609 course. You know what the say: the best way to learn is to teach! Here, I will try to solve all the problems as we go and prepare some questions for the undergrads for when we meet. Additionally, I will document my foray into more advanced exploration of topics introduced in the textbook.

          The worked exercises are collected separately in Reinforcement learning: An introduction: Exercises. What stays here are the conceptual asides and the open questions I want to raise with the undergrads.

          Dynamic Programming

          • November 24, 2024
          • Kellen Kanarios
          Remark. Value Iteration as Linear Algebra. During my brief stint at IPAM, I spent a lot of time focused on solving large systems for discretized PDEs. From this, I learned about iterative methods, such as Gauss-Jacobi and Gauss-Seidel. Interestingly, these methods can be used to interpret some of RL's most fundamental algorithms. If we define the following matrices, \[ \begin {align*} R &= \begin {bmatrix} \mathbb {E}[r(s = 1)]\\ \vdots \\ \mathbb {E}[r(s = n)] \end {bmatrix}, \quad P = \begin {bmatrix} P_{\pi }(s'=1 | s=1) & \cdots & P_{\pi }(s'=n | s=1) \\ \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ P_{\pi }(s'=1 | s=n) & \cdots & P_{\pi }(s'=n | s=n) \end {bmatrix}, \\ V_k &= \begin {bmatrix} V_k(s = 1)\\ \vdots \\ V_k(s = n) \end {bmatrix} \end {align*} \] Then we can write the value function \(V_{\pi }\) as the solution to the linear system \[ V_{\pi } = R + PV_{\pi } \iff V_{\pi } = (1 - P)^{-1} R \] This is just inverting a matrix! Updating one state with the canonical update \[ \begin {align*} v_{k + 1}(s) = \sum _{a}\pi (a|s)\sum _{s^{\prime },r}p(s^{\prime },r\,|\,s,a)\Big [r+\gamma v_{k}(s^{\prime })\Big ] \end {align*} \] Is actually just one iteration of Gauss-Seidel!
          Remark. (Number of updates as pseudo discount factor).

          On-policy Prediction with Approximation

          • November 24, 2024
          • Kellen Kanarios

          In my opinion, the most important part of this chapter is now that when we update say a \(Q\) function for a specific state action pair \((s,a)\), then this update can affect the value of the \(Q(s', a')\) due to the reuse of the internal parameters.

          Question.
          1. In section 9.5.2, what do they mean when they say you can select \(n\) so all the fourier features can be used?
            1. Pick \(n\) so that \((n + 1)^k < mk^2\).
            2. Pick \(n\) so that \((n + 1)^k\) is reasonable.

            2. In the tabular case, I think (a) is correct. My initial understanding of state representation is as a representation learning i.e. compression type objective. If we assume that \(s_i \in [m]\), then we do not gain anything in the tabular setting if our value function vector is the same size as the underlying transition kernel. When in the continuous state space regime i.e. \(s_i \in [0,1]\), there is no amount of features that would overfit the transition kernel. Therefore, it is just about trying to learn as much as possible about the underlying relations of the state dimensions.

            In the \(2\)-dimensional case, the feature vector \(c_i = [1,1]\) would provide information on how \(s_1\) and \(s_2\) relate not just their specific values. You want the learning algorithm to understand the relationships, so that it can make better use of the internal parameters when learning something like a \(Q\) function. This is basically just SVD but instead of classification you are learning a \(Q\) function. The compression

          Question.
          1. In Figure 9.5, why do fourier features outperform polynomial features?
            1. The fourier features got lucky on the seeds (lol).
            2. The choice of \(\boldsymbol {c}\) is not specified. A good choice can provide improvement specific to the problem?
            3. Polynomial features range is very large. Can suffer from blowup or vanishing of features.
            2. One of the advantages of fourier features mentioned previously is the ability to select which features to serve as your basis. However, for this setup I assume they just use all of the fourier features. This likely means it is more of an issue with the polynomial features and (c). If you have a large polynomial then even relative similar states \(s_1 = 1.1\), \(s_2 = 0.9\), \(\ldots \) can blow up or vanish making them likely more unstable when using gradient-based methods.
          Remark. I think that RBF as a continuous generalization coarse-coding is a nice intuition I want to remember here. Essentially, you just weight a state by how close it is to the center of the receptive field. This weighting is done via a Gaussian kernel, which I believe is arbitrary and can be any distance measure of choice.

          2. Multi-armed Bandits [sutton-ch2]

          • November 24, 2024
          • Kellen Kanarios

          Exercise 2.1. How often greedy is chosen with two actions

          • November 24, 2024
          • Kellen Kanarios

          In \(\epsilon \)-greedy action selection with two actions, how often is the greedy action selected?

          Solution

          Assuming \(Q_*(a_1) > Q_*(a_2)\), the greedy action is selected with probability \(1 - \epsilon \), or \(0.5\) when exploration lands on it by chance.

          Exercise 2.2. Which exploration rate wins in the long run

          • November 24, 2024
          • Kellen Kanarios

          On the 10-armed testbed, which value of \(\epsilon \) achieves the highest reward in the long run, and by how much?

          Solution

          \(\epsilon = 0.01\). Expected reward under an \(\epsilon \)-greedy policy that has converged is

          \[ \begin {align*} R^* = \max _{a} q^*(a) + \frac {\epsilon }{n}\sum _{i \neq a}^{n} q^*(i) \end {align*} \]

          so a smaller \(\epsilon \) pays less exploration tax once the right arm is identified. The exception is \(\epsilon = 0\), which comes with no guarantee at all: with zero initialization, a suboptimal arm whose empirical average stays positive is never abandoned. Some \(\epsilon > 0\) is what buys convergence to the optimal arm.

          Exercise 2.4. Weights on the initial estimate under a varying step size

          • November 24, 2024
          • Kellen Kanarios

          Derive the weighting of the initial estimate and of each reward when the step-size parameter \(\alpha _n\) varies from step to step.

          Solution

          Unrolling the update as in (2.6),

          \[ \begin {align*} Q_{n + 1} &= Q_n + \alpha _n [R_n - Q_n] \\ &= Q_{n - 1} + \alpha _{n - 1}[R_{n - 1} - Q_{n - 1}] + \alpha _n \Big [R_n - (Q_{n - 1} + \alpha _{n - 1}[R_{n - 1} - Q_{n - 1}])\Big ] \\ &\vdots \\ & = \left (\prod _{i = 1}^{n} (1 - \alpha _{i})\right ) Q_1 + \sum _{i = 1}^{n} \alpha _n \left (\prod _{i = 1}^{n} (1 - \alpha _{n - i})\right )R_i \end {align*} \]

          Exercise 2.6. The spikes in the optimistic-initialization curve

          • November 24, 2024
          • Kellen Kanarios

          Optimistic initialization produces oscillations and a pronounced early spike in the optimal-action curve. Why?

          Solution

          Every arm on the testbed has support well below \(5\), so an unpulled arm's optimistic estimate beats the empirical estimate of anything already pulled. The early steps are therefore a round robin over all arms, and — with rewards deterministic — the optimal arm keeps being pulled until its estimate falls below the remaining optimistic ones. That alternation between "sweep the untried" and "exploit the best so far" is the oscillation.

          Exercise 2.8. The UCB spike at step 11

          • November 24, 2024
          • Kellen Kanarios

          UCB performance shows a pronounced spike on the 11th step of the 10-armed testbed, then drops. Why?

          Solution

          With \(10\) arms at equal initialization the exploration bonus forces the first \(10\) pulls to be a round robin. On step \(11\) all bonuses are equal again, so the tie is broken by empirical reward and the best-so-far arm is pulled — the spike. It drops immediately after, because that pull shrinks the chosen arm's bonus and hands the next steps to other, possibly worse, arms.

          Exercise 2.9. Soft-max over two actions is the logistic

          • November 24, 2024
          • Kellen Kanarios

          Show that in the two-action case, the soft-max distribution over preferences is the logistic (sigmoid) function used in statistics.

          Solution

          Expand the denominator:

          \[ \begin {align*} \Pr \{A_t = a\} &= \frac {e^{H_t(a)}}{e^{H_t(a)} + e^{H_t(b)}} \\ &= \frac {1}{1 + e^{\frac {H_t(b)}{H_t(a)}}} \\ &= \frac {1}{1 + e^{-\frac {H_t(a)}{H_t(b)}}} \\ \end {align*} \]

          Exercise 2.10. The value of knowing which case you are in

          • November 24, 2024
          • Kellen Kanarios

          A two-armed bandit alternates between two cases with equal probability. In case A, \(q_*(1) = 10\) and \(q_*(2) = 20\); in case B, \(q_*(1) = 90\) and \(q_*(2) = 80\). What is the best expected reward achievable, and how does it change if you are told which case you are in?

          Solution

          Without the case label, the two arms are indistinguishable in expectation:

          \[ \begin {align*} \mathbb {E}[R(1)] &= 0.5 \cdot 10 + 0.5 \cdot 90 = 50, \\ \mathbb {E}[R(2)] &= 0.5 \cdot 20 + 0.5 \cdot 80 = 50 \end {align*} \]

          so the ceiling is \(50\). Told the case, you can condition on it and pick the better arm in each:

          \[ \begin {align*} R^* &= 0.5 \cdot \max _{a}\mathbb {E}[R(a) \mid x = 1] + 0.5 \cdot \max _{a}\mathbb {E}[R(a) \mid x = 2] \\ &= 0.5 \cdot 20 + 0.5 \cdot 90 \\ &= 55 \end {align*} \]

          The \(5\) points of difference are the value of the observation — which is what turns a bandit into an associative (contextual) problem.

          3. Finite Markov Decision Processes [sutton-ch3]

          • November 24, 2024
          • Kellen Kanarios

          Exercise 3.3. Where to draw the agent-environment boundary

          • November 24, 2024
          • Kellen Kanarios

          Where should the line between agent and environment be drawn — at the steering wheel, at the muscles, at the intent to drive somewhere? Is any level fundamentally preferable?

          Solution

          Draw it where you can already execute the behavior that carries you from one state to another. Fixing the boundary above the level of reliable control means the agent must relearn what it already has; fixing it below means solving a control problem you did not need to solve. This is precisely the premise of hierarchical reinforcement learning, which raises the boundary over time by learning subpolicies and then treating them as primitive.

          Exercise 3.5. Adapting the continuing formulation to episodic tasks

          • November 24, 2024
          • Kellen Kanarios

          Restate the equations of the continuing case so they apply to episodic tasks.

          Solution

          Add a terminal state — some \(t\) adjoined to \(\mathcal {S}\) — and split the normalization condition on whether we have reached it:

          \[ \begin {cases} p(t, 0 \mid s, a) = 1, &\text { if } s = t\\ \sum _{s^{\prime }\in \mathcal {S}}\sum _{r\in \mathcal {R}}p(s^{\prime },r|s,a)=1,\mathrm {~for~all~}s\in \mathcal {S},a\in \mathcal {A}(s), &\text { if } s \neq t \end {cases} \]

          The content of this is just that once you hit a terminal state you can reach nothing else, and accrue nothing further.

          Exercise 3.6. Return under an episodic pole-balancing failure signal

          • November 24, 2024
          • Kellen Kanarios

          Treat pole-balancing as episodic with discounting and a reward of \(-1\) on failure. What is the return at each time?

          Solution

          With \(T\) the length of the episode and the only nonzero reward at the end,

          \[ \begin {align*} G_t &= R_{t+1} + \gamma R_{t + 2} + \cdots + \gamma ^{T - {t + 1}} R_T = - \gamma ^{T - {t + 1}} \end {align*} \]

          Exercise 3.7. The maze-runner that never learns to hurry

          • November 24, 2024
          • Kellen Kanarios

          A maze-running agent gets \(+1\) for escaping and \(0\) otherwise, and after many episodes shows no improvement. What is going wrong?

          Solution

          The task has not actually been communicated. Every escaping trajectory earns the same return regardless of how long it took, so the agent has no reason to prefer a fast escape to a slow one. Fix it by paying \(-1\) per timestep, or by discounting so that a reward collected later is worth less.

          Exercise 3.8. Computing returns backwards

          • November 24, 2024
          • Kellen Kanarios

          With \(\gamma = 0.5\) and the reward sequence \(R_1 = -1\), \(R_2 = 2\), \(R_3 = 6\), \(R_4 = 3\), \(R_5 = 2\), what are \(G_0\) through \(G_5\)?

          Solution

          The recursion \(G_t = R_{t+1} + \gamma G_{t+1}\) is solved from the back:

          \[ \begin {align*} G_5 &= 0 \\ G_4 &= R_{5} + \gamma G_5 = 2 \\ G_3 &= R_{4} + \gamma G_4 = 4 \\ G_2 &= R_{3} + \gamma G_3 = 8 \\ G_1 &= R_{2} + \gamma G_2 = 6 \\ G_0 &= R_{1} + \gamma G_1 = 2 \end {align*} \]

          Exercise 3.9. Return of an infinite constant reward stream

          • November 24, 2024
          • Kellen Kanarios

          With \(\gamma = 0.9\), a reward of \(2\) followed by an infinite sequence of \(7\)s, what are \(G_1\) and \(G_0\)?

          Solution

          Peel off the leading term and sum the geometric tail:

          \[ \begin {align*} G_0 &= R_{1} + \gamma R_{2} + \gamma ^2 R_{3} + \cdots \\ &= 2 + \sum _{i = 1}^{\infty } \gamma ^{i} R_{i} \\ &= 2 + \gamma \sum _{i = 0}^{\infty } \gamma ^{i} R_{i + 2} \\ &= 2 + \frac {7 \gamma }{1 - \gamma } \\ &= 65 \end {align*} \]

          and

          \[ \begin {align*} G_1 &= R_{2} + \gamma R_{2} + \gamma ^2 R_{3} + \cdots \\ &= 7 + \sum _{i = 1}^{\infty } \gamma ^{i} R_{i} \\ &= 7 + \gamma \sum _{i = 0}^{\infty } \gamma ^{i} R_{i + 3} \\ &= 7 + \frac {7 \gamma }{1 - \gamma } \\ &= 70 \end {align*} \]

          Exercise 3.11. Expected reward in terms of the policy and dynamics

          • November 24, 2024
          • Kellen Kanarios

          If the current state is \(S_t\) and actions are drawn from \(\pi \), what is the expectation of \(R_{t+1}\) in terms of \(\pi \) and the four-argument dynamics \(p\)?

          Solution

          Marginalize over the action, then over the successor and the reward:

          \[ \begin {align*} \mathbb {E}[R_{t + 1} \mid S_{t} = s] = \sum _{a} \pi (a \mid s) \sum _{s'} \sum _{r} p(s', r \mid s, a) \cdot r \end {align*} \]

          Exercise 3.12. State value from action values

          • November 24, 2024
          • Kellen Kanarios

          Give an equation for \(v_{\pi }\) in terms of \(q_{\pi }\) and \(\pi \).

          Solution \[ \begin {align*} v_{\pi }(s) &= \sum _{a} \pi (a \mid s) q_{\pi }(s, a) \end {align*} \]

          Exercise 3.13. Action value from state values

          • November 24, 2024
          • Kellen Kanarios

          Give an equation for \(q_{\pi }\) in terms of \(v_{\pi }\) and the four-argument dynamics \(p\).

          Solution \[ \begin {align*} q_{\pi }(s, a) = \sum _{s', r} p(s', r \mid s, a) \big (r + \gamma v_{\pi }(s')\big ) \end {align*} \]

          Exercise 3.15. Adding a constant to every reward

          • November 24, 2024
          • Kellen Kanarios

          In gridworld the rewards are positive, so what matters is their differences. Show that adding a constant \(c\) to every reward adds a constant \(v_c\) to the value of every state, and give \(v_c\) in terms of \(c\) and \(\gamma \).

          Solution

          Starting from

          \[ \begin {align*} v_{\pi }(s) = \mathbb {E}_{\pi } \left [\sum _{k = 0}^{\infty } \gamma ^{k} R_{t + k + 1} \mid S_t = s\right ] \end {align*} \]

          and shifting every reward by \(c\), the shift factors out of the expectation as its own geometric series:

          \[ \begin {align*} v_{\pi }'(s) &= \mathbb {E}_{\pi } \left [\sum _{k = 0}^{\infty } \gamma ^{k} (R_{t + k + 1} + c) \mid S_t = s\right ] \\ &= \mathbb {E}_{\pi } \left [\sum _{k = 0}^{\infty } \gamma ^{k} R_{t + k + 1}\mid S_t = s\right ] + \sum _{k = 0}^{\infty } \gamma ^{k} c \\ &= v_{\pi }(s) + \frac {c}{1 - \gamma } \end {align*} \]

          so \(v_c = \frac {c}{1 - \gamma }\), the same for every state — and therefore no change to the ordering of policies.

          Exercise 3.16. Why the same shift is not harmless in the episodic case

          • November 24, 2024
          • Kellen Kanarios

          Does the previous exercise's conclusion survive in an episodic task? Give an example.

          Solution

          It does not. The shift is \(c\) summed over the episode's length, so it is not constant across states — \(v_c\) is larger for states from which episodes run longer. In the maze runner, a positive \(c\) therefore rewards dawdling, which is the exact opposite of the intended task.

          Exercise 3.18. The value of a state as an expectation over actions

          • November 24, 2024
          • Kellen Kanarios

          The value of a state depends on the values of the actions available in it. Express \(v_{\pi }(s)\) accordingly.

          Solution

          Same identity as Exercise 3.12 — the state's value is its action values averaged under the policy:

          \[v_{\pi }(s) = \mathbb {E}_{\pi }[q_{\pi }(s, a)] = \sum _{a} \pi (a \mid s) q_{\pi }(s, a)\]

          4. Dynamic Programming [sutton-ch4]

          • November 24, 2024
          • Kellen Kanarios

          Exercise 4.1. Action values in the gridworld under the random policy

          • November 24, 2024
          • Kellen Kanarios

          In the gridworld example, with \(\pi \) the equiprobable random policy, what are \(q_{\pi }(11, \mathrm {down})\) and \(q_{\pi }(7, \mathrm {down})\)?

          Solution

          From state \(11\), moving down terminates the episode, so there is no recursion to unroll:

          \[ \begin {align*} q_{\pi }(11, \mathrm {down}) &= -1 \end {align*} \]

          From state \(7\), moving down lands in \(11\) and picks up its value:

          \[ \begin {align*} q_{\pi }(7, \mathrm {down}) &= -1 + v(11) \\ &= -1 - 14 \\ &= -15 \end {align*} \]

          Review: Part I [sutton-review-1]

          • November 24, 2024
          • Kellen Kanarios

          Not a numbered exercise but the question the first part of the book leaves you with: review the tabular methods. What are their strengths and weaknesses, and when should each be used?

          Solution
          Strength Weakness Use case
          Bandits Simplest case. Can isolate exploration problem. No credit assignment. Action only affects the next timestep. Clinical trials. Things without temporally extended outcomes.
          Dynamic Programming Exact solution. Complexity blows up with state and action space. Model-based. Tabular MDPs.
          Monte Carlo Unbiased estimator. Model-free. Extremely high variance. Must wait till end of episode. When interacting with the environment is inexpensive and episodes are short.
          TD methods Model-free. Online. Biased estimator. Environment interaction is cheap but episodes are long or continuing.
          N step Balances the bias-variance tradeoff. Must choose \(n\). Lower variance in continuing environments.
          Dyna Sample efficiency. Model-based. When interacting with the environment is costly — driving, say.

          8. Planning and Learning with Tabular Methods [sutton-ch8]

          • November 24, 2024
          • Kellen Kanarios

          Exercise 8.1. Can multi-step bootstrapping match Dyna with a perfect model?

          • November 24, 2024
          • Kellen Kanarios

          The nonplanning method in the maze example is a special case of the \(n\)-step method. Could a multi-step bootstrapping method do as well as a Dyna agent given a perfect model?

          Solution

          Take \(n\) large enough and the first pass is just as good, in the sense that every \((s,a)\) pair on the encountered trajectory gets updated. But Dyna updates from \(Q\)-values that have themselves been updated, so it is not confined to the \(n\)-step trajectory it actually walked. That extra reach is what an \(n\)-step method cannot reproduce, so I do not think it can match Dyna even with a perfect model.

          Exercise 8.5. Dyna-Q+ in stochastic and changing environments

          • November 24, 2024
          • Kellen Kanarios

          How might the tabular Dyna-Q algorithm be modified for stochastic environments? How might it handle environments that change over time?

          Solution

          Replace the deterministic transition entry with an empirical distribution over successor states and rewards. For a changing environment, weight recent observations more heavily when updating that empirical model, e.g.

          \[\hat {R}_{t + 1}(S,A) = \lambda \hat {R}_{t}(S, A) + (1 - \lambda )R_{t + 1}(S, A)\]

          which is exponential recency-weighting — the same instrument used for nonstationary bandits in Chapter 2.

          Exercise 8.6. When skewed transition probabilities favor sample updates

          • November 24, 2024
          • Kellen Kanarios

          Suppose the branching factor \(b\) is large but the transition probabilities are highly skewed, so a few successors are far more likely than the rest. Does this strengthen or weaken the case for sample updates over expected updates?

          Solution

          It strengthens it. Samples concentrate where the probability mass is, so a handful of them recovers most of what the expected update computes — and the expected update pays for the whole tail to get there.

          9. On-policy Prediction with Approximation [sutton-ch9]

          • November 24, 2024
          • Kellen Kanarios

          Exercise 9.1. Tabular methods as linear function approximation

          • November 24, 2024
          • Kellen Kanarios

          Show that tabular methods are a special case of linear function approximation. What are the feature vectors?

          Solution

          Linear function approximation carries two objects, \(\boldsymbol {w}\) and \(\boldsymbol {x}(s)\), updated as

          \[w_{t + 1} = w_{t} + \alpha (r_t + \gamma w_{t}^{\top } x_{t+1} - w_t^{\top } x_t) x_t\]

          The tabular setting is the one where we can afford a coordinate per state, \(x(s) \in \mathbb {R}^{|S|}\). Take the features to be one-hot, \(x : s_i \mapsto \boldsymbol {e}_i\), and identify

          \[r_i = \mathbb {E}_{a \sim \pi , s \sim p}[r(s_i)], \quad w_i = v_{\pi }(s_i)\]

          Substituting,

          \[w_{t + 1} = w_{t} + \alpha (\mathbb {E}_{a \sim \pi , s \sim p}[r(s_i)] + v(s_{t + 1}) - v(s_{t})) \cdot \boldsymbol {e}_i\]

          Since \(\boldsymbol {w}\) is the table of values and \(\boldsymbol {e}_i\) zeroes out everything else, updating the \(i\)th entry is exactly one tabular update to \(v_{\pi }(s_i)\). Generalization across states is precisely what the one-hot encoding refuses to do.

          Exercise 9.2. Counting polynomial features

          • November 24, 2024
          • Kellen Kanarios

          Why does (9.17) define \((n + 1)^k\) distinct features for dimension \(k\)?

          Solution

          Each of the \(k\) state components \(s_j\) carries an exponent \(c_{i,j}\) chosen from \(\{0, 1, \ldots , n\}\) — that is \(n + 1\) options — and the choices are independent, so there are \((n + 1)^k\) distinct exponent vectors, hence that many features.

          Exercise 9.3. Recovering the order and exponents from a feature vector

          • November 24, 2024
          • Kellen Kanarios

          What \(n\) and \(c_{i,j}\) produce the feature vector \[\mathbf {x}(s)=(1,s_{1},s_{2},s_{1}s_{2},s_{1}^{2},s_{2}^{2},s_{1}^{2}s_{2}^{2},s_{1}s_{2}^{2},s_{1}^{2}s_{2}^{2})^{\top }?\]

          Solution

          \(n = 2\), with exponent vectors

          \[\boldsymbol {c_0} = [0, 0], \quad \boldsymbol {c_1} = [1, 0] \\ \boldsymbol {c_2} = [0, 1], \quad \boldsymbol {c_3} = [1, 1] \\ \boldsymbol {c_4} = [2, 0], \quad \boldsymbol {c_5} = [0, 2] \\ \boldsymbol {c_6} = [2, 2], \quad \boldsymbol {c_7} = [1, 2], \quad \boldsymbol {c_8} = [2, 2] \]

          Exercise 9.4. Tile shape as a statement about generalization

          • November 24, 2024
          • Kellen Kanarios

          Suppose you believe one of two state dimensions is more likely to have an effect on the value function than the other. What tilings could take advantage of that?

          Solution

          Use anisotropic tiles — long in the direction you want to generalize along, thin in the direction you do not. Reading the two state dimensions as \((x, y)\) coordinates: to make states sharing an \(x\) coordinate resemble one another, tile with tall narrow rectangles. States at the same \(x\) then fall in a common vertical tile and share their features, while any change in \(x\) moves you into disjoint tiles. Tile shape is how a prior about which dimension matters gets stated.

          Definition. Action Value Function [0011]

          • November 22, 2024
          • Kellen Kanarios

          For a fixed policy and a starting state \(s_{0}=s\), we define the action value function \(Q_{M}^{s}:S \times A \to \mathbb {R}\) as the discounted sum of future rewards after taking action \(A\). \[Q_{M}^{s}(s, a)=\mathbb {E}\Big [\sum _{t=0}^{\infty }\gamma ^{t}r(s_{t},a_{t})\mid \pi , s_{0}=s, a_{0} = a\Big ]\]

          Definition. Markov Decision Process [000Z]

          • November 22, 2024
          • Kellen Kanarios

          A Markov Decision Process \(M=(S,A,P,\tau ,\gamma ,\mu )\) is a tuple, where

          • A state space \(S\), which may be finite or infinite. For mathematical convenience, we will assume that \(S\) is finite or countably infinite.
          • A action space \(A\), which also may be discrete or infinite. For mathematical convenience, we will assume that \(A\) is finite.
          • A transition function \(P:S\times A\to \Delta (S)\), where \(\Delta (S)\) is the space of probability distributions over \(S\) (i.e., the below) \(P_{S}\) is \(\mathcal {P}(S|\tau _{0})\) is the probability of transitioning to state \(s^{\prime }\) upon taking action \(a\) in state \(s\).
          • A reward function \(r: S\times A \to [0,1]\). \(r(s, a)\) is the immediate reward associated with taking action \(a\) in state \(s\). More generally, the \(r(s,a)\) could be a random variable (where the distribution depends on \(a\), \(0\)). While we largely focus on the case where \(r(s,a)\) is deterministic, the extension to methods with stochastic rewards are often straightforward.
          • A discount factor \(\gamma \in (0,1)\), which defines a horizon for the problem.

          Markov Decision Processes [000Y]

          • November 22, 2024
          • Kellen Kanarios

          In reinforcement learning, the interactions between the agent and the environment are often described by an infinite-horizon, discounted Markov Decision Process (MDP).

          Definition. Markov Decision Process [000Z]

          • November 22, 2024
          • Kellen Kanarios

          A Markov Decision Process \(M=(S,A,P,\tau ,\gamma ,\mu )\) is a tuple, where

          • A state space \(S\), which may be finite or infinite. For mathematical convenience, we will assume that \(S\) is finite or countably infinite.
          • A action space \(A\), which also may be discrete or infinite. For mathematical convenience, we will assume that \(A\) is finite.
          • A transition function \(P:S\times A\to \Delta (S)\), where \(\Delta (S)\) is the space of probability distributions over \(S\) (i.e., the below) \(P_{S}\) is \(\mathcal {P}(S|\tau _{0})\) is the probability of transitioning to state \(s^{\prime }\) upon taking action \(a\) in state \(s\).
          • A reward function \(r: S\times A \to [0,1]\). \(r(s, a)\) is the immediate reward associated with taking action \(a\) in state \(s\). More generally, the \(r(s,a)\) could be a random variable (where the distribution depends on \(a\), \(0\)). While we largely focus on the case where \(r(s,a)\) is deterministic, the extension to methods with stochastic rewards are often straightforward.
          • A discount factor \(\gamma \in (0,1)\), which defines a horizon for the problem.

          From an MDP and a policy \(\pi : S \to A\), we can define a Value function for \(\pi \).

          Definition. Value Function [0010]

          • November 22, 2024
          • Kellen Kanarios

          For a fixed policy and a starting state \(s_{0}=s\), we define the value function \(V_{M}^{s}:S\to \mathbb {R}\) as the discounted sum of future rewards \[V_{M}^{s}(s)=\mathbb {E}\Big [\sum _{t=0}^{\infty }\gamma ^{t}r(s_{t},a_{t})\mid \pi ,s_{0}=s\Big ]\]

          The expectation is over the randomness of the the transitions \(P\) and if the policy \(\pi \) is stochastic. When determining a policy we are more interested with the value of an action in a specific state rather than just the state itself. To get this, we can define a \(Q\)-function in a similar way.

          Definition. Action Value Function [0011]

          • November 22, 2024
          • Kellen Kanarios

          For a fixed policy and a starting state \(s_{0}=s\), we define the action value function \(Q_{M}^{s}:S \times A \to \mathbb {R}\) as the discounted sum of future rewards after taking action \(A\). \[Q_{M}^{s}(s, a)=\mathbb {E}\Big [\sum _{t=0}^{\infty }\gamma ^{t}r(s_{t},a_{t})\mid \pi , s_{0}=s, a_{0} = a\Big ]\]

          If the reward \(r(s,a)\) is bounded by some \(R_{\text {max}}\). Then we can trivially bound both the value and action value function by \((R_{max}/1 - \gamma )\)

          Proof. This is just a geometric series i.e. \[\begin {align*} V_{M}^{s}(s)&=\mathbb {E}\Big [\sum _{t=0}^{\infty }\gamma ^{t}r(s_{t},a_{t})\mid \pi ,s_{0}=s\Big ] \\ &\leq \mathbb {E}\Big [\sum _{t=0}^{\infty }\gamma ^{t}R_{\text {max}}\mid \pi ,s_{0}=s\Big ] \\ &= R_{\text {max}} \sum _{t=0}^{\infty }\gamma ^{t} \\ &= R_{\text {max}}/ 1 - \gamma \end {align*} \]

          Definition. Value Function [0010]

          • November 22, 2024
          • Kellen Kanarios

          For a fixed policy and a starting state \(s_{0}=s\), we define the value function \(V_{M}^{s}:S\to \mathbb {R}\) as the discounted sum of future rewards \[V_{M}^{s}(s)=\mathbb {E}\Big [\sum _{t=0}^{\infty }\gamma ^{t}r(s_{t},a_{t})\mid \pi ,s_{0}=s\Big ]\]

          Definition. Kullback-Liebler Divergence [000W]

          • November 21, 2024
          • Kellen Kanarios

          The KL-divergence between two probability distributions is defined as \[\mathrm {KL}(p || q) = \mathbb {E}_{x \sim p}\left [\log \frac {p(x)}{q(x)}\right ] = \sum _{x \in \mathcal {X}} p(x) \log \frac {p(x)}{q(x)}\]

          Definition. Mutual Information [000V]

          • November 21, 2024
          • Kellen Kanarios

          The mutual information between two random variables \(X, Y\) is defined with respect to their joint distribution. Namely, it is the Kullback-Liebler Divergence between the joint distribution \(p(x,y)\) and the product of the marginals \(p(x)p(y)\) i.e. \[H(X || Y) = \mathbb {E}_{x,y \sim p(x,y)}\left [\log \frac {p(x, y)}{p(x)p(y)}\right ]\]

          Definition. Outer Measure [000T]

          • November 21, 2024
          • Kellen Kanarios

          For each subset \(A\) of \(\Omega \), \[P^{*}(A)=\mathrm {inf}\,\sum _{n}P(A_{n}),\] where \(A \subset \bigcup _{n = 1}^{\infty } A_n.\)

          Definition. \(P^*\)-measurable [000U]

          • November 21, 2024
          • Kellen Kanarios

          \(A\) is \(P^*\)-measurable if for every \(E \subset \Omega \), we have that \[P^*(A \cap E) + P^*(A^c \cap E) = P^*(E)\]

          Theorem. Additivity of Intervals [000S]

          • November 20, 2024
          • Kellen Kanarios

          We have the following properties

          1. If \(\bigcup _{k}I_{k}\subset I\), and the \(I_{k}\) are disjoint, then \(\sum _{k}|I_{k}|\leq |I|\).
          2. If \(I\subset \bigcup _{k}I_{k}\) (the \(I_{k}\) need not be disjoint), then \(|I|\leq \sum _{k}|I_{k}|\).
          3. If \(I=\bigcup _{k}I_{k}\), and the \(I_{k}\) are disjoint, then \(|I|=\sum _{k}|I_{k}|\).

          Theorem. Continuity and countable subadditivity of a probability measure [000R]

          • November 20, 2024
          • Kellen Kanarios

          Let \(P\) be a probability measure on a field \(\mathscr {F}\).

          1. Continuity from below: If \(A_{n}\) and \(A\) lie in \(\mathscr {F}\) and \(\mathscr {A}_{n}\uparrow A\), then \(P(A_{n})\uparrow P(A)\).
          2. Continuity from above: If \(A_{n}\) and \(A\) lie in \(\mathscr {F}\) and \(A_{n}\downarrow A\), then \(P(A_{n})\downarrow P(A)\).
          3. Countable subadditivity: If \(A_{1},A_{2},\ldots \) and \(\bigcup _{k=1}^{\infty }A_{k}\) lie in \(\mathscr {F}\) (the \(A_{k}\) need not be disjoint), then \[P\left (\bigcup _{k=1}^{\infty }A_{k}\right )\leq \sum _{k=1}^{\infty }P(A_{k})\]

          Definition. Probability Measure [000P]

          • November 20, 2024
          • Kellen Kanarios

          A set function is a real-valued function defined on some class of subsets of \(\Omega \). A set function \(P\) on a field \(\mathscr {F}\) is a probability measure if it satisfies these conditions:

          1. \(0\leq P(A)\leq 1\) for \(A\in \mathscr {F}\);
          2. \(P(\varnothing )=0\), \(P(\Omega )=1\);
          3. if \(A_{1},A_{2},\ldots \) is a disjoint sequence of \(\mathscr {F}\) sets and if \(\bigcup _{k=1}^{\infty }A_{k}\in \mathscr {F}\), then \[P\Big (\bigcup _{k=1}^{\infty }A_{k}\Big )=\sum _{k=1}^{\infty }P(A_{k}).\]

          Definition. Probability Space [000Q]

          • November 20, 2024
          • Kellen Kanarios

          If \(\mathscr {F}\) is a \(\sigma \)-field in \(\Omega \) and \(P\) is a probability measure on \(\mathscr {F}\), the triple \((\Omega ,\mathscr {F},P)\) is called a probability measure space, or simply a probability space. A support of \(P\) is any \(\mathscr {F}\)-set \(A\) for which \(P(A)=1\).

          Definition. \(\sigma \)-field [000O]

          • November 20, 2024
          • Kellen Kanarios

          A class of subsets \(\mathscr {F}\) of \(\Omega \) is a \(\sigma \)-field if the following holds

          1. \(\Omega \in \mathscr {F}\)
          2. If \(A \in \mathscr {F}\) then \(A^c \in \mathscr {F}\)
          3. If \(A_1, A_2, \ldots \in \mathscr {F}\) then \(\bigcup _{i = 1}^{\infty } A_i \in \mathscr {F}\)

          1. Borel's Normal Number Theorem [billingsley-s1]

          • November 17, 2024
          • Kellen Kanarios

          Exercise 1.1. No infinite fair independent sequence on a discrete space

          • November 17, 2024
          • Kellen Kanarios

          Show that a discrete probability space cannot carry an infinite sequence of independent events \(A_1, A_2, \ldots \), each of probability \(1/2\).

          Solution

          Denote the sample space \(\mathcal {X}\). Independence of \(A_1\) and \(A_2\) splits it into four cells of probability \(1/4\) apiece:

          \[P(A_1 \cap A_2) + P(A_1 \cap A_2^c) + P(A_1^c \cap A_2) + P(A_1^c \cap A_2^c) = 1\]

          Every \(x \in \mathcal {X}\) lies in exactly one of the four, so \(\mathbb {P}(\{x\}) \leq 1/4\). Running the same construction on \(A_1, \ldots , A_n\) gives \(n\) disjoint cells and the bound \(\mathbb {P}(\{x\}) \leq 1/n\) for every \(x\); the sequence is infinite, so \(n\) is unbounded and \(\mathbb {P}(\{x\}) = 0\).

          But the space is discrete, so all of its mass sits on its atoms:

          \[\sum _{x \in \mathcal {X}} \mathbb {P}(\{x\}) = 1\]

          A countable sum of zeros cannot be one, and we have our contradiction.

          3. Uniqueness [billingsley-s3]

          • November 17, 2024
          • Kellen Kanarios

          Exercise 3.2. Measurability as agreement of inner and outer measure

          • November 17, 2024
          • Kellen Kanarios

          Let \(P\) be a probability measure on a field \(\mathscr {F}_{0}\), define \(P^{\star }(A)\) for every subset \(A\) of \(\Omega \) by (3.1), and denote also by \(P\) the extension of \(P\) to \(\mathscr {F}=\sigma (\mathscr {F}_{0})\). Show that \(A\) is \(P^*\)-measurable if and only if \(P^*(A) = P_*(A)\).

          Solution

          Suppose \(P^*(A) = P_*(A)\) and fix \(E \subset \Omega \). We must show

          \[P^*(E \cap A) + P^*(E \cap A^c) = P^*(E)\]

          The preceding part of the exercise supplies \(\overline {A}, \underline {A} \in \mathscr {F}\) with \(\underline {A} \subset A \subset \overline {A}\), and the hypothesis collapses their measures onto each other:

          \[P(\overline {A}) = P^*(A) = P_*(A) = P(\underline {A})\]

          Approximate \(E\) the same way — there is \(B \in \mathscr {F}\) with \(E \subset B\) and \(P^*(E) = P(B)\). Then

          \[P^*(E \cap A) \leq P^*(B \cap \overline {A}) = P(B \cap \overline {A})\]

          and

          \[P^*(B \cap A) \leq P^*(B \cap \underline {A}^c) = P(B \cap \underline {A}^c)\]

          so that

          \[P^*(E \cap A) + P^*(E \cap A^c) \leq P(B \cap \underline {A}^c) + P(B \cap \overline {A}) = P^*(E)\]

          as desired.

          Remark. The difficulty is bookkeeping, not measure theory: three objects live on three different domains, and conflating them is what makes the problem look impenetrable.
          1. \(P\) is defined on the initial field \(\mathscr {F}_0\), the closure over finite unions and complements of \(\Omega \).
          2. \(P^*\) is defined on the whole powerset \(\mathcal {P}(\Omega )\), but is not a measure there. In particular \(E\) need not lie in \(\mathscr {F}\), which is exactly why the argument has to route through \(B\).
          3. \(P\) (abusing notation) is \(P^*\) restricted to the \(P^*\)-measurable subsets of \(\Omega \).
          The tempting shortcut — apply finite additivity and conclude everything is \(P^*\)-measurable — fails because \(P^*\) is countably subadditive only on the \(P^*\)-measurable sets, not on \(\mathcal {P}(\Omega )\).

          Definition. Consistent estimator [000F]

          • November 4, 2024
          • Kellen Kanarios

          Formally speaking, an estimator \(T_{n}\) of parameter \(\theta \) is said to be weakly consistent. If it converges in probabilty to the true value of the parameter i.er \[\lim \limits _{n\rightarrow \infty }T_{n}=\theta . \quad \text { i.e. for all t>0 } \quad \lim \limits _{n\rightarrow \infty }\Pr \left (\left |T_{n}-\theta \right |>c\right )=0.\]

          Definition. InfoNCE [000B]

          • November 4, 2024
          • Kellen Kanarios

          InfoNCE recasts representation learning as classification: given a context \(c_t\) and a batch \(\mathcal {X}\) holding one positive future sample \(x_{t+k}\) among \(N-1\) distractors, it trains a score \(f_k\) to pick the positive out of the batch. This is the workhorse objective of contrastive learning.

          The loss is the cross-entropy of that identification: \[\mathcal {L}_{N} = - \mathbb {E}_{\mathcal {X}} \left [\log \frac {f_k(x_{t + k}, c_t)}{\sum _{x_j \in \mathcal {X}} f_k(x_j, c_t)}\right ]\] The numerator rewards a high score on the true pair; the denominator normalizes over the positive plus every negative, so a score only counts by being large relative to the distractors. Minimizing \(\mathcal {L}_N\) maximizes a lower bound on the mutual information \(I(x_{t+k}; c_t)\), and the bound tightens with \(N\) — which is the mechanistic reason contrastive methods reward large batches and many negatives.

          Theorem. Maximize Mutual info [000C]

          • November 4, 2024
          • Kellen Kanarios

          \(\mathcal {L}_N\) from InfoNCE paper maximizes a lower bound on the Mutual Information between \(x_{t + k}\) and \(c_t\).

          Proof.All we must do is plug \(\frac {p(x \mid c)}{p(x)}\) back into the objective. \[\begin {align*} \mathcal {L}_{\mathbb {N}}^{\text {opt}}&=-\,\mathbb {E}\log \left [\frac {\frac {p(x_{t+k}|c_{t})}{p(x_{t+k})}}{\frac {p(x_{t+k}|c_{t})}{p(x_{t+k})}+\sum _{x_{j}\in X_{\text {neg}}}\frac {p(x_{j}|c_{t})}{p(x_{j})}}\right ] \\ &=\mathbb {E}\log \left [1+\frac {p(x_{t+k})}{p(x_{t+k}|c_{t})}\sum _{x_{j}\in X_{\text {neg}}}\frac {p(x_{j}|c_{t})}{p(x_{j})}\right ] \\ &\approx \mathbb {E}\log \left [1+\frac {p(x_{t+k})}{p(x_{t+k}|c_{t})}(N-1)\,\mathbb {E}\,\frac {p(x_{j}|c_{t})}{p(x_{j})}\right ] \\ &=\mathbb {E}\log \left [1+\frac {p(x_{t+k})}{p(x_{t+k} \mid c_t)}N\right ] \\ &\geq \mathbb {E} \log \left [\frac {p(x_{t + k})}{p(x_{t + k} \mid c_t)}N \right ] \\ &= - I(x_{t + k}, c_t) + \log N \end {align*} \]

          Definition. NCE loss [000E]

          • November 4, 2024
          • Kellen Kanarios

          The NCE loss aims to minimize the following objective \[\mathcal {L}_{N} = - \sum _{t} \log \left [h(x_t; \theta )\right ] + \log \left [1 - h(y_t; \theta )\right ],\] where \(x_t\) are samples from the data distribution and \(y_t\) are randomly generated samples and \[\begin {array}{r c l}{{h({\bf u};\theta )}}&{{=}}&{{\frac {1}{1+\exp \left [-G({\bf u};\theta )\right ]},}}\\ {{G({\bf u};\theta )}}&{{=}}&{{\ln p_{m}({\bf u};\theta )-\ln p_{n}({\bf u}).}}\end {array}\]

          Contrastive Learning [0009]

          • October 31, 2024
          • with contributions from Kellen Kanarios

          Recall the longstanding objective of machine learning i.e. given data \(\mathcal {X}\) find the distribution \(p(x)\) that generated the data \(\mathcal {X}\). The most fundamental approach is maximum likelihood estimation. Namely, we want to maximize the log-likelhood of the data \[\max _{\theta } \sum _{x \in \mathcal {X}} \log p_{\theta }(x) \]

          NCE

          • October 31, 2024

          Suppose we are given \(N\) dog samples \(\mathcal {D}\) from some distribution \(p_d(x)\). We want to learn \(\theta \) so that \(p_{\theta }(x) \approx p_d(x)\). The idea is to learn to distinguish the dogs from our dataset and random samples according to some noisy distribution \(g(x)\). We can now return to the supervised learning setting, where we treat \(\mathcal {D}\) and \(\mathcal {R}\) as two classes. If we recall standard supervised learning practice, given a sample \(x\), we can easily estimate \[p(x \text { is a dog}) = 1 - p(x \text { is random noise})\] via binary classification.

          Explicitly, we will use logistic regression with the parametrization \[p_{\theta }(x) = \frac {1}{1 + e^{-G_{\theta }(x)}}.\] However, solving the logistic regression problem will yield \(p_{\theta ^*}(x) \approx p(x \text { is a dog})\). Recall that we want to estimate \(p_d(x)\) which is the distribution over the "dog manifold".

          To estimate the correct quantity, we need to leverage our knowledge of the noise distribution. Recall that if \(p_{\theta }(x) = p(\mathcal {D} \mid x)\) then \(G_{\theta }(x) = \log \frac {p(x \mid \mathcal {D})}{p(x \mid \mathcal {R})}\). Since we generated the samples from \(\mathcal {R}\), we have the explicit distribution i.e. \(p(x \mid \mathcal {R}) = p_{\mathcal {R}}(x)\). Therefore, we can restrict \(G_{\theta }\) to explicitly learn \(p(x \mid \mathcal {D})\) by considering \[G_{\theta }(x) = \log p_{\theta }(x \mid \mathcal {D}) - \log p_{\mathcal {R}}(x),\] considering the cross entropy loss we get the NCE loss

          Definition. NCE loss [000E]

          • November 4, 2024
          • Kellen Kanarios

          The NCE loss aims to minimize the following objective \[\mathcal {L}_{N} = - \sum _{t} \log \left [h(x_t; \theta )\right ] + \log \left [1 - h(y_t; \theta )\right ],\] where \(x_t\) are samples from the data distribution and \(y_t\) are randomly generated samples and \[\begin {array}{r c l}{{h({\bf u};\theta )}}&{{=}}&{{\frac {1}{1+\exp \left [-G({\bf u};\theta )\right ]},}}\\ {{G({\bf u};\theta )}}&{{=}}&{{\ln p_{m}({\bf u};\theta )-\ln p_{n}({\bf u}).}}\end {array}\]

          In the NCE paper, they show under mild conditions that the estimator \(p_{\theta }(x \mid D) \to p_{\mathcal {D}}(x)\) in probability as the number of samples in the loss goes to infinity. Equivalently, the estimator is consistent.

          Temporally Contrastive Learning in Time Series

          • October 31, 2024

          Before we get to contrastive RL, it is a natural question to wonder how does this apply to temporal sequences? Concretely, we want to make predictions about the future given the current "context". However, we want to do so in an unsupervised way, meaning we are only given trajectories not a notion of what it means for a trajectory to be good. Naively, one can try to do this in a supervised manner.

          For a \(k\) step prediction, this would just be your model predicting what will happen in \(k\) steps then seeing if it matches what occured \(k\) steps in the future in the sample trajectory. However, if your sample space \(\mathcal {X}\) is very high-dimensional, modeling this relationship can require an exorbinant amount of trajectories.

          This is a central question in the InfoNCE paper, where they propose the following loss:

          Definition. InfoNCE [000B]

          • November 4, 2024
          • Kellen Kanarios

          InfoNCE recasts representation learning as classification: given a context \(c_t\) and a batch \(\mathcal {X}\) holding one positive future sample \(x_{t+k}\) among \(N-1\) distractors, it trains a score \(f_k\) to pick the positive out of the batch. This is the workhorse objective of contrastive learning.

          The loss is the cross-entropy of that identification: \[\mathcal {L}_{N} = - \mathbb {E}_{\mathcal {X}} \left [\log \frac {f_k(x_{t + k}, c_t)}{\sum _{x_j \in \mathcal {X}} f_k(x_j, c_t)}\right ]\] The numerator rewards a high score on the true pair; the denominator normalizes over the positive plus every negative, so a score only counts by being large relative to the distractors. Minimizing \(\mathcal {L}_N\) maximizes a lower bound on the mutual information \(I(x_{t+k}; c_t)\), and the bound tightens with \(N\) — which is the mechanistic reason contrastive methods reward large batches and many negatives.

          Now we need to unpack this very ominous loss. To start, what are \(x_k\) and \(c_t\)?

          Theorem. Maximize Mutual info [000C]

          • November 4, 2024
          • Kellen Kanarios

          \(\mathcal {L}_N\) from InfoNCE paper maximizes a lower bound on the Mutual Information between \(x_{t + k}\) and \(c_t\).

          Proof.All we must do is plug \(\frac {p(x \mid c)}{p(x)}\) back into the objective. \[\begin {align*} \mathcal {L}_{\mathbb {N}}^{\text {opt}}&=-\,\mathbb {E}\log \left [\frac {\frac {p(x_{t+k}|c_{t})}{p(x_{t+k})}}{\frac {p(x_{t+k}|c_{t})}{p(x_{t+k})}+\sum _{x_{j}\in X_{\text {neg}}}\frac {p(x_{j}|c_{t})}{p(x_{j})}}\right ] \\ &=\mathbb {E}\log \left [1+\frac {p(x_{t+k})}{p(x_{t+k}|c_{t})}\sum _{x_{j}\in X_{\text {neg}}}\frac {p(x_{j}|c_{t})}{p(x_{j})}\right ] \\ &\approx \mathbb {E}\log \left [1+\frac {p(x_{t+k})}{p(x_{t+k}|c_{t})}(N-1)\,\mathbb {E}\,\frac {p(x_{j}|c_{t})}{p(x_{j})}\right ] \\ &=\mathbb {E}\log \left [1+\frac {p(x_{t+k})}{p(x_{t+k} \mid c_t)}N\right ] \\ &\geq \mathbb {E} \log \left [\frac {p(x_{t + k})}{p(x_{t + k} \mid c_t)}N \right ] \\ &= - I(x_{t + k}, c_t) + \log N \end {align*} \]

          Contrastive Learning as GCRL [P658]

          • August 17, 2025

          \[ \operatorname *{max}_{f(u,v)}\mathbb {E}_{(u,v^{+})\sim p(u,v)}\left [\log \sigma (\underbrace {f(u,{\green v^{+}})}_{\phi (u)^{T}\psi ({\green v^{+}})})+\log (1-\sigma (\underbrace {f(u,{\red v^{-}})}_{\phi (u)^{T}\psi ({\red v^{-}})}))\right ] \]\[ \begin {align*} &\operatorname *{max}_{f}\mathbb {E}_{(s,a)\sim p(s,a),s_{f}^{-}\sim p(s_{f})}\left [\mathcal {L}(s,a,s_{f}^{+},s_{f}^{-})\right ] \\ \end {align*} \]\[ \mathcal {L}_1(\theta ) = \log \sigma (f_{\theta }(s_1,a_1,{\color {green} s_{8}})) + \log (1-\sigma (f_{\theta }(s_1,a_1, {\color {red} s_3}))) \]\[ \begin {align*} \widehat {\mathcal {L}}(\theta ) &= \frac {1}{n} \sum _{i = 1}^{n} \mathcal {L}_i \\ &= \frac {1}{n} \sum _{i = 1}^{n} \Big [\log \sigma (f_{\theta }(s_i,a_i,{\color {green} s_{f}^{+}})) + \log (1-\sigma (f_{\theta }(s_i,a_i, {\color {red} s_{f}^{-}})))\Big ] \end {align*} \]\[ \mathcal {L}(\theta ) = \mathbb {E}_{x \sim p_X, y \sim p_Y}\Big [\log \sigma (f_{\theta }(x)) + \log (1-\sigma (f_{\theta }(y)))\Big ] \]\[f^*(s, a, s_g) = \log \left (\frac {p^{\pi (\cdot \mid \cdot )}(s_g \mid s, a)}{p(s_g)}\right )\]
