                                            Kellen Kanarios [index]

                                              I am a PhD student at the University of Michigan as part of the Electrical and Computer Engineering program, where my work \(\in \) {programming languages} \(\cap \) {computer architecture} \(\cap \) {LLMs} \(\cap \) {reinforcement learning}. I am co-advised by Xinyu Wang and Satish Narayanasamy. Currently, I am interested in automated kernel generation across accelerators backends. In particular, neurosymbolic approaches to preserve guarantees and limit costs. With this, I am looking into {kernel DSLs, MLIR, formal synthesis, LLM "vibe compilers"}. I am also recreationally interested in Unix (see my dotfiles) and in a past life I did research in reinforcement learning algorithms.

                                              I earned my BS in Mathematics and Computer Science from the University of Michigan, graduating with honors and high honors, followed by an MS in Electrical and Computer Engineering. During this time, I was fortunate enough to be advised by Lei Ying.

                                              This is my forest (shoutout to Jon Sterling who is remarkably helpful). This website functions both as a personal knowledge management system, where I store my notes in notebooks, some accompanying solutions in the solution manuals, and any external resources I have made in /dev/null. Explore this site via Ctrl+K.

                                              Reference. Learning Options via Compression [jiangLearningOptionsCompression]

                                              • Yiding Jiang, Evan Zheran Liu, Benjamin Eysenbach, J Zico Kolter, Chelsea Finn

                                                @article{jiangLearningOptionsCompression,
 title = {Learning {{Options}} via {{Compression}}},
 author = {Jiang, Yiding and Liu, Evan Zheran and Eysenbach, Benjamin and Kolter, J Zico and Finn, Chelsea},
 file = {/home/kellen/Downloads/papers/Learning Options via Compression - Jiang et al..pdf},
 langid = {english},
 abstract = {Identifying statistical regularities in solutions to some tasks in multi-task reinforcement learning can accelerate the learning of new tasks. Skill learning offers one way of identifying these regularities by decomposing pre-collected experiences into a sequence of skills. A popular approach to skill learning is maximizing the likelihood of the pre-collected experience with latent variable models, where the latent variables represent the skills. However, there are often many solutions that maximize the likelihood equally well, including degenerate solutions. To address this underspecification, we propose a new objective that combines the maximum likelihood objective with a penalty on the description length of the skills. This penalty incentivizes the skills to maximally extract common structures from the experiences. Empirically, our objective learns skills that solve downstream tasks in fewer samples compared to skills learned from only maximizing likelihood. Further, while most prior works in the offline multi-task setting focus on tasks with low-dimensional observations, our objective can scale to challenging tasks with high-dimensional image observations.}
}

                                                Reference. Neural Ordinary Differential Equations [chenNeuralOrdinaryDifferential]

                                                • Tian Qi Chen, Yulia Rubanova, Jesse Bettencourt, David K Duvenaud

                                                  @article{chenNeuralOrdinaryDifferential,
 title = {Neural {{Ordinary Differential Equations}}},
 author = {Chen, Tian Qi and Rubanova, Yulia and Bettencourt, Jesse and Duvenaud, David K},
 file = {/home/kellen/Downloads/papers/Neural Ordinary Differential Equations - Chen et al..pdf},
 langid = {english},
 abstract = {We introduce a new family of deep neural network models. Instead of specifying a discrete sequence of hidden layers, we parameterize the derivative of the hidden state using a neural network. The output of the network is computed using a blackbox differential equation solver. These continuous-depth models have constant memory cost, adapt their evaluation strategy to each input, and can explicitly trade numerical precision for speed. We demonstrate these properties in continuous-depth residual networks and continuous-time latent variable models. We also construct continuous normalizing flows, a generative model that can train by maximum likelihood, without partitioning or ordering the data dimensions. For training, we show how to scalably backpropagate through any ODE solver, without access to its internal operations. This allows end-to-end training of ODEs within larger models.}
}

                                                    Reference. Variational Inference with Normalizing Flows [rezendeVariationalInferenceNormalizing]

                                                    • Danilo Jimenez Rezende, Shakir Mohamed

                                                      @article{rezendeVariationalInferenceNormalizing,
 title = {Variational {{Inference}} with {{Normalizing Flows}}},
 author = {Rezende, Danilo Jimenez and Mohamed, Shakir},
 file = {/home/kellen/Downloads/papers/Variational Inference with Normalizing Flows - Rezende and Mohamed.pdf},
 langid = {english},
 abstract = {The choice of approximate posterior distribution is one of the core problems in variational inference. Most applications of variational inference employ simple families of posterior approximations in order to allow for efficient inference, focusing on mean-field or other simple structured approximations. This restriction has a significant impact on the quality of inferences made using variational methods. We introduce a new approach for specifying flexible, arbitrarily complex and scalable approximate posterior distributions. Our approximations are distributions constructed through a normalizing flow, whereby a simple initial density is transformed into a more complex one by applying a sequence of invertible transformations until a desired level of complexity is attained. We use this view of normalizing flows to develop categories of finite and infinitesimal flows and provide a unified view of approaches for constructing rich posterior approximations. We demonstrate that the theoretical advantages of having posteriors that better match the true posterior, combined with the scalability of amortized variational approaches, provides a clear improvement in performance and applicability of variational inference.}
}

                                                        Exercise 1.1. int8 matmul

                                                        • August 5, 2026
                                                        • Kellen Kanarios

                                                        Multiplying \(X (B \times D)\) and \(Y (D \times F)\) in int8.

                                                        1. How many bytes loaded from memory?
                                                        2. How many total OPs performed?
                                                        3. What is arithmetic intensity?
                                                        4. What is roofline estimate for \(T_{math}\) and \(T_{comms}\)? What are reasonable upper and lower bounds for runtime of whole operation?
                                                        Solution
                                                        1. The only difference here from before is that the loaded / written bytes are divided by \(2\). This means we load \(BD\) bytes for \(X\) and \(DF\) bytes for \(Y\), which is a total of \(BD + DF\) bytes.
                                                        2. The same number of total ops is performed. Namely, for each element in the output matrix (\(BF\) of them) we must perform \(2D\) OPs. This leaves a total of \(2DBF\) OPs.
                                                        3. The arithmetic intensity is now just \(2 \times \) the old arithmetic intensity because we are loading half as many bytes i.e. \(\frac {2DBF}{BD + DF + BF}\).
                                                          4. Remark. After looking at the solution, they also mention that the rule on batch size to saturate arithmetic intensity remains unchanged. Namely, using the heuristic \(B \ll D, F\), we can get that the arithmetic intensity \(\approx \frac {2DBF}{DF} = 2B\). One may think that this means that we can use smaller batch size. However, recall that our in8 peak OPs/s has now doubled to \(3.94e14\). Therefore, the computation is effectively \[2B > \frac {2 \cdot \text {Peak OPs / s}}{\text {HBM Bandwidth}} \iff B > \frac {\text {Peak OPs / s}}{\text {HBM Bandwidth}} = 240\]
                                                          Question. So what is the point of int8?
                                                          Answer.Within each batch, we are actually performing FLOPs \(2 \times \) as fast. Therefore, our computation is actually twice as fast wall clock time!
                                                        4. From above, we know that we are performing \(2DBF\) FLOPs. Assuming our int8 peak OPs/s is \(3.94e14\), this gives \(T_{math} = \frac {2DBF}{3.94e14}\). Similarly, we have that \(T_{comm} = \frac {BD + DF + BF}{8.2e11}\). We know that \(\max \{T_{max}, T_{comm}\} \) is a good lower bound, and that \(T_{max} + T_{comm}\) is a good upper bound.

                                                        Exercise 1.2. int8 + bf16 matmul

                                                        • August 5, 2026
                                                        • Kellen Kanarios

                                                        In practice we often do different weight vs. activation quantization, so we might store our weights in very low precision but keep activations (and compute) in a higher precision. Say we want to quantize our weights in int8 but keep activations (and compute) in bfloat16. At what batch size do we become compute bound? Assume \(1.97e14\) bfloat16 FLOPs/s.

                                                        Solution

                                                        Following the computation in the above remark / from the notes, the only thing that changes is now in the bytes loaded we have \(2BD + DF + 2BF\). Using the approximation, this gives us once again that the computational intensity is \(2B\). However, unlike in the previous question, we now remain doing computation at the speed of bf16 which means the previous cancellation no longer occurs. Thus, we have that

                                                        \[2B > \frac {\text {Peak FLOPs / s}}{\text {HBM Bandwidth}} \implies 2B > 240 \implies B > 120.\]

                                                        Exercise 1.4. Batched matrices

                                                        • August 5, 2026
                                                        • Kellen Kanarios

                                                        What if we wanted to perform int8[B,D] \(\cdot \) int8[B,D,F] \(\to \) int8[B,F] where we imagine having a different matrix for each batch element. What is the arithmetic intensity of this operation?

                                                        Solution

                                                        This dramatically reduces arithmetic intensity because it requires loading \(B \times \) more bytes from memory. In particular, we now have \(BD + BDF + BF\) total bytes moved. Even making the same approximation as before, this gives \(\frac {2BDF}{BDF} = 2\). Recall to saturate TPU we need this to be greater than \(240\)...

                                                        Exercise 1.5. Memory rooflines for GPUs

                                                        • August 5, 2026
                                                        • Kellen Kanarios

                                                        For the H100 SXM, calculate the batch size at which a bfloat16 matrix multiplication will become compute-bound. Note that the Tensor Core FLOPs numbers are twice the true value since they’re only achievable with structured sparsity.

                                                        Solution

                                                        We only need to find two quantities in the spec sheet 1. the bf16 peak FLOPs/s and 2. the HBM bandwidth. From the spec sheet, a bf16 tensor core on the H100 sxm can achieve \(1.979e15\) FLOPs / s and has a memory bandwidth of \(3.35e12\) bytes / s. Using the approximation from above, we will become compute bound when \(B > \frac {1.979e15}{3.35e12} \approx 591\).

                                                        Remark. From the solution, the number we used was with sparsity. It turns out the true number is \(9.89e14\), which gives \(295\) instead of \(590\).

                                                        Exercise Pop Quiz. 2D sharding across 1 axis

                                                        • August 5, 2026
                                                        • Kellen Kanarios
                                                         Consider an array fp32[1024, 4096] with sharding \(A[I_{XY},J]\) and mesh {'X': 8, 'Y': 2}. How much data is held by each device? How much time would it take to load this array from HBM on H100s (assuming 3.4e12 memory bandwidth per chip)?
                                                        Solution

                                                        The notation indicates that we are sharding the first axis \((1024)\) across both \(x\) and \(y\)? This means we are dividing into fp32[64, 4096] chunks or \(4\cdot 64\cdot 4096\) bytes per device, which would then take

                                                        \[\frac {4\cdot 64\cdot 4096}{3.4e12} = .308 \mu s\]

                                                        Exercise Pop Quiz. 2D sharding across 1 axis of 3D mesh

                                                        • August 5, 2026
                                                        • Kellen Kanarios
                                                         Let \(A\) be an array with shape int8[128, 2048], sharding \(A[I_{XY},J]\), and mesh Mesh({'X': 2, 'Y': 8, 'Z': 2}) (so 32 devices total). How much memory does \(A\) use per device? How much total memory does \(A\) use across all devices?
                                                        Solution

                                                        Since there is no sharding across the Z axis. I assume this means it is replicated. This still gives \(8\cdot 2048\) bytes per device but now total memory is still multiplied by \(32\) giving \(32\cdot 8\cdot 2048\) bytes across all devices.

                                                        Exercise Pop Quiz. AllGather

                                                        • August 5, 2026
                                                        • Kellen Kanarios
                                                         How long does it take to perform the AllGatherY([EY, F]) → [E, F] on a TPU v5e with a 2D mesh {'X': 8, 'Y': 4}, for \(E = 2048\), \(F = 8192\) in bf16? What about for \(E = F = 256\)?
                                                        Solution

                                                        For the large \(E\) and \(F\), we will clearly not be latency bound, so we can just perform the ICI cost. We will have \(N = 2\cdot 2048\cdot 8192\) bytes and the TPU v5e uni-directional bandwidth is \(4.5e 10\). Since we are only gathering over \(1\) dimension, we do not get any additional bandwidth. Thus, it will take \(\frac {N}{4.5e10} = 3.72\text {ms}\).

                                                        For the small \(E\) and \(F\), we now need to consider the latency time given by

                                                        \[T_{\text {latency}} = \frac {|Y|\cdot T_{\min }}{2} = 2\mu s.\]

                                                        Computing the ICI cost, we have \(N = 2\cdot 256\cdot 256\) bytes and \(T_{\text {ICI}} = \frac {N}{4.5e 10} = 0.73 \mu s\). Thus, the total time is \(T = \max \{T_{\text {latency}}, T_{\text {ICI}} = 2\mu s\).

                                                        Remark. I divided the latency time by \(2\), when once again the TPU v5e sub-mesh does not support wrap-around links and therefore the hop count is NOT upperbounded by \(|Y|\). Also the hop count is actually \(|Y| - 1\) not \(|Y|\), so the correct answer was just \(T_{\text {min}}\cdot (|Y| - 1) = 3\mu s\).

                                                        Exercise 3.1. replicated sharding

                                                        • August 5, 2026
                                                        • Kellen Kanarios
                                                         An array is sharded \(A[I_X,J,K,…]\) (i.e., only sharded across \(X\) ), with a mesh Mesh({'X': 4, 'Y': 8, 'Z': 2}). What is the ratio of the total number of bytes taken up by \(A\) across all chips to the size of one copy of the array?
                                                        Solution It is sharded across \(X\), so that on each chip there is only \(1/4\) of \(A\). However, it must be replicated across \(Y\) and \(Z\) which are \(8\cdot 2 = 16\) copies. This leaves us with \(16 \times \) the total number of bytes across all copies.

                                                        Exercise 3.2. AllGather latency

                                                        • August 5, 2026
                                                        • Kellen Kanarios
                                                         How long should \(\text {AllGather}_{X}([B_X,D_Y])\) take on a TPU v4p 4x4x4 slice with mesh Mesh({'X': 4, 'Y': 4, 'Z': 4}) if \(B=1024\) and \(D=4096\) in bfloat16? How about \(\text {AllGather}_{XY}([B_X,D_Y])\) How about \(\text {AllReduce}_{Z}([B_X,D_Y]\{U_Z\})\)?
                                                        Solution

                                                        1. We cannot use bi-directional because we are on a non-16 dim axes on TPU v4p. Therefore, the ICI bandwidth is \(W_{\text {ICI}} = 4.5e10\). From AllGather, we know that the communication time is independent of \(|X|\) and is \(\frac {N}{W_{\text {ICI}}}\). For this problem, we have \(N = 1024\cdot 4096\cdot 2\). Thus, it will take \(.186\text {ms}\).

                                                          Remark. I do not understand wrap-around rules at allor maybe they are just highly unintuitive, but we actually do have bi-directional bandwidth. I also needed to take into consideration that \(|X|\) cancels out but we only have \(N/|Y|\) bytes. Correct answer is \[\frac {1024\cdot 4096\cdot 2}{9e10\cdot |Y|}\]

                                                        2. In this case, we now have double the bandwidth because we are reducing across both dimensions. However, the total number of bytes is now \(4\times \), which means this will be double the previous part.

                                                        3. An AllReduce requires each device to send the full \(A\) across \(Z\). This should be \(\frac {2BD}{W_{\text {ICI}}}\) or \(2 \times \) the previous part.
                                                          Remark. Completely misunderstood this question. For starters, when reducing along the \(Z\) axis, we still stay sharded across \(x\) and \(y\) and therefore do not make hops across those links. Therefore, we must divide by \(|X| \cdot |Y|\). Also, I guess the heuristic that AllReduce is roughly \(2 \times \) AllGather is used in calculations, which gives final answer \[\frac {4BD}{|X|\cdot |Y|\cdot W_{\text {ICI}}}\]

                                                        Exercise 3.3. latency-bound AllGather

                                                        • August 5, 2026
                                                        • Kellen Kanarios
                                                         Let’s say we’re performing an \(\text {AllGather}_X([B_X])\) but \(B\) is very small (say 128). How long should this take on a TPU v4p 4x4x4 slice with mesh Mesh({'X': 4, 'Y': 4, 'Z': 4}) in bfloat16?
                                                        Solution

                                                        Since \(|X| = 4\), the hop latency time is \(\approx 4 \mu \)s. We have \(N = 2\cdot 128 = 256\)bytes and \(W_{\text {ICI}} = 9e10\). This gives \(.0028 \mu \)s. So we are severely latency bound.

                                                        Remark. Only need to do \(2\) hops in bi-directional case, so true answer is \(\approx 2\mu s\): still latency bound.

                                                        Exercise 3.4. matmul strategies

                                                        • August 5, 2026
                                                        • Kellen Kanarios
                                                         To perform \(X[B,D]\cdot _D Y[D_X,F] \to Z[B,F]\), in this section we tell you to perform \(\text {AllGather}_X(Y[D_X,F])\) and multiply the fully replicated matrices (Case 2, Strategy 1). Instead, you could multiply the local shards like \(X[B,D_X]\cdot _D Y[D_X,F] \to Z[B,F]\{U_X\}\) (Case 3, Strategy 2), and then \(\text {AllReduce}_X(Z[B,F]\{U_X\})\). How many FLOPs and comms does each of these perform? Which is better and why?
                                                        Solution

                                                        Case 2, strategy 1. In this case, the AllGather will take \(\frac {DF}{W_{\text {ICI}}}\) for communication over \(ICI\) and \(BD + DF + BF\) over HBM with \(2BDF\) FLOPs.

                                                        Case 3, strategy 2. For local shards, each will only need to do \(\frac {2BDF}{X}\) FLOPs and \(BD + D_X F + BF\) HBM cost. However, the ICI cost would then be the whole matrix which is \(X \times \) as much over ICI.

                                                        Remark.

                                                        I was roughly correct. However, an important distinction (and gap in my understanding I gues) is that we have been ignoring HBM cost when communicating over ICI because these transfers are done concurrently and are therefore bottlenecked by the slower one (ICI).

                                                        Exercise 3.5. minimum latency

                                                        • August 5, 2026
                                                        • Kellen Kanarios
                                                         Let’s say I want to do a matmul \(A[I,J]\cdot JB[J,K]\to C[I,K]\) on a TPU v4p 4x4x4 with the lowest possible latency. Assume the inputs can be sharded arbitrarily but the result should be fully replicated. How should my inputs be sharded? What is the total FLOPs and comms time?
                                                        Solution

                                                        My initial intuition is we do not want to shard along the contracting dimension. If we have a large enough matrix, then I think the best sharding strategy would be to shard \(A[I_{XYZ}, J], B[J, K]\). The multiplication then requires no communication, and the only communication is an AllGather across all \(3\) axis, which should triple bandwidth. Since we shard over every axis of our mesh, we do not have any additional replicated bytes. This gives us \(N = 2IK\)bytes in bf16. Since we are on a \(4\times 4\times 4\) cube, we have bi-directional bandwidth availability. Therefore, the communication time on TPU v4p is \(\frac {2IK}{3\cdot 9e10}\). The total flops is still just \(2IJK\).

                                                        Exercise 3.6. comparing shardings

                                                        • August 5, 2026
                                                        • Kellen Kanarios
                                                         Let’s say we want to perform \(A[I_X,J_Y]\cdot _J B[J_Y,K]\to C[I_X,K]\) on TPU v5e 4x4. What communication do we perform? How much time is spent on communication vs. computation?
                                                        • What about \(A[I_X,J]\cdot _J B[J_X,K_Y]\to C[I_X,K_Y]\)? This is the most standard setting for training where we combine data, tensor, and ZeRO sharding.
                                                        • What about \(A[I_X,J]\cdot _J B[J,K_Y]\to C[I_X,K_Y]\)? This is standard for inference, where we do pure tensor parallelism.
                                                        Solution

                                                        1. Since this is a matmul over the sharded axis, we need to perform a reduction at some point. After performing the matmul, we should have \(C[I_X, K]\{U_Y\}\). Therefore, we need to do an AllReduce over \(Y\). This is then a ReduceScatter and an AllGather. For computation, each chip does the partial sum, which takes \(\frac {2IJK}{|X||Y|}\) FLOPs. For communication, the AllReduce is \(2 \times \) an AllGather. We are still sharded over \(X\), so the total bytes is \(N = \frac {2IK}{|X|}\). We do not have bi-directional because the v5e is a 2d topology and \(4 \times 4\) is not full in either axis. Thus, the communication is

                                                          \[\frac {2\cdot N}{W_{\text {ICI}}} = \frac {4IK}{4.5e10\cdot |X|}\]

                                                          To see where we are bound, the v5e can do \(1.97e 14\) bf16 FLOPs/s. Therefore, we are compute bound when

                                                          \[ \begin {align*} \frac {2IJK}{|X|\cdot |Y|\cdot 1.97e 14} > \frac {4IK}{4.5e10\cdot |X|} \iff J > \frac {8 \cdot 1.97e 14}{4.5e10} .\end {align*} \]

                                                          Thus, we are almost surely communication bound because it is determined by the contracting dimension, which is \(d_{\text {model}}\) in practice.

                                                          Remark. No solutions available. Prayers up this right...

                                                        2. This is Case 1 with an additional sharding over the contracting dim in \(B\). I believe this means when we do the matmul, we are gonna end up with scattered partial sums i.e. unlike in the ReduceScatter case, where we have partial sums the same dimension as \(C\), the partial sums will now be \(\frac {I}{|X|} \times \frac {K}{|Y|}\). Another ReduceScatter would cause this smaller matrix to be further divided and scattered, so it is not what we want.

                                                          Instead, we should just perform \(\text {AllGather}_X(B[J_X, K_Y])\). Then, this will directly reduce to Case 1 and we will need no further communication. We only need to send \(N = \frac {2JK}{|Y|}\) bytes. Once again, we do not have bi-directional bandwidth. Thus, the communication is

                                                          \[\frac {N}{W_{\text {ICI}}} = \frac {4JK}{4.5e10\cdot |Y|}\]

                                                          The FLOPs per-device are still \(\frac {2IJK}{|X|\cdot |Y|}\). To see where we are bound, the v5e can do \(1.97e 14\) bf16 FLOPs/s. Therefore, we are compute bound when

                                                          \[ \begin {align*} \frac {2IJK}{|X|\cdot |Y|\cdot 1.97e 14} > \frac {2JK}{4.5e10\cdot |Y|} \iff I > \frac {4 \cdot 1.97e 14}{4.5e10} .\end {align*} \]

                                                          Thus, we have a smaller bound than the previous part but are now dependent on \(I\) instead of \(J\). This is likely in practice because \(I\) corresponds to sequence length, which can get very large.

                                                        3. This is pure case 1 with no communication, so we instead need to worry about memory instead of communication overhead.

                                                        Exercise 3.7. transformer block

                                                        • August 5, 2026
                                                        • Kellen Kanarios
                                                         A typical Transformer block has two matrices \(W_{in}[D,F]\) and \(W_{out}[F,D]\) where \(F \gg DF \gg D\) . Say we have a batch size B. Then the full block is \(In[B,D]\cdot W_{in}[D,F]\cdot W_{out}[F,D]\). Let’s pick D=8192 , F=32768, and B=128 and assume everything is in bfloat16. Assume we’re running on a TPU v5e 2x2 slice but let’s pretend each TPU only has 300MB of free memory. How should In, \(W_{in}\), \(W_{out}\), and Out be sharded to stay below the memory limit while minimizing overall time? How much time is spent on comms and FLOPs? Hint: the final output doesn’t need to be fully replicated, but it should be sharded the same as the input so the “layer” can be repeated.
                                                        Solution

                                                        To start, lets compute how big everything is.

                                                        \[ \begin {align*} In &= 2\cdot B\cdot D \\ &= 2\cdot 8192\cdot 128 = 2^{21} \\ W_{in} &= 2\cdot D\cdot F \\ &= 2\cdot 8192\cdot 32768 = 2^{29} \\ W_{out} &= 2\cdot D\cdot F \\ &= 2\cdot 8192\cdot 32768 = 2^{29} \end {align*} \]

                                                        and each TPU has \(300\)MB \(\approx 300 \cdot 2^{20} \approx 2^{28}\) in this example. Therefore, each TPU can fit just over one half of \(W_{in}\) and \(W_{out}\), which leads us to have to fully shard both across \(X\) and \(Y\). The remaining \(11 \cdot 2^{22}\) can fit \(\text {In}\). However, we need to satisfy the constraint that \(\text {Out}\) is sharded in the same way as \(\text {In}\). We adopt the following strategy:

                                                        1. Shard \(\text {In}[B_{XY}, D]\), \(W_{in}[D,F_{XY}]\)
                                                          • First, we need to AllGather \(\text {In}\) along \(B\).
                                                          • Then, we have \(\text {In}[B, D]\cdot W_{in}[D, F_{XY}]\to \text {Tmp}[B, F_{XY}]\)
                                                        2. Shard \(W_{out}[F_{XY}, D]\)
                                                          • Now we have \(\text {Tmp}[B, F_{XY}]\cdot W_{out}[F_{XY}, D] \to \text {Out}[B, D]\{U_{XY}\} \)
                                                          • Then we need to do a ReduceScatter over \(XY\) in the \(B\) axis to get back to our input shape.

                                                        Now lets count up the communication cost.

                                                        1. First, we have an AllGather over \(XY\) of \(\text {In}\). This is \(N = 2\cdot B\cdot D\) bytes. We only have unidirectional bandwidth. However, we are gathering over 2 axes, which doubles our bandwidth. Thus, this will take \[\frac {2\cdot 128\cdot 8192}{2\cdot 4.5e 10} = 23.3\mu s\]
                                                        2. Then we have a ReduceScatter of \(\text {Out}[B, D]\{U_{XY}\}\), which takes the same time as AllGather and is another \(23.3 \mu s\).

                                                        Thus, the whole communication cost is only \(46.6 \mu s\).

                                                        Remark. In the solution, they instead propose to shard \(\text {In}[B, D_{XY}]\), which is equivalent in communication cost. According to Claude, there is a subtle distinction.
                                                        1. If you are in decoding (i.e. \(B = 1\)), then you cannot even shard along \(B\) but can still shard along \(D\).
                                                        2. However, it seems preferable to shard over \(B\) if you can. This way, for activations / reductions over \(D\) you do not need any communication.

                                                        Exercise 3.9. another strategy for sharded matmuls

                                                        • August 5, 2026
                                                        • Kellen Kanarios
                                                         Above we claimed that when only one input to a matmul is sharded along its contracting dimension, we should AllGather the sharded matrix and perform the resulting contraction locally. Another strategy you might think of is to perform the sharded matmul and then AllReduce the result (as if both inputs were sharded along the contracting dimension), i.e. \(A[I,J_X]\cdot _J B[J,K]\to C[I,K]\) by way of
                                                        1. \(C[I, K]\{U_{X}\} = A[I, J_{X}]\cdot B[J_{x}, K] \)
                                                        2. \(C[I, K]\{U_{X}\} = \text {AllReduce}(C[I,K]\{U_{X}\})\)
                                                        Answer the following
                                                        1. Explicitly write out this algorithm for matrices \(A[N,M]\) and \(B[M,K]\), using indices to show exactly what computation is done on what device. Assume \(A\) is sharded as \(A[I,J_X]\) across ND devices, and you want your output to be replicated across all devices.
                                                        2. Now suppose you are ok with the final result not being replicated on each device, but instead sharded (across either the N or K dimension). How would the algorithm above change?
                                                        3. Looking purely at the communication cost of the strategy above (in part 2, not 1), how does this communication cost compare to the communication cost of the algorithm in which we first AllGather A and then do the matmul?
                                                        Solution
                                                        1. On the device, we can only make use of the \(J_{X}\) rows of \(B\) and compute the corresponding partial sums. This corresponds to the outer product \[C'[i] = \sum _{n=i\cdot \frac {J}{ND}}^{i(\frac {J}{ND} + 1)} A_{:,n} \oplus B_{n,:}\]
                                                        2. The above algorithm would change by replacing the AllReduce with a ReduceScatter. This is better communication wise because AllReduce is two collectives, not one.
                                                        3. The communication cost is the same because ReduceScatter has the same communication cost as AllGather, but it is likely preferable if you are compute bound because you can distribute computation across devices.
                                                          Remark. In the solutions, they make the (excellent) point that in the ReduceScatter case we are sending the output \(N\times K\) matrix, whereas in the AllGather case we are sending the \(N\times M\) matrix. Therefore, if we have a large contraction dim, then the second case might also be preferable.

                                                        Exercise 3.10. Fun with AllToAll

                                                        • August 5, 2026
                                                        • Kellen Kanarios
                                                         In the table above, it was noted that the time to perform an AllToAll is a factor of 4 lower than the time to perform an AllGather or ReduceScatter (in the regime where we are throughput-bound). In this problem we will see where that factor of 4 comes from, and also see how this factor would change if we only had single-direction ICI links, rather than bidirectional ICI links.
                                                        1. Let’s start with the single-direction case first. Imagine we have D devices in a ring topology and want to do either an AllGather or a ReduceScatter on an N x N matrix \(A[I_X,J]\) (say D divides N for simplicity). Describe the comms involved in these two collectives, and calculate the total number of scalars (floats or ints) which are transferred across a single ICI link during the entirety of this algorithm.
                                                        2. Now let’s think about an AllToAll, still in the single-directional ICI case. How is the algorithm different in this case than the all-gather case? Calculate the number of scalars that are transferred across a single ICI link in this algorithm.
                                                        3. You should have found that the ratio between your answers to part (a) and part (b) is a nice number. Explain where this factor comes from in simple terms.
                                                        4. Now let’s add bidirectional communication. How does this affect the total time needed in the all-gather case?
                                                        5. How does adding bidirectional communication affect the total time needed in the AllToAll case?
                                                        6. Now simply explain the ratio between AllGather time and AllToAll time in a bidirectional ring.
                                                        Solution
                                                        1. The communication involved in either of these collectives is each chip in the ring sending a chunk of \(A\) of size \(\frac {N^2}{D}\) to the right neighbor. A single ICI link sees every chunk and therefore \(N^2(D-1)\) scalars must cross a single ICI link. The \(D - 1\) comes from the fact that each device already owns one \(\frac {N^2}{D}\) chunk.
                                                        2. AllToAll differs than AllGather because each subsequent forwarding is \(\frac {N^2}{D^2}\) less bytes. Namely, each device has an \(\frac {N^2}{D}\) shard of \(A\). Then in AllToAll, you forward to a neighbor who takes a \(\frac {1}{D}\) of this chunk and forwards the remaining. Therefore, a single ICI link only sees the following bytes of ICI traffic \[\frac {N^2}{D} \sum _{i=1}^{D} (D - i) = \frac {N^2\cdot D(D-1)}{2D} = \frac {N^2(D-1)}{2}\]
                                                        3. From the previous 2 parts, we see that the ratio is exactly \(\frac {1}{2}\). This comes from the fact that, for farther devices, a link needs to transfer a much smaller number of bytes in AllToAll. Whereas, in AllGather, you must see all bytes of a chunk for every device uniformly.
                                                        4. In the AllGather case, bidirectional communication still requires each link to see every byte. Therefore, only the ICI bandiwdth changes and not the total bytes seen per-link.
                                                        5. In the AllToAll case, each chip only needs its sub-chunk of each chunk. Therefore, we can divide the chunk into the front and back half and send in each direction. This halves the total bytes seen per link, reducing to \(\frac {N^2(D-1)}{4}\).
                                                        6. In the bidirectional case, we can effectively reduce our AllToAll to 2 unidirectional AllToAll's of half the size. This then halves the bytes-per-link, which was already half of an AllGather. Since every device needs every byte of each chunk in the AllGather case, it gets no reduction in the bidirectional case.

                                                        Exercise 2.2. TPU details

                                                        • August 5, 2026
                                                        • Kellen Kanarios
                                                         Consider a full TPU v5e pod. How many total CPU hosts are there? How many TPU TensorCores? What is the total FLOPs/s for the whole pod? What is the total HBM? Do the same exercise for TPU v5p pod.
                                                        Solution

                                                        TPU v5e. From the TPU specs, a TPU v5e has a pod size of \(16\times 16\) and a host size of \(4\times 2\). The host size is the topology of the subunit connected to a single host. So the number of hosts is actually the pod size / host size.                                                         Exercise 2.4. General matmul latency

                                                        • August 5, 2026
                                                        • Kellen Kanarios
                                                         Let’s say we want to multiply a weight matrix int8[16384, 4096] by an activation matrix of size int8[B, 4096] where B is some unknown batch size. Let’s say we’re on 1 TPU v5e to start.
                                                        1. How long will this multiplication take as a function of B?
                                                        2. What if we wanted to run this operation out of VMEM? How long would it take as a function of B?
                                                        Solution

                                                        For the first part, we need to load

                                                        \[16384 \cdot 4096 + 4096B~\text {bytes}\]

                                                        and store \(B \cdot 16384\) bytes. We need to perform

                                                        \[2\cdot B\cdot 16384\cdot 4096~\text {FLOPs}\]

                                                        Therefore, the communication time is

                                                        \[T_{comm} = (16384 \cdot 4096 + 4096\cdot B + 16384\cdot B)/8.2e11\]

                                                        and the math time is

                                                        \[T_{math} = (2\cdot B\cdot 16384\cdot 4096)/3.94e14\]

                                                        The total computation time will then be \(\max \{T_{math}, T_{comm}\}\) and the ridge point is when \(T_{math} = T_{comm}\). This gives us

                                                        \[ \begin {align*} \frac {2\cdot B\cdot 16384\cdot 4096}{3.94e14} &= \frac {16384 \cdot 4096 + 4096\cdot B + 16384\cdot B}{8.2e11} \\ &\iff B = 259 \end {align*} \]

                                                        For the second part, VMEM is \(10\times \) faster than HBM. Therefore, our batch size can be \(10\times \) smaller.

                                                        Remark. The solution says that VMEM is \(22\times \) faster. So the numbers are adjusted accordingly.

                                                        Exercise 2.5. ICI Bandwidth

                                                        • August 5, 2026
                                                        • Kellen Kanarios
                                                         Let’s say we have a TPU v5e 4x4 slice. Let’s say we want to send an array of type bf16[8, 128, 8192] from TPU{0,0} to TPU{3, 3}. Let’s say the per-hop latency for TPU v5e is 1μs.
                                                        1. How soon will the first byte arrive at its destination?
                                                        2. How long will total transfer take?
                                                        Solution

                                                        I believe since we have wrap-around links in the Torus topology we can make it from \((0,0) \to (3,3)\) in \(4\) hops. If each hop latency is \(1\mu s\) then it should take \(4 \mu s\).

                                                        From TPU specs, the TPU v5e has ICI bandwidth \(4.5e 10\). We need to transfer \(2\cdot 8\cdot 128\cdot 8192\) bytes. Naively, I am going to say that this means it will take

                                                        \[\frac {2\cdot 8\cdot 128\cdot 8192}{4.5e 10} s,\] factoring in latency this gives \(372 + 4 \mu s\).
                                                        Remark. So the wraparound links are actually only on pods of \(16 \times 16\) or larger. This means it is actually \(6\) hops from \((0,0) \to (3,3)\). Also, we can use the bi-directional capabilities of the network to half the time it will take to send the whole array.

                                                        Exercise 2.6. pulling it all together

                                                        • August 5, 2026
                                                        • Kellen Kanarios
                                                         Imagine you have a big matrix \(A\): int8[128 * 1024, 128 * 1024] sharded evenly across a TPU v5e 4x4 slice but offloaded to host DRAM on each chip. Let’s say you want to copy the entire array to TPU{0, 0} and multiply it by a vector bf16[8, 128 * 1024]. How long will this take?
                                                        Solution

                                                        From the question wording, we are assuming the vector is already on TPU{0,0}.

                                                        From TPU specs, the host configuration for TPU v5e is \(4 \times 2\). I believe this means in a \(4 \times 4\) pod there will be \(2\) CPUs. If this is the case, then for the half of chips on the other host, we first have to transfer to our host via DCN which has bandwidth \(3.125e 9\) for v5e. Since it is sharded evenly, this would be \((1/2) \cdot 128 \cdot 128 \cdot 1024 \cdot 1024\) bytes we must send over DCN, taking

                                                        \[\frac {(1/2) \cdot 128 \cdot 128 \cdot 1024 \cdot 1024}{3.125e 9} = 2.75 s\]

                                                        However, now looking at the notes again, we only use DCN for chips not connected via ICI (which makes sense because it clearly slow AF).

                                                        Instead, we can first transfer all the bytes to the respective chips over PCIe and then to TPU{0,0} over ICI. To load into HBM, PCIe bandwidth is \(1.6e 10\) bytes/second. Since we can divide across all 16 chips, it will take

                                                        \[\frac {128 \cdot 128 \cdot 1024 \cdot 1024}{16\cdot 1.6e 10} = 67.1ms\]

                                                        Now to actually get all of the weights onto a single chip, we can follow the previous part. Using bi-directional bandwidth \(9e 10\), we have

                                                        \[\frac {128 \cdot 128 \cdot 1024 \cdot 1024}{9e 10} = 190.9ms\]

                                                        The remaining time comes from \(\max \{T_{comm}, T_{math}\}\), which are \[T_{math} = \frac {2\cdot 128\cdot 1024\cdot 128 \cdot 1024\cdot 8}{1.97e 14} = 1.39ms\] and \[T_{comm} = \frac {128\cdot 1024\cdot 128\cdot 1024 + 2\cdot 8\cdot 128\cdot 1024 + 2\cdot 128\cdot 1024\cdot 8}{8.2e 11} = 20.9ms \]

                                                        Thus, the total is \(67.1 + 190.9 + 20.9 = 278.9ms\).

                                                        Remark.

                                                        I think I might be so fucking him it is actually unbelievable. My numbers are all off, but the process seems pretty much the same. I also SNIPED the DCN stuff.

                                                        However, it seems there is a bit more nuance to the ICI links than I thought. In particular, our number is a lower bound dependent on the amount of utilized inbound links. Since \((0,0)\) is a corner, it only has \(2\) links and that is why the denominator is \(2\cdot 4.5e 10\) and is not because of bi-directional bandwidth. I imagine if there were wraparound links then we could divide the ICI time by \(2\) because there are \(4\) total inbound links.

                                                        Exercise 1. fork() copies the address space, not the variable

                                                        • May 12, 2026
                                                        • Kellen Kanarios

                                                        Write a program that calls fork(). Before forking, set a variable — say x — to 100. What is its value in the child? What happens when parent and child both change it?

                                                        Solution

                                                        The child gets a copy of the parent's address space, \(x\) included. Each subsequent write lands in that process's own copy, so neither sees the other's change.

                                                        Exercise 2. A file descriptor survives the fork

                                                        • May 12, 2026
                                                        • Kellen Kanarios

                                                        Open a file with open() and then fork(). Can both child and parent use the returned descriptor? What happens when they write to the file concurrently?

                                                        Solution

                                                        Both have access to the same descriptor. Concurrent writes can in principle interleave, but in my runs whichever process was scheduled first always finished writing before the other started — plausibly a scheduling artifact rather than a guarantee.

                                                        Exercise 3. Ordering child before parent without wait()

                                                        • May 12, 2026
                                                        • Kellen Kanarios

                                                        Write a program where the child prints "hello" and the parent prints "goodbye", with the child always printing first. Can you do it without calling wait() in the parent?

                                                        Solution

                                                        Reusing the shared file from the previous exercise: have the child write a value, and have the parent spin in a while loop until it reads that value back. It works, and it is miserable — which is presumably why wait() exists.

                                                        Exercise 4. What wait() returns, and what it does in the child

                                                        • May 12, 2026
                                                        • Kellen Kanarios

                                                        Now use wait() in the parent to wait for the child. What does it return? What happens if you call wait() in the child?

                                                        Solution

                                                        It returns the pid of the child that died. Called in the child — which has no children of its own — it returns \(-1\) immediately.

                                                        Exercise 5. Why exec() has so many variants

                                                        • May 12, 2026
                                                        • Kellen Kanarios

                                                        Write a program that calls fork() and then some form of exec() to run /bin/ls. Try the variants — execl(), execle(), execlp(), execv(), execvp(), execvP(). Why are there so many spellings of one call?

                                                        Solution

                                                        The suffixes are a small matrix of three independent choices. The v family takes a variable-size argument vector where the l family takes a fixed argument list. The e family takes an explicit environment — the list of environment variables the new program will see — instead of inheriting the caller's. The p family resolves the program name against PATH, the way a shell does, instead of requiring a path.

                                                        • May 12, 2026
                                                        • Kellen Kanarios

                                                        Rewrite the previous program using waitpid() instead of wait(). When is waitpid() the one you want?

                                                        Solution

                                                        When a parent has several children. wait() returns on whichever dies first; waitpid() lets you name the child you care about.

                                                        7. Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces: Exercises › Scheduling: Introduction [ostep-ch7]

                                                        • May 12, 2026

                                                        Exercise 1. When SJF matches FIFO

                                                        • May 12, 2026
                                                        • Kellen Kanarios

                                                        For what types of workloads does SJF scheduling deliver the same turnaround times as FIFO scheduling?

                                                        Solution

                                                        Workloads that arrive in increasing order of total job time — FIFO is then already running them shortest-first.

                                                        Exercise 2. When SJF matches round robin

                                                        • May 12, 2026
                                                        • Kellen Kanarios

                                                        For what workloads and quantum lengths does SJF deliver the same response times as Round-robin scheduling?

                                                        Solution

                                                        Short jobs and long quanta. A quantum long enough to hold a whole job turns round robin into run-to-completion, and short jobs make the ordering hardly matter.

                                                        Exercise 3. Response time under SJF as jobs grow

                                                        • May 12, 2026
                                                        • Kellen Kanarios

                                                        What happens to response time under SJF as job lengths increase?

                                                        Solution

                                                        It degrades: the longest job waits out every shorter one ahead of it, so as those grow the response time grows with them.

                                                        Exercise 4. Worst-case response time under round robin

                                                        • May 12, 2026
                                                        • Kellen Kanarios

                                                        What happens to response time under round robin as the quantum grows? Can you write the worst-case response time for \(N\) jobs?

                                                        Solution

                                                        Job \(i\) waits out the \(i - 1\) slices ahead of it, so with quantum \(S\) the worst case is the last job's:

                                                        \[\mathrm {RT}_{\max } = S(N - 1)\]

                                                        and averaging over the \(N\) jobs halves it,

                                                        \[\overline {\mathrm {RT}} = \frac {1}{N} \sum _{i = 1}^{N} (i - 1)S = \frac {S}{N} \cdot \frac {N(N-1)}{2} = \frac {S(N - 1)}{2}\]

                                                        Both grow linearly in the quantum: round robin's responsiveness is precisely what a long quantum spends.

                                                        Exercise 4.1. Action values in the gridworld under the random policy

                                                        • November 24, 2024
                                                        • Kellen Kanarios

                                                        In the gridworld example, with \(\pi \) the equiprobable random policy, what are \(q_{\pi }(11, \mathrm {down})\) and \(q_{\pi }(7, \mathrm {down})\)?

                                                        Solution

                                                        From state \(11\), moving down terminates the episode, so there is no recursion to unroll:

                                                        \[ \begin {align*} q_{\pi }(11, \mathrm {down}) &= -1 \end {align*} \]

                                                        From state \(7\), moving down lands in \(11\) and picks up its value:

                                                        \[ \begin {align*} q_{\pi }(7, \mathrm {down}) &= -1 + v(11) \\ &= -1 - 14 \\ &= -15 \end {align*} \]
